title: 9  Sound Waves and the Doppler Effect
text:
9.1 Oscillation Equation
Sound waves are small perturbations of pressure and density that propagate through a fluid, like the ones in Figure 9.1.
The equations of fluid mechanics are nonlinear and only few analytic solutions are known. However, significant insight into astrophysical systems can be obtained by considering small perturbations around a background flow. Typically the background is chosen to be a hydrostatic solution, e.g., the density profile of an atmosphere. However, this method can be applied to more general situations. This is the key working principle of asteroseismology (helioseismology in the case of the Sun). Sound waves are also one of the key tools to learn about the early Universe, as they generate the baryon acoustic oscillations seen in the CMB and in the distribution of galaxies.
To set the stage, consider a gas flow with density, pressure, and velocity \[
\rho_0 (t ; \mathcal{V}), \quad p_0 (t ; \mathcal{V}), \quad \mathbf{v}_0 (t
; \mathcal{V}) .
\tag{9.1}\] We describe its perturbation in terms of a small displacement vector \(\boldsymbol{\xi} (t ; \mathcal{V})\) describing the offset of each fluid element from its background state.
The density, pressure, and velocity of each fluid element change according to \[
\rho (t ; \mathcal{V}) = \rho_0 (t ; \mathcal{V}) + \delta \rho (t ;
\mathcal{V}), \quad p (t ; \mathcal{V}) = p_0 (t ; \mathcal{V}) + \delta p
(t ; \mathcal{V}), \quad \mathbf{v} (t ; \mathcal{V}) =\mathbf{v}_0 (t ;
\mathcal{V}) + \frac{\mathrm{d} \boldsymbol{\xi} (t ; \mathcal{V})}{\mathrm{d} t} .
\tag{9.2}\] The quantities with the \(\delta\) in front are the Lagrangian perturbations1. The Eulerian perturbation of a quantity is given by \[
q' (t, \mathbf{x}) = q_0 (t, \mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\xi}) + \delta q (t,
\mathbf{x}) - q_0 (t, \mathbf{x}) = \delta q (t, \mathbf{x}) -\boldsymbol{\xi}
\cdot \nabla q_0 .
\tag{9.3}\] The difference between Lagrangian and Eulerian perturbations is that the Lagrangian perturbations are specific to individual fluid elements, while the Eulerian perturbations record the difference in the flow at a fixed position. This distinction turns out to be crucial when perturbing non-homogeneous backgrounds, for which \(\nabla q_0 \neq 0\), as we will see in Chapter 10.
For the moment, we consider a homogeneous medium in which \(\rho_0\), \(p_0\), and \(\mathbf{v}_0 = 0\) are constant. We perturb it by displacing the fluid elements by a small amount \(\boldsymbol{\xi}\) and let it evolve freely. How do the perturbations evolve? To find out, we need to insert the Lagrangian perturbations into the Lagrangian equations (Chapter 5).
The continuity equation (Equation 1.15) reads \[
\frac{\mathrm{d} \rho}{\mathrm{d} t} = - \rho \nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}
\longrightarrow \frac{\mathrm{d} (\rho_0 + \delta \rho )}{\mathrm{d} t} = - (\rho_0
+ \delta \rho) \nabla \cdot \left( \frac{\mathrm{d} \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\mathrm{d} t}
\right) .
\tag{9.4}\] Dropping quantities that are quadratic or higher order in the perturbation, and integrating in time with the condition that \(\delta \rho = 0\) when \(\boldsymbol{\xi} = 0\), we obtain \[
\frac{\mathrm{d} \delta \rho}{\mathrm{d} t} = - \rho_0 \nabla \cdot \frac{\mathrm{d}
\boldsymbol{\xi}}{\mathrm{d} t} \longrightarrow \boxed{\delta \rho = - \rho_0
\nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}} .
\tag{9.5}\] To find the perturbed momentum equation, first note that \[
\frac{\mathrm{d} \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\mathrm{d} t} = \frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial
t} + (\mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla) \boldsymbol{\xi}= \frac{\partial
\boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial t} + (\mathbf{v}_0 \cdot \nabla) \boldsymbol{\xi}+ \left(
\frac{\mathrm{d} \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\mathrm{d} t} \cdot \nabla \right) \boldsymbol{\xi}=
\frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial t} + O (| \boldsymbol{\xi} |^2),
\tag{9.6}\] so \[
\mathbf{v}= \frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial t}, \qquad \frac{\mathrm{d}
\mathbf{v}}{\mathrm{d} t} = \frac{\partial \mathbf{v}}{\partial t} +
(\mathbf{v}_0 \cdot \nabla) \mathbf{v}+ \left( \frac{\mathrm{d}
\boldsymbol{\xi}}{\mathrm{d} t} \cdot \nabla \right) \mathbf{v}= \frac{\partial^2
\boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial t^2} + O (| \boldsymbol{\xi} |^2) .
\tag{9.7}\] The momentum equation (Equation 4.12) becomes \[
\rho \frac{\mathrm{d} \mathbf{v}}{\mathrm{d} t} = - \nabla p \rightarrow
\frac{\partial^2 \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial t^2} = - \frac{1}{\rho_0} \nabla p =
- \frac{1}{\rho_0} \nabla \delta p.
\tag{9.8}\] Here we have used the fact that, for a homogeneous background, the Eulerian and Lagrangian perturbations are the same, \(p' = \delta p\) (Equation 9.3). This is not true in a stratified atmosphere, as we will see in Chapter 10.
We will consider only the case of adiabatic perturbations, for which \[
p = p (\rho) .
\tag{9.9}\] In other words, we are taking the pressure at constant entropy. For example, for an ideal gas, we have already seen that for adiabatic processes (Equation 2.24) \[
p = (\Gamma - 1) \rho \varepsilon \longrightarrow p = K \rho^{\Gamma} ,
\tag{9.10}\] with \(K = (\Gamma - 1) \rho^{1 - \Gamma} \varepsilon\).
Why should sound waves be adiabatic? A sound wave compresses some regions of the fluid and expands others, so the compressed regions become hotter. Heat flows from the hot to the cold regions, but this takes time. Heat needs to diffuse over a distance comparable to the wavelength \(\lambda_w\) of the wave, which takes a time \(t_{\mathrm{diff}} \sim \lambda_w^2 / D\), where \(D \sim \lambda v_{\mathrm{th}}\) and \(\lambda\) is the mean free path (Chapter 6). The period of the wave is \(\sim \lambda_w / c_s\), where \(c_s\) is the sound speed defined below, which is comparable to the thermal velocity of the particles \(v_{\mathrm{th}}\). So we have \[
\frac{t_{\mathrm{diff}}}{\lambda_w / c_s} \sim \frac{\lambda_w}{\lambda} \gg 1,
\tag{9.11}\] whenever the fluid description is valid. In other words, heat does not have time to leave the compressed regions during one period, and the perturbations are adiabatic. The opposite limit, isothermal perturbations, happens when the gas can cool very quickly, for example by radiation. This is the case in cold molecular clouds (Chapter 8, Section 11.5.3).
In this case, we can use the chain rule to rewrite \(\nabla \delta p\) in terms of \(\nabla \delta \rho\): \[
\frac{\partial^2 \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial t^2} = - \frac{1}{\rho_0}
\frac{\mathrm{d} p}{\mathrm{d} \rho} \nabla \delta \rho = \frac{\mathrm{d} p}{\mathrm{d}
\rho} \nabla \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}.
\tag{9.12}\] Defining the sound speed \(c_s = \sqrt{\mathrm{d} p / \mathrm{d} \rho}\), we obtain the oscillation equation: \[
\boxed{\frac{\partial^2 \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial t^2} - c_s^2 \nabla
\nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}= 0.}
\tag{9.13}\] In general, the sound speed needs to be evaluated at constant entropy, that is \[
\boxed{c_s = \sqrt{\left( \frac{\partial p}{\partial \rho} \right)_s} .}
\tag{9.14}\]
If, instead, the perturbations are isothermal, we need to take the derivative of the pressure at constant temperature. For an ideal gas, this gives the isothermal sound speed \[
c_{\mathrm{iso}} = \sqrt{\left( \frac{\partial p}{\partial \rho} \right)_T} = \sqrt{\frac{k_B T}{\mu m_u}} = \frac{c_s}{\sqrt{\Gamma}} .
\tag{9.16}\] This is the sound speed that appears in the equation of state of an isothermal gas, \(p = c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2 \rho\) (Chapter 4, Chapter 8).
The oscillation Equation 9.13 is the fundamental equation to describe sound waves. Taking the divergence on both sides and using Equation 9.5, we find that the density perturbation \(\delta \rho\) satisfies the wave equation: \[
\frac{\partial^2 \delta \rho}{\partial t^2} - c_s^2 \nabla^2 \delta \rho =
0.
\tag{9.17}\] To solve the oscillation equation, we consider the ansatz \[
\boldsymbol{\xi}=\boldsymbol{\xi}_1 \exp [\mathrm{i} (\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{x}-
\omega t)],
\tag{9.18}\] which describes a plane sound wave propagating in the direction \(\mathbf{k}\) and having frequency \(\omega\). \(\boldsymbol{\xi}_1\) is the polarization vector, describing the way in which fluid elements oscillate as the wave propagates. As usual, the physical displacement is the real part of Equation 9.18. Inserting this ansatz into Equation 9.13, we find \[
\omega^2 \boldsymbol{\xi}_1 = c_s^2 \mathbf{k} (\mathbf{k} \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}_1)
.
\tag{9.19}\] This means that plane wave solutions to Equation 9.13 exist only for specific choices of \(\boldsymbol{\xi}_1, \omega\) and \(\mathbf{k}\). We see that the RHS is parallel to \(\mathbf{k}\), so solutions with \(\omega \neq 0\) can exist only if \(\boldsymbol{\xi}_1 \parallel \mathbf{k}\). This means that sound waves are longitudinal. Displacements with \(\boldsymbol{\xi}_1 \perp \mathbf{k}\) are also solutions, but with \(\omega = 0\). They do not compress the fluid, so there is no restoring force (recall that a fluid at rest cannot sustain shear, Chapter 4). This is opposite from electromagnetic waves in vacuum, in which the electric and magnetic fields oscillate in the plane perpendicular to the direction of propagation. Setting \(\boldsymbol{\xi}_1 = \xi_1 \hat{\mathbf{k}}\), we find \[
\omega^2 = c_s^2 k^2 .
\tag{9.20}\] This is the dispersion relation for sound waves. It means that both phase and group velocity for sound waves are given by \(c_s\) \[
v_{\mathrm{phase}} = \frac{\omega}{k} = c_s, \qquad v_{\mathrm{group}} =
\frac{\mathrm{d} \omega}{\mathrm{d} k} = c_s .
\tag{9.21}\] This justifies the name sound speed for \(c_s\). Since \(v_{\mathrm{phase}}\) does not depend on \(k\), sound waves are non-dispersive: a pulse made of many waves with different wavelengths propagates without changing its shape.
What happens to fluid elements when a sound wave passes through them? They are displaced along the direction of the wave. This causes a compression of the fluid. From Equation 9.5, we find: \[
\delta \rho = - \mathrm{i} \rho_0  (\mathbf{k} \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}_1) \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}
(\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{x}- \omega t)} .
\tag{9.22}\]
The same method can be applied to a homogeneous fluid moving with constant velocity \(\mathbf{v}_0\). In this case the sound waves are carried by the flow, and the dispersion relation becomes \[
\omega = \mathbf{v}_0 \cdot \mathbf{k} \pm c_s k .
\tag{9.25}\] This means that the frequency of the sound measured by an observer at rest is shifted with respect to the frequency \(c_s k\) measured by an observer moving with the fluid. This is the Doppler effect. We derive Equation 9.25 in the in-class worksheet (Section 9.3).

title: 9  Sound Waves and the Doppler Effect
text:
Figure 9.2: Lagrangian displacement of a fluid element from position \(\mathbf{x}\) to position \(\mathbf{x}+\boldsymbol{\xi}\).















TipExample



For an ideal gas, with \(p = (\Gamma - 1) \rho \varepsilon = \frac{\rho}{\mu m_u} k_B T\), the sound speed is \[
c_s^2 = \left( \frac{\partial p}{\partial \rho} \right)_s = \Gamma K
\rho^{\Gamma - 1} = (\Gamma - 1) \Gamma \varepsilon = \frac{\Gamma k_B
T}{\mu m_u} .
\tag{9.15}\]









TipExample



Consider air at room temperature, \(T = 293\,\mathrm{K}\). Air is mostly made of \(\mathrm{N}_2\) and \(\mathrm{O}_2\), so \(\mu \approx 29\) and \(\Gamma = 7/5\). From Equation 9.15 we find \(c_s \approx 343\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), which is the measured value. Newton was the first to compute the speed of sound, but he assumed that the perturbations were isothermal. He found \(c_{\mathrm{iso}} \approx 290\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), about 15% too small. The discrepancy was only explained a century later by Laplace, who realized that sound waves are adiabatic.
In astrophysics, sound speeds span a large range. In a cold molecular cloud with \(T = 10\,\mathrm{K}\) and \(\mu \approx 2.3\), we have \(c_s \approx 0.2\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}\). At the center of the Sun, \(T \approx 1.6 \times 10^7\,\mathrm{K}\) and \(\mu \approx 0.85\), so \(c_s \approx 500\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}\). This means that sound takes about one hour to cross the Sun (Exercise 9.1).










TipExample



Consider a sound wave propagating along \(z\) with wave number \(k\). Then \(\mathbf{k}= k \hat{\mathbf{z}}\) and \(\omega = c_s k\). The only non-zero component of \(\boldsymbol{\xi}\) is the \(z\)-component \[
\xi_z = \mathrm{Re} \left\{ \xi_1 \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i} k (z - c_s t)} \right\} = A \cos [k (z - c_s t)] + B \sin [k
(z - c_s t)] \Longleftrightarrow \xi_1 = A - \mathrm{i} B
\tag{9.23}\] The density perturbation is given by \[
\frac{\delta \rho}{\rho_0} = - \frac{\partial \xi_z}{\partial z} = k \{ A
\sin [k (z - c_s t)] - B \cos [k (z - c_s t)] \} .
\tag{9.24}\] Note that the density perturbation is shifted by a quarter of a wavelength with respect to the displacement. The gas is most compressed where \(\xi_z\) changes sign, not where it is largest. This is shown in Figure 9.3.








Figure 9.3: A plane sound wave at a fixed time. Top: displacement \(\xi_z\) and density perturbation \(\delta\rho/\rho_0\). Bottom: positions of fluid elements, initially equally spaced, after being displaced by \(\xi_z\).
crumbs: 9  Sound Waves and the Doppler Effect

title: 9  Sound Waves and the Doppler Effect
text:
9.2 Wave Energy and Momentum
Sound waves also transport energy and momentum. The deposition of energy by breaking waves (Chapter 11) is thought to play an important role in phenomena such as core-collapse supernovae, stellar eruptions, and the evolution of giant molecular clouds.






NoteGoing further: Normal Modes



Before we can compute the energy carried by waves, we need to develop some general perturbation theory. In general, the oscillation equation takes the form \[
\rho_0  \frac{\partial^2 \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial t^2} = \hat{\mathbf{F}}
\boldsymbol{\xi},
\tag{9.26}\] where \(\hat{\mathbf{F}}\) is a differential operator. For example, for sound waves in a homogeneous medium \(\hat{\mathbf{F}} \boldsymbol{\xi}= \rho_0 c_s^2 \nabla \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}\). We can find a dispersion relation by looking for solutions such that \[
\boldsymbol{\xi} (t, \mathbf{x}) =\boldsymbol{\eta} (\mathbf{x}) \mathrm{e}^{- \mathrm{i}
\omega t} .
\tag{9.27}\] Inserting this ansatz in Equation 9.26, we find an eigenvalue problem \[
- \omega^2 \rho_0 \boldsymbol{\eta} (\mathbf{x}) = \hat{\mathbf{F}}
\boldsymbol{\eta} (\mathbf{x}) .
\tag{9.28}\] In most applications, \(\hat{\mathbf{F}}\) is self-adjoint: \[
\int \boldsymbol{\zeta} (\mathbf{x}) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{F}} \boldsymbol{\xi}
(\mathbf{x}) \mathrm{d} V = \int \boldsymbol{\xi}
(\mathbf{x}) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{F}} \boldsymbol{\zeta} (\mathbf{x}) \mathrm{d} V .
\tag{9.29}\] For sound waves, this can be shown by integrating by parts: both sides are equal to \(- \int \rho_0 c_s^2 (\nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\zeta}) (\nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}) \mathrm{d} V\). An important consequence of Equation 9.29 is that \(\omega^2\) is always real. So each mode either oscillates, if \(\omega^2 > 0\), or grows exponentially, if \(\omega^2 < 0\). We will use this to study instabilities later in the course (Chapter 14).
The general theory of linear operators then implies that Equation 9.28 has an infinite set of eigenvalues \(\{ \omega_n \}\) and eigenfunctions \(\{ \boldsymbol{\eta}_n \}\) and that any perturbation (not just plane waves) can be written as an infinite superposition of elementary solutions: \[
\boldsymbol{\xi} (t, \mathbf{x}) = \sum_n \boldsymbol{\eta}_n (\mathbf{x}) \mathrm{e}^{-
\mathrm{i} \omega_n t} .
\tag{9.30}\] The quantities \(\boldsymbol{\eta}_n (\mathbf{x})\) are also called the normal modes of oscillations. Note that the normal modes need not be countable. For example, for sound waves in a homogeneous infinite medium all positive sound frequencies \(\omega\) are allowed. In this case, Equation 9.30 takes the form of an integral. For plane waves in a homogeneous medium, Equation 9.30 is just the Fourier transform: \[
\boldsymbol{\xi} (t, \mathbf{x}) = \int \mathrm{d}^3 \mathbf{k}\boldsymbol{\eta}
(\mathbf{k}) \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i} \mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{x}} \mathrm{e}^{- \mathrm{i} c_s kt} ,
\tag{9.31}\] where the real part is understood. However, when we consider sound waves in a finite medium, for example a star of a given radius, standing waves must fit an integer number of half wavelengths inside the star. This makes the frequencies \(\{ \omega_n \}\) quantized.






TipExample



Consider a rigid, cylindrical pipe of length \(L\) filled with gas at constant density and temperature. The ends of the pipe are sealed. The displacement equation for sound waves propagating in the pipe is \[
\left\{\begin{array}{ll}
\partial_t^2 \xi (t, z) = c_s^2 \partial_z^2 \xi (t, z), & 0 < z < L,\\
\xi (t, 0) = \xi (t, L) = 0. &
\end{array}\right.
\tag{9.32}\] If we look for solutions in the form \(\xi (t, z) = \eta (z) \mathrm{e}^{- \mathrm{i} \omega t}\), we find the eigenvalue problem \[
\left\{\begin{array}{ll}
\partial_z^2 \eta (z) + \left( \frac{\omega}{c_s} \right)^2 \eta (z) =
0, & 0 < z < L\\
\eta (0) = \eta (L) = 0. &
\end{array}\right.
\tag{9.33}\] This equation is just the equation for a harmonic oscillator. The general solution is \[
\eta (z) = A \cos (k z) + B \sin (k z), \qquad k =
\frac{\omega}{c_s} .
\tag{9.34}\] However, not all solutions satisfy the boundary conditions. To satisfy the boundary conditions, we require \[
A = 0, \qquad k = k_n = \frac{n \pi}{L} \Longrightarrow \omega = c_s
\left( \frac{n \pi}{L} \right), \quad n = 1, 2, \ldots
\tag{9.35}\] For example, for a pipe of length \(L = 1\,\mathrm{m}\) filled with air, the frequency of the fundamental mode is \(\omega_1 / 2 \pi = c_s / (2 L) \approx 170\,\mathrm{Hz}\). This is how organ pipes work. The first few normal modes are plotted in Figure 9.4.






Figure 9.4: Normal modes for gas in a cylindrical pipe.



This means that all sound waves propagating along the pipe are in the form \[
\begin{aligned}
\xi (t, z) = \sum_{n = 1}^{\infty} \biggl[ & A_n \sin \left( \frac{n \pi c_s t}{L} \right) \\
& {} + B_n \cos \left( \frac{n \pi c_s t}{L} \right) \biggr] \sin \left( \frac{n \pi z}{L} \right),
\end{aligned}
\tag{9.36}\] where \(A_n\) and \(B_n\) are determined by the initial velocity \(\partial_t \xi (0, z)\) and displacement \(\xi (0, z)\), respectively.










NoteGoing further: Work Integral



We might be tempted to define the energy density of a wave in the general form \(\boldsymbol{\xi} (t, \mathbf{x}) =\boldsymbol{\eta} (\mathbf{x}) \mathrm{e}^{- \mathrm{i} \omega t}\) as \[
K_{\mathrm{wave}} = \frac{1}{2} \rho_0  \left\langle \left| \frac{\partial
\boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial t } \right|^2 \right\rangle = \frac{1}{2} \rho_0  |
\boldsymbol{\eta} |^2  \omega^2 \langle \sin^2 (\omega t) \rangle =
\frac{\omega^2}{4} \rho_0  | \boldsymbol{\eta} |^2,
\tag{9.37}\] where \(\langle \cdot \rangle\) denotes averaging over a period \(T = 2 \pi / \omega\) of the wave. Equation 9.37 is the kinetic energy density associated with the wave. However, it turns out that the kinetic energy is just one portion of the wave energy.
The energy of the wave is related to \(\xi^2\), so it cannot be computed directly from linear theory. However, we can use a trick:

adiabatically perturb the system to create a wave with an external force;
compute the work done by the external force on the system.

To achieve this we add a source term to the oscillation equation: \[
\rho_0  \frac{\partial^2 \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial t^2} = \hat{\mathbf{F}}
\boldsymbol{\xi}+\mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{ext}} (t) .
\tag{9.38}\] Suppose we want to excite the mode \(\boldsymbol{\xi} (t, \mathbf{x}) =\boldsymbol{\eta} (\mathbf{x}) \mathrm{e}^{- \mathrm{i} \omega t}\), where \(\boldsymbol{\eta}\) is such that \(\hat{\mathbf{F}} \boldsymbol{\eta}= - \rho_0 \omega^2 \boldsymbol{\eta}\). Then we can take \(\mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{ext}} (t) = F_0 \mathrm{e}^{\gamma t} \boldsymbol{\eta} (\mathbf{x})\), where \(F_0\) is chosen so that for \(t \lesssim 0\), \(\boldsymbol{\xi} (t, \mathbf{x}) = \mathrm{e}^{\gamma t} \boldsymbol{\eta} (\mathbf{x})\). Inserting this into the oscillation equation yields \[
\rho_0  \frac{\partial^2 \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial t^2} = \rho_0 \gamma^2
\mathrm{e}^{\gamma t} \boldsymbol{\eta}= \mathrm{e}^{\gamma t}  \hat{\mathbf{F}}
\boldsymbol{\eta}+ F_0 \mathrm{e}^{\gamma t} \boldsymbol{\eta}= (- \rho_0 \omega^2 + F_0)
\mathrm{e}^{\gamma t} \boldsymbol{\eta}.
\tag{9.39}\] We can solve for \(F_0\) to find that \[
F_0 = \rho_0  (\omega^2 + \gamma^2) .
\tag{9.40}\] The work done by the external force per unit volume is given by the work integral \[
W_{\mathrm{ext}} = \int_{- \infty}^0 \mathrm{d} t \frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial t}
\cdot \mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{ext}} = \int_{- \infty}^0 \mathrm{d} t \rho_0 \gamma
(\gamma^2 + \omega^2) \mathrm{e}^{2 \gamma t} \boldsymbol{\eta} \cdot \boldsymbol{\eta}=
\rho_0  | \boldsymbol{\eta} |^2  \int_{- \infty}^0 \mathrm{d} t \gamma (\gamma^2 +
\omega^2) \mathrm{e}^{2 \gamma t},
\tag{9.41}\] where we have used the fact that \(\boldsymbol{\eta}\) is time independent. The last integral can be computed analytically, so the previous expression yields \[
W_{\mathrm{ext}} = \rho_0  | \boldsymbol{\eta} |^2  \left( \frac{\gamma^2}{2} +
\frac{\omega^2}{2} \right) .
\tag{9.42}\] The energy density of the wave is obtained in the limit in which \(\gamma \downarrow 0\): \[
\boxed{E_{\mathrm{wave}} = \frac{\omega^2}{2} \rho_0  | \boldsymbol{\eta} |^2
.}
\tag{9.43}\] Note that \(E_{\mathrm{wave}} = 2 K_{\mathrm{wave}}\), meaning that half of the wave energy is potential energy. For example, for a sound wave with \(\boldsymbol{\eta}=\mathbf{A} \cos (\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{x})\), the mean energy density (averaging over one wave-length) is \[
E_{\mathrm{wave}} = \frac{\omega^2}{4} \rho_0 A^2 .
\tag{9.44}\] It is possible to compute the linear momentum density \(\mathbf{P}_{\mathrm{wave}}\) carried by waves in a similar way. One finds \[
\boxed{\mathbf{P}_{\mathrm{wave}} = \frac{\mathbf{k}}{\omega}
E_{\mathrm{wave}} .}
\tag{9.45}\]

9.3 In-class worksheets

9.3.1 Sound waves
Consider an ideal gas with \[
p = (\Gamma - 1) \rho \varepsilon = \frac{\rho}{\mu m_u} k_B T.
\tag{9.46}\] What is the sound speed \(c_s\) as a function of \(\rho\) and \(T\)? Does it depend on \(\rho\)?
Show that \[
\boldsymbol{\xi}= f (z - c_s t)  \hat{\mathbf{z}}
\tag{9.47}\] is a solution of \[
\frac{\partial^2 \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial t^2} - c_s^2 \nabla \nabla \cdot
\boldsymbol{\xi}= 0.
\tag{9.48}\] Sketch the solution for different times if \(f (x) = \mathrm{e}^{- x^2 / 2}\). What is the corresponding density perturbation? Is \(f (z + c_s t) \hat{\mathbf{z}}\) also a solution? What does it describe?


9.3.2 The Doppler effect
Consider an initially homogeneous flow with \[
\rho = \rho_0 = \mathrm{const}, \qquad p = p_0 = \mathrm{const}, \qquad
\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{v}_0 = \mathrm{const} .
\tag{9.49}\] Introduce a small perturbation in the form of a Lagrangian displacement \(\boldsymbol{\xi}\).

Show that the Lagrangian density perturbation is given by \[
\delta \rho = - \rho_0 \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}.
\tag{9.50}\]
Use the results from part 1) to show that the oscillation equation reads \[
\left[ \frac{\partial}{\partial t} + (\mathbf{v}_0 \cdot \nabla)
\right]^2 \boldsymbol{\xi}= c_s^2 \nabla \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}.
\tag{9.51}\]
Introduce the ansatz \(\boldsymbol{\xi}=\boldsymbol{\eta}\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i} (\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{x}- \omega t)}\) and show that the dispersion relation is \[
\omega_{\pm} =\mathbf{v}_0 \cdot \mathbf{k} \pm c_s k.
\tag{9.52}\] What is the physical meaning of the \(\pm\) solutions?
Consider a sound wave propagating at an angle \(\theta\) with respect to \(\mathbf{v}_0\). Let \(\omega_0 = c_s k\) be the frequency of sound in the fluid frame. Show that the frequency of sound in the lab frame is \[
\omega = \omega_0  \left( 1 + \frac{v_0}{c_s} \cos \theta \right),
\tag{9.53}\] where \(v_0 = | \mathbf{v}_0 |\).

9.4 Exercises

Exercise 9.1 (Helioseismology) The surface of the Sun oscillates with periods of about 5 minutes. These oscillations are due to sound waves trapped inside the Sun. In this exercise, we estimate their frequencies with a very simple model. Assume \(\Gamma = 5/3\).

Estimate the sound speed at the center of the Sun, where \(T \approx 1.6 \times 10^7\,\mathrm{K}\) and \(\mu \approx 0.85\), and at the base of the convection zone, at \(r \approx 0.7\,R_\odot\), where \(T \approx 2 \times 10^6\,\mathrm{K}\) and \(\mu \approx 0.6\).
Estimate the time \(t_s\) it takes for sound to travel from the center to the surface of the Sun. For \(r < 0.7\,R_\odot\), use the average of the two sound speeds you found in part 1. For \(r > 0.7\,R_\odot\), assume that the temperature decreases linearly to zero at the surface, and that \(\mu\) is constant.
Model the Sun as a pipe of length \(R_\odot\), closed at both ends. What is the frequency of the fundamental mode? What is the order \(n\) of a mode with a period of 5 minutes?
The observed frequencies of consecutive modes of this type differ by about \(135\,\mu\mathrm{Hz}\). Compare with your estimate. What do these observations measure?

title: 10  Waves in Stratified Atmospheres
text:
10.1 Waves in Isothermal Atmospheres
Consider a stratified, static, isothermal atmosphere. We assume constant acceleration \(g\) in the negative \(z\) direction. The hydrostatic equilibrium equations are (Chapter 4) \[
\partial_z p_0 = - \rho_0 g, \qquad p_0 = c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2 \rho_0,
\tag{10.1}\] where \(c_{\mathrm{iso}} = \sqrt{k_B T / (\mu m_u)}\) is the isothermal sound speed (Equation 9.16).
Combining these two we find \[
\partial_z \rho_0 = - \frac{g}{c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2} \rho_0 \Longrightarrow \rho_0 =
\tilde{\rho} \mathrm{e}^{- z / H} .
\tag{10.2}\] \(H = c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2 / g\) is called the scale height of the atmosphere and has units of a length.
We want to study the propagation of waves in this atmosphere. The continuity equation still gives (Equation 9.5) \[
\delta \rho = - \rho_0 \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi},
\tag{10.3}\] and the velocity perturbation is \[
\mathbf{v}' = \delta \mathbf{v}- (\boldsymbol{\xi} \cdot \nabla) \mathbf{v}_0 =
\delta \mathbf{v}= \frac{\mathrm{d} \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\mathrm{d} t} = \frac{\partial
\boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial t} + (\mathbf{v}_0 \cdot \nabla) \boldsymbol{\xi}=
\frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial t} .
\tag{10.4}\] The sound speed is given by \[
c_s^2 = \left( \frac{\partial p}{\partial \rho} \right)_s = \Gamma c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2 ,
\tag{10.5}\] which implies that \(\delta p = c_s^2 \delta \rho\) for adiabatic perturbations. However, \(p' \neq c_s^2 \rho'\), because the Eulerian and Lagrangian perturbations differ when \(\nabla p_0 \neq 0\) (Equation 9.3). Instead we have \[
\delta p = c_s^2 \delta \rho \Longrightarrow (p' +\boldsymbol{\xi} \cdot
\nabla p_0) = c_s^2 \delta \rho \Longrightarrow p' = c_s^2 \delta
\rho + g \rho_0 \xi_z .
\tag{10.6}\] The momentum equation reads \[
\rho \frac{\mathrm{d} \mathbf{v}}{\mathrm{d} t} = - \nabla p - g \rho
\hat{\mathbf{z}} .
\tag{10.7}\] Setting \(\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{v}'\), \(p = p_0 + p'\), and \(\rho = \rho_0 + \rho'\) yields \[
\rho_0  \frac{\partial^2 \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial t^2} = - \nabla p_0 - g
\rho_0  \hat{\mathbf{z}} - \nabla p' - g \rho'  \hat{\mathbf{z}} + \ldots,
\tag{10.8}\] where the dots denote terms of second order in the perturbation. The first two terms on the RHS cancel out. Dropping the higher order terms we find \[
\rho_0  \frac{\partial^2 \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial t^2} = - c_s^2 \nabla
\delta \rho + g \frac{\rho_0}{H} \xi_z  \hat{\mathbf{z}} - g \rho_0 \nabla
\xi_z - g \left( \delta \rho + \frac{\rho_0}{H} \xi_z  \right)
\hat{\mathbf{z}},
\tag{10.9}\] where we have used Equation 10.6 and \[
\rho' = \delta \rho - (\boldsymbol{\xi} \cdot \nabla) \rho_0 = \delta \rho +
\frac{\rho_0}{H} \xi_z .
\tag{10.10}\] The second and last term on the RHS of Equation 10.9 cancel out leaving \[
\rho_0  \frac{\partial^2 \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial t^2} = - c_s^2 \nabla
\delta \rho - g \rho_0 \nabla \xi_z - g \delta \rho \hat{\mathbf{z}} .
\tag{10.11}\] Using the fact that \[
\begin{aligned}
\nabla \delta \rho &= \nabla (- \rho_0 \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}) \\
&= - \rho_0 \nabla \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}- \nabla \rho_0 \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi} \\
&= - \rho_0 \nabla \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}+ \frac{\rho_0}{H} \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi} \hat{\mathbf{z}},
\end{aligned}
\tag{10.12}\] we obtain \[
\begin{aligned}
\rho_0 \frac{\partial^2 \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial t^2} = {}& c_s^2 \rho_0 \nabla \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}- \rho_0 \Gamma g \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi} \hat{\mathbf{z}} \\
& - g \rho_0 \nabla \xi_z + g \rho_0 \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi} \hat{\mathbf{z}} .
\end{aligned}
\tag{10.13}\] This can be simplified to \[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial^2 \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial t^2} = {}& c_s^2 \left( \nabla \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}- \frac{c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2}{c_s^2} \frac{1}{H} \nabla \xi_z \right) \\
& - \frac{(c_s^2 - c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2)}{H} \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi} \hat{\mathbf{z}} .
\end{aligned}
}
\tag{10.14}\] We are going to analyze the consequences of this equation shortly. Before we do that, we show that this equation reduces to Eq. (6.31) of Clarke and Carswell (2007) in the limit of vertical oscillations in the \(z\) direction. To do that, we take the divergence of Equation 10.14 and use \(\nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi} = - \delta \rho / \rho_0\) to obtain \[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial^2 \delta \rho}{\partial t^2} &= c_s^2 \left( \nabla^2 \delta \rho + \frac{2}{H} \partial_z \delta \rho + \frac{\delta \rho}{H^2} \right) \\
&\qquad + g \rho_0 \nabla^2 \xi_z \\
&\qquad - \frac{(c_s^2 - c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2)}{H} \left( \partial_z \delta \rho + \frac{\delta \rho}{H} \right) \\
&= c_s^2 \nabla^2 \delta \rho + \frac{c_s^2 + c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2}{H} \partial_z \delta \rho \\
&\qquad + \frac{c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2}{H} \rho_0 \nabla^2 \xi_z + c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2 \frac{\delta \rho}{H^2} .
\end{aligned}
\tag{10.15}\] Assuming that \(\delta \rho = \delta \rho (t, z)\) and \(\boldsymbol{\xi}= \xi_z \hat{\mathbf{z}}\), we obtain, \[
\frac{\partial^2 \delta \rho}{\partial t^2} - c_s^2  \frac{\partial^2 \delta
\rho}{\partial z^2} - \frac{c_s^2}{H}  \frac{\partial \delta \rho}{\partial
z} = 0,
\tag{10.16}\] where we have used the fact that \[
\nabla^2 \xi_z = \partial_z^2 \xi_z = \partial_z  \left( - \frac{\delta
\rho}{\rho_0} \right) = - \frac{\partial_z \delta \rho}{\rho_0} -
\frac{\delta \rho}{\rho_0 H} .
\tag{10.17}\] Equation 10.16 is identical to Eq. (6.31) of Clarke and Carswell (2007). It describes the propagation of density modes in a stratified atmosphere, but neglects an entirely different class of modes, the gravity waves, in which the fluid elements move up and down, while the wave propagates mostly in the horizontal direction. We discuss them in Section 10.2.
As before, we look for traveling wave solutions \[
\boldsymbol{\xi}=\boldsymbol{\eta}\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i} (\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{x}- \omega t)}
,
\tag{10.18}\] where now we allow the components of \(\mathbf{k}\) to be complex. Inserting this into Equation 10.14 we obtain \[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\omega^2 \boldsymbol{\eta} = {}& c_s^2 \left( \mathbf{k} \cdot \boldsymbol{\eta}+ \mathrm{i} \frac{c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2}{c_s^2} \frac{1}{H} \eta_z \right) \mathbf{k} \\
& + \mathrm{i} \frac{(c_s^2 - c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2)}{H} \mathbf{k} \cdot \boldsymbol{\eta} \hat{\mathbf{z}} .
\end{aligned}
}
\tag{10.19}\]

title: 10  Waves in Stratified Atmospheres
text:
In the limit \(kH \gg 1\), that is, when the wavelength is much smaller than the scale height of the atmosphere, the terms proportional to \(1/H\) can be neglected and we recover the dispersion relation for waves in a homogeneous medium, namely \(\omega^2 = c_s^2 k^2\), as expected.
Purely horizontal waves, with \(\boldsymbol{\eta}, \mathbf{k} \perp \hat{\mathbf{z}}\), cannot satisfy the dispersion relation, unless \(c_s = c_{\mathrm{iso}}\), that is for isothermal as opposed to adiabatic perturbations. Physically this means that density fluctuations become buoyant, so they acquire a \(k_z \neq 0\) component in their wave vector.
For waves with \(\boldsymbol{\eta} \parallel \mathbf{k} \parallel \hat{\mathbf{z}}\), the dispersion relation simplifies to \[
\omega^2 = c_s^2  \left( k^2 + \mathrm{i} \frac{1}{H} k \right)
\Longrightarrow k_{1, 2} = - \frac{\mathrm{i}}{2 H} \pm \sqrt{\left(
\frac{\omega}{c_s} \right)^2 - \left( \frac{1}{2 H} \right)^2} .
\tag{10.20}\] These are the so-called pressure or p-modes of the atmosphere. They are the generalization of sound waves. Note that \(k\) has a real part only if \(\omega\) is larger than the acoustic cutoff frequency \[
\omega_{\mathrm{ac}} = \frac{c_s}{2 H} .
\tag{10.21}\]

If \(\omega \gg \omega_{\mathrm{ac}}\), then the dispersion relation for p-modes can be approximated as: \[
k_{1, 2} \approx - \frac{\mathrm{i}}{2 H} \pm \frac{\omega}{c_s} .
\tag{10.22}\] In this case the displacement grows exponentially with height: \[
\xi_z = \eta_z \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i} (\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{x}- \omega t)} =
\eta_z \exp \left[ \mathrm{i} \omega \left( \pm \frac{z}{c_s} - t \right)
\right] \exp \left( \frac{z}{2 H} \right) .
\tag{10.23}\] This makes sense, because the energy flux carried by the wave, which is the energy density (Equation 9.43) times \(c_s\), \(\sim \rho_0 \omega^2 |\boldsymbol{\xi}|^2 c_s\), must be the same at all heights. Since \(\rho_0\) decreases with height, \(|\boldsymbol{\xi}|\) must increase as \(\rho_0^{-1/2} \propto \mathrm{e}^{z / 2 H}\). The density perturbation of the wave propagating upward is \[
\begin{aligned}
\delta \rho &= - \rho_0 \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi} \\
&= - \tilde{\rho} \eta_z
\left( \frac{\mathrm{i} \omega}{c_s} + \frac{1}{2 H} \right) \\
&\quad {} \times \exp \left[ \mathrm{i} \omega \left( \frac{z}{c_s} - t \right) \right] \\
&\quad {} \times \exp \left( - \frac{z}{2 H} \right) .
\end{aligned}
\tag{10.24}\] Note that the density perturbation itself decreases with height. However, the background density decreases faster, so the relative perturbation \(\delta \rho / \rho_0 \propto \mathrm{e}^{z / 2 H}\) grows. This means that waves propagating upward through an isothermal atmosphere eventually become nonlinear, \(\delta \rho \sim \rho_0\), and break, forming shocks (Chapter 11). Waves breaking in this way are thought to contribute to the heating of the solar chromosphere.
If \(\omega < \omega_{\mathrm{ac}}\), then \(k\) is purely imaginary and the waves do not propagate. In the limit \(\omega \ll \omega_{\mathrm{ac}}\), we find \[
k_{1, 2} \approx 0, - \frac{\mathrm{i}}{H} \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad
[\xi_z]_{1, 2} = \eta_z  \mathrm{e}^{- \mathrm{i} \omega t}, \eta_z \mathrm{e}^{z / H} \mathrm{e}^{- \mathrm{i}
\omega t} .
\tag{10.25}\] In other words, the atmosphere responds to the perturbation as a whole, rather than with a wave propagating upward.

Let us now consider the case of perturbations with horizontal displacement. We can align the \(x\)-axis with \(\boldsymbol{\eta}\), meaning that \(\boldsymbol{\eta}= \eta \hat{\mathbf{x}}\). In this case, the dispersion relation becomes \[
\omega^2 \eta \hat{\mathbf{x}} = c_s^2  (k_x \eta) \mathbf{k}+ \mathrm{i}
\frac{(c_s^2 - c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2)}{H} k_x \eta \hat{\mathbf{z}} .
\tag{10.26}\] This means that there are two components of \(\mathbf{k}= (k_x, 0, k_z)\). The \(x\)-component of Equation 10.26 is \[
\omega^2 = c_s^2 k_x^2 \Longrightarrow k_x = \pm \frac{\omega}{c_s} .
\tag{10.27}\] The \(z\)-component of Equation 10.26 is \[
k_z = - \mathrm{i} \left( 1 - \frac{c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2}{c_s^2} \right)  \frac{1}{H} .
\tag{10.28}\] The corresponding displacement is \[
\begin{aligned}
\boldsymbol{\xi} (t, \mathbf{x}) &= \eta \exp \left[ \mathrm{i} \omega \left( \pm
\frac{x}{c_s} - t \right) \right] \\
&\quad {} \times \exp \left[ \left( 1 - \frac{c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2}{c_s^2}
\right) \frac{z}{H} \right] \hat{\mathbf{x}} .
\end{aligned}
\tag{10.29}\] These are called Lamb waves. They are sound waves that propagate horizontally and are trapped near the bottom of the atmosphere. Indeed, their energy density \(\rho_0 |\boldsymbol{\xi}|^2 \propto \mathrm{e}^{(1 - 2 / \Gamma) z / H}\) decreases with height for \(\Gamma < 2\). Lamb waves generated by the eruption of the Hunga Tonga volcano in 2022 were observed to travel around the Earth several times. In the limit in which \(c_s \rightarrow c_{\mathrm{iso}}\), that is \(\Gamma \rightarrow 1\) (isothermal perturbations), these waves reduce to horizontal sound waves.







TipExample



Consider the atmosphere of the Earth. It is not isothermal, but we can estimate its properties taking \(T \approx 288\,\mathrm{K}\), \(\mu \approx 29\), and \(\Gamma = 7/5\). We find \(H = k_B T / (\mu m_u g) \approx 8\,\mathrm{km}\), \(c_s \approx 340\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), and an acoustic cutoff period \(2 \pi / \omega_{\mathrm{ac}} \approx 5\,\mathrm{min}\).
For the solar photosphere, \(T \approx 5800\,\mathrm{K}\), \(\mu \approx 1.3\), \(g \approx 2.7 \times 10^2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\), and \(\Gamma = 5/3\). We find \(H \approx 140\,\mathrm{km}\), \(c_s \approx 8\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}\), and \(\omega_{\mathrm{ac}} / 2 \pi \approx 4.6\,\mathrm{mHz}\), corresponding to a period of about 3.6 minutes. The measured value is about \(5.3\,\mathrm{mHz}\). The solar oscillations with periods of about 5 minutes have lower frequencies, about \(3.3\,\mathrm{mHz}\), so they cannot propagate into the solar atmosphere. They are reflected at the surface and remain trapped inside the Sun. This is why the Sun rings like a pipe (Exercise 9.1).

title: 10  Waves in Stratified Atmospheres
text:
10.2 Gravity Waves
To understand the second class of waves, consider a fluid element that is displaced upward by a small distance \(\xi_z\). We assume that the displacement is slow enough for the fluid element to stay in pressure equilibrium with its surroundings, and that it is adiabatic. The pressure of the fluid element changes by \(\delta p = \xi_z \partial_z p_0 = - \rho_0 g \xi_z\), so its density changes by \[
\delta \rho = \frac{\delta p}{c_s^2} = - \frac{g}{c_s^2} \rho_0 \xi_z .
\tag{10.30}\] The density of the surrounding gas at the new position is \(\rho_0 + \xi_z \partial_z \rho_0 = \rho_0 - (g / c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2) \rho_0 \xi_z\). Since \(c_s > c_{\mathrm{iso}}\), the fluid element is denser than its surroundings, by \[
\Delta \rho = \delta \rho - \xi_z \partial_z \rho_0 = g \left( \frac{1}{c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2} - \frac{1}{c_s^2} \right) \rho_0 \xi_z .
\tag{10.31}\] So gravity pulls it back down. The equation of motion of the fluid element is \[
\rho_0 \frac{\mathrm{d}^2 \xi_z}{\mathrm{d} t^2} = - g \Delta \rho = - \rho_0 N^2 \xi_z, \qquad
N^2 = g^2 \left( \frac{1}{c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2} - \frac{1}{c_s^2} \right) = \frac{(\Gamma - 1) g^2}{c_s^2} .
\tag{10.32}\] In other words, the fluid element oscillates up and down with frequency \(N\), which is called the buoyancy frequency or Brunt–Väisälä frequency. Note that \(N = 0\) if \(\Gamma = 1\). This makes sense, because, if the perturbations are isothermal, a displaced fluid element always has the same density as its surroundings. If the atmosphere were stratified in such a way that \(N^2 < 0\), the displaced fluid element would be lighter than its surroundings and would keep rising. This is the onset of convection, which we will discuss in Chapter 14.
To find the waves associated with this oscillation, we go back to Equation 10.19 and consider a general wave vector. We can always align the \(x\)-axis with the horizontal component of \(\mathbf{k}\), so that \(\mathbf{k} = (k_x, 0, k_z)\). Equation 10.19 is a linear system of equations for \(\boldsymbol{\eta}\), which has non-trivial solutions only if its determinant vanishes. To simplify the result, it is useful to write \(k_z = K - \mathrm{i} / (2 H)\), with \(K\) real. This takes into account the growth of the amplitude with height, \(\mathrm{e}^{z / 2 H}\), that we found for the p-modes. After some algebra, we find the dispersion relation \[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\omega^4 - \omega^2 \left[ c_s^2 (k_x^2 + K^2) + \omega_{\mathrm{ac}}^2 \right]& \\
{} + N^2 c_s^2 k_x^2 &= 0 .
\end{aligned}
}
\tag{10.33}\] This is a quadratic equation for \(\omega^2\), so for each wave vector there are two solutions:

The larger solution describes the acoustic waves, or p-modes. One can show that these have \(\omega > \omega_{\mathrm{ac}}\). For \(c_s k \gg \omega_{\mathrm{ac}}\) they reduce to sound waves, \(\omega^2 \approx c_s^2 (k_x^2 + K^2)\).
The smaller solution describes the gravity waves, or g-modes, in which the restoring force is buoyancy. These have \(\omega < N\). For \(c_s k \gg \omega_{\mathrm{ac}}\) we find \[
\omega^2 \approx N^2 \frac{k_x^2}{k_x^2 + K^2} .
\tag{10.34}\] Interestingly, the frequency of gravity waves depends only on the direction of \(\mathbf{k}\), not on the wavelength. Gravity waves with \(K = 0\), propagating horizontally, have the largest frequency, \(\omega \approx N\). In these waves, the fluid elements move up and down, like the fluid element we considered above.

For an isothermal atmosphere, \(\omega_{\mathrm{ac}}^2 - N^2 = (g / c_s)^2 (\Gamma / 2 - 1)^2 \geq 0\), so \(N \leq \omega_{\mathrm{ac}}\). Waves with frequencies between \(N\) and \(\omega_{\mathrm{ac}}\) cannot propagate vertically. The two branches are shown in Figure 10.1. The Lamb waves we found before lie between the two branches, because they do not propagate vertically.






Figure 10.1: Dispersion relation for waves in an isothermal atmosphere with \(\Gamma = 5/3\), for vertical wave number \(K = 0\). Acoustic waves (p-modes) can propagate in the region above the upper curve and gravity waves (g-modes) in the region below the lower curve. Waves with \(K \neq 0\) move further into these regions. The dotted line is the Lamb wave, \(\omega = c_s k_x\).

title: 10  Waves in Stratified Atmospheres
text:
10.3 In-class worksheet
We consider small disturbances in a plane parallel, isothermal atmosphere. We will assume \(z\) to be the vertical direction and \(g\) to be the gravitational acceleration, assumed to be constant and towards the negative \(z\) direction. Let \(c_{\mathrm{iso}} = \sqrt{k_B T / (\mu m_u)}\) be the isothermal sound speed.

Show that the static background density \(\rho_0\) satisfies \[
\rho_0 (z) = \tilde{\rho} \mathrm{e}^{- z / H},
\tag{10.35}\] where \(H = c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2 / g\) is the scale height of the atmosphere.
Let \(\delta \rho\) and \(\rho'\) be the Lagrangian and Eulerian perturbations of the density. Show that \[
\rho' = \delta \rho + \frac{\rho_0}{H} \xi_z .
\tag{10.36}\]
Let \(p'\) be the Eulerian pressure perturbation. Show that \[
p' = c_s^2 \delta \rho + g \rho_0 \xi_z,
\tag{10.37}\] where \(c_s^2 = \Gamma c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2\) is the square of the sound speed and \(\xi_z\) is the \(z\)-component of the displacement.
Use the results from the previous two points to show that \[
\rho_0  \frac{\partial^2 \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial t^2} = - c_s^2 \nabla
\delta \rho - g \rho_0 \nabla \xi_z - g \delta \rho \hat{\mathbf{z}} .
\tag{10.38}\]
If time allows: consider vertical waves, \(\boldsymbol{\xi} = \xi_z (t, z) \hat{\mathbf{z}}\), and look for solutions \(\xi_z \propto \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i} (k z - \omega t)}\). Show that \[
\omega^2 = c_s^2 \left( k^2 + \frac{\mathrm{i} k}{H} \right),
\tag{10.39}\] and that the waves can propagate, that is, \(k\) has a real part, only if \(\omega > c_s / (2 H)\).

title: 10  Waves in Stratified Atmospheres
text:
10.4 Exercises

Exercise 10.1 (Waves in a polytropic atmosphere) An isentropic atmosphere sits in a uniform gravitational field \(g\), with pressure \(p_0 = K \rho_0^{1 + 1/n}\) and \(K\) constant. Let \(x\) be the depth below the top of the atmosphere, and suppose that the unperturbed density is \(\rho_0 = (bx)^n\) with \(b\) constant.

Show that hydrostatic equilibrium requires \(g = Kb (1 + n)\).
Perturb the atmosphere with a small vertical velocity \(v\), taken positive upward, together with adiabatic perturbations \(p' \ll p_0\) of the pressure and \(\rho' \ll \rho_0\) of the density. Show that \(p' = (gx / n) \rho'\).
Show that the linearized continuity and momentum equations are \[
\frac{\partial \rho'}{\partial t} - v \frac{\partial \rho_0}{\partial x} - \rho_0 \frac{\partial v}{\partial x} = 0
\tag{10.40}\] and \[
\frac{\partial v}{\partial t} + \left( \frac{\rho'}{\rho_0} \right) g - \frac{g}{n \rho_0} \frac{\partial (x \rho')}{\partial x} = 0.
\tag{10.41}\]
For \(n = 1/2\), combine these equations to show that \[
\frac{\partial^2 v}{\partial t^2} = 2 gx \frac{\partial^2 v}{\partial x^2} + 3 g \frac{\partial v}{\partial x} .
\tag{10.42}\]
Look for solutions \(v (t, x) = v_1 (x) \mathrm{e}^{- \mathrm{i} \omega t}\) and change variable to \(\tau = (2 x / g)^{1/2}\). Show that Equation 10.42 becomes \[
\frac{1}{\tau} \frac{\mathrm{d}^2}{\mathrm{d} \tau^2} (\tau v_1) + \omega^2 v_1 = 0.
\tag{10.43}\] Find the solution that stays finite at \(x = 0\) and interpret it physically.

Adapted from Clarke and Carswell (2007), Problem 22.

title: 11  Shock Waves
text:
11.1 Discontinuous solutions
Shock waves are thin regions in which the density, pressure, and velocity of a fluid change abruptly. They form, for example, when sound waves steepen (Chapter 9), in front of supersonic objects (Figure 11.1), and in explosions such as supernovae (Chapter 3). The thickness of a shock is of the order of the mean free path, so in the fluid approximation we can treat shocks as discontinuities.
First, we need to learn how to deal with discontinuous solutions. Consider a conservation law in one dimension (see Table 6.1), \[
\partial_t U + \partial_x F (U) = 0 .
\tag{11.1}\] Suppose that \(U\) has a discontinuity moving with speed \(s\), so that \(U = U_{\mathrm{L}}\) for \(x < s t\) and \(U = U_{\mathrm{R}}\) for \(x > s t\) (Figure 11.2). The derivatives in Equation 11.1 are not defined at the discontinuity, but we can still integrate the equation over the region \(0 \leq t \leq T\), \(0 \leq x \leq X\): \[
\begin{aligned}
& \int_0^T \mathrm{d} t \int_0^X \mathrm{d} x \left[ \partial_t U + \partial_x F (U) \right] = 0 \\
\Longrightarrow \quad & \int_0^X \mathrm{d} x \left[ U \right]_{t = 0}^{t = T} = - \int_0^T \mathrm{d} t \left[ F (U) \right]_{x = 0}^{x = X} .
\end{aligned}
\tag{11.2}\] At \(t = T\), \(U = U_{\mathrm{L}}\) for \(0 < x < s T\) and \(U = U_{\mathrm{R}}\) for \(s T < x < X\), while at \(t = 0\), \(U = U_{\mathrm{R}}\) everywhere. So \[
\begin{aligned}
& U_{\mathrm{L}} s T + U_{\mathrm{R}} (X - s T) - U_{\mathrm{R}} X \\
& \qquad = T \left[ F (U_{\mathrm{L}}) - F (U_{\mathrm{R}}) \right],
\end{aligned}
\tag{11.3}\] that is \[
\boxed{s (U_{\mathrm{L}} - U_{\mathrm{R}}) = F (U_{\mathrm{L}}) - F (U_{\mathrm{R}}) .}
\tag{11.4}\] This is called a jump condition. In the frame of the discontinuity, \(s = 0\), it reads \(F (U_{\mathrm{L}}) = F (U_{\mathrm{R}})\). In other words, the flux is continuous across the discontinuity. This makes sense, because whatever flows into the discontinuity from one side must flow out of the other side.

title: 11  Shock Waves
text: Figure 11.2: A discontinuity moving with speed \(s\) in the \(x\)–\(t\) plane.

title: 11  Shock Waves
text:
11.2 Rankine–Hugoniot conditions
The equations of hydrodynamics in one dimension, without external forces and heating or cooling, can be written as (Table 6.1) \[
\begin{gathered}
\partial_t \mathbf{U} + \partial_x \mathbf{F} (\mathbf{U}) = 0, \\
\mathbf{U} = \begin{pmatrix} \rho \\ \rho v \\ \rho \varepsilon + \frac{1}{2} \rho v^2 \end{pmatrix}, \\
\mathbf{F} (\mathbf{U}) = \begin{pmatrix} \rho v \\ \rho v^2 + p \\ \rho h v + \frac{1}{2} \rho v^3 \end{pmatrix},
\end{gathered}
\tag{11.5}\] where \(h = \varepsilon + p / \rho\) is the specific enthalpy and \(p = p (\rho, \varepsilon)\) is given by the equation of state. Each component of Equation 11.5 satisfies the jump condition Equation 11.4. It is easiest to write them in the frame of the shock, where \(s = 0\) and the fluid velocity is \(u = v - s\) (Figure 11.3). We denote with \(1\) the upstream state, from which the gas flows into the shock, and with \(2\) the downstream state. We obtain the Rankine–Hugoniot conditions: \[
\begin{aligned}
\rho_1 u_1 &= \rho_2 u_2, \\
\rho_1 u_1^2 + p_1 &= \rho_2 u_2^2 + p_2, \\
\rho_1 h_1 u_1 + \tfrac{1}{2} \rho_1 u_1^3 &= \rho_2 h_2 u_2 + \tfrac{1}{2} \rho_2 u_2^3 .
\end{aligned}
\tag{11.6}\] These are three equations for seven quantities: \(\rho_i\), \(v_i\), \(p_i\) (\(i = 1, 2\)), and \(s\). So, given the upstream state, one more quantity, for example \(p_2\) or \(s\), determines the downstream state.






Figure 11.3: A shock in its rest frame. The gas flows from the upstream to the downstream side.



To manipulate Equation 11.6, we define the specific volume \(V_i = 1 / \rho_i\) (not to be confused with a volume) and the mass flux through the shock \[
j = \rho_1 u_1 = \rho_2 u_2 \Longrightarrow u_i = j V_i .
\tag{11.7}\] The momentum condition becomes \(V_1 j^2 + p_1 = V_2 j^2 + p_2\), so that \[
\boxed{j^2 = \frac{p_2 - p_1}{V_1 - V_2} .}
\tag{11.8}\] Note that, since \(j^2 > 0\), pressure and density must both increase or both decrease across the shock. Dividing the left-hand side of the energy condition by \(\rho_1 u_1\) and the right-hand side by \(\rho_2 u_2\), which are both equal to \(j\), we obtain \[
h_1 + \frac{1}{2} j^2 V_1^2 = h_2 + \frac{1}{2} j^2 V_2^2 ,
\tag{11.9}\] and, using Equation 11.8, \[
\boxed{h_2 = h_1 + \frac{1}{2} (p_2 - p_1) (V_1 + V_2) .}
\tag{11.10}\] This relation is called the shock adiabat, or Hugoniot adiabat. Note that it only involves the thermodynamic state of the gas on the two sides of the shock.

11.2.1 Polytropic gas
For an ideal gas with a \(\Gamma\)-law equation of state (Equation 2.15) \[
\begin{gathered}
h = \varepsilon + p V, \qquad \varepsilon = \frac{p V}{\Gamma - 1} \\
\Longrightarrow \quad h = \frac{\Gamma}{\Gamma - 1} p V = \Gamma \varepsilon,
\end{gathered}
\tag{11.11}\] so Equation 11.10 becomes \[
\begin{aligned}
\Gamma p_2 V_2 &= \Gamma p_1 V_1 \\
&\quad + \frac{1}{2} (\Gamma - 1) (p_2 - p_1) (V_1 + V_2) .
\end{aligned}
\tag{11.12}\] Solving for the pressure ratio or for the volume ratio, we find \[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{p_2}{p_1} &= \frac{(\Gamma + 1) V_1 - (\Gamma - 1) V_2}{(\Gamma + 1) V_2 - (\Gamma - 1) V_1}, \\
\frac{V_2}{V_1} &= \frac{(\Gamma + 1) p_1 + (\Gamma - 1) p_2}{(\Gamma - 1) p_1 + (\Gamma + 1) p_2} .
\end{aligned}
\tag{11.13}\] We will use these relations in the in-class worksheet (Section 11.6). Note that \(V_2 / V_1\) decreases as \(p_2 / p_1\) increases, and for a strong shock, \(p_2 \gg p_1\), \[
\frac{V_2}{V_1} \to \frac{\Gamma - 1}{\Gamma + 1} .
\tag{11.14}\] In other words, a shock can heat the gas without limit, but it can compress it at most by a factor \((\Gamma + 1) / (\Gamma - 1)\).






TipExample



For a monoatomic gas, \(\Gamma = 5 / 3\), the compression is \(\rho_2 / \rho_1 \leq 4\). For a gas dominated by radiation or relativistic particles, \(\Gamma = 4 / 3\), it is \(\rho_2 / \rho_1 \leq 7\).


The shock adiabat is shown in Figure 11.4, together with the adiabats \(p V^{\Gamma} = K = \mathrm{const}\). Recall that \(K\) is a function of the entropy only (Equation 2.24). For compressions, \(V_2 < V_1\), the shock adiabat lies above the adiabat of the upstream gas, so the gas leaves the shock with a larger entropy. For expansions, \(V_2 > V_1\), it lies below, so the entropy would decrease. Since the entropy of the gas crossing the shock cannot decrease, only compression shocks, with \(p_2 > p_1\) and \(\rho_2 > \rho_1\), are physical.






Figure 11.4: Shock adiabat (black) and adiabats (blue) for \(\Gamma = 5/3\), on logarithmic axes. The dashed part of the shock adiabat describes expansion shocks, which would decrease the entropy.









NoteGoing further: Shocks with energy losses



So far, we have assumed that the composition of the gas does not change across the shock. However, the gas heated by a shock can be ionized, or its molecules or nuclei can be dissociated. These processes absorb an energy \(\Delta \varepsilon\) per unit mass, which is no longer available to heat the gas. The conservation of mass and momentum is unchanged, while the energy condition, divided by \(j\) as in Equation 11.9, becomes \[
h_1 + \frac{1}{2} u_1^2 = h_2 + \frac{1}{2} u_2^2 + \Delta \varepsilon .
\tag{11.15}\] For example, the ionization of atomic hydrogen requires an energy \(\chi = 13.6\,\mathrm{eV} = 2.18 \times 10^{-18}\,\mathrm{J}\) per atom, so \[
\Delta \varepsilon = \frac{\chi}{m_p} \approx 1.3 \times 10^9\,\mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}} .
\tag{11.16}\] The dissociation of iron nuclei into free nucleons requires about \(8.8\,\mathrm{MeV}\) per nucleon, so \(\Delta \varepsilon \approx 8.8\,\mathrm{MeV} / m_u \approx 8.5 \times 10^{14}\,\mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}}\). This is the energy lost by the shock of a core-collapse supernova as it moves through the iron core of the star (Chapter 3).
Consider now a strong shock in a cold gas, \(p_1 = 0\) and \(h_1 = 0\). The momentum condition gives \(j^2 = p_2 / (V_1 - V_2)\), and the energy condition becomes \[
\begin{aligned}
& \frac{1}{2} j^2 V_1^2 = h_2 + \Delta \varepsilon + \frac{1}{2} j^2 V_2^2 \\
\Longrightarrow \quad & h_2 = \frac{1}{2} p_2 (V_1 + V_2) - \Delta \varepsilon .
\end{aligned}
\tag{11.17}\] For a polytropic gas, \(h_2 = \Gamma p_2 V_2 / (\Gamma - 1)\), so \[
\boxed{\frac{V_2}{V_1} = \frac{\Gamma - 1}{\Gamma + 1} - \frac{2 (\Gamma - 1)}{\Gamma + 1} \frac{\Delta \varepsilon}{p_2 V_1} .}
\tag{11.18}\] In other words, energy losses increase the density jump across the shock, because the energy spent on ionization or dissociation does not contribute to the pressure. Conversely, if the reactions release energy, \(\Delta \varepsilon < 0\), as in a detonation, the compression is reduced.




11.2.2 Mach numbers
From Equation 11.8 and Equation 11.13, \[
\begin{aligned}
j^2 &= \frac{p_2 - p_1}{V_1} \frac{1}{1 - V_2 / V_1} \\
&= \frac{p_2 - p_1}{V_1} \frac{(\Gamma - 1) p_1 + (\Gamma + 1) p_2}{2 (p_2 - p_1)} \\
&= \frac{1}{2 V_1} \left[ (\Gamma - 1) p_1 + (\Gamma + 1) p_2 \right] .
\end{aligned}
\tag{11.19}\] So the velocity upstream of the shock is \[
\begin{aligned}
u_1^2 &= V_1^2 j^2 = \frac{V_1}{2} \left[ (\Gamma - 1) p_1 + (\Gamma + 1) p_2 \right] \\
&= \frac{\Gamma p_1 V_1}{2 \Gamma} \left[ \Gamma \left( 1 + \frac{p_2}{p_1} \right) + \left( \frac{p_2}{p_1} - 1 \right) \right],
\end{aligned}
\tag{11.20}\] where \(c_{s, 1}^2 = \Gamma p_1 V_1\) is the upstream sound speed (Equation 9.15). The upstream Mach number is then \[
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{Ma}_1^2 &= \frac{u_1^2}{c_{s, 1}^2} \\
&= \frac{1}{2 \Gamma} \left[ \Gamma \left( 1 + \frac{p_2}{p_1} \right) + \left( \frac{p_2}{p_1} - 1 \right) \right] \geq 1,
\end{aligned}
\tag{11.21}\] since \(p_2 \geq p_1\) for a physical shock. Similarly, \[
\begin{aligned}
u_2^2 &= V_2^2 j^2 = \frac{V_2}{2} \frac{V_2}{V_1} \left[ (\Gamma - 1) p_1 + (\Gamma + 1) p_2 \right] \\
&= \frac{V_2}{2} \left[ (\Gamma + 1) p_1 + (\Gamma - 1) p_2 \right],
\end{aligned}
\tag{11.22}\] so that \[
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{Ma}_2^2 &= \frac{u_2^2}{c_{s, 2}^2} \\
&= \frac{1}{2 \Gamma} \left[ \Gamma \left( 1 + \frac{p_1}{p_2} \right) + \left( \frac{p_1}{p_2} - 1 \right) \right] \leq 1 .
\end{aligned}
\tag{11.23}\] Therefore, the gas enters the shock with a supersonic velocity and leaves it with a subsonic velocity. In other words, shocks separate supersonic from subsonic flows. Note that, in the limit of a weak shock, \(p_2 \to p_1\), both Mach numbers tend to one: a very weak shock is a sound wave.






TipExample



Stars and pulsars moving supersonically through the interstellar medium are surrounded by bow shocks, like the one in front of the sphere in Figure 11.1. Figure 11.5 shows the bow shock around the millisecond pulsar PSR J0437−4715 (Bell et al. 1995), made visible by the Hα emission of the shocked interstellar gas. In this case, the obstacle is the wind of the pulsar.






Figure 11.5: Hα image of the bow shock around the millisecond pulsar PSR J0437−4715, taken at the Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory. The arrow shows the direction of motion of the pulsar. From Fruchter (1995); reproduced for non-commercial educational use and not covered by the license of these notes.

title: 11  Shock Waves
text:
11.3 Stability of shocks
The Rankine–Hugoniot conditions admit many solutions, but not all of them are realized in nature. A shock must also be stable with respect to small perturbations. Consider a shock in its rest frame and perturb it, so that it is displaced by a small amount \(\eta\), which can vary along the shock (Figure 11.6). The perturbation generates small-amplitude waves on both sides of the shock. In a uniform flow with velocity \(u\), these are sound waves moving with velocities \(u \pm c_s\) (Equation 9.25) and entropy perturbations, which are carried by the flow with velocity \(u\).
The waves moving towards the shock are given, while the waves moving away from it, together with \(\eta\), have to be determined from the three (linearized) jump conditions. Upstream, the waves moving away from the shock have negative velocity. The sound wave with velocity \(u_1 - c_{s, 1} < 0\) exists only if \(u_1 < c_{s, 1}\). Downstream, the waves moving away from the shock have positive velocity. These are the entropy perturbation, with velocity \(u_2\), and the sound wave with velocity \(u_2 + c_{s, 2}\), and, if \(u_2 > c_{s, 2}\), also the sound wave with velocity \(u_2 - c_{s, 2}\).
If \(u_1 > c_{s, 1}\) and \(u_2 < c_{s, 2}\), we have three unknowns: \(\eta\), the entropy perturbation, and one sound wave. These can be determined using the three jump conditions. If \(\eta\) varies along the shock, the flow downstream also carries vorticity perturbations, with velocity \(u_2\). However, there is also one more jump condition, for the velocity tangential to the shock, so the counting does not change. In all other cases, there are more unknowns than equations, so the evolution of a small perturbation is not determined. Such shocks cannot exist (Landau and Lifshitz 1987, sec. 88). So the jump conditions can be solved only if \(u_1 > c_{s, 1}\) and \(u_2 < c_{s, 2}\). This is the same result that we have obtained in Equation 11.21 and Equation 11.23, but here we have not made any assumption on the equation of state.






Figure 11.6: Small perturbations of a shock, in its rest frame, for \(u_1 > c_{s,1}\) and \(u_2 < c_{s,2}\). Gray: waves moving towards the shock. Blue: waves moving away from it.

title: 11  Shock Waves
text:
11.4 Structure of shocks
The Rankine–Hugoniot conditions describe the conservation of mass, momentum, and energy across a shock, but they do not tell us anything about its internal structure. Inside a shock the velocity and the temperature change over very short distances, so viscosity and heat conduction cannot be neglected. In the shock frame, the steady one-dimensional equations become \[
\begin{gathered}
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} x} (\rho u) = 0, \qquad \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} x} \left( p + \rho u^2 - \sigma \right) = 0, \\
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} x} \left[ \rho u \left( h + \frac{u^2}{2} \right) - u \sigma + F_{\mathrm{heat}} \right] = 0,
\end{gathered}
\tag{11.24}\] where \(\sigma \propto \mathrm{d} u / \mathrm{d} x\) is the viscous stress (Chapter 15) and \(F_{\mathrm{heat}} \propto - \mathrm{d} T / \mathrm{d} x\) is the heat flux (Chapter 6). Far upstream the flow is homogeneous, so the diffusive terms disappear, and we can integrate Equation 11.24 to obtain \[
\begin{aligned}
\rho u &= \rho_1 u_1, \\
p + \rho u^2 - \sigma &= p_1 + \rho_1 u_1^2, \\
\rho u \left( h + \frac{u^2}{2} \right) &- u \sigma + F_{\mathrm{heat}} \\
&= \rho_1 u_1 \left( h_1 + \frac{u_1^2}{2} \right) .
\end{aligned}
\tag{11.25}\] The solution of these equations determines the structure of the shock (Figure 11.7). Far downstream the diffusive terms disappear again, and we recover the Rankine–Hugoniot conditions.






Figure 11.7: Velocity (left) and pressure (right) across a viscous shock of thickness \(\delta\). The dotted lines show the corresponding discontinuity. Redrawn after Mihalas and Weibel Mihalas (1984).



The thickness \(\delta\) of a strong shock is of the order of the mean free path of the particles that carry momentum and energy across it (weak shocks are thicker). Shocks in terrestrial applications are mediated by collisions between molecules, and in air \(\delta \sim 100\,\mathrm{nm}\). Shocks in astrophysical applications are often mediated by photons (radiation-mediated shocks), or they are collisionless, that is mediated by interactions between particles and waves in a plasma (Chapter 18). However, for many applications the nature of the shock is not important: the downstream state \(\rho_2\), \(u_2\), \(h_2\) only depends on the upstream state and on the strength of the shock, through the Rankine–Hugoniot conditions. The most comprehensive reference on the physics of shocks is Zel’dovich and Raizer (2002).

title: 11  Shock Waves
text:
11.5 Radiative shocks
So far, we have assumed that the gas does not exchange energy with the radiation. However, the gas behind a strong shock is hot, and it radiates. The structure of the shock then depends on whether the gas is optically thick or optically thin to its own radiation.

11.5.1 Optically thick shocks
If the gas is optically thick, the photons emitted by the hot gas behind the shock diffuse upstream and heat the gas ahead of it, in a region called the radiative precursor (Figure 11.8). Behind the viscous shock, the gas and the radiation relax to equilibrium in a relaxation layer. Since no energy escapes, the Rankine–Hugoniot conditions still connect the states on the two sides of the whole structure, if we include the pressure and the energy of the radiation in \(p\) and \(h\).






Figure 11.8: Structure of a radiatively thick shock.



In weak, subcritical shocks, the precursor heats the upstream gas to a temperature lower than the final temperature \(T_2\). In strong, supercritical shocks, the precursor heats the upstream gas all the way to \(T_2\). In both cases, the temperature just behind the viscous shock can exceed \(T_2\) (Mihalas and Weibel Mihalas 1984).


11.5.2 Optically thin shocks
If the gas is optically thin, the radiation escapes and carries energy away. The structure of the shock is shown in Figure 11.9. Cold gas moving rapidly (1) crosses the viscous shock and is heated (2), as described by the Rankine–Hugoniot conditions. The hot gas then cools in a radiative relaxation layer, until it reaches thermal equilibrium (3). As the gas cools, it slows down and it is compressed further. The profile of the relaxation layer can be found by solving \[
\begin{gathered}
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} x} (\rho u) = 0, \qquad \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} x} \left( \rho u^2 + p \right) = 0, \\
\rho u \frac{\mathrm{d} \varepsilon}{\mathrm{d} x} = - p \frac{\mathrm{d} u}{\mathrm{d} x} - \rho \dot{Q},
\end{gathered}
\tag{11.26}\] where \(\dot{Q}\) is the net cooling rate per unit mass. Note that energy is not conserved. Instead, the conditions downstream of the shock can be found from the conservation of mass and momentum, and from the condition of thermal equilibrium: \[
\begin{gathered}
\rho_1 u_1 = \rho_3 u_3, \qquad p_1 + \rho_1 u_1^2 = p_3 + \rho_3 u_3^2, \\
\dot{Q} (\rho_3, T_3) = 0 .
\end{gathered}
\tag{11.27}\]






Figure 11.9: Structure of an optically thin radiative shock (top), with sketches of the density and temperature profiles (bottom). Redrawn after Shu (1992).





11.5.3 Isothermal shocks
For the interstellar medium, a good approximation is often \(T_3 = T_1\): the gas cools back to the temperature set by the balance of heating and cooling. In this case the equation of state is \(p = c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2 \rho\) (Equation 9.16), and Equation 11.27 becomes \[
\begin{aligned}
\rho_3 u_3 &= \rho_1 u_1, \\
c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2 \rho_3 + \rho_3 u_3^2 &= c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2 \rho_1 + \rho_1 u_1^2 .
\end{aligned}
\tag{11.28}\] These can be solved to find \[
\boxed{\frac{\rho_3}{\rho_1} = \left( \frac{u_1}{c_{\mathrm{iso}}} \right)^2 = \mathrm{Ma}_1^2 ,}
\tag{11.29}\] where the Mach number is now defined with the isothermal sound speed. Note the difference with adiabatic shocks. The compression is not limited to \((\Gamma + 1) / (\Gamma - 1)\) (Equation 11.14), but grows as the square of the Mach number. This is why radiative shocks can produce very dense layers of gas, for example when interstellar clouds collide (Exercise 11.2).

title: 11  Shock Waves
text:
11.6 In-class worksheet

11.6.1 Shock waves I

Consider a shock wave in an ideal gas with adiabatic index \(\Gamma\). Let \(\rho_1, p_1\), and \(T_1\) be the upstream (unshocked) gas density, pressure, and temperature. Let \(\rho_2, p_2,\) and \(T_2\) be the corresponding downstream (post-shock) quantities.

Show that the ratio of downstream to upstream temperature across the shock is \[
\frac{T_2}{T_1} = \frac{p_2}{p_1}  \frac{(\Gamma + 1) p_1 + (\Gamma - 1)
p_2}{(\Gamma - 1) p_1 + (\Gamma + 1) p_2} .
\tag{11.30}\]
If \(T_2 = 4 T_1\), what are \(p_2\) and \(\rho_2\) as a function of \(\rho_1, p_1,\) and \(T_1\)?




11.6.2 Shock waves II

The Bullet Cluster (1E 0657-56) consists of two colliding clusters of galaxies. The name comes from the characteristic shape of a shock formed by the interaction of the gas from the two clusters, which is visible in X-ray. The image in Figure 11.10 has been obtained with the Chandra X-ray space telescope.






Figure 11.10: Chandra/ACIS 0.5–5 keV image of the Bullet Cluster. From Markevitch et al. (2002); © The American Astronomical Society, reproduced for non-commercial educational use and not covered by the license of these notes.



This data can be fitted to infer the following parameters for the upstream and downstream electron density and temperature: \[
\begin{aligned}
n_1 &= 3.7 \times 10^{- 3}\, \mathrm{cm}^{- 3}, \\
T_1 &= 9.3 \times 10^7 \,\mathrm{K}, \\
n_2 &= 9.3 \times 10^{- 3}\, \mathrm{cm}^{- 3}, \\
T_2 &= 2.2 \times 10^8 \,\mathrm{K}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{11.31}\] Estimate

the Mach number of the shock (defined as the Mach number of the upstream flow);
the relative velocity of approach of the two clusters of galaxies.

title: 11  Shock Waves
text:
11.7 Exercises

Exercise 11.1 (Piston-driven shock) A piston drives a strong shock wave through a cold gas that is initially at rest; similar considerations are used to describe young supernova remnants. The piston moves at speed \(v_p\) and has a mass per unit surface area \(\Sigma_p\). The gas follows a gamma-law equation of state \[
p = (\Gamma - 1) \rho \varepsilon .
\tag{11.32}\]

Express the shock speed \(s\), and the downstream density \(\rho_2\) and pressure \(p_2\), in terms of the upstream density \(\rho_1\). Keep \(\Gamma\) general (do not set \(\Gamma = 5/3\)) and do not use the expression for \(s\) given by Kulsrud, which contains a typo.
Calculate the work that the piston does on the gas and estimate when the piston begins to decelerate. Compare the mass of the piston with the mass of the gas that the shock has swept up by that time. For this estimate, take the piston velocity to stay constant until the piston has lost a significant fraction of its kinetic energy.

Adapted from Kulsrud (2005), Problem 4.6.


Exercise 11.2 (Colliding clouds) Two identical clouds, each of radius \(3 \times 10^{16}\, \mathrm{m}\) (about 1 pc) and temperature \(10\,\mathrm{K}\), collide with each other at a relative velocity of \(4\, \mathrm{km} \, \mathrm{s}^{- 1}\).

Estimate the time \(t_{\mathrm{coll}}\) that each cloud needs to run entirely into the shock.
The shocked gas cools at a rate \(\dot{Q} = 10^{- 7}\, \mathrm{W} \, \mathrm{kg}^{- 1}\). Decide whether the shock is approximately adiabatic or isothermal.
Suppose the collision produces an isothermal shock. How thick is the shocked layer, \(x\), at the moment when the whole of each cloud has been shocked?
At later times the layer settles into a structure that can be approximated by a hydrostatic isothermal slab with column density \(10^{- 2}\, \mathrm{g} \, \mathrm{cm}^{- 2} = 0.1\, \mathrm{kg} \, \mathrm{m}^{- 2}\). In this hydrostatic structure, what fraction of the clouds’ mass lies within the thickness \(x\)? Neglect edge effects and variations of the column density across the plane of the slab. [Hint. The density of a self-gravitating isothermal slab is \(\rho (z) = \rho_0 / \cosh^2 (z / H)\), where \(\rho_0\) is the density in the midplane and \(H = c_{\mathrm{iso}} / \sqrt{2 \pi G \rho_0}\) (Clarke and Carswell 2007, sec. 5.2).]

Adapted from Clarke and Carswell (2007), Problem 24.

title: 12  Blast Waves
text:
12.1 Similarity analysis
Supernova explosions sweep the interstellar medium (ISM), creating bubbles of superheated plasma, with \(T \sim 10^7\,\mathrm{K}\) (Figure 12.1). These supernova remnants remain bright X-ray sources for about \(10^5\) years before cooling down. In this chapter, we model supernova remnants as point explosions in the ISM, and derive the Sedov–Taylor solution. This is also an excuse to present an example of similarity analysis, which has many applications, but is seldom discussed in (astro)physics courses.
Consider an energy \(E\) released at a point in a uniform gas with density \(\rho_1\). The explosion drives a spherical shock with radius \(r_{\mathrm{sh}}\), moving outwards with speed \(U_{\mathrm{sh}}\). In the limit in which the pressure of the ambient gas can be neglected, that is for a strong shock (Equation 11.14), this problem is characterized by only two parameters: \(E\) and \(\rho_1\). No combination of them has the dimensions of a length or a time. So the problem has no characteristic length or time: the flow at a later time must look like a scaled-up copy of the flow at an earlier time. The solution behind the shock must be in the form \[
q (t, r) = f_q \left( \xi \right), \qquad \xi = \frac{r}{r_0 (t)},
\tag{12.1}\] where \(q\) is any of the fluid variables and \(r_0\) is a characteristic length scale of the problem. \(r_0\) can only depend on \(E\), \(\rho_1\), and \(t\). We write \(r_0 = \rho_1^{\alpha} E^{\beta} t^{\gamma}\), so that \[
\begin{gathered}
\mathrm{m} = \left( \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}} \right)^{\alpha} \left( \mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-2}} \right)^{\beta} \mathrm{s}^{\gamma} \\
\Longrightarrow \quad \alpha + \beta = 0, \quad 2 \beta - 3 \alpha = 1, \quad \gamma - 2 \beta = 0 \\
\Longrightarrow \quad \alpha = - 1 / 5, \quad \beta = 1 / 5, \quad \gamma = 2 / 5 .
\end{gathered}
\tag{12.2}\] So the dimensionless radius is \[
\xi = r \left( \frac{\rho_1}{E t^2} \right)^{1 / 5} .
\tag{12.3}\] The shock must sit at a fixed value \(\xi = \xi_0\), so \[
\boxed{r_{\mathrm{sh}} = \xi_0 \left( \frac{E t^2}{\rho_1} \right)^{1 / 5} ,}
\tag{12.4}\] and the shock velocity is \[
U_{\mathrm{sh}} = \frac{\mathrm{d} r_{\mathrm{sh}}}{\mathrm{d} t} = \frac{2}{5} \xi_0 \left( \frac{E}{\rho_1 t^3} \right)^{1 / 5} = \frac{2}{5}  \frac{r_{\mathrm{sh}}}{t} .
\tag{12.5}\] \(\xi_0\) is a number of order one, which we will compute in Section 12.2.4. Note that \(U_{\mathrm{sh}} \propto t^{- 3 / 5}\) and \(r_{\mathrm{sh}} \propto t^{2 / 5}\), so \[
\rho_1 r_{\mathrm{sh}}^3 U_{\mathrm{sh}}^2 = \mathrm{const} .
\tag{12.6}\] In other words, the kinetic energy of the swept-up gas is constant: the phase that is described by this similarity solution is energy conserving.

title: 12  Blast Waves
text:
12.2 Supernova remnants
A supernova ejects a mass \(M_{\mathrm{ej}} \sim M_{\odot}\) with kinetic energy \(E \sim 10^{51}\,\mathrm{erg} = 10^{44}\,\mathrm{J}\) into the ISM. The remnant goes through three phases, which we discuss in turn (Figure 12.3).






Figure 12.3: Velocity of the shock in the three phases of the evolution of a supernova remnant, on logarithmic axes.




12.2.1 Free expansion
At early times, the ejecta expand ballistically into the ISM, with velocity \[
v \sim \sqrt{\frac{2 E}{M_{\mathrm{ej}}}} \sim 10^4\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}} .
\tag{12.7}\] The ejecta drive a shock into the ISM, the forward shock. When the ejecta have swept up a mass of ISM comparable to their own, \((4 \pi / 3) \rho_1 r^3 \sim M_{\mathrm{ej}}\), they are slowed down, and a second shock, the reverse shock, forms (Figure 12.4). During the free expansion the ejecta have cooled adiabatically, so their sound speed is small, and the deceleration can only be communicated to them by a shock. The reverse shock moves inwards with respect to the gas and heats the ejecta. For \(\rho_1 = 2 \times 10^{-24}\,\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}} = 2 \times 10^{-21}\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}\), that is about one proton per \(\mathrm{cm}^3\), this happens at \(r \sim 2\,\mathrm{pc}\), after \(t \sim r / v \sim 200\,\mathrm{yr}\). This marks the end of the free-expansion phase, \(t_0\) in Figure 12.3.






Figure 12.4: Density in the free-expansion phase (left) and after the formation of the reverse shock (right).





12.2.2 Is hydrodynamics applicable?
The ejecta are mostly ionized hydrogen moving at \(v \sim 10^4\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}\). What is the mean free path \(\lambda\) of the protons? Each proton has an energy \[
\begin{aligned}
\varepsilon_p &= \frac{1}{2} m_p v^2 = \frac{1}{2} \left( \frac{v}{c} \right)^2 m_p c^2 \\
&\approx 5 \times 10^{-4} m_p c^2 \approx 0.5\,\mathrm{MeV} .
\end{aligned}
\tag{12.8}\] Protons are slowed down by ionizing hydrogen atoms (if the ISM is ionized, Coulomb collisions give an even longer mean free path). The cross section for this process is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ion}} \sim 10^{-17}\,\mathrm{cm^2} = 10^{-21}\,\mathrm{m^2}\), and the density of targets is \(n_H \sim 1\,\mathrm{cm^{-3}} = 10^6\,\mathrm{m^{-3}}\). Assuming that \(50\,\mathrm{eV}\) are lost in each ionization, we find \[
\begin{aligned}
\lambda &\sim \left( \frac{0.5\,\mathrm{MeV}}{50\,\mathrm{eV}} \right) \frac{1}{n_H \sigma_{\mathrm{ion}}} \sim 10^{19}\,\mathrm{m} \\
&\approx 300\,\mathrm{pc} \gg r_{\mathrm{sh}} .
\end{aligned}
\tag{12.9}\] However, the protons are stuck on the magnetic field lines. For \(B \sim 0.1\,\mathrm{nT}\) (\(1\,\mu\mathrm{G}\)), the Larmor radius (Equation 18.44) is \(r_L \sim 10^9\,\mathrm{m}\). This makes the plasma behave like a fluid on the scales of interest, \(r \sim 1\,\mathrm{pc} \approx 3 \times 10^{16}\,\mathrm{m}\) (Chapter 18). Shocks in which the particles are coupled by the magnetic field, rather than by collisions, are called collisionless shocks.


12.2.3 Sedov–Taylor phase
Once the swept-up mass is much larger than \(M_{\mathrm{ej}}\), the remnant forgets the details of the ejecta, and it is described by the point explosion of Section 12.1. Radiative losses are still negligible, because the shocked gas is too hot and too tenuous to radiate efficiently. Table 12.1 gives typical numbers.



Table 12.1: Sedov–Taylor solution for \(E = 10^{51}\,\mathrm{erg}\), \(\rho_1 = 2 \times 10^{-24}\,\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}\), \(\xi_0 = 1.15\), and \(\mu = 0.6\).
