The post-shock conditions can be found from the Rankine–Hugoniot conditions in the strong-shock limit (Section 11.2). In the frame of the shock, the upstream velocity is \(u_1 = U_{\mathrm{sh}}\), and, using Equation 11.8 with \(p_1 = 0\), \[
\begin{gathered}
\rho_2 = \frac{\Gamma + 1}{\Gamma - 1} \rho_1, \\
p_2 = j^2 (V_1 - V_2) = \rho_1 U_{\mathrm{sh}}^2 \left( 1 - \frac{V_2}{V_1} \right) .
\end{gathered}
\tag{12.10}\] The velocity of the gas behind the shock, in the rest frame of the ISM, is \(v_2 = U_{\mathrm{sh}} - u_2 = U_{\mathrm{sh}} (1 - V_2 / V_1)\). Accordingly, the post-shock pressure and velocity are \[
p_2 = \frac{2}{\Gamma + 1} \rho_1 U_{\mathrm{sh}}^2, \qquad v_2 = \frac{2}{\Gamma + 1} U_{\mathrm{sh}} .
\tag{12.11}\] The post-shock temperature is \[
\begin{aligned}
T_2 &= \frac{\mu m_u p_2}{k_B \rho_2} = 2 \frac{\Gamma - 1}{(\Gamma + 1)^2}  \frac{\mu m_u}{k_B} U_{\mathrm{sh}}^2 \\
&= \frac{3}{16}  \frac{\mu m_u}{k_B} U_{\mathrm{sh}}^2 \qquad \left( \Gamma = \frac{5}{3} \right) .
\end{aligned}
\tag{12.12}\] For the ionized ISM, \(\mu \approx 0.6\), so at \(t \sim 1000\,\mathrm{yr}\) the temperature is \(T_2 \approx 5 \times 10^7\,\mathrm{K}\). Since \(U_{\mathrm{sh}} \propto t^{- 3 / 5}\), the temperature decreases as \(T_2 \propto t^{- 6 / 5}\) (Table 12.1).


12.2.4 The Sedov solution
Behind the shock, we look for a similarity solution in the form \[
\begin{gathered}
\rho (t, r) = \rho_2 \hat{\rho} (\xi), \qquad v (t, r) = v_2 \frac{r}{r_{\mathrm{sh}}} \hat{v} (\xi), \\
p (t, r) = p_2 \left( \frac{r}{r_{\mathrm{sh}}} \right)^2 \hat{p} (\xi),
\end{gathered}
\tag{12.13}\] where \(\xi\) is given by Equation 12.3, and \(\rho_2\), \(v_2\), and \(p_2\) are the post-shock values, which depend on time through \(U_{\mathrm{sh}}\). The dimensionless density, velocity, and pressure satisfy \[
\hat{\rho} (\xi_0) = \hat{v} (\xi_0) = \hat{p} (\xi_0) = 1 .
\tag{12.14}\] We can convert the time and radial derivatives into total derivatives with respect to \(\xi\): \[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial}{\partial t} &= \frac{\partial \xi}{\partial t}  \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} \xi} = - \frac{2}{5}  \frac{\xi}{t}  \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} \xi}, \\
\frac{\partial}{\partial r} &= \frac{\partial \xi}{\partial r}  \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} \xi} = \frac{\xi}{r}  \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} \xi} .
\end{aligned}
\tag{12.15}\] Inserting these into the equations of hydrodynamics in spherical symmetry (Table 6.1) yields \[
\begin{aligned}
& - \xi \frac{\mathrm{d} \hat{\rho}}{\mathrm{d} \xi} + \frac{2}{\Gamma + 1} \left[ 3 \hat{\rho} \hat{v} + \xi \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} \xi} (\hat{\rho} \hat{v}) \right] = 0, \\
& - \hat{v} - \frac{2}{5} \xi \frac{\mathrm{d} \hat{v}}{\mathrm{d} \xi} + \frac{4}{5 (\Gamma + 1)} \left( \hat{v}^2 + \hat{v} \xi \frac{\mathrm{d} \hat{v}}{\mathrm{d} \xi} \right) \\
& \qquad = - \frac{2}{5}  \frac{\Gamma - 1}{\Gamma + 1}  \frac{1}{\hat{\rho}} \left( 2 \hat{p} + \xi \frac{\mathrm{d} \hat{p}}{\mathrm{d} \xi} \right), \\
& - 2 (\hat{p} + \hat{\rho} \hat{v}^2) - \frac{2}{5} \xi \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} \xi} (\hat{p} + \hat{\rho} \hat{v}^2) \\
& \qquad + \frac{4}{5 (\Gamma + 1)} \biggl\{ 5 \hat{v} (\Gamma \hat{p} + \hat{\rho} \hat{v}^2) \\
& \qquad \qquad + \xi \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} \xi} \left[ \hat{v} (\Gamma \hat{p} + \hat{\rho} \hat{v}^2) \right] \biggr\} = 0 .
\end{aligned}
\tag{12.16}\] These are three ordinary differential equations, which can be integrated numerically from the shock, \(\xi = \xi_0\), towards the centre. Note that \(\xi_0\) only enters through \(\xi / \xi_0 = r / r_{\mathrm{sh}}\). Its value is set by the requirement of energy conservation: \[
4 \pi \int_0^{r_{\mathrm{sh}}} \rho \left( \varepsilon + \frac{1}{2} v^2 \right) r^2 \mathrm{d} r = E .
\tag{12.17}\] Using Equation 12.11 and Equation 12.13, this requires \[
\frac{32 \pi}{25 (\Gamma^2 - 1)} \int_0^{\xi_0} \left[ \hat{p} + \hat{\rho} \hat{v}^2 \right] \xi^4 \mathrm{d} \xi = 1 .
\tag{12.18}\] For \(\Gamma = 5 / 3\), we find \(\xi_0 \approx 1.15\). The solution is shown in Figure 12.5. Note that most of the mass is in a thin shell behind the shock, while the interior is filled with hot gas at low density and nearly uniform pressure. Since the shock compresses the gas by a factor \((\Gamma + 1) / (\Gamma - 1) = 4\), the swept-up mass would fill a uniform shell of thickness \(r_{\mathrm{sh}} / 12\).






Figure 12.5: The Sedov solution for \(\Gamma = 5/3\). The pressure at the centre is \(0.31\,p_2\).





12.2.5 Snowplough phase
As the remnant expands, its temperature decreases, and radiative cooling becomes important. An optically thin gas (Section 11.5) radiates an energy \(n_H^2 \Lambda (T)\) per unit volume and unit time, where \(\Lambda\) is called the cooling function. For the ISM at \(T \sim 10^5\)–\(10^6\,\mathrm{K}\), \(\Lambda \sim 10^{-35}\)–\(10^{-34}\,\mathrm{W\,m^3}\) (\(10^{-22}\)–\(10^{-21}\,\mathrm{erg\,cm^3\,s^{-1}}\)). So the energy radiated by \(t \sim 10^5\,\mathrm{yr}\) is \[
n_H^2 \Lambda t \left( \frac{4 \pi}{3} r_{\mathrm{sh}}^3 \right) \sim 10^{44}\text{–}10^{45}\,\mathrm{J} .
\tag{12.19}\] So the supernova blast wave radiates away all its energy in \(t \sim 10^5\,\mathrm{yr}\). Cooling is fastest in the dense gas behind the shock, since the energy radiated per unit volume scales as \(n_H^2\). So, at \(t \gtrsim t_1 \sim 5 \times 10^4\,\mathrm{yr}\), when \(r_{\mathrm{sh}} = r_1\), the swept-up gas condenses into a thin shell of cold material, pushed by the hot gas in the interior (Figure 12.6). The shell sweeps up the ISM like a snowplough.






Figure 12.6: Structure of a supernova remnant in the snowplough phase.



The hot bubble does not radiate efficiently, because of its low density, but it loses energy by doing work on the shell. Due to these adiabatic losses, \(p_{\mathrm{hot}} V_{\mathrm{hot}}^{\Gamma} = \mathrm{const}\), so, for \(\Gamma = 5 / 3\), \[
\begin{gathered}
p_{\mathrm{hot}} \propto V_{\mathrm{hot}}^{- \Gamma} \propto r_{\mathrm{sh}}^{- 3 \Gamma} = r_{\mathrm{sh}}^{- 5} \\
\Longrightarrow \quad p_{\mathrm{hot}} = p_{\mathrm{hot}} (t_1) \left( \frac{r_{\mathrm{sh}}}{r_1} \right)^{- 5} .
\end{gathered}
\tag{12.20}\] The momentum of the shell changes because of the pressure of the hot gas: \[
\begin{gathered}
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} t} \int_{\mathrm{shell}} \rho v_r \mathrm{d} V = \oint_{\mathrm{shell}} p \mathrm{d} A \\
\Longrightarrow \quad \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} t} (M_{\mathrm{sh}} U_{\mathrm{sh}}) = 4 \pi r_{\mathrm{sh}}^2 p_{\mathrm{hot}},
\end{gathered}
\tag{12.21}\] where \(M_{\mathrm{sh}} = (4 \pi / 3) \rho_1 r_{\mathrm{sh}}^3\) is the swept-up mass. We assume \(r_{\mathrm{sh}} \propto t^{\eta}\). Then \(U_{\mathrm{sh}} \propto t^{\eta - 1}\), \(M_{\mathrm{sh}} \propto t^{3 \eta}\), and \[
\begin{gathered}
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} t} (M_{\mathrm{sh}} U_{\mathrm{sh}}) \propto t^{4 \eta - 2}, \\
r_{\mathrm{sh}}^2 p_{\mathrm{hot}} \propto r_{\mathrm{sh}}^{- 3} \propto t^{- 3 \eta} \\
\Longrightarrow \quad \eta = \frac{2}{7} .
\end{gathered}
\tag{12.22}\] That is \[
\begin{gathered}
\boxed{r_{\mathrm{sh}} = r_1 \left( \frac{t}{t_1} \right)^{2 / 7},} \\
U_{\mathrm{sh}} = \frac{2}{7}  \frac{r_{\mathrm{sh}}}{t} \propto t^{- 5 / 7}, \qquad p_{\mathrm{hot}} \propto t^{- 10 / 7} .
\end{gathered}
\tag{12.23}\] Note that \(U_{\mathrm{sh}}\) drops by a factor \(5 / 7\) at \(t_1\) (Figure 12.3), because \(U_{\mathrm{sh}} = (2 / 5) r_{\mathrm{sh}} / t\) just before \(t_1\) (Equation 12.5) and \(U_{\mathrm{sh}} = (2 / 7) r_{\mathrm{sh}} / t\) just after. In reality, the transition is gradual. Eventually, the hot interior also cools, and the shell coasts with constant momentum, \(M_{\mathrm{sh}} U_{\mathrm{sh}} = \mathrm{const}\), so that \(r_{\mathrm{sh}} \propto t^{1 / 4}\). The remnant merges with the ISM when \(U_{\mathrm{sh}}\) becomes comparable to the sound speed of the ISM.


12.2.6 Breakout from the galactic disk
So far, we have assumed that the ISM is uniform. However, the gas of a galaxy is concentrated in a thin disk. Bubbles that grow larger than the thickness of the disk, for example because they are inflated by many supernovae in a star cluster, expand faster in the vertical direction, where the density drops. Eventually, they break out of the disk and vent their hot gas into the halo of the galaxy (Figure 12.7 and Exercise 12.1).






Figure 12.7: Hubble Space Telescope image of a bubble of hot gas rising above the disk of the galaxy NGC 3079. Credit: NASA, G. Cecil, S. Veilleux, J. Bland-Hawthorn, and A. Filippenko; not covered by the license of these notes.









NoteGoing further: Strömgren spheres and ionization fronts



Consider a young, massive star that emits ultraviolet (UV) photons with energies above \(13.6\,\mathrm{eV}\), which can ionize hydrogen, at a rate \(\dot{N}_{\mathrm{UV}}\). Initially, the star is in a cloud of neutral hydrogen (H I) with density \(n_H\), but the UV photons ionize the gas, forming an H II region (Figure 12.8).
In equilibrium, photoionization balances recombination. The number of recombinations per unit time in a sphere of radius \(R\) is \[
\frac{4 \pi}{3} R^3 \alpha_B n_e n_p = \frac{4 \pi}{3} R^3 \alpha_B n_H^2 ,
\tag{12.24}\] where \(\alpha_B \approx 2.6 \times 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{m^3\,s^{-1}}\) is the recombination coefficient at \(T \approx 10^4\,\mathrm{K}\). This does not include recombinations to the ground state, because these emit a new ionizing photon, which is absorbed nearby. The neutral gas is very opaque to UV photons, so each photon is absorbed and ionizes one atom. So the radius of the H II region, the Strömgren radius, is \[
\boxed{R_S = \left( \frac{3 \dot{N}_{\mathrm{UV}}}{4 \pi \alpha_B n_H^2} \right)^{1 / 3} .}
\tag{12.25}\] For example, an O star emits \(\dot{N}_{\mathrm{UV}} \sim 10^{49}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}\). In a cloud with \(n_H = 100\,\mathrm{cm^{-3}} = 10^8\,\mathrm{m^{-3}}\), we find \(R_S \approx 10^{17}\,\mathrm{m} \approx 3\,\mathrm{pc}\). The boundary of the H II region, the ionization front, is much thinner than this. Its thickness is the mean free path of the UV photons in the neutral gas, \(1 / (n_H \sigma) \sim 10^{13}\,\mathrm{m}\), where \(\sigma \approx 6 \times 10^{-22}\,\mathrm{m^2}\) is the photoionization cross section of hydrogen.
In the early stages of its formation, the H II region grows rapidly under the sole effect of the radiation: the front reaches \(R_S\) in a few recombination times, \(1 / (n_H \alpha_B) \approx 1200\,\mathrm{yr}\). However, as the electrons thermalize, the ionized gas heats up to \(T_2 \approx 10^4\,\mathrm{K}\), while the neutral gas is cold, \(T_1 \sim 100\,\mathrm{K}\). So the ionized gas has a much larger pressure than its surroundings and wants to expand. Hydrodynamic effects become important after about one sound-crossing time, \(R_S / c_2 \sim 2 \times 10^5\,\mathrm{yr}\), which is still short compared with the lifetime of the star.
Like a shock, the ionization front is a thin layer in which the state of the gas changes abruptly, so we can describe it with jump conditions (Section 11.2). In the frame of the front, the neutral gas (1) flows into the front with speed \(u_1\) and leaves it ionized (2) with speed \(u_2\). Heating and cooling keep both sides at their equilibrium temperatures, so the gas is isothermal, \(p_i = c_i^2 \rho_i\), with \(c_1 \approx 1\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}\) for H I at \(100\,\mathrm{K}\) and \(c_2 \approx 13\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}\) for H II at \(10^4\,\mathrm{K}\) (\(\mu \approx 1\) and \(1 / 2\), respectively). The conservation of mass and momentum gives (compare Equation 11.28) \[
\begin{aligned}
\rho_1 u_1 &= \rho_2 u_2 = m_p F_{\mathrm{UV}}, \\
\rho_1 (u_1^2 + c_1^2) &= \rho_2 (u_2^2 + c_2^2),
\end{aligned}
\tag{12.26}\] where \(F_{\mathrm{UV}}\) is the number of UV photons that reach the front per unit time and area. Note that the last equality in the first line is a new condition: each photon that reaches the front ionizes one atom, so the mass flux through the front is fixed by the radiation. We do not need an energy condition, because the temperatures on the two sides are fixed. Setting \(x = \rho_2 / \rho_1\) and eliminating \(u_2 = u_1 / x\), we find \[
\begin{aligned}
& c_2^2 x^2 - (u_1^2 + c_1^2) \, x + u_1^2 = 0 \\
\Longrightarrow \quad & x = \frac{u_1^2 + c_1^2 \pm \sqrt{\Delta}}{2 c_2^2} , \\
& \Delta = (u_1^2 + c_1^2)^2 - 4 c_2^2 u_1^2 .
\end{aligned}
\tag{12.27}\] Real solutions exist only if \(\Delta \geq 0\), or \(u_1^2 + c_1^2 \geq 2 c_2 u_1\), that is, for \(u_1 \geq u_R\) or \(u_1 \leq u_D\), where \[
u_R = c_2 + \sqrt{c_2^2 - c_1^2} \approx 2 c_2, \qquad u_D = c_2 - \sqrt{c_2^2 - c_1^2} \approx \frac{c_1^2}{2 c_2} .
\tag{12.28}\] For a given photon flux, \(u_1 = m_p F_{\mathrm{UV}} / \rho_1\), so the front moves fast into rarefied gas and slowly into dense gas. For this reason, fronts with \(u_1 \geq u_R\) are called R-type, for “rare”, and fronts with \(u_1 \leq u_D\) are called D-type, for “dense” (Spitzer 1978). At \(u_1 = u_R\) and \(u_1 = u_D\), the two roots coincide, and the ionized gas leaves the front exactly at its sound speed, \(u_2 = c_2\).

For R-type fronts with \(u_1 \gg u_R\), the root with the minus sign gives \(x \approx 1 + c_2^2 / u_1^2 \approx 1\). The ionized region expands rapidly, but there is no compression: the gas is ionized before it has time to move.
For D-type fronts with \(u_1 \ll u_D\), the root with the plus sign gives \(x \approx c_1^2 / c_2^2 \sim 10^{-2}\), that is, \(\rho_2 c_2^2 \approx \rho_1 c_1^2\). The gas is ionized and expands, but at nearly constant pressure, as at a contact discontinuity.

At early times, the front is R-type. As it approaches \(R_S\), it slows down, and when \(u_1 < u_R\) no single front can connect the neutral and the ionized gas. The front then splits in two: an isothermal shock (Section 11.5.3), which compresses the neutral gas ahead of it, followed by a D-type front. At the same time, a rarefaction wave moves inwards into the ionized gas (Figure 12.8).






Figure 12.8: Structure of an expanding H II region. The D-type ionization front is preceded by an isothermal shock, which compresses the neutral gas, and a rarefaction wave moves inwards into the ionized gas.



From this point on, the H II region evolves like a supernova remnant in the snowplough phase: the hot ionized gas pushes a dense shell of swept-up neutral gas. The ionized gas is nearly uniform, because its sound speed is large, and it stays in ionization equilibrium, so, from Equation 12.25, its density decreases as \(n_2 = n_H (R_S / R)^{3 / 2}\). The shell moves with speed \(U = \mathrm{d} R / \mathrm{d} t \gg c_1\), so the pressure behind the isothermal shock is \(\rho_1 U^2\) (Equation 11.29). Setting it equal to the pressure of the ionized gas, \(\rho_2 c_2^2\), with \(\rho_2 / \rho_1 = n_2 / n_H\), we find \[
\frac{\mathrm{d} R}{\mathrm{d} t} = c_2 \left( \frac{R_S}{R} \right)^{3 / 4} \Longrightarrow \boxed{R = R_S \left( 1 + \frac{7}{4} \frac{c_2 t}{R_S} \right)^{4 / 7} .}
\tag{12.29}\] At late times, \(R \propto t^{4 / 7}\) (Spitzer 1978). The expansion stops when the pressure of the ionized gas drops to that of the neutral gas, \(n_2 c_2^2 = n_H c_1^2\), that is, at \(R = R_S (c_2 / c_1)^{4 / 3} \approx 30 R_S\). In practice, this takes much longer than the lifetime of the star (compare Exercise 12.1).

Exercise 12.1 (Ionized cavities around star clusters) A cluster of ionizing stars with total luminosity \(L\) clears out a cavity in the interstellar medium, which has an undisturbed density \(\rho_0\).

Use the similarity-solution method to find how the cavity radius \(r\) grows with time \(t\). [Hint. Take \(r \propto L^{\alpha} \rho_0^{\beta} t^{\gamma}\) and determine \(\alpha\), \(\beta\), \(\gamma\).]
Such bubbles stall once their expansion speed becomes comparable to the sound speed of the interstellar medium. Show that the area covered by a stalled bubble is proportional to \(L\). title: 13  Stellar Winds and Spherical Accretion
text:
13.1 Vorticity, circulation, and Bernoulli’s theorem
All stars lose mass through winds. Their mass-loss rates span 10 orders of magnitude, \(\dot{M} \sim 10^{-14}\)–\(10^{-4}\,M_{\odot}/\mathrm{yr}\), and have terminal velocities in the wide range \(v_{\infty} \sim 10\)–\(3000\,\mathrm{km/s}\) (Figure 13.1). Depending on the mechanism that accelerates them, we distinguish:
The most sensitive diagnostics of the winds of hot stars are P Cygni line profiles (Figure 13.2), named after the star P Cygni, where they were first observed. The gas in front of the star moves towards us and absorbs the light of the star at blue-shifted wavelengths, up to \(v_{\infty}\), while the rest of the wind scatters photons into our line of sight, with both red and blue shifts. Other diagnostics are optically thin emission lines (at low \(\dot{M}\)), the bremsstrahlung emission of the wind, and molecular lines (for the winds of cool stars).
In this chapter we study the simplest model of a stellar wind, the isothermal wind of Parker (1958). Before we can do that, we will take a little detour to introduce the concept of vorticity and Bernoulli’s theorem. The latter will give us the equation describing the acceleration of the wind.

title: 13  Stellar Winds and Spherical Accretion
text:
13.1.1 Kelvin’s circulation theorem
Consider now a surface \(A (t)\), bounded by a closed curve \(C (t)\), that moves with the fluid. In a time \(\mathrm{d} t\), each element \(\mathrm{d} \mathbf{l}\) of \(C (t)\) sweeps an area \(\mathrm{d} \mathbf{A} = \mathbf{v} \times \mathrm{d} \mathbf{l} \, \mathrm{d} t\) (Figure 13.3). So \[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\mathrm{d} \mathcal{C}}{\mathrm{d} t} &= \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} t} \int_{A (t)} \boldsymbol{\omega} \cdot \mathrm{d} \mathbf{A} \\
&= \int_{A (t)} \frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\omega}}{\partial t} \cdot \mathrm{d} \mathbf{A} + \oint_{C (t)} \boldsymbol{\omega} \cdot (\mathbf{v} \times \mathrm{d} \mathbf{l}) \\
&= \int_{A (t)} \frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\omega}}{\partial t} \cdot \mathrm{d} \mathbf{A} + \oint_{C (t)} \mathrm{d} \mathbf{l} \cdot (\boldsymbol{\omega} \times \mathbf{v}) \\
&= \int_{A (t)} \left[ \frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\omega}}{\partial t} + \nabla \times (\boldsymbol{\omega} \times \mathbf{v}) \right] \cdot \mathrm{d} \mathbf{A} = 0,
\end{aligned}
\tag{13.7}\] where we have used Stokes’ theorem and Equation 13.6 (the first step also uses \(\nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\omega} = 0\): no vortex lines start or end inside the volume swept by the surface). This is Kelvin’s circulation theorem: the number of vortex lines that thread any surface moving with the fluid does not change in the barotropic flow of an ideal fluid. In other words, vortex lines are material lines: they move with the fluid.






Figure 13.3: A curve \(C (t)\) that moves with the fluid. In a time \(\mathrm{d} t\), the element \(\mathrm{d} \mathbf{l}\) moves by \(\mathbf{v} \, \mathrm{d} t\) and sweeps the shaded area \(\mathrm{d} \mathbf{A} = \mathbf{v} \, \mathrm{d} t \times \mathrm{d} \mathbf{l}\). The displacement is exaggerated.









NoteGoing further: Potential flows



Kelvin’s theorem tells us that a barotropic flow that starts irrotational remains irrotational. A flow that is both incompressible and irrotational has \[
\nabla \cdot \mathbf{v} = 0, \qquad \nabla \times \mathbf{v} = 0 .
\tag{13.8}\] The second equation implies that \(\mathbf{v} = \nabla \Phi\) (a potential flow). The first equation then gives \[
\boxed{\nabla^2 \Phi = 0 .}
\tag{13.9}\] For example, the flow with speed \(U\) around a cylinder of radius \(a\) has \(\Phi = U (R + a^2 / R) \cos \phi\) in cylindrical coordinates (Figure 13.4).






Figure 13.4: Streamlines of the potential flow around a cylinder.



More generally, for an incompressible flow the curl of the vorticity is \[
\nabla \times \boldsymbol{\omega} = \nabla \times (\nabla \times \mathbf{v}) = \nabla (\nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}) - \nabla^2 \mathbf{v} \Longrightarrow \nabla^2 \mathbf{v} = - \nabla \times \boldsymbol{\omega} .
\tag{13.10}\] Together with the vorticity equation, Equation 13.6, this completely determines the flow. We can then find the pressure from the velocity, by taking the divergence of the momentum equation with \(\rho = \rho_0\): \[
\rho_0 \left[ \frac{\partial \mathbf{v}}{\partial t} + (\mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla) \mathbf{v} \right] = - \nabla p \Longrightarrow \nabla^2 p = - \rho_0 \nabla \cdot \left[ (\mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla) \mathbf{v} \right] .
\tag{13.11}\] The pressure is no longer a function of the density! Instead, it takes whatever value is needed to keep \(\nabla \cdot \mathbf{v} = 0\): in the limit \(c_s \to \infty\), sound waves adjust the pressure instantaneously.
When can we treat a flow as incompressible? Consider a quasi-steady, adiabatic flow. The continuity equation gives \[
0 \approx - \frac{\partial \rho}{\partial t} = \mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla \rho + \rho \nabla \cdot \mathbf{v} \Longrightarrow \frac{1}{c_s^2} \mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla p \approx - \rho \nabla \cdot \mathbf{v},
\tag{13.12}\] where we have used \(\nabla p = c_s^2 \nabla \rho\). The momentum equation, Equation 13.4 without gravity, gives \[
0 \approx - \frac{\partial \mathbf{v}}{\partial t} = \nabla \left( \frac{1}{2} v^2 \right) + \boldsymbol{\omega} \times \mathbf{v} + \frac{\nabla p}{\rho} \Longrightarrow \mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla p \approx - \rho \mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla \left( \frac{1}{2} v^2 \right) .
\tag{13.13}\] Combining the two, we find \[
\nabla \cdot \mathbf{v} \approx \frac{1}{c_s^2} \mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla \left( \frac{1}{2} v^2 \right) \sim \left( \frac{v}{c_s} \right)^2 \frac{v}{L} = \mathrm{Ma}^2 \frac{v}{L},
\tag{13.14}\] where \(L\) is the length scale of the flow. In practice, this means that the equation of state does not matter for flows with \(\mathrm{Ma} \lesssim 0.3\).




13.1.2 Bernoulli’s theorem
For a barotropic fluid, we can introduce the enthalpy as the indefinite integral \[
\mathcal{H} = \int \frac{\mathrm{d} p}{\rho}, \qquad \nabla \mathcal{H} = \frac{\nabla p}{\rho},
\tag{13.15}\] and write Equation 13.4 as \[
\frac{\partial \mathbf{v}}{\partial t} + \nabla \mathcal{B} + \boldsymbol{\omega} \times \mathbf{v} = 0, \qquad \mathcal{B} = \frac{1}{2} v^2 + \mathcal{H} + \Psi .
\tag{13.16}\] For an isentropic flow, \(\mathcal{H}\) is the specific enthalpy \(h\) of Chapter 11; for other barotropic flows, such as isothermal ones, it is not. For a pressureless fluid, \(\mathcal{H} = 0\), and \(\mathcal{B}\) is just the mechanical energy (kinetic plus potential) per unit mass. In a steady state, \(\partial_t \mathbf{v} = 0\). Taking the dot product of Equation 13.16 with \(\mathbf{v}\), we find \(\mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla \mathcal{B} = 0\), that is (Bernoulli’s theorem) \[
\boxed{\begin{aligned}
\mathcal{B} &= \frac{1}{2} v^2 + \mathcal{H} + \Psi \\
&= \text{const along streamlines.}
\end{aligned}}
\tag{13.17}\] This theorem generalizes the conservation of mechanical energy, which is so useful to solve problems in mechanics, to the domain of fluids. As we will see, Bernoulli’s theorem can be used to solve many fluid-related problems with minimal effort. If the flow is also irrotational, then \(\nabla \mathcal{B} = 0\), and \(\mathcal{B}\) has the same value everywhere.

title: 13  Stellar Winds and Spherical Accretion
text:
13.2 Isothermal winds
Consider a spherical, steady, isothermal wind, \(p = c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2 \rho\), from a star with mass \(M\). The wind starts at a radius \(r_0\), the photosphere or the corona of the star, and is accelerated outwards.
For an isothermal fluid, Equation 13.15 gives \[
\mathcal{H} = \int c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2 \frac{\mathrm{d} \rho}{\rho} = c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2 \ln \rho,
\tag{13.18}\] and the wind is described by the conservation of mass and by Bernoulli’s theorem: \[
\dot{M} = 4 \pi r^2 \rho v = \mathrm{const}, \qquad \frac{1}{2} v^2 + c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2 \ln \rho - \frac{GM}{r} = \mathrm{const} .
\tag{13.19}\] Differentiating the first equation, we find \[
2 r \rho v + r^2 v \frac{\mathrm{d} \rho}{\mathrm{d} r} + r^2 \rho \frac{\mathrm{d} v}{\mathrm{d} r} = 0 \Longrightarrow \frac{1}{\rho} \frac{\mathrm{d} \rho}{\mathrm{d} r} = - \frac{2}{r} - \frac{1}{v} \frac{\mathrm{d} v}{\mathrm{d} r} .
\tag{13.20}\] Differentiating the second, we find \[
v \frac{\mathrm{d} v}{\mathrm{d} r} + \frac{c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2}{\rho} \frac{\mathrm{d} \rho}{\mathrm{d} r} = - \frac{GM}{r^2} .
\tag{13.21}\] Combining the two, we obtain the wind equation \[
\boxed{(v^2 - c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2) \frac{1}{v} \frac{\mathrm{d} v}{\mathrm{d} r} = \frac{2 c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2}{r} - \frac{GM}{r^2} .}
\tag{13.22}\] At this point, before we analyze this equation in detail, it is important to remark that energy is not conserved in this problem. The assumption of constant temperature requires that heat is supplied to the wind: by thermal conduction and non-radiative heating in the solar corona, by the radiation of the star in hot stars. Remember that, if energy is conserved, an expanding flow cools adiabatically, like the hot bubble of a supernova remnant in the snowplough phase (Section 12.2). What is happening here is that energy is being injected into the flow and that this heating is implicit in our assumption that the flow is isothermal. We will come back to this in Section 13.2.3.

13.2.1 The critical point
Close to the star, where the wind is almost in hydrostatic equilibrium, \(v \ll c_{\mathrm{iso}}\), while far from it, \(v \gg c_{\mathrm{iso}}\). So, if the wind accelerates, it must cross the sound speed somewhere. At that point the left-hand side of Equation 13.22 vanishes, so the right-hand side must also vanish. This happens only at the critical point, or sonic point, \[
\boxed{r_c = \frac{GM}{2 c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2} .}
\tag{13.23}\] Note that \(c_{\mathrm{iso}} = v_{\mathrm{esc}} (r_c) / 2\), where \(v_{\mathrm{esc}} = (2GM / r)^{1/2}\) is the escape velocity. In the worksheet, you will show that the acceleration at the critical point is finite: \[
\left( \frac{\mathrm{d} v}{\mathrm{d} r} \right)_{r_c} = \pm \frac{2 c_{\mathrm{iso}}^3}{GM} .
\tag{13.24}\]
The wind equation can be written as \[
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} r} \left[ \frac{v^2}{2} - c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2 \ln v \right] = \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} r} \left[ \frac{GM}{r} + 2 c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2 \ln r \right] .
\tag{13.25}\] Integrating, dividing by \(- c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2\), and taking the exponential of both sides, we find \[
v \exp \left( - \frac{v^2}{2 c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2} \right) = \frac{C}{r^2} \exp \left( - \frac{2 r_c}{r} \right),
\tag{13.26}\] where \(C\) is an integration constant. Figure 13.5 shows the solutions for different values of \(C\). The solution that passes through the critical point, \(v = c_{\mathrm{iso}}\) at \(r = r_c\), has \[
c_{\mathrm{iso}} \mathrm{e}^{- 1 / 2} = \frac{C}{r_c^2} \mathrm{e}^{- 2} \Longrightarrow C = c_{\mathrm{iso}} r_c^2 \mathrm{e}^{3 / 2},
\tag{13.27}\] so \[
\boxed{\begin{aligned}
v \exp \left( - \frac{v^2}{2 c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2} \right) &= c_{\mathrm{iso}} \left( \frac{r_c}{r} \right)^2 \\
&\quad {} \times \exp \left( - \frac{2 r_c}{r} + \frac{3}{2} \right) .
\end{aligned}}
\tag{13.28}\]






Figure 13.5: Solutions of the isothermal wind equation, Equation 13.26, for different values of the integration constant \(C\). Thick lines: the two solutions that pass through the critical point.



Only one of the solutions in Figure 13.5 starts subsonic close to the star and becomes supersonic: this is the wind. The other solutions are double valued, or supersonic already at the base of the wind, or subsonic everywhere. The last ones, the breezes, have \(v \to 0\) and a finite density at large radii, so their pressure at infinity is much larger than that of the ISM (Parker 1958). At the base of the wind, \(v_0 \ll c_{\mathrm{iso}}\), so Equation 13.28 gives \[
v_0 \approx c_{\mathrm{iso}} \left( \frac{r_c}{r_0} \right)^2 \exp \left( - \frac{2 r_c}{r_0} + \frac{3}{2} \right) .
\tag{13.29}\] In other words, the speed at the base of the wind is set by the critical point. The wind regulates itself. If the speed at the base is too large, the gas reaches the sound speed before \(r_c\), where \(\mathrm{d} v / \mathrm{d} r \to \infty\): the flow stalls, and a shock forms, which slows down the wind. If the speed at the base is too small, the gas remains subsonic, and a rarefaction wave forms, which lowers the pressure and accelerates the wind.


13.2.2 Velocity and density of the wind
Far from the star, \(r \gg r_c\), the wind is supersonic, and Equation 13.28 gives \[
\frac{v^2}{2 c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2} \approx 2 \ln \left( \frac{r}{r_c} \right) + \ln \left( \frac{v}{c_{\mathrm{iso}}} \right) - \frac{3}{2} \Longrightarrow v \approx 2 c_{\mathrm{iso}} \left[ \ln \left( \frac{r}{r_c} \right) \right]^{1 / 2} .
\tag{13.30}\] The isothermal wind keeps accelerating, albeit slowly.
Dividing Equation 13.28 by Equation 13.29, we find \[
\frac{v}{v_0} \exp \left( - \frac{v^2}{2 c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2} \right) \approx \left( \frac{r_0}{r} \right)^2 \exp \left[ \frac{GM}{c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2} \left( \frac{1}{r_0} - \frac{1}{r} \right) \right] .
\tag{13.31}\] So, from the conservation of mass, in the subsonic part of the wind \[
\frac{\rho}{\rho_0} = \left( \frac{r_0}{r} \right)^2 \frac{v_0}{v} \approx \exp \left[ - \frac{GM}{c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2} \left( \frac{1}{r_0} - \frac{1}{r} \right) \right],
\tag{13.32}\] which is the density of an isothermal atmosphere in hydrostatic equilibrium. The mass-loss rate is \(\dot{M} = 4 \pi r_c^2 \rho_c c_{\mathrm{iso}}\), where \(\rho_c = \rho_0 (r_0 / r_c)^2 v_0 / c_{\mathrm{iso}}\) is the density at the critical point. Using Equation 13.29, \[
\boxed{\dot{M} = 4 \pi \rho_0 c_{\mathrm{iso}} r_c^2 \exp \left( \frac{3}{2} - \frac{r_0}{H_0} \right),}
\tag{13.33}\] where \(H_0 = c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2 / g_0 = c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2 r_0^2 / (GM) = r_0^2 / (2 r_c)\) is the pressure scale height at the base of the wind. The mass-loss rate is exponentially sensitive to \(r_0 / H_0\), that is, to the temperature at the base of the wind.

In reality, the corona is not isothermal: it cools as the wind expands.

For a hot star, with \(M = 50\,M_{\odot}\), \(r_0 = 15\,R_{\odot}\), and \(T = 4 \times 10^4\,\mathrm{K}\) at the photosphere, \(r_0 / H_0 \approx 10^3\), so thermal pressure cannot drive a wind. The winds of hot stars are driven by radiation (see Exercise 13.1 for a simple model).




13.2.3 Energy of the wind
The energy per unit mass of the wind is \[
e = \frac{v^2}{2} - \frac{GM}{r} + \frac{p}{(\Gamma - 1) \rho} = \frac{v^2}{2} - \frac{GM}{r} + \frac{c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2}{\Gamma - 1},
\tag{13.34}\] where \(\Gamma\) is the adiabatic index of the gas. At the base of the wind, \(v^2 \ll c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2 = v_{\mathrm{esc}}^2 (r_c) / 4 \ll v_{\mathrm{esc}}^2 (r_0)\), so \(e (r_0) \approx - GM / r_0 < 0\). Far from the star, \(v \gg c_{\mathrm{iso}}\), so \(e \approx v^2 / 2 > 0\). This means that energy is not conserved in an isothermal wind: the wind must be heated to stay isothermal. Polytropic winds, \(p \propto \rho^{\Gamma}\) with polytropic exponent \(\Gamma\), have the same qualitative features, as long as \(\Gamma < 3 / 2\) (Lamers and Cassinelli 1999). An adiabatic wind with \(\Gamma = 5 / 3\) cannot accelerate to supersonic speeds.


13.2.4 The de Laval nozzle
Surprisingly, there is an exact mathematical equivalence between stellar winds and transonic flows in nozzles. Consider a one-dimensional, barotropic flow in a pipe with cross-sectional area \(A (s)\), \(s\) being a coordinate along the pipe (Figure 13.6). The flow is described by the conservation of mass and by Bernoulli’s theorem: \[
\rho v A = \mathrm{const}, \qquad \frac{1}{2} v^2 + \mathcal{H} = \mathrm{const} .
\tag{13.35}\] Differentiating the first equation, we obtain \[
\frac{1}{\rho} \frac{\mathrm{d} \rho}{\mathrm{d} s} + \frac{1}{v} \frac{\mathrm{d} v}{\mathrm{d} s} + \frac{1}{A} \frac{\mathrm{d} A}{\mathrm{d} s} = 0 .
\tag{13.36}\] Bernoulli’s theorem gives, with \(c_s^2 = \mathrm{d} p / \mathrm{d} \rho\) and \(\mathrm{Ma} = v / c_s\), \[
v \frac{\mathrm{d} v}{\mathrm{d} s} + \frac{c_s^2}{\rho} \frac{\mathrm{d} \rho}{\mathrm{d} s} = 0 \Longrightarrow \frac{1}{\rho} \frac{\mathrm{d} \rho}{\mathrm{d} s} = - \mathrm{Ma}^2 \frac{1}{v} \frac{\mathrm{d} v}{\mathrm{d} s} .
\tag{13.37}\] Combining the last two equations, we find \[
\boxed{(1 - \mathrm{Ma}^2) \frac{1}{v} \frac{\mathrm{d} v}{\mathrm{d} s} = - \frac{1}{A} \frac{\mathrm{d} A}{\mathrm{d} s} .}
\tag{13.38}\] We will see below that this equation coincides with the wind equation, Equation 13.22, with the proper choice of \(A (s)\).






Figure 13.6: A de Laval nozzle. The flow is subsonic before the throat, where the area \(A (s)\) is smallest, and supersonic after it.




If \(\mathrm{Ma} < 1\), the flow accelerates where the pipe narrows, \(\mathrm{d} A / \mathrm{d} s < 0\). The opposite happens for \(\mathrm{Ma} > 1\).
The flow can become supersonic without a shock, that is with a finite \(\mathrm{d} v / \mathrm{d} s\), only at a throat, where \(\mathrm{d} A / \mathrm{d} s = 0\).
In principle, we could reverse the nozzle and have a flow that decelerates smoothly from supersonic to subsonic. In practice, this almost always produces shocks. Shocks, and dissipation in general, break the time symmetry of the fluid equations, even though these are derived from classical mechanics, which is time reversible (compare the famous Loschmidt paradox).
Rocket engines use de Laval nozzles to accelerate their exhaust to supersonic speeds.
The flow regulates itself, as the wind does. A sonic point before the throat makes \(\mathrm{d} v / \mathrm{d} s\) diverge: a shock forms, and the flow stalls. The additional pressure moves the sonic point towards the throat. A sonic point after the throat also makes \(\mathrm{d} v / \mathrm{d} s\) diverge, but now a rarefaction wave forms, which decreases the pressure and brings the sonic point back to the throat.

For an isothermal gas, \(c_s = c_{\mathrm{iso}}\), and Equation 13.38 becomes \[
(v^2 - c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2) \frac{1}{v} \frac{\mathrm{d} v}{\mathrm{d} s} = c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2 \frac{\mathrm{d} \ln A}{\mathrm{d} s} .
\tag{13.39}\] This is the wind equation, Equation 13.22, if \(c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2 \, \mathrm{d} \ln A / \mathrm{d} r = 2 c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2 / r - GM / r^2\), that is if \(A \propto r^2 \exp (2 r_c / r)\). This effective area has a minimum at \(r = r_c\): the critical point is the throat of the nozzle.

title: 13  Stellar Winds and Spherical Accretion
text:
13.3 Spherical accretion
The same equations, with \(v < 0\), describe the steady accretion of gas onto a star from a uniform medium, at rest far from the star. The physical solution is the one labelled “accretion” in Figure 13.5: the gas falls in subsonically at large radii, and it crosses the sound speed at \(r_c\). This is called Bondi accretion (Bondi 1952). We work it out in Exercise 13.2.

\tag{13.40}\] Find the acceleration of the wind at the sonic point \[
r_c = \frac{GM}{2 c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2} .

text:
13.5 Exercises

Exercise 13.1 (Radiation-driven winds) Consider an isothermal steady stellar wind. Radiation pressure in optically thin conditions produces an additional force per unit mass that can be parameterized as \[
f = \frac{A}{r^2},
\tag{13.42}\] where \(A > 0\).

Show that the momentum equation becomes \[
(v^2 - c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2)  \frac{1}{v}  \frac{\mathrm{d} v}{\mathrm{d} r} = \frac{2 c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2}{r} -
\frac{GM}{r^2} + \frac{A}{r^2},
\tag{13.43}\] where \(c_{\mathrm{iso}}\) is the isothermal sound speed.
Assuming \(A < GM\), how does the structure of the wind change?
How does the radial profile of the velocity change if \(A > GM\)? Give a physical interpretation of the results.



Exercise 13.2 (Isothermal Bondi accretion) Far from a star of mass \(M\) located at the origin, isothermal gas has pressure \(p_{\infty} = c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2 \rho_{\infty}\) and density \(\rho_{\infty}\). This gas is steadily accreted onto the star.

Find the accretion rate, assuming that the gas remains isothermal. At what radius does the infalling gas reach the sound speed?
Let \(c_{\mathrm{iso}} = 1\, \mathrm{km} /\mathrm{s}\) and \(n_{\infty} = 10^3\) hydrogen atoms per \(\mathrm{cm}^{3}\), and take the mass of the hydrogen atom to be \(1.66 \times 10^{- 27}\, \mathrm{kg}\). Express this radius in units of the solar radius \(R_{\odot} = 7 \times 10^8\, \mathrm{m}\).
Calculate the time that a star of mass \(M\) needs to double its mass.
The gas is captured by the star inside the Bondi radius \(r_B\), where the gravitational energy per unit mass, \(GM / r\), becomes comparable to the thermal energy per unit mass, \(c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2\). Find \(r_B\) and compare it with the radius of part 1. Estimate the accretion rate as the mass flux \(\rho_{\infty} c_{\mathrm{iso}}\) through a disk of radius \(r_B\), and compare your estimate with the result of part 1.

title: 14  Fluid Instabilities
text:
14.1 Convective instability
A flow is unstable when small perturbations can grow exponentially. We have already seen in Chapter 9 that the normal modes of a fluid at rest have real \(\omega^2\) (Equation 9.29), so each mode either oscillates or grows exponentially. This is no longer true when the fluid is moving, as we will see for the Kelvin–Helmholtz instability. In this chapter we will look at a few examples of instabilities that are particularly useful in astrophysics. There are many more instabilities, each with its own dimensionless numbers. The definitive reference is Chandrasekhar (1961).
Consider a stratified medium in a uniform gravitational field \(\mathbf{g} = - g \hat{\mathbf{z}}\), in hydrostatic equilibrium, \(\partial_z p = - \rho g\). We displace a small fluid element upwards by a distance \(\delta z\), as shown in Figure 14.1. Initially, the fluid element has the same density \(\rho\) and pressure \(p\) as its surroundings. After the displacement, its density and pressure are \(\rho^*\) and \(p^*\), while the background at the new location has density \(\rho (z + \delta z)\) and pressure \(p (z + \delta z)\). What will the fluid element do?
As in Section 10.2, we assume that the displacement is slow enough for the fluid element to stay in pressure equilibrium with its surroundings, \(p^* = p (z + \delta z)\), and that it is adiabatic. The force per unit volume experienced by the fluid element in the vertical direction is \[
f_z = - \partial_z p - \rho^* g = g \left[ \rho (z + \delta z) - \rho^* \right] .
\tag{14.1}\] So, if \(\rho^* < \rho (z + \delta z)\), the fluid element is lighter than its surroundings and it is pushed further upwards. In this case we say that the fluid is convectively unstable. Otherwise, the fluid element is pushed back down.
For an adiabatic displacement, \((\partial p / \partial \rho)_s = \Gamma p / \rho\), so, to linear order, \[
\rho^* = \rho + \left( \frac{\partial \rho}{\partial p} \right)_s \frac{\mathrm{d} p}{\mathrm{d} z} \delta z = \rho \left[ 1 + \frac{1}{\Gamma p} \frac{\mathrm{d} p}{\mathrm{d} z} \delta z \right] .
\tag{14.2}\] On the other hand, the density of the background at the new location is \[
\rho (z + \delta z) = \rho + \frac{\mathrm{d} \rho}{\mathrm{d} z} \delta z .
\tag{14.3}\] The fluid is stable if \(\rho^* \geq \rho (z + \delta z)\) for \(\delta z > 0\), that is if \((\rho / \Gamma p) \, \mathrm{d} p / \mathrm{d} z \geq \mathrm{d} \rho / \mathrm{d} z\). Since both the pressure and the density decrease with height, the condition for stability is \[
\boxed{\frac{\rho}{\Gamma p} \left| \frac{\mathrm{d} p}{\mathrm{d} z} \right| \leq \left| \frac{\mathrm{d} \rho}{\mathrm{d} z} \right| .}
\tag{14.4}\] Note that \(\rho / \Gamma p = c_s^{- 2}\). In words, the density of the background has to decrease with height at least as fast as the density of a fluid element that is moved up adiabatically.

title: 14  Fluid Instabilities
text:
Figure 14.1: A fluid element is displaced upwards by \(\delta z\). Its density and pressure change from \(\rho\) and \(p\) to \(\rho^*\) and \(p^*\). The background at the new location has density \(\rho (z + \delta z)\) and pressure \(p (z + \delta z)\).






14.1.1 The Schwarzschild criterion
For an ideal gas with uniform composition (constant \(\mu\)), \(p = \rho k_B T / (\mu m_u)\), so \[
\begin{aligned}
\rho = \frac{\mu m_u p}{k_B T} \Longrightarrow \mathrm{d} \rho &= \frac{\mu m_u}{k_B T} \mathrm{d} p - \frac{\mu m_u p}{k_B T^2} \mathrm{d} T \\
&= \frac{\rho}{p} \mathrm{d} p - \frac{\rho}{T} \mathrm{d} T .
\end{aligned}
\tag{14.5}\] Combining Equation 14.2, Equation 14.3, and Equation 14.5, we find \[
\begin{aligned}
& \rho^* - \rho (z + \delta z) \\
& \quad = \left[ - \left( 1 - \frac{1}{\Gamma} \right) \frac{\rho}{p} \frac{\mathrm{d} p}{\mathrm{d} z} + \frac{\rho}{T} \frac{\mathrm{d} T}{\mathrm{d} z} \right] \delta z .
\end{aligned}
\tag{14.6}\] So the condition for instability is that \[
\frac{\mathrm{d} T}{\mathrm{d} z} < \left( 1 - \frac{1}{\Gamma} \right) \frac{T}{p} \frac{\mathrm{d} p}{\mathrm{d} z} .
\tag{14.7}\] What is the meaning of the right-hand side? Suppose that the background is isentropic, \(p = p_0 (\rho / \rho_0)^{\Gamma}\). Then \(\mathrm{d} \rho = \rho \, \mathrm{d} p / (\Gamma p)\) and \[
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{d} p &= \frac{k_B T}{\mu m_u} \mathrm{d} \rho + \frac{\rho k_B}{\mu m_u} \mathrm{d} T = \frac{1}{\Gamma} \mathrm{d} p + \frac{p}{T} \mathrm{d} T \\
\Longrightarrow \mathrm{d} T &= \left( 1 - \frac{1}{\Gamma} \right) \frac{T}{p} \mathrm{d} p .
\end{aligned}
\tag{14.8}\] So the right-hand side of Equation 14.7 is the adiabatic temperature gradient, \((\mathrm{d} T / \mathrm{d} z)_{\mathrm{ad}}\), that is the temperature gradient that the fluid would have if it were isentropic, with the same pressure gradient. Since the temperature decreases with height, the condition for instability is \[
\boxed{\left| \frac{\mathrm{d} T}{\mathrm{d} z} \right| > \left| \frac{\mathrm{d} T}{\mathrm{d} z} \right|_{\mathrm{ad}} .}
\tag{14.9}\] This is the Schwarzschild criterion: a fluid is convectively unstable if its temperature decreases with height faster than it would in an isentropic fluid.
When the fluid is unstable, hot fluid elements rise, give heat to their surroundings, sink, and take heat from their surroundings at the bottom (Figure 14.2). So convection transports heat upwards. The convective heat flux grows with the difference \(|\mathrm{d} T / \mathrm{d} z| - |\mathrm{d} T / \mathrm{d} z|_{\mathrm{ad}}\); in the mixing-length theory used in stellar evolution codes, \(F_{\mathrm{conv}} \propto (|\mathrm{d} T / \mathrm{d} z| - |\mathrm{d} T / \mathrm{d} z|_{\mathrm{ad}})^{3 / 2}\). Convection is very efficient, so a small excess over the adiabatic gradient is enough to carry a large heat flux. In well developed convection, the average temperature gradient is very close to the adiabatic one: \[
\left\langle \left| \frac{\mathrm{d} T}{\mathrm{d} z} \right| \right\rangle \approx \left| \frac{\mathrm{d} T}{\mathrm{d} z} \right|_{\mathrm{ad}} .
\tag{14.10}\]






Figure 14.2: Schematic convection cycle. Hot fluid elements rise adiabatically and heat their surroundings at the top; cool fluid elements sink adiabatically and take heat from their surroundings at the bottom.



Convection transports energy in the cores of massive stars and in the envelopes of low-mass stars like the Sun. Three-dimensional simulations of convection in stars, such as those of Herwig et al. (2023), show a turbulent flow, with fluid elements moving on a wide range of scales. Convection is also important in core-collapse supernovae (Chapter 3). After core bounce, the gas behind the stalled shock is heated from below by the neutrinos emitted by the proto-neutron star, so it becomes convectively unstable. This neutrino-driven convection helps the shock to revive (Abdikamalov et al. 2022).


14.1.2 The Brunt–Väisälä frequency
The equation of motion of the displaced fluid element is \[
\begin{aligned}
\rho \frac{\mathrm{d}^2 \delta z}{\mathrm{d} t^2} &= - g \left[ \rho^* - \rho (z + \delta z) \right] \\
&= - g \rho \biggl[ - \left( 1 - \frac{1}{\Gamma} \right) \frac{1}{p} \frac{\mathrm{d} p}{\mathrm{d} z} \\
&\qquad {} + \frac{1}{T} \frac{\mathrm{d} T}{\mathrm{d} z} \biggr] \delta z ,
\end{aligned}
\tag{14.11}\] where we have used Equation 14.1 and Equation 14.6. This can be written as \[
\frac{\mathrm{d}^2 \delta z}{\mathrm{d} t^2} + N^2 \delta z = 0 ,
\tag{14.12}\] where \(N\) is the Brunt–Väisälä frequency \[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
N^2 &= \frac{g}{T} \left[ \frac{\mathrm{d} T}{\mathrm{d} z} - \left( 1 - \frac{1}{\Gamma} \right) \frac{T}{p} \frac{\mathrm{d} p}{\mathrm{d} z} \right] \\
&= \frac{g}{T} \left[ \frac{\mathrm{d} T}{\mathrm{d} z} - \left( \frac{\mathrm{d} T}{\mathrm{d} z} \right)_{\mathrm{ad}} \right] .
\end{aligned}
}
\tag{14.13}\] This generalizes Equation 10.32, which we derived for an isothermal atmosphere, to an arbitrary stratification.

If \(N^2 > 0\), the fluid element oscillates with frequency \(N\): \[
\delta z (t) = A \sin (N t) + B \cos (N t) .
\tag{14.14}\] The fluid is stable against convection.
If \(N^2 < 0\), the displacement grows exponentially: \[
\delta z (t) = A \exp \left( \sqrt{- N^2} \, t \right) + B \exp \left( - \sqrt{- N^2} \, t \right) .
\tag{14.15}\] The fluid is unstable against convection, and the growth rate of the instability is \(\lambda = \sqrt{- N^2}\).







TipExample



Consider the atmosphere of the Earth, with \(\mu \approx 29\) and \(\Gamma = 7/5\) (Chapter 10), and neglect the water vapour. Using hydrostatic equilibrium, \(\mathrm{d} p / \mathrm{d} z = - \rho g\), the adiabatic temperature gradient is \[
\left( \frac{\mathrm{d} T}{\mathrm{d} z} \right)_{\mathrm{ad}} = - \left( 1 - \frac{1}{\Gamma} \right) \frac{\mu m_u g}{k_B} \approx - 9.8\,\mathrm{K\,km^{-1}} .
\tag{14.16}\] The average temperature gradient in the lower atmosphere is about \(- 6.5\,\mathrm{K\,km^{-1}}\), so the atmosphere is, on average, stable against convection. With \(T \approx 288\,\mathrm{K}\), we find \(N^2 \approx (g / T) \times 3.3\,\mathrm{K\,km^{-1}} \approx 1.1 \times 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{s^{-2}}\), so a displaced parcel of air oscillates with a period \(2 \pi / N \approx 10\,\mathrm{min}\). On a sunny day, however, the ground heats the air above it, the temperature gradient near the ground becomes steeper than the adiabatic one, and the air starts to convect. The rising bubbles of warm air, called thermals, are used by birds and glider pilots to gain altitude.

title: 14  Fluid Instabilities
text:
14.2 The Rayleigh–Taylor instability
Suppose now that the density changes over a distance much shorter than the pressure scale height, for example at the interface between two layers with different composition or temperature. Then the change in the density of the fluid element in Equation 14.2, which is of order \(\rho \, \delta z / (\Gamma H)\), with \(H\) the pressure scale height, is negligible compared with the change in the density of the background in Equation 14.3. The fluid element keeps its density as it moves, \(\rho^* \approx \rho\), as if the fluid were incompressible, so \(\rho^* - \rho (z + \delta z) = - (\mathrm{d} \rho / \mathrm{d} z) \, \delta z\), and \[
\boxed{N^2 = - \frac{g}{\rho} \frac{\mathrm{d} \rho}{\mathrm{d} z} .}
\tag{14.17}\] For an ideal gas with uniform composition, at nearly constant pressure, \(\mathrm{d} \rho / \rho \approx - \mathrm{d} T / T\), so this agrees with Equation 14.13 without the \(\mathrm{d} p / \mathrm{d} z\) term. Equation 14.17 tells us that a heavy fluid on top of a light fluid is unstable. This is the Rayleigh–Taylor instability. The heavy fluid sinks in fingers, while the light fluid rises in bubbles that take the shape of mushrooms (Figure 14.3). The fingers slide past the surrounding fluid, so their sides are in turn unstable to the Kelvin–Helmholtz instability (Section 14.3), which rolls them up into vortices. In the in-class worksheet (Section 14.4), we estimate the growth rate of the instability for a sharp interface between two fluids.






Figure 14.3: Development of the Rayleigh–Taylor instability in a two-dimensional simulation with \(1024 \times 2048\) grid points, at three times (in code units). The colour shows a passive tracer, equal to 1 in the heavy fluid, initially on top, and to 0 in the light fluid below. The interface is initially perturbed with a small sinusoidal displacement.



What matters is the gravitational acceleration felt by the fluid. In a fluid that is accelerated with acceleration \(\mathbf{a}\), the effective gravity, in the frame of the fluid, is \(\mathbf{g} - \mathbf{a}\). So a fluid that is stable in a gravitational field can become Rayleigh–Taylor unstable when it is accelerated. This happens in supernovae. When the shock launched by a core-collapse supernova (Chapter 3) passes through the layers of the star, it sets them in motion outwards. The gas behind the shock is then decelerated, for example when the shock reaches the hydrogen envelope and has to sweep up more mass. In the frame of the decelerating gas, the effective gravity points outwards, so the interfaces between layers with different composition, where the density drops outwards, have heavy fluid “on top” of light fluid and become unstable. The instability mixes the heavy elements produced in the explosion, including hot bubbles of radioactive \(^{56}\)Ni, into the outer layers of the star (Wongwathanarat et al. 2015). When the acceleration is impulsive, as when a shock crosses the interface between two fluids (for example between the oxygen and the carbon layers of a star), the corresponding instability is called the Richtmyer–Meshkov instability (Richtmyer 1960; Meshkov 1969).

title: 14  Fluid Instabilities
text:
14.3 The Kelvin–Helmholtz instability
Consider an incompressible fluid with uniform density and a shear flow \[
\mathbf{v}_0 (x) = V (x) \hat{\mathbf{y}} .
\tag{14.18}\] We perturb it with a small velocity field in the \((x, y)\) plane, \[
\mathbf{v}_1 (t, x, y) = \hat{\mathbf{z}} \times \nabla \phi (t, x, y) = \partial_x \phi \, \hat{\mathbf{y}} - \partial_y \phi \, \hat{\mathbf{x}} ,
\tag{14.19}\] where \(\phi\) is called the stream function. Note that \(\nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}_1 = - \partial_x \partial_y \phi + \partial_y \partial_x \phi = 0\), so the perturbation is automatically incompressible.
We study the stability of this flow using the vorticity equation (Equation 13.6) together with \(\nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}_1 = 0\): \[
\frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\omega}}{\partial t} + \nabla \times (\boldsymbol{\omega} \times \mathbf{v}) = 0 .
\tag{14.20}\] The vorticity of the background and of the perturbation are \[
\begin{aligned}
\boldsymbol{\omega}_0 &= \nabla \times \mathbf{v}_0 = \frac{\mathrm{d} V}{\mathrm{d} x} \hat{\mathbf{z}} , \\
\boldsymbol{\omega}_1 &= \nabla \times \mathbf{v}_1 = (\partial_x^2 \phi + \partial_y^2 \phi) \, \hat{\mathbf{z}} = \nabla^2 \phi \, \hat{\mathbf{z}} .
\end{aligned}
\tag{14.21}\] Inserting \(\boldsymbol{\omega} = \boldsymbol{\omega}_0 + \boldsymbol{\omega}_1\) and \(\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{v}_0 + \mathbf{v}_1\) in Equation 14.20 and keeping only the terms of first order, we find \[
\frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\omega}_1}{\partial t} + \nabla \times (\boldsymbol{\omega}_0 \times \mathbf{v}_1) + \nabla \times (\boldsymbol{\omega}_1 \times \mathbf{v}_0) = 0 .
\tag{14.22}\] The zeroth-order term vanishes: \(\boldsymbol{\omega}_0 \times \mathbf{v}_0 = - V \, (\mathrm{d} V / \mathrm{d} x) \, \hat{\mathbf{x}}\) depends only on \(x\), so its curl is zero. Since \(\boldsymbol{\omega}_1\) is parallel to \(\hat{\mathbf{z}}\), we need only the \(z\)-component of Equation 14.22. We have \[
\begin{aligned}
\boldsymbol{\omega}_1 \times \mathbf{v}_0 &= \nabla^2 \phi \, \hat{\mathbf{z}} \times V \hat{\mathbf{y}} \\
&= - V \nabla^2 \phi \, \hat{\mathbf{x}} , \\
\left\{ \nabla \times [\boldsymbol{\omega}_1 \times \mathbf{v}_0] \right\} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{z}} &= V \partial_y \nabla^2 \phi , \\
\boldsymbol{\omega}_0 \times \mathbf{v}_1 &= - \frac{\mathrm{d} V}{\mathrm{d} x} (\partial_x \phi \hat{\mathbf{x}} + \partial_y \phi \hat{\mathbf{y}}) , \\
\left\{ \nabla \times [\boldsymbol{\omega}_0 \times \mathbf{v}_1] \right\} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{z}} &= - \frac{\mathrm{d}^2 V}{\mathrm{d} x^2} \partial_y \phi .
\end{aligned}
\tag{14.23}\] In the last line, the terms with \(\partial_x \partial_y \phi\) cancel. So \[
\partial_t \nabla^2 \phi + V \partial_y \nabla^2 \phi - \frac{\mathrm{d}^2 V}{\mathrm{d} x^2} \partial_y \phi = 0 .
\tag{14.24}\] The coefficients of this equation depend only on \(x\), so we look for solutions of the form \[
\phi (t, x, y) = \Psi (x) \, \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i} (k y - \omega t)} ,
\tag{14.25}\] with \(k > 0\). Then \(\partial_t \phi = - \mathrm{i} \omega \phi\), \(\partial_y \phi = \mathrm{i} k \phi\), and \(\nabla^2 \phi = (\mathrm{d}^2 \Psi / \mathrm{d} x^2 - k^2 \Psi) \, \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i} (k y - \omega t)}\). Inserting these in Equation 14.24 and dividing by \(- \mathrm{i} k\), we obtain \[
\boxed{(c - V) \left( \frac{\mathrm{d}^2 \Psi}{\mathrm{d} x^2} - k^2 \Psi \right) + \frac{\mathrm{d}^2 V}{\mathrm{d} x^2} \Psi = 0 ,}
\tag{14.26}\] where \(c = \omega / k\), with boundary conditions \(\Psi (\pm \infty) = 0\). This is Rayleigh’s stability equation. It is an eigenvalue problem: for a given \(V (x)\) and \(k\), it has non-trivial solutions only for some values of \(c\). The flow is unstable if one of these has a positive imaginary part. Writing \(\omega = \omega_r + \mathrm{i} \omega_i\), the perturbation grows as \(\mathrm{e}^{\omega_i t}\), so the growth rate of the instability is \(\omega_i\).

14.3.1 A vortex sheet
As an example, consider a shear layer of zero thickness, a vortex sheet, in which \[
\mathbf{v}_0 (x) = V (x) \hat{\mathbf{y}} = \begin{cases}
V_1 \hat{\mathbf{y}}, & x < 0, \\
V_2 \hat{\mathbf{y}}, & x > 0 .
\end{cases}
\tag{14.27}\] Let \(\xi (t, x, y) = X (x) \, \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i} (k y - \omega t)}\) be the displacement of the fluid elements in the \(x\)-direction (Figure 14.4). The \(x\)-component of the velocity perturbation is the rate of change of \(\xi\) following the fluid: \[
v_{1 x} = \frac{\mathrm{d} \xi}{\mathrm{d} t} = \partial_t \xi + V (x) \, \partial_y \xi = \mathrm{i} \left[ - \omega + V (x) k \right] \xi = - \mathrm{i} k \phi ,
\tag{14.28}\] where the last equality follows from Equation 14.19. So \[
\phi = \begin{cases}
(c - V_1) \, \xi, & x < 0, \\
(c - V_2) \, \xi, & x > 0 .
\end{cases}
\tag{14.29}\]






Figure 14.4: A perturbed vortex sheet. The fluid moves with velocity \(V_2\) above the sheet (\(x > 0\)) and \(V_1\) below it (\(x < 0\)). The sheet is displaced by \(\xi\).



Away from the vortex sheet, \(V\) is constant, so \(\mathrm{d}^2 V / \mathrm{d} x^2 = 0\), and Equation 14.26 becomes \[
\frac{\mathrm{d}^2 \Psi}{\mathrm{d} x^2} - k^2 \Psi = 0 \Longrightarrow \Psi (x) = \begin{cases}
A_- \mathrm{e}^{k x}, & x < 0, \\
A_+ \mathrm{e}^{- k x}, & x > 0,
\end{cases}
\tag{14.30}\] where we have used the boundary conditions at \(\pm \infty\). Using Equation 14.29, with \(X = X (0)\) the displacement of the sheet, which is the same on both sides (otherwise a gap would open between the two fluids), \(A_- = (c - V_1) X\) and \(A_+ = (c - V_2) X\). So, just below and just above the sheet, \[
\frac{\mathrm{d} \Psi}{\mathrm{d} x} = \begin{cases}
k (c - V_1) X, & x = 0^-, \\
- k (c - V_2) X, & x = 0^+ .
\end{cases}
\tag{14.31}\] To find the dispersion relation, we integrate Equation 14.26 across the vortex sheet. It is convenient to note that \[
(c - V) \frac{\mathrm{d}^2 \Psi}{\mathrm{d} x^2} + \frac{\mathrm{d}^2 V}{\mathrm{d} x^2} \Psi = \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} x} \left[ (c - V) \frac{\mathrm{d} \Psi}{\mathrm{d} x} + \frac{\mathrm{d} V}{\mathrm{d} x} \Psi \right] ,
\tag{14.32}\] so that \[
\begin{aligned}
0 &= \int_{- \epsilon}^{\epsilon} \biggl[ (c - V) \left( \frac{\mathrm{d}^2 \Psi}{\mathrm{d} x^2} - k^2 \Psi \right) \\
&\qquad {} + \frac{\mathrm{d}^2 V}{\mathrm{d} x^2} \Psi \biggr] \mathrm{d} x \\
&= \left[ (c - V) \frac{\mathrm{d} \Psi}{\mathrm{d} x} + \frac{\mathrm{d} V}{\mathrm{d} x} \Psi \right]_{- \epsilon}^{\epsilon} \\
&\qquad {} - k^2 \int_{- \epsilon}^{\epsilon} (c - V) \Psi \, \mathrm{d} x \\
&\xrightarrow{\epsilon \to 0} - k X \left[ (c - V_1)^2 + (c - V_2)^2 \right] ,
\end{aligned}
\tag{14.33}\] where we have used \(\mathrm{d} V / \mathrm{d} x = 0\) at \(x = \pm \epsilon\) and the fact that the last integral vanishes as \(\epsilon \to 0\). So the dispersion relation is \[
2 c^2 - 2 c (V_1 + V_2) + V_1^2 + V_2^2 = 0 \Longrightarrow
\boxed{c = \frac{1}{2} (V_1 + V_2) \pm \frac{\mathrm{i}}{2} |V_1 - V_2| .}
\tag{14.34}\] The real part of \(c\) tells us that the perturbations are carried along at the average velocity of the two layers. One of the two solutions has a positive imaginary part, so the vortex sheet is always unstable. This is the Kelvin–Helmholtz instability. Its growth rate is \[
\omega_i = \frac{k}{2} |V_1 - V_2| .
\tag{14.35}\] Note that smaller scales grow faster. If the shear layer has a finite thickness \(\delta\), Equation 14.35 is valid only for \(k \lesssim 1 / \delta\). The fastest-growing modes have \(k \sim 1 / \delta\), and \[
\omega_{i, \max} \sim \frac{|V_1 - V_2|}{\delta} \sim \left| \frac{\mathrm{d} V}{\mathrm{d} x} \right| .
\tag{14.36}\] Viscosity can also damp the instability at large \(k\).
We have assumed the fluid to be incompressible, which is a good approximation if \(|V_1 - V_2|\) is much smaller than the sound speed. Compressibility reduces the growth rate. For two fluids with the same sound speed \(c_s\), a vortex sheet is stable against perturbations along the flow if \(|V_1 - V_2| > 2 \sqrt{2} \, c_s\) (Landau and Lifshitz 1987, sec. 84). A perturbation with a wave vector at an angle to the flow only feels the component of the velocity jump along \(\mathbf{k}\), so in three dimensions a supersonic shear layer is never completely stable, but it is much less unstable than a subsonic one. This is one of the reasons why supersonic astrophysical jets can travel large distances without being disrupted.


14.3.2 Effect of viscosity
With the inclusion of viscosity, which we will discuss in Chapter 15, the vorticity equation acquires a diffusion term, and Rayleigh’s equation becomes the Orr–Sommerfeld equation: \[
(c - V) \tilde{\nabla}^2 \Psi + \frac{\mathrm{d}^2 V}{\mathrm{d} x^2} \Psi = \frac{\mathrm{i}}{k \mathrm{Re}} \tilde{\nabla}^4 \Psi , \qquad \tilde{\nabla}^2 = \frac{\mathrm{d}^2}{\mathrm{d} x^2} - k^2 .
\tag{14.37}\] Here we have measured lengths in units of a characteristic length \(L\) of the flow (for example the thickness of the shear layer) and velocities in units of a characteristic velocity \(U\) (for example \(|V_1 - V_2|\)), and introduced the Reynolds number \[
\mathrm{Re} = \frac{U L}{\nu} ,
\tag{14.38}\] where \(\nu\) is the kinematic viscosity. The Reynolds number is the most important parameter describing the stability of a flow.
In the limit of small Reynolds number, viscosity dominates and we can neglect the terms with \(V\). For a perturbation with \(\tilde{\nabla}^2 \Psi \approx - k^2 \Psi\), Equation 14.37 gives \[
\begin{aligned}
- c k^2 = \mathrm{i} \frac{k^3}{\mathrm{Re}} &\Longrightarrow \omega = - \frac{\mathrm{i}}{\mathrm{Re}} k^2 \\
&\Longrightarrow \phi (t, x, y) \sim \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i} k y} \mathrm{e}^{- k^2 t / \mathrm{Re}} .
\end{aligned}
\tag{14.39}\] The perturbation decays: viscosity has a stabilizing effect. In physical units, \(\mathrm{e}^{- k^2 t / \mathrm{Re}}\) is \(\mathrm{e}^{- \nu k^2 t}\), so the vorticity of the perturbation diffuses away in a time \(1 / (\nu k^2)\). In general, a flow becomes unstable when the Reynolds number exceeds a critical value, \(\mathrm{Re} > \mathrm{Re}_{\mathrm{crit}}\), which depends on the flow. As \(\mathrm{Re}\) increases, the eigenvalues \(\omega\) move upwards in the complex plane, and some of them cross into the upper half plane (Figure 14.5, left). For a shear layer, all sufficiently long wavelengths are unstable. For small \(k\) the modes behave as for the vortex sheet, with \(\omega_r \propto k\) and \(\omega_i \propto k\), while the modes with large \(k\) are damped by viscosity (Figure 14.5, right).






Figure 14.5: Sketch of the eigenvalues \(\omega = \omega_r + \mathrm{i} \omega_i\) in the complex plane. Left: as the Reynolds number increases, the eigenvalues move upwards, and the flow becomes unstable when one of them crosses the real axis. Right: the modes of a shear layer for increasing wave number \(k\), starting from the origin. Long wavelengths are unstable, while short wavelengths are damped by viscosity.



The Kelvin–Helmholtz instability is everywhere: it produces the billows that we sometimes see in clouds, and it makes jets and the boundaries of astrophysical outflows turbulent. It also plays an important role in turbulence (Chapter 17): large eddies are destroyed by the Kelvin–Helmholtz instability and generate smaller eddies.

In the vertical (\(z\)) direction, the disk is held up by a balance between the pressure gradient and the \(z\)-component of the gravitational force exerted by the central object.

Is the disk stable against convection if it consists of ionized hydrogen?

Adapted from Clarke and Carswell (2007), Problem 40.

The pipe is filled with incompressible fluid: the upper half of the pipe contains fluid of density \(\rho_1\) and the lower half contains fluid of density \(\rho_0\), with \(\rho_1 > \rho_0\).

Name the instability that develops, and identify the energy source that powers it.
Compute the energy \(E_1\) per unit length of the pipe that is available to the instability.

Adapted from Clarke and Carswell (2007), Problem 41.


Exercise 14.3 (Thermal balance of a slab) A slab of gas held together by its own gravity is heated by cosmic rays, at a constant rate per unit mass. It cools by optically thin thermal bremsstrahlung, with a cooling rate per unit mass proportional to \(\rho T^{1 / 2}\).

A gas in thermal equilibrium, \(\dot{Q} = 0\), is thermally unstable if \((\partial \dot{Q} / \partial T)_p < 0\). This is the Field criterion, which is discussed in Clarke and Carswell 2007, sec. 10.4.)
Is the slab stable against the Rayleigh–Taylor instability?

title: 15  Diffusion and Viscous Flows
text:
15.1 Random walks and diffusion
The diffusion equation is used to model many processes in astrophysics. Examples are:
In this chapter we first derive the diffusion equation from a simple model of a random walk. We then include bulk and shear viscosity in the momentum equation, we discuss how viscosity dissipates the kinetic energy of the flow, and we write the complete equations for a viscous fluid, the Navier–Stokes equations.
Consider a particle moving on a one-dimensional lattice with spacing \(\Delta x\), as in Figure 15.1. At each time step \(\Delta t\) the particle jumps to one of the two neighboring sites, to the left or to the right, with equal probability \(1/2\). For example, the particle could be a photon traveling at the speed of light \(c\) between two scatterings, in which case \(\Delta x = c \Delta t\).
Suppose that the particle starts at \(x = 0\). After \(n\) steps, its average position is still \(\langle x \rangle = 0\), because each step is equally likely to go to the left or to the right. However, the mean square displacement grows with the number of steps: \[
\langle x^2 \rangle = n \Delta x^2 .
\tag{15.1}\] This is the same result that we used in Chapter 3 to estimate the number of scatterings needed by a photon to escape from a supernova (Equation 3.16). Figure 15.2 shows a few examples of random walks. The typical distance from the origin after a time \(t = n \Delta t\) is \(X = \sqrt{\langle x^2 \rangle} = \sqrt{n} \Delta x\), so the combination \[
\frac{X^2}{2 t} = \frac{\Delta x^2}{2 \Delta t}
\tag{15.2}\] does not depend on \(n\). So we expect it to be a characteristic scale of the problem.
Let \(P(t, x)\) be the probability of finding the particle at the position \(x\) at time \(t\). The particle can be at \(x\) at time \(t + \Delta t\) only if it was at \(x - \Delta x\) or at \(x + \Delta x\) at time \(t\), so \[
P (t + \Delta t, x) = \frac{1}{2} \left[ P (t, x - \Delta x) + P (t, x + \Delta x) \right] .
\tag{15.3}\] To take the continuum limit, we expand both sides in Taylor series: \[
\begin{aligned}
P (t + \Delta t, x) &= P (t, x) + \Delta t \, \frac{\partial P}{\partial t} + O (\Delta t^2), \\
P (t, x \pm \Delta x) &= P (t, x) \pm \Delta x \, \frac{\partial P}{\partial x} \\
&\quad {} + \frac{1}{2} \Delta x^2 \, \frac{\partial^2 P}{\partial x^2} + O (\Delta x^3) .
\end{aligned}
\tag{15.4}\] Inserting these expansions in Equation 15.3, the terms with \(P(t, x)\) and the first derivatives in \(x\) cancel, and we obtain \[
\frac{\partial P}{\partial t} = \left( \frac{\Delta x^2}{2 \Delta t} \right) \frac{\partial^2 P}{\partial x^2} .
\tag{15.5}\] If we now take the limit \(\Delta x, \Delta t \to 0\) keeping \(\Delta x^2 / \Delta t\) fixed, we obtain the diffusion equation \[
\boxed{\frac{\partial P}{\partial t} = D \frac{\partial^2 P}{\partial x^2},}
\tag{15.6}\] where \[
D = \frac{\Delta x^2}{2 \Delta t}
\tag{15.7}\] is the diffusion coefficient. This is the same combination we found in Equation 15.2. In the continuum limit, \(P (t, x)\) becomes a probability distribution function (pdf), meaning that \(P (t, x) \mathrm{d} x\) is the probability of finding the particle between \(x\) and \(x + \mathrm{d} x\) at time \(t\).
The diffusion coefficient has units of \(\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}\), as in Equation 6.30. For the photon, \(\Delta x\) is the mean free path \(\lambda\) and \(D = \lambda c / 2\). This agrees with Equation 6.28, apart from the factor \(1/2\) in place of \(1/3\). The exact factor depends on the number of dimensions and on the distribution of the distances traveled between two scatterings, which in our model are all equal to \(\Delta x\).
The solution of Equation 15.6 for a particle that starts at \(x = 0\), that is with \(P (0, x) = \delta (x)\), is called the fundamental solution: \[
\Gamma (t, x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{4 \pi D t}} \mathrm{e}^{- \frac{x^2}{4 D t}} .
\tag{15.8}\] This can be found from the central limit theorem, or using separation of variables. The fundamental solution is a Gaussian with variance \(\langle x^2 \rangle = 2 D t\), which is Equation 15.1 with \(n = t / \Delta t\). As shown in Figure 15.3, the peak decreases and the distribution spreads out with time, while the area under the curve, the total probability, stays equal to 1. The width of the distribution grows as \(\sqrt{D t}\), so the time needed to diffuse over a distance \(L\) is \(\sim L^2 / D\).
In three dimensions, and allowing \(D\) to depend on position, the diffusion equation reads \[
\frac{\partial P}{\partial t} = \nabla \cdot (D \nabla P) .
\tag{15.9}\] Note that this has the form of a conservation law, \(\partial_t P + \nabla \cdot \mathbf{F} = 0\), with a flux given by Fick’s law, \(\mathbf{F} = - D \nabla P\) (Equation 6.29). If, instead of a single particle, we consider many particles, then \(P\) is replaced by their density. We will study the solutions of the diffusion equation, also in the presence of a flow, in the in-class worksheet (Section 15.5).
