title: 15  Diffusion and Viscous Flows
text:
15.2 Viscous flows
In Chapter 6 we wrote the momentum equation in terms of the stress tensor \(\mathbf{T}\). In the absence of external forces, it reads \[
\rho \frac{\mathrm{d} \mathbf{v}}{\mathrm{d} t} = \nabla \cdot \mathbf{T} .
\tag{15.10}\] So far we have only considered ideal fluids, for which \(\mathbf{T} = - p \mathbf{I}\). We now write \[
\mathbf{T} = - p \mathbf{I} + \boldsymbol{\tau},
\tag{15.11}\] where \(\boldsymbol{\tau}\) is the viscous stress tensor. Viscous stresses arise when neighboring fluid elements move with different velocities, so \(\boldsymbol{\tau}\) must depend on the derivatives of the velocity, and it must vanish for a uniform flow. The simplest choice is to take \(\boldsymbol{\tau}\) to be linear in \(\nabla \mathbf{v}\). It is convenient to introduce the rate-of-strain (or shear) tensor \[
\mathbf{S} = \frac{1}{2} \left( \nabla \mathbf{v} + \nabla \mathbf{v}^T \right) .
\tag{15.12}\] Note that \(\mathbf{S}\) is symmetric and that it vanishes for a rigid rotation, as it should, because a rigidly rotating fluid has no internal friction. If the fluid is isotropic, the only symmetric tensors that we can build from \(\nabla \mathbf{v}\) to first order are \(\mathbf{S}\) and \((\nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}) \mathbf{I}\). So the most general viscous stress tensor can be written as \[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\boldsymbol{\tau} &= \zeta (\nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}) \mathbf{I} \\
&\quad + \rho \nu \left[ \left( \nabla \mathbf{v} + \nabla \mathbf{v}^T \right) - \frac{2}{3} (\nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}) \mathbf{I} \right],
\end{aligned}}
\tag{15.13}\] where \(\nu\) is the kinematic shear viscosity, \(\rho \nu\) the dynamic shear viscosity, and \(\zeta\) the bulk viscosity. This is the form used in Clarke and Carswell (2007). Note that \(\nu\) has units of \(\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}\), like a diffusion coefficient, while \(\rho \nu\) and \(\zeta\) have units of \(\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-1}} = \mathrm{Pa\,s}\). The term in square brackets has zero trace, so the shear viscosity describes the response of the fluid to a deformation that does not change its volume, while the bulk viscosity describes the response to a compression or expansion. Some books write the coefficient of \((\nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}) \mathbf{I}\), that is \(\zeta - \frac{2}{3} \rho \nu\), as a single coefficient, called the second coefficient of viscosity.
To compute the divergence of \(\boldsymbol{\tau}\), we first compute the divergence of \(\mathbf{S}\). Writing \(\mathbf{S}\) row by row, we have \[
\mathbf{S} = \frac{1}{2}
\begin{pmatrix}
\partial_x \mathbf{v}^T + \nabla v_x^T \\
\partial_y \mathbf{v}^T + \nabla v_y^T \\
\partial_z \mathbf{v}^T + \nabla v_z^T
\end{pmatrix},
\tag{15.14}\] so that \[
\begin{aligned}
\nabla \cdot \mathbf{S} &= \frac{1}{2} \partial_x \left[ \partial_x \mathbf{v} + \nabla v_x \right] \\
&\quad {} + \frac{1}{2} \partial_y \left[ \partial_y \mathbf{v} + \nabla v_y \right] + \ldots \\
&= \frac{1}{2} \left[ \nabla^2 \mathbf{v} + \nabla (\nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}) \right] .
\end{aligned}
\tag{15.15}\] Assuming that \(\rho \nu\) and \(\zeta\) are constant, we then find \[
\nabla \cdot \mathbf{T} = - \nabla \left[ p - \left( \zeta + \frac{1}{3} \rho \nu \right) (\nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}) \right] + \rho \nu \nabla^2 \mathbf{v} .
\tag{15.16}\] The term \(- (\zeta + \frac{1}{3} \rho \nu) (\nabla \cdot \mathbf{v})\) acts like an additional pressure, the bulk viscous pressure. It is positive in a compression, \(\nabla \cdot \mathbf{v} < 0\), and it opposes the compression. The last term in Equation 15.16 is the shear viscosity term. Accordingly, the momentum equation becomes \[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\rho \frac{\mathrm{d} \mathbf{v}}{\mathrm{d} t} &= - \nabla p + \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\tau} \\
&= - \nabla \left[ p - \left( \zeta + \frac{1}{3} \rho \nu \right) (\nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}) \right] \\
&\quad {} + \rho \nu \nabla^2 \mathbf{v} .
\end{aligned}}
\tag{15.17}\] This is the Navier–Stokes equation. For an incompressible flow, \(\nabla \cdot \mathbf{v} = 0\), it reduces to \[
\frac{\partial \mathbf{v}}{\partial t} + (\mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla) \mathbf{v} = - \frac{1}{\rho} \nabla p + \nu \nabla^2 \mathbf{v},
\tag{15.18}\] which is the form we will use in Chapter 17 (Equation 17.1). Note that, if we neglect the advection and the pressure terms, Equation 15.18 becomes \(\partial_t \mathbf{v} = \nu \nabla^2 \mathbf{v}\), which is a diffusion equation for each component of the velocity, with \(D = \nu\). In other words, the shear viscosity describes the diffusion of momentum.






TipExample



Consider a fluid with only shear viscosity, \(\zeta = 0\), and no external forces. The momentum equation is \[
\rho \frac{\mathrm{d} \mathbf{v}}{\mathrm{d} t} = - \nabla p + \rho \nu \left[ \nabla^2 \mathbf{v} + \frac{1}{3} \nabla (\nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}) \right] .
\tag{15.19}\] Consider a situation in which \(p = \mathrm{const}\) and the tangential velocity \(v_y\) changes sharply across the plane \(x = 0\), over a distance \(\ell\). If the velocity is \(\mathbf{v} = v_y (t, x) \hat{\mathbf{y}}\), then \(\nabla \cdot \mathbf{v} = 0\), \((\mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla) \mathbf{v} = 0\), and the \(y\) component of Equation 15.19 becomes \[
\frac{\partial v_y}{\partial t} = \nu \frac{\partial^2 v_y}{\partial x^2} .
\tag{15.20}\] We expect the velocity profile to diffuse, and the front to advance with an effective velocity \[
| v_{\mathrm{eff}} | = \left| \nu \frac{\partial_x v_y}{v_y} \right| \sim \frac{\nu}{\ell} .
\tag{15.21}\] This estimate is actually off, because the shear layer is unstable to the Kelvin–Helmholtz instability (Section 14.3). The flow becomes turbulent (Chapter 17), and the two layers mix on a much shorter timescale.








TipExample



Consider a molecular cloud with number density \(n \sim 10^3\,\mathrm{cm^{-3}} = 10^9\,\mathrm{m^{-3}}\), temperature \(T \sim 10\,\mathrm{K}\), and mean molecular weight \(\mu \approx 2.3\). In a gas, momentum is carried from one fluid element to the next by the particles, which move with the thermal speed \(v_{\mathrm{th}} \sim \sqrt{k_B T / (\mu m_u)}\) over a distance of about one mean free path \(\lambda\) between collisions. So, by analogy with Equation 15.7, we can estimate the kinematic viscosity as \(\nu \sim \lambda v_{\mathrm{th}}\), up to a factor of order unity. Taking \(\sigma \sim 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{m^2}\), as in Chapter 1, we find \[
\lambda = \frac{1}{n \sigma} \sim 10^{10}\,\mathrm{m}, \qquad v_{\mathrm{th}} \approx 190\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}, \qquad \nu \sim 2 \times 10^{12}\,\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}} .
\tag{15.22}\] This is a very large viscosity compared with that of water, \(\nu \approx 10^{-6}\,\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}\), but the cloud is also very large. For a cloud of size \(L \sim 10\,\mathrm{pc} \approx 3.1 \times 10^{17}\,\mathrm{m}\), the time needed for momentum to diffuse across the cloud is \[
t_{\mathrm{visc}} \sim \frac{L^2}{\nu} \sim 5 \times 10^{22}\,\mathrm{s} \approx 2 \times 10^{15}\,\mathrm{yr},
\tag{15.23}\] about \(10^5\) times the age of the Universe. On the other hand, the gas in molecular clouds moves with velocities \(v \sim 2\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}\), so the cloud changes its shape on a timescale \(t_{\mathrm{dyn}} \sim L / v \approx 1.5 \times 10^{14}\,\mathrm{s}\), or about \(5\,\mathrm{Myr}\). In other words, viscosity has no time to act on the scale of the cloud. Note that the ratio \[
\frac{t_{\mathrm{visc}}}{t_{\mathrm{dyn}}} = \frac{L v}{\nu} \sim 3 \times 10^8
\tag{15.24}\] is the Reynolds number of the flow, which we will meet again in Chapter 17 (Equation 17.16). Such large values are typical of astrophysical flows, which are almost always turbulent. Viscosity becomes important only on much smaller scales, where \(L^2 / \nu\) is comparable to \(L / v\).

title: 15  Diffusion and Viscous Flows
text:
15.3 Kinetic energy dissipation
To see how viscosity affects the energy of the flow, we multiply Equation 15.17 by \(\mathbf{v}\). Following the same steps as in Chapter 6 (Equation 6.21), we obtain \[
\begin{aligned}
&\frac{\partial \left( \frac{1}{2} \rho v^2 \right)}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \left[ \left( \frac{1}{2} \rho v^2 + p \right) \mathbf{v} \right] \\
&\qquad = p \nabla \cdot \mathbf{v} + (\nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\tau}) \cdot \mathbf{v} .
\end{aligned}
\tag{15.25}\] The last term is new and describes the viscous dissipation of kinetic energy.
Consider first the incompressible case. Integrating over a volume \(V\), we find \[
\begin{aligned}
\int_V (\nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\tau}) \cdot \mathbf{v} \mathrm{d} V &= \int_V \rho \nu \nabla^2 \mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{v} \mathrm{d} V \\
&= \int_V \rho \nu \nabla \cdot \left[ \nabla \left( \tfrac{1}{2} v^2 \right) \right] \mathrm{d} V \\
&\quad {} - \rho \nu \int_V | \nabla \mathbf{v} |^2 \mathrm{d} V .
\end{aligned}
\tag{15.26}\] The first term on the RHS can be written as a surface integral using the divergence theorem, and it vanishes if, for example, the fluid is at rest on the boundary of \(V\). So the shear viscosity always decreases the kinetic energy of the flow, and it does so at a rate proportional to \(\int_V | \nabla \mathbf{v} |^2 \mathrm{d} V\). For an incompressible flow, and if the boundary terms vanish, this integral is equal to \(\int_V | \boldsymbol{\omega} |^2 \mathrm{d} V\), where \(\boldsymbol{\omega} = \nabla \times \mathbf{v}\) is the vorticity (Equation 13.2). This is the enstrophy of the flow. We will use this result in Chapter 17 (Equation 17.11).
If instead the flow is compressible and \(\nu = 0\), we find \[
\begin{aligned}
\int_V (\nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\tau}) \cdot \mathbf{v} \mathrm{d} V &= \zeta \int_V \nabla (\nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}) \cdot \mathbf{v} \mathrm{d} V \\
&= \zeta \int_V \nabla \cdot \left[ (\nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}) \mathbf{v} \right] \mathrm{d} V \\
&\quad {} - \zeta \int_V (\nabla \cdot \mathbf{v})^2 \mathrm{d} V .
\end{aligned}
\tag{15.27}\] Once again, the first term on the RHS is a surface term that vanishes for suitable boundary conditions. So the bulk viscosity dissipates kinetic energy whenever the fluid is compressed or expanded. As we will see next, the kinetic energy lost to viscous dissipation is not destroyed, but it is converted into internal energy.

title: 15  Diffusion and Viscous Flows
text:
15.4 The Navier–Stokes equations
To complete the description of a viscous fluid, we need an equation for the total energy. The rate of change of the energy in a fixed region \(\Omega\) is given by the work done by external forces in \(\Omega\), plus the work done by the stresses on the boundary \(\partial \Omega\), minus the energy carried out of \(\Omega\) by the flow and by the heat flux \(\mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{heat}}\): \[
\begin{aligned}
&\frac{\partial}{\partial t} \int_{\Omega} \rho \left( \varepsilon + \tfrac{1}{2} v^2 \right) \mathrm{d} V \\
&\quad = \int_{\Omega} \mathbf{f} \cdot \mathbf{v} \mathrm{d} V + \int_{\partial \Omega} \mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{T} \cdot \mathbf{n} \mathrm{d} A \\
&\qquad {} - \int_{\partial \Omega} \left[ \rho \left( \varepsilon + \tfrac{1}{2} v^2 \right) \mathbf{v} + \mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{heat}} \right] \cdot \mathbf{n} \mathrm{d} A .
\end{aligned}
\tag{15.28}\] Here \(\mathbf{T} \cdot \mathbf{n} \mathrm{d} A\) is the force exerted on the surface element \(\mathrm{d} A\) by the fluid outside of \(\Omega\) (for an ideal fluid it is \(- p \mathbf{n} \mathrm{d} A\)), so \(\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{T} \cdot \mathbf{n} \mathrm{d} A\) is the work done per unit time by this force. Using the divergence theorem, we can rewrite this as \[
\begin{aligned}
&\int_{\Omega} \biggl\{ \frac{\partial \left[ \rho \left( \varepsilon + \frac{1}{2} v^2 \right) \right]}{\partial t} \\
&\quad {} + \nabla \cdot \biggl[ \left( \rho \varepsilon + \tfrac{1}{2} \rho v^2 \right) \mathbf{v} \\
&\qquad\quad {} - \mathbf{T} \cdot \mathbf{v} + \mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{heat}} \biggr] \biggr\} \mathrm{d} V \\
&\quad = \int_{\Omega} \mathbf{f} \cdot \mathbf{v} \mathrm{d} V,
\end{aligned}
\tag{15.29}\] where we have used the fact that \(\mathbf{T}\) is symmetric. Since this must hold for any region \(\Omega\), and using \(\mathbf{T} = - p \mathbf{I} + \boldsymbol{\tau}\), we obtain \[
\begin{aligned}
&\frac{\partial \left[ \rho \left( \varepsilon + \frac{1}{2} v^2 \right) \right]}{\partial t} \\
&\quad {} + \nabla \cdot \left[ \left( \rho \varepsilon + \tfrac{1}{2} \rho v^2 + p \right) \mathbf{v} - \boldsymbol{\tau} \cdot \mathbf{v} + \mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{heat}} \right] \\
&\quad = \mathbf{f} \cdot \mathbf{v} .
\end{aligned}
\tag{15.30}\] Compared with Equation 6.22, the energy flux has two new terms. The first, \(- \boldsymbol{\tau} \cdot \mathbf{v}\), describes the work done by the viscous stresses, while the second is the heat flux \(\mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{heat}}\).
The equations for a viscous, heat-conducting fluid are called the Navier–Stokes equations. Adding a heating rate per unit mass \(\dot{q}\), they read \[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
&\frac{\partial \rho}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot (\rho \mathbf{v}) = 0, \\
&\frac{\partial (\rho \mathbf{v})}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot [\rho \mathbf{v} \otimes \mathbf{v} - \mathbf{T}] = \mathbf{f}, \\
&\frac{\partial \left[ \rho \left( \varepsilon + \frac{1}{2} v^2 \right) \right]}{\partial t} \\
&\quad {} + \nabla \cdot \biggl[ \left( \rho \varepsilon + \tfrac{1}{2} \rho v^2 + p \right) \mathbf{v} \\
&\qquad\quad {} - \boldsymbol{\tau} \cdot \mathbf{v} + \mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{heat}} \biggr] \\
&\quad = \rho \dot{q} + \mathbf{f} \cdot \mathbf{v},
\end{aligned}}
\tag{15.31}\] with \(\mathbf{T} = - p \mathbf{I} + \boldsymbol{\tau}\) and \(\boldsymbol{\tau}\) given by Equation 15.13. In non-conservation form, the momentum equation is Equation 15.17 with the external force \(\mathbf{f}\) added to the RHS. Subtracting Equation 15.25, with \(\mathbf{f} \cdot \mathbf{v}\) added to its RHS, from the energy equation, and using \(\nabla \cdot (\boldsymbol{\tau} \cdot \mathbf{v}) = (\nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\tau}) \cdot \mathbf{v} + \boldsymbol{\tau} : \nabla \mathbf{v}\), we find the equation for the internal energy: \[
\rho \frac{\mathrm{d} \varepsilon}{\mathrm{d} t} = \rho \dot{q} - p \nabla \cdot \mathbf{v} + \boldsymbol{\tau} : \nabla \mathbf{v} - \nabla \cdot \mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{heat}} .
\tag{15.32}\] The term \(\boldsymbol{\tau} : \nabla \mathbf{v}\) is the viscous heating. Using Equation 15.13, it can be written as \[
\boldsymbol{\tau} : \nabla \mathbf{v} = 2 \rho \nu \left| \mathbf{S} - \frac{1}{3} (\nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}) \mathbf{I} \right|^2 + \zeta (\nabla \cdot \mathbf{v})^2 \geq 0,
\tag{15.33}\] where \(| \mathbf{A} |^2 = \mathbf{A} : \mathbf{A}\) is the sum of the squares of the components of \(\mathbf{A}\). So viscosity always heats the fluid. This is the energy that the shear and bulk viscosity remove from the kinetic energy of the flow (Equation 15.26 and Equation 15.27).

title: 15  Diffusion and Viscous Flows
text:
15.5 In-class worksheet

Core-collapse supernovae inject metals, such as oxygen, into the interstellar medium (ISM). After the supernova remnant has stalled its expansion, the diffusion of these elements throughout the galaxy can be modeled through an advection-diffusion equation: \[
\frac{\partial \rho}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot (\rho \mathbf{v}) = \nabla
\cdot (D \nabla \rho),
\tag{15.34}\] where \(\rho\) is the mass density of the newly synthesized elements, \(\mathbf{v}\) is the local velocity of the ISM, and \(D\) is a diffusion coefficient.

Show that, under suitable assumptions, \[
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} t} \int_V \rho \mathrm{d}^3 \mathbf{r}= 0.
\tag{15.35}\]
Assume that \(\mathbf{v}= \mathrm{const}\), \(D = \mathrm{const} > 0\), and look for solutions in the form \[
\rho (t, \mathbf{x}) = \rho_0 \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i} (\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{x}-
\omega t)} .
\tag{15.36}\] Sketch the solution for different times and give a physical interpretation of the results.
How do the results change if \(D < 0\)?
Show that Equation 15.34 can be written as \[
\frac{\partial \rho}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \left[ \rho \left(
\mathbf{v}- D \frac{\nabla \rho}{\rho} \right)  \right] = 0.
\tag{15.37}\] Interpret the term in round brackets as an effective propagation velocity \(\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{eff}}\). How does \(\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{eff}}\) depend on the wave number \(\mathbf{k}\) if \(\rho\) is as in Equation 15.36?

title: 15  Diffusion and Viscous Flows
text:
15.6 Exercises

Exercise 15.1 (Steady viscous vortex) Consider a steady-state, axisymmetric solution of the incompressible, viscous, Navier–Stokes equations in cylindrical coordinates \((R, \phi, z)\) in the form \[
v_R = - \alpha R, \qquad v_{\phi} = \frac{\mathcal{C}}{2 \pi R} g (R), \qquad
v_z = 2 \alpha z,
\tag{15.38}\] where \(\alpha > 0\) and \(\mathcal{C} > 0\) are given constants, while \(g (R)\) is a function satisfying \[
\lim_{R \rightarrow 0} g (R) = 0, \qquad \lim_{R \rightarrow \infty} g (R)
= 1.
\tag{15.39}\] Let \(\nu > 0\) be the kinematic viscosity.

Show that the flow is incompressible.
Derive an equation for \(g (R)\) assuming the flow to be steady state.
Compute the vorticity \(\boldsymbol{\omega}\) of the flow.



Exercise 15.2 (Sound waves and bulk viscosity) Consider a fluid with bulk viscosity \(\zeta\), but no shear viscosity (\(\nu = 0\)). In one dimension, the continuity and momentum equations are \[
\partial_t \rho + \partial_x (\rho v) = 0, \qquad \rho (\partial_t v + v \partial_x v) = - \partial_x p + \zeta \partial_x^2 v .
\tag{15.40}\] The background is homogeneous, with \(\rho = \rho_0\), \(v = 0\), and \(p = p_0\). Consider small adiabatic perturbations of the form \(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i} (k x - \omega t)}\).

Derive the dispersion relation \(\omega (k)\). How is it modified compared with the case \(\zeta = 0\) (Chapter 9)?
Show that, if \(\zeta\) is small, sound waves are damped, and find the damping rate. Which waves are damped faster, short or long ones?
What happens to perturbations with \(k > 2 \rho_0 c_s / \zeta\)?

title: 16  Accretion Disks
text:
16.1 Vertically integrated equations
Accretion disks are found in a wide range of astrophysical systems. Young stars are surrounded by protoplanetary disks, which are the sites of planet formation. For example, the ALMA image of the disk around the young star HL Tau shows a series of bright rings separated by dark gaps, which might have been carved by forming planets (ALMA Partnership et al. 2015). Accretion disks around white dwarfs, neutron stars, and stellar-mass black holes power cataclysmic variables and X-ray binaries. On much larger scales, accretion onto supermassive black holes powers active galactic nuclei (AGN). The Event Horizon Telescope image of the black hole at the center of the galaxy M87 shows the emission from the innermost region of one such accretion flow (Figure 16.1). Note that the gas around this black hole is very hot and dilute, so this flow is not well described by the thin disks that we will discuss in this chapter.
Disks are so common because gas falling towards a central object almost always has some angular momentum. The gas can lose energy, for example through shocks and radiation, much more easily than it can lose angular momentum. Since, for a given angular momentum, the orbit with the lowest energy is a circular orbit, the gas settles on circular orbits in the plane perpendicular to its angular momentum. In other words, the gas forms a ring at the circularization radius \(R_c\), where the specific angular momentum of a circular orbit, \(\sqrt{G M R_c}\), is equal to that of the gas. However, gas on circular orbits cannot fall onto the central object. In order to be accreted, the gas needs to get rid of its angular momentum. In this chapter, we will see that viscosity can do this, by transporting angular momentum outwards and mass inwards. We will then compute the luminosity and the spectrum of a disk in a steady state.
We use cylindrical coordinates \((R, \phi, z)\) and we take the disk to lie in the plane \(z = 0\). In the in-class worksheet (Section 16.7), we will show that the continuity equation in cylindrical coordinates reads \[
\frac{\partial \rho}{\partial t} + \frac{1}{R} \left[ \frac{\partial (\rho R v_R)}{\partial R} + \frac{\partial (\rho v_{\phi})}{\partial \phi} \right] + \frac{\partial (\rho v_z)}{\partial z} = 0 .
\tag{16.1}\] We assume that the disk is axisymmetric, \(\partial_{\phi} = 0\), and thin, so that we can neglect \(v_z\). We also assume that the gas rotates with angular velocity \(\Omega\), that is \(v_{\phi} = R \Omega\). It is convenient to introduce the surface density \[
\Sigma = \int_{- \infty}^{\infty} \rho \mathrm{d} z ,
\tag{16.2}\] which is the mass per unit area of the disk. If we integrate Equation 16.1 in the vertical direction, we obtain \[
\frac{\partial \Sigma}{\partial t} + \frac{1}{R} \frac{\partial (R \Sigma v_R)}{\partial R} = 0 .
\tag{16.3}\]
To find an equation for \(v_R\), we use the conservation of angular momentum (Chapter 6). The \(z\)-component of the angular momentum density is \(\rho R v_{\phi} = \rho R^2 \Omega\). The pressure does not exert any torque on the gas, since \(\partial_{\phi} p = 0\), and neither does the gravity of the central object. However, the viscous stresses do. The only component of the viscous stress tensor (Equation 15.13) that can exert a torque on the gas is \[
\tau_{R \phi} = \rho \nu R \frac{\partial \Omega}{\partial R} .
\tag{16.4}\] Note that \(\tau_{R \phi}\) depends only on the shear, \(R \, \partial_R \Omega\), so it vanishes for a rigid rotation, as it should. The flux of angular momentum in the radial direction is then \(\rho R v_{\phi} v_R - R \tau_{R \phi}\), where the second term is the torque per unit area exerted by the viscous stresses. Accordingly, the conservation of angular momentum reads \[
\begin{aligned}
&\frac{\partial (\rho R^2 \Omega)}{\partial t} + \frac{1}{R} \frac{\partial}{\partial R} \left( \rho R^3 \Omega v_R - \rho \nu R^3 \frac{\partial \Omega}{\partial R} \right) \\
&\qquad + \frac{\partial (\ldots)}{\partial z} = 0 .
\end{aligned}
\tag{16.5}\] When we integrate in the vertical direction, the last term vanishes and we find \[
\frac{\partial (\Sigma R^2 \Omega)}{\partial t} + \frac{1}{R} \frac{\partial (\Sigma R^3 \Omega v_R)}{\partial R} = \frac{1}{R} \frac{\partial}{\partial R} \left( \nu \Sigma R^3 \frac{\partial \Omega}{\partial R} \right) ,
\tag{16.6}\] where \(\nu\) now denotes the density-weighted average of the viscosity, \(\nu \Sigma = \int \rho \nu \mathrm{d} z\).
We still need an equation for \(\Omega\), which is given by the radial component of the momentum equation. The radial pressure gradient term is of order \(p / (\rho R) \sim c_s^2 / R\). As we will see below, this is smaller than the gravitational acceleration, \(G M / R^2 = \Omega^2 R\), by a factor \((H / R)^2\), where \(H\) is the thickness of the disk. So, for a thin disk, the gas moves on nearly circular Keplerian orbits. The angular velocity and the specific angular momentum \(j\) of a Keplerian disk are \[
\Omega = \left( \frac{G M}{R^3} \right)^{1 / 2}, \qquad j = R^2 \Omega = \sqrt{G M R} .
\tag{16.7}\] Since \(\partial_R \Omega = - \frac{3}{2} \Omega / R\), we have \(\nu \Sigma R^3 \partial_R \Omega = - \frac{3}{2} \nu \Sigma j\), and Equation 16.6 can be written as \[
\frac{\partial (\Sigma j)}{\partial t} + \frac{1}{R} \frac{\partial}{\partial R} \left[ R \Sigma j \left( v_R + \frac{3}{2} \frac{\nu}{R} \right) \right] = 0 .
\tag{16.8}\] This is a conservation law for the angular momentum per unit area \(\Sigma j\). The first contribution to the flux, \(\Sigma j v_R\), is the angular momentum carried by the gas as it moves in the radial direction. The second contribution, \(\frac{3}{2} \nu \Sigma j / R\), is due to viscosity, and it is always positive. In other words, viscosity transports angular momentum outwards. This makes sense, because \(\Omega\) decreases with \(R\), so each ring of gas rotates faster than the ring just outside of it. The friction between the two rings slows down the inner ring and speeds up the outer one. Since \(j\) increases with \(R\), the inner ring, having lost angular momentum, has to move inwards.

title: 16  Accretion Disks
text:
16.2 Viscous evolution
We now eliminate \(v_R\) to obtain an equation for \(\Sigma\) alone. Using Equation 16.3, we can rewrite the LHS of Equation 16.6 as \[
\begin{aligned}
&\frac{\partial (\Sigma R^2 \Omega)}{\partial t} + \frac{1}{R} \frac{\partial}{\partial R} \left( R \Sigma v_R \cdot R^2 \Omega \right) \\
&\qquad = R^2 \Omega \left[ \frac{\partial \Sigma}{\partial t} + \frac{1}{R} \frac{\partial (R \Sigma v_R)}{\partial R} \right] \\
&\qquad\qquad {} + \Sigma v_R \frac{\partial (R^2 \Omega)}{\partial R} \\
&\qquad = \Sigma v_R \frac{\partial (R^2 \Omega)}{\partial R} ,
\end{aligned}
\tag{16.9}\] where we have used the fact that \(\Omega\) depends only on \(R\). Combining this with Equation 16.6 yields \[
R \Sigma v_R = \left[ \frac{\partial (R^2 \Omega)}{\partial R} \right]^{- 1} \frac{\partial}{\partial R} \left( \nu \Sigma R^3 \frac{\partial \Omega}{\partial R} \right) .
\tag{16.10}\] For a Keplerian disk, \(\partial_R (R^2 \Omega) = \frac{1}{2} R \Omega = \frac{1}{2} \sqrt{G M} R^{- 1 / 2}\) and \(\nu \Sigma R^3 \partial_R \Omega = - \frac{3}{2} \sqrt{G M} \nu \Sigma R^{1 / 2}\), so \[
R \Sigma v_R = - 3 R^{1 / 2} \frac{\partial}{\partial R} \left( \nu \Sigma R^{1 / 2} \right) .
\tag{16.11}\] Plugging this into the continuity equation, Equation 16.3, gives \[
\boxed{\frac{\partial \Sigma}{\partial t} = \frac{3}{R} \frac{\partial}{\partial R} \left[ R^{1 / 2} \frac{\partial}{\partial R} \left( \nu \Sigma R^{1 / 2} \right) \right] .}
\tag{16.12}\] This is a diffusion-like equation for \(\Sigma\), similar to those we have discussed in Chapter 15. Note that the equation is nonlinear if \(\nu\) depends on \(\Sigma\). We will study some of its properties in Exercise 16.2 and Exercise 16.3, and in the in-class worksheet.
To see how this works, we consider a ring of mass \(m\) that is initially located at \(R = R_0\), and we take \(\nu\) to be constant. In this case, Equation 16.12 can be solved exactly (Lynden-Bell and Pringle 1974). The solution is shown in Figure 16.2 as a function of \(x = R / R_0\) and of the dimensionless time \(\tau = 12 \nu t / R_0^2\). The ring spreads both inwards and outwards. As time goes on, most of the mass moves inwards and is accreted by the central object, while a small fraction of the mass moves to large radii, carrying with it almost all of the angular momentum. In other words, the disk can accrete mass while conserving its angular momentum, as long as some of the gas moves outwards.






Figure 16.2: Viscous spreading of a ring of mass \(m\) initially located at \(R = R_0\), for a constant viscosity \(\nu\), at different times \(\tau = 12 \nu t / R_0^2\). Computed from the solution of Lynden-Bell and Pringle (1974).




16.2.1 Accretion timescale
Equation 16.11 tells us that the radial velocity is of order \(v_R \sim \nu / R\). This is also what we would expect from dimensional analysis, since \(\nu\) has units of \(\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}\). So the typical timescale for accretion is \[
t_* \sim \frac{R}{v_R} \sim \frac{R^2}{\nu} = \frac{R}{v_{\phi}} \frac{v_{\phi} R}{\nu} = \frac{\mathrm{Re}}{\Omega} ,
\tag{16.13}\] where \(\mathrm{Re} = v_{\phi} R / \nu\) is the Reynolds number of the disk. The Reynolds numbers of astrophysical disks are very large, so \(t_* \gg \Omega^{- 1}\). In other words, the gas completes many orbits before being accreted.






TipExample



Consider the solar nebula, which is the protoplanetary disk from which the planets of the Solar System formed. At \(1\,\mathrm{AU}\), we take \(T \approx 300\,\mathrm{K}\) and \(\rho \approx 10^{-9}\,\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}} = 10^{-6}\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}\), for molecular gas with \(\mu = 2.3\). The isothermal sound speed is \(c_{\mathrm{iso}} \approx 1\,\mathrm{km/s}\) and the number density is \(n = \rho / (\mu m_u) \approx 3 \times 10^{20}\,\mathrm{m^{-3}}\). The cross section for collisions between hydrogen molecules is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{H_2}} \approx 2 \times 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{m^2}\), so the mean free path is \(\lambda = 1 / (n \sigma_{\mathrm{H_2}}) \approx 2\,\mathrm{cm}\) and the molecular viscosity is \(\nu \sim \lambda c_{\mathrm{iso}} \approx 20\,\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}\). The orbital velocity is \(v_{\phi} \approx 30\,\mathrm{km/s}\), so \[
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{Re} = \frac{v_{\phi} R}{\nu} &\approx \frac{(3 \times 10^4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}) (1.5 \times 10^{11}\,\mathrm{m})}{20\,\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}} \\
&\approx 2 \times 10^{14} .
\end{aligned}
\tag{16.14}\] With \(\Omega = 2 \pi / \mathrm{yr}\), the accretion timescale is \(t_* \sim \mathrm{Re} / \Omega \sim 3 \times 10^{13}\,\mathrm{yr}\). This is much longer than the age of the Universe. On the other hand, protoplanetary disks are observed to disappear in a few million years.


The previous Example shows that the molecular viscosity is too small to explain the accretion of gas in disks. Instead, the viscosity to use is an effective viscosity \(\nu_T \gg \nu\) due to turbulence (Chapter 17). What is the source of this turbulence? We will see in Chapter 23 that a weak magnetic field makes the disk unstable, and that the resulting turbulence can transport angular momentum. For the moment, we estimate \(\nu_T\) on dimensional grounds. The disk is in hydrostatic equilibrium in the vertical direction, with a scale height \[
H = \frac{c_s}{\Omega} ,
\tag{16.15}\] where \(c_s\) is the sound speed, which is equal to \(c_{\mathrm{iso}}\) for an isothermal disk (Exercise 16.1). The largest turbulent eddies cannot be larger than \(H\), and their velocity cannot be much larger than \(c_s\), otherwise they would produce shocks and be dissipated. So we write \[
\nu_T = \alpha c_s H = \alpha \Omega H^2 , \qquad \alpha \lesssim 1 .
\tag{16.16}\] This is the so-called α-viscosity model of Shakura and Sunyaev (1973). Observations and simulations suggest \(\alpha \sim 0.01\)–\(0.1\). For the solar nebula at \(1\,\mathrm{AU}\), we have \(H / R = c_s / v_{\phi} \approx 0.035\), and \(\alpha = 0.01\) gives \(t_* \sim R^2 / \nu_T = \alpha^{- 1} (R / H)^2 \Omega^{- 1} \sim 10^4\,\mathrm{yr}\). Note also that the radial pressure gradient term is of order \(c_s^2 / R = \Omega^2 H^2 / R\), which is smaller than the gravitational acceleration \(\Omega^2 R\) by the factor \((H / R)^2\) that we anticipated in Section 16.1.

title: 16  Accretion Disks
text:
16.3 Steady disks
We now look for steady-state solutions, that is solutions with \(\partial_t = 0\). These describe a disk that is fed at a constant rate at large radii, for example by a companion star in a binary system. From the continuity equation, Equation 16.3, it follows that \(R \Sigma v_R\) is constant, so we can write \[
2 \pi R \Sigma v_R = - \dot{M} ,
\tag{16.17}\] where \(\dot{M} > 0\) is the accretion rate. Similarly, Equation 16.6 tells us that the total flux of angular momentum through a ring of radius \(R\) is constant, \[
2 \pi \left( \Sigma R^3 \Omega v_R - \nu \Sigma R^3 \frac{\partial \Omega}{\partial R} \right) = - \dot{J} ,
\tag{16.18}\] where \(\dot{J}\) is the rate at which angular momentum is carried onto the central object. We use Equation 16.17 to eliminate \(v_R\) and we find \[
\dot{M} R^2 \Omega + 2 \pi \nu \Sigma R^3 \frac{\partial \Omega}{\partial R} = \dot{J} .
\tag{16.19}\]
To find \(\dot{J}\), we need a boundary condition at the surface of the central star, \(R_*\). If the star rotates more slowly than the Keplerian velocity at its surface, then \(\Omega\) has to decrease from the Keplerian value in the disk to the angular velocity of the star in a thin boundary layer. So \(\Omega\) has a maximum very close to \(R_*\), where \(\partial_R \Omega = 0\). At this point the viscous torque vanishes, and angular momentum is carried onto the star only by the accreted gas, so \[
\dot{J} = \dot{M} j_* = \dot{M} \sqrt{G M R_*} ,
\tag{16.20}\] where \(j_*\) is the specific angular momentum of a Keplerian orbit at the surface of the star. For a black hole, which does not have a surface, a similar argument applies at the innermost stable circular orbit, inside of which the gas plunges into the black hole. Since \(\partial_R \Omega = - \frac{3}{2} \sqrt{G M} R^{- 5 / 2}\), Equation 16.19 becomes \[
\dot{M} R^{1 / 2} - 3 \pi \nu \Sigma R^{1 / 2} = \dot{M} R_*^{1 / 2} ,
\tag{16.21}\] that is \[
\boxed{\nu \Sigma = \frac{\dot{M}}{3 \pi} \left[ 1 - \left( \frac{R_*}{R} \right)^{1 / 2} \right] .}
\tag{16.22}\] As shown in Figure 16.3, \(\nu \Sigma\) vanishes at \(R_*\) and approaches the constant value \(\dot{M} / (3 \pi)\) for \(R \gg R_*\). It is important to note that the structure of the disk depends on the viscosity only through the combination \(\nu \Sigma\), which is fixed by \(\dot{M}\). A larger viscosity simply gives a smaller surface density. As we will see next, this implies that the luminosity and the spectrum of a steady disk do not depend on the viscosity, which is poorly known.

title: 16  Accretion Disks
text:
16.4 Disk luminosity
Viscosity converts the kinetic energy of the shear flow into heat (Section 15.3). For \(\mathbf{v} = R \Omega (R) \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}\), the flow is incompressible and the only non-zero components of the rate-of-strain tensor are \(S_{R \phi} = S_{\phi R} = \frac{1}{2} R \, \partial_R \Omega\). So the viscous heating (Equation 15.33) is \(\boldsymbol{\tau} : \nabla \mathbf{v} = \rho \nu R^2 (\partial_R \Omega)^2\). If we integrate in the vertical direction, we find that the energy dissipated per unit time and per unit area of the disk is \[
\begin{aligned}
D (R) &= \int_{- \infty}^{\infty} \rho \nu R^2 \left( \frac{\partial \Omega}{\partial R} \right)^2 \mathrm{d} z \\
&= \nu \Sigma R^2 \left( \frac{\partial \Omega}{\partial R} \right)^2 = \frac{9}{4} \nu \Sigma \Omega^2 .
\end{aligned}
\tag{16.23}\] Using Equation 16.22, we obtain \[
D (R) = \frac{3 G M \dot{M}}{4 \pi R^3} \left[ 1 - \left( \frac{R_*}{R} \right)^{1 / 2} \right] .
\tag{16.24}\] The total energy dissipated in the disk per unit time is \[
\begin{aligned}
L &= 2 \pi \int_{R_*}^{\infty} D (R) R \mathrm{d} R \\
&= \frac{3}{2} G M \dot{M} \left[ - \frac{1}{R} + \frac{2}{3} \frac{R_*^{1 / 2}}{R^{3 / 2}} \right]_{R_*}^{\infty} \\
&= \frac{G M \dot{M}}{2 R_*} .
\end{aligned}
\tag{16.25}\] If the disk is optically thick, all of this energy is radiated away, so \(L\) is the luminosity of the disk. Note that this is only half of the gravitational energy released per unit time by gas falling from infinity to \(R_*\), which is \(G M \dot{M} / R_*\). This should not be surprising, because the gas reaches \(R_*\) on a Keplerian orbit, so it still has a kinetic energy per unit mass \(\frac{1}{2} G M / R_*\). If the star rotates slowly, this kinetic energy is dissipated in the boundary layer, which can then be as luminous as the whole disk.
It is instructive to compare Equation 16.24 with the gravitational energy released locally. Gas moving from \(R + \mathrm{d} R\) to \(R\) on Keplerian orbits releases a binding energy \(\dot{M} \, \mathrm{d} (G M / 2 R) = G M \dot{M} \mathrm{d} R / (2 R^2)\) per unit time. Dividing by the area of the ring, \(2 \pi R \mathrm{d} R\), we find \(G M \dot{M} / (4 \pi R^3)\). So, for \(R \gg R_*\), the energy dissipated is three times larger than the energy released locally. The difference is carried outwards from the inner regions of the disk by the viscous torque. On the other hand, for \(R < \frac{9}{4} R_*\), the energy dissipated is smaller than the energy released locally.

title: 16  Accretion Disks
text:
16.5 Emergent spectrum
If the disk is optically thick, each ring radiates approximately as a blackbody with an effective temperature \(T_{\mathrm{eff}} (R)\). The disk has two faces, each radiating a flux \(\sigma T_{\mathrm{eff}}^4\), so \[
2 \sigma T_{\mathrm{eff}}^4 (R) = D (R) = \frac{3 G M \dot{M}}{4 \pi R^3} \left[ 1 - \left( \frac{R_*}{R} \right)^{1 / 2} \right] .
\tag{16.26}\] It is convenient to write this as \[
\begin{aligned}
T_{\mathrm{eff}} (R) &= T_* \left( \frac{R_*}{R} \right)^{3 / 4} \left[ 1 - \left( \frac{R_*}{R} \right)^{1 / 2} \right]^{1 / 4}, \\
T_* &= \left( \frac{3 G M \dot{M}}{8 \pi \sigma R_*^3} \right)^{1 / 4} .
\end{aligned}
\tag{16.27}\] The effective temperature is shown in Figure 16.3. It has a maximum \(T_{\mathrm{max}} \approx 0.49\, T_*\) at \(R = (49/36) R_*\), and for \(R \gg R_*\) it decreases as \(T_{\mathrm{eff}} \approx T_* (R_* / R)^{3 / 4}\).






Figure 16.3: Structure of a steady disk around a star of radius \(R_*\). The solid line shows the combination \(\nu \Sigma\) (Equation 16.22), the dashed line the effective temperature (Equation 16.27).









TipExample



Consider a black hole with \(M = 10\,M_{\odot}\) accreting from a companion star at a rate \(\dot{M} = 10^{-8}\,M_{\odot}/\mathrm{yr} \approx 6 \times 10^{14}\,\mathrm{kg\,s^{-1}}\). For \(R_*\) we take the radius of the innermost stable circular orbit, \(R_* = 6 G M / c^2 \approx 90\,\mathrm{km}\). Equation 16.25 gives \(L \approx 5 \times 10^{30}\,\mathrm{W}\), which is more than \(10^4\,L_{\odot}\), and Equation 16.27 gives \(T_* \approx 7 \times 10^6\,\mathrm{K}\). The innermost regions of the disk have \(k_B T_{\mathrm{max}} \approx 0.3\,\mathrm{keV}\), so they emit X-rays. If we repeat the calculation for a white dwarf with \(M = 1\,M_{\odot}\), \(R_* = 5600\,\mathrm{km}\), and \(\dot{M} = 10^{-9}\,M_{\odot}/\mathrm{yr}\), we find \(T_* \approx 10^5\,\mathrm{K}\), so disks around white dwarfs emit mostly in the UV. Indeed, the X-ray spectra of black-hole binaries in their so-called “soft” state are well described by the sum of blackbodies that we will compute next, after a correction for the scattering of photons by electrons in the atmosphere of the disk, which makes the spectrum look hotter than \(T_{\mathrm{eff}}\) (Davis et al. 2006).


Consider an observer at a distance \(d\) who sees the disk inclined by an angle \(i\), where \(i = 0\) corresponds to a disk seen face on. A ring of area \(2 \pi R \mathrm{d} R\) subtends a solid angle \(2 \pi R \mathrm{d} R \cos i / d^2\), so the flux received at the frequency \(\nu\) is \[
\begin{aligned}
F_{\nu} &= \frac{2 \pi \cos i}{d^2} \int_{R_*}^{R_{\mathrm{out}}} B_{\nu} \big( T_{\mathrm{eff}} (R) \big) R \mathrm{d} R, \\
B_{\nu} (T) &= \frac{2 h \nu^3}{c^2} \frac{1}{\mathrm{e}^{h \nu / k_B T} - 1} ,
\end{aligned}
\tag{16.28}\] where \(R_{\mathrm{out}}\) is the outer radius of the disk and \(B_{\nu}\) is the Planck function. Note that here \(\nu\) denotes the frequency and not the viscosity. The resulting spectrum, shown in Figure 16.4, is called a multi-color blackbody spectrum. To understand its shape, we consider three limits, and we define \(T_{\mathrm{out}} = T_{\mathrm{eff}} (R_{\mathrm{out}})\).

For \(h \nu \gg k_B T_{\mathrm{max}}\), all rings emit in the Wien part of their spectrum, and the emission is dominated by the hottest ones, so \(F_{\nu} \sim \exp (- h \nu / k_B T_{\mathrm{max}})\), up to a power of \(\nu\).
For \(h \nu \ll k_B T_{\mathrm{out}}\), all rings emit in the Rayleigh–Jeans part of their spectrum, where \(B_{\nu} \approx 2 \nu^2 k_B T / c^2\), so \(F_{\nu} \propto \nu^2\). This is the Rayleigh–Jeans tail.
For \(k_B T_{\mathrm{out}} \ll h \nu \ll k_B T_*\), the emission comes mostly from rings with \(R \gg R_*\), where \(T_{\mathrm{eff}} \approx T_* (R_* / R)^{3 / 4}\). So \[
F_{\nu} \propto \int_{R_*}^{R_{\mathrm{out}}} \frac{\nu^3 R \mathrm{d} R}{\exp \left( \frac{h \nu R^{3 / 4}}{k_B T_* R_*^{3 / 4}} \right) - 1} .
\tag{16.29}\] We introduce the new variable \[
\begin{aligned}
x &= \frac{h \nu}{k_B T_*} \left( \frac{R}{R_*} \right)^{3 / 4}, \\
R &= \left( \frac{k_B T_* x}{h \nu} \right)^{4 / 3} R_*, \\
\mathrm{d} R &= \frac{4}{3} \left( \frac{k_B T_*}{h \nu} \right)^{4 / 3} R_* x^{1 / 3} \mathrm{d} x ,
\end{aligned}
\tag{16.30}\] to find \[
F_{\nu} \propto \nu^{1 / 3} \int_{x_{\mathrm{in}}}^{x_{\mathrm{out}}} \frac{x^{5 / 3}}{\mathrm{e}^x - 1} \mathrm{d} x ,
\tag{16.31}\] with \(x_{\mathrm{in}} = h \nu / k_B T_* \ll 1\) and \(x_{\mathrm{out}} \approx h \nu / k_B T_{\mathrm{out}} \gg 1\). Since the integrand is small for both \(x \ll 1\) and \(x \gg 1\), we can extend the integral from \(0\) to \(\infty\). The integral then does not depend on \(\nu\), so \(F_{\nu} \propto \nu^{1 / 3}\). This part of the spectrum is a distinctive feature of accretion disks, which is not present in the spectrum of a single blackbody.







Figure 16.4: Spectrum of a steady accretion disk with \(R_{\mathrm{out}} = 10^4 R_*\), computed from Equation 16.28. The dashed and dash-dotted lines show the \(\nu^2\) and \(\nu^{1/3}\) power laws. Compare with the sketch in Pringle (1981).

title: 16  Accretion Disks
text:
16.6 Limitations of the model
The model that we have discussed explains many of the observed properties of accretion disks. However, it also has some important problems.

Under some conditions, the disk models that we have discussed are unstable. For example, this happens in the inner regions of very luminous disks, where radiation pressure dominates, and in the regions where hydrogen is partially ionized. If the heating rate grows with temperature faster than the cooling rate, then a small increase in the temperature leads to runaway heating. This is called thermal instability. In disks around white dwarfs, it is thought to cause the outbursts of dwarf novae. Similarly, under some conditions, a small overdensity in the disk keeps growing, and the disk breaks up into rings. This is called viscous instability. We will find the condition for viscous instability in the in-class worksheet.
We have not explained the origin of the viscosity. As we have seen, the molecular viscosity is much too small, and the α-viscosity model does not tell us where the turbulence comes from. We will come back to this point when we discuss turbulence (Chapter 17) and the magnetorotational instability (Chapter 23). Modern studies of accretion disks rely on magnetohydrodynamic simulations, in which angular momentum is transported by the turbulence driven by the magnetorotational instability.

title: 16  Accretion Disks
text:
16.7 In-class worksheet

Cylindrical coordinates \((R, \phi, z)\) are defined as follows \[
x = R \cos \phi, \qquad y = R \sin \phi, \qquad z = z.
\tag{16.32}\] The unit vectors in the \(R, \phi\), and \(z\) directions are \[
\begin{gathered}
\hat{\mathbf{R}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}}  \left(\begin{array}{c}
x\\
y\\
0
\end{array}\right), \\
\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{x^2 +
y^2}}  \left(\begin{array}{c}
- y\\
x\\
0
\end{array}\right), \\
\hat{\mathbf{z}} = \left(\begin{array}{c}
0\\
0\\
1
\end{array}\right) .
\end{gathered}
\tag{16.33}\]

Given the fluid velocity written as \(\mathbf{v}= v_R \hat{\mathbf{R}} + v_{\phi} \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}} + v_z \hat{\mathbf{z}}\), find its Cartesian components \(v_x, v_y,\) and \(v_z\).
Use the chain rule for derivatives to show that \[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial}{\partial R} &= \frac{x}{R}  \frac{\partial}{\partial x}
+ \frac{y}{R}  \frac{\partial}{\partial y}, \\
\frac{\partial}{\partial \phi} &= - y \frac{\partial}{\partial x} + x
\frac{\partial}{\partial y} .
\end{aligned}
\tag{16.34}\]
Using the results from the previous points show that \[
\nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}= \frac{1}{R}  \frac{\partial (Rv_R)}{\partial
R} + \frac{1}{R}  \frac{\partial v_{\phi}}{\partial \phi} +
\frac{\partial v_z}{\partial z} .
\tag{16.35}\]
Conclude that the continuity equation in cylindrical coordinates is \[
\frac{\partial \rho}{\partial t} + \frac{1}{R}  \left[ \frac{\partial
(\rho Rv_R)}{\partial R} + \frac{\partial (\rho v_{\phi})}{\partial
\phi} \right] + \frac{\partial (\rho v_z)}{\partial z} = 0.
\tag{16.36}\]

Viscous instability in accretion disks. The equation describing the evolution of the surface density \(\Sigma\) in an accretion disk is given by \[
\partial_t \Sigma = \frac{3}{R} \partial_R  [R^{1 / 2} \partial_R (\nu
\Sigma R^{1 / 2})] .
\tag{16.37}\] Assume that the viscosity \(\nu\) is in the form \(\nu = \nu (\Sigma, R)\).

Introduce the quantity \(\psi = \nu \Sigma\) and consider a small perturbation \(\delta \Sigma\) in the surface density of the disk. Find the equation describing the evolution of the corresponding perturbation \(\delta \psi\) of \(\psi\).
Under what condition is the disk stable?

title: 16  Accretion Disks
text:
16.8 Exercises

Exercise 16.1 (α-disks: scale height, viscosity, Reynolds number)  

Consider gas in an accretion disk that is in hydrostatic equilibrium in the vertical direction, with the vertical pressure gradient balancing the vertical component of the gravitational acceleration due to the central object. Show that the angular frequency of rotation \(\Omega\), the sound speed \(c_s\), and the vertical scale height \(H\) of the disk satisfy \(c_s \sim H \Omega\).
Suppose now that the \(R \phi\) component of the viscous stress tensor equals a factor \(\alpha\) times the thermal pressure. Show that (i) \(\nu \sim \alpha c_s H\) and (ii) the Reynolds number is \(\mathrm{Re} \sim \frac{1}{\alpha} \left( \frac{R}{H} \right)^2\).

Adapted from Clarke and Carswell (2007), Problem 47.


Exercise 16.2 (Similarity form of the disk equation)  

Show that the viscous evolution equation of a Keplerian accretion disk, \[
\frac{\partial \Sigma}{\partial t} = \frac{3}{R}
\frac{\partial}{\partial R} \left[ R^{1 / 2}  \frac{\partial}{\partial
R} (\nu \Sigma R^{1 / 2}) \right],
\tag{16.38}\] can be recast as \[
\frac{\partial S}{\partial t} = \frac{\partial^2 Y}{\partial X^2},
\tag{16.39}\] with \(S = \Sigma R^{3 / 2}\), \(Y = 3 \nu \Sigma R^{1 / 2}\), and \(X = 2 R^{1 / 2}\).
Obtain also a partial differential equation for \(S (t, X)\) when \(Y = Y_0 + \beta (S - S_0)\), where \(Y_0\), \(S_0\), and \(\beta\) are constants.
Describe how \(S\) evolves in the two cases (a) \(\beta > 0\) and (b) \(\beta < 0\).

Adapted from Clarke and Carswell (2007), Problem 49.


Exercise 16.3 (Numerical evolution of an accretion disk)  

Show that Equation 16.38 can be written as \[
\frac{\partial S}{\partial T} = \frac{\partial^2 (SX^{- 2})}{\partial
X^2},
\tag{16.40}\] where \(S\) and \(X\) are defined as in Exercise 16.2 and \(T = 12 \nu t\).
To solve Equation 16.40 numerically, introduce a grid \[
\begin{aligned}
&\{ (T_n, X_k) = (n \Delta T, X_{\min} + k \Delta X) : \\
&\qquad n = 0, 1, \ldots, N_T, k = 0, 1, \ldots, N_X \},
\end{aligned}
\tag{16.41}\] where \(\Delta T\), \(X_{\min}\), and \(\Delta X\) are fixed parameters. Let \(S^n_k\) be the approximation of \(S\) at \((T_n, X_k)\)1. Then \(S_k^n\) for \(k = 1, \ldots, N_X - 1\) can be written as \[
\frac{S^{n + 1}_k - S^n_k}{\Delta T} = \frac{S^{n + 1}_{k + 1} X_{k +
1}^{- 2} - 2 S^{n + 1}_k X_k^{- 2} + S^{n + 1}_{k - 1} X_{k - 1}^{-
2}}{\Delta X^2} .
\tag{16.42}\] The boundary conditions for this problem are \[
S_0 = S_{N_X} = 0,
\tag{16.43}\] corresponding to Dirichlet boundary condition for \(S\).
Show that Equation 16.42 can be written as \[
(I - \Delta TA) \mathbf{S}^{n + 1} =\mathbf{S}^n,
\tag{16.44}\] where \(\mathbf{S}^n = (S_1^n, S_2^n, \ldots, S^n_{N_X - 1})\) is a vector of values, \(I\) is the identity matrix, and \(A\) is a tridiagonal matrix. Find the explicit form of \(A\).
Write code to evolve in time the density in the disk by repeatedly solving Equation 16.44 starting from some initial condition \(\mathbf{S}^0\). You can use scipy.linalg.solve_banded to solve the linear equations.
Consider as initial conditions \[
S (t = 0, X) = \mathrm{e}^{- (X - 10)^2},
\tag{16.45}\] with \(X_{\min} = 1\). Plot the numerical solutions at successive times. Interpret the results in a few sentences.



Exercise 16.4 (Accretion-disk spectrum) Model an accretion disk as a set of concentric rings \(i = 1, 2, \ldots, N\), each with median radius \(R_i\) and radial extent \(\Delta R\). Let the disk extend from an inner radius \(R_{\mathrm{in}}\) to an outer radius \(R_{\mathrm{out}}\) and the temperature be \[
T (R) = T_{\mathrm{in}}  \left( \frac{R_{\mathrm{in}}}{R} \right)^{3 / 4} .
\tag{16.46}\] Assume that the \(i\)th ring emits as a blackbody with a fixed temperature \(T_i = T (R_i)\) \[
B_{\nu} (T) = \frac{2 h \nu^3}{c^2}  \frac{1}{\mathrm{e}^{h \nu / k_B T} - 1},
\tag{16.47}\] where \(h\) is the Planck constant, \(c\) the speed of light, and \(k_B\) the Boltzmann constant.

Write a code to compute and plot the emergent spectrum from a single ring at radius \(R_i\). Plot the emergent spectrum for several radii. You can work in units in which \(k_B = h = c = 1\). You can take \(T_{\mathrm{in}} = 1\) in these units.
Write a code to compute the emergent spectrum from the full disk by summing up the contribution from each ring. Plot the resulting spectrum and discuss its physical interpretation. Verify that the spectrum approximately scales as \(\nu^{1 / 3}\) for \(T_{\mathrm{out}} \lesssim \nu \lesssim T_{\mathrm{in}}\). You can work in the same units as in the previous point. Additionally assume that \(R_{\mathrm{out}} / R_{\mathrm{in}} = 10^4\), so that \(T_{\mathrm{out}} = 10^{-3}\, T_{\mathrm{in}}\).

title: 17  Turbulence
text:
17.1 What is Turbulence?
Turbulence is the chaotic, complex motion observed in fluids across all scales, from the chaotic motion of the quark–gluon plasma produced in heavy-ion collisions (fm scale) to the motion of gas in the intracluster medium (Mpc scale). Turbulence plays an important role in many terrestrial and astrophysical flows. For example, turbulence in the interstellar medium is thought to generate overdensities that eventually grow up to become stars. Turbulence also shapes the evolution and death of stars. Turbulent flows efficiently mix fluid: think of the way in which milk and coffee mix once turbulence is generated with a spoon. Turbulent flows also efficiently dissipate kinetic energy and develop large effective shear viscosity, e.g., triggering angular momentum transport.
Despite its importance for a number of applications, including many of practical, industrial impact, and despite the fact that turbulence has been studied for more than 500 years, we still lack a rigorous theory of turbulence. The closest thing we have to a theory is Kolmogorov’s 1941 theory (K41). These notes contain an introductory-level description of K41 and some example applications. For a more in depth description, I would recommend Landau–Lifshitz Vol. 6 (Landau and Lifshitz 1987) and Pope, Turbulent Flows, 2000 (Pope 2000).
