title: 17  Turbulence
text:
17.2 Mean Flow and Fluctuations
We will assume that the flow is incompressible, which is a good approximation if the velocity fluctuations are small compared to the sound speed (Chapter 9). As we will see, the velocity fluctuations become smaller at smaller scales, so this is always true at sufficiently small scales, except in shocks. The flow is then described by the Navier–Stokes equations (Chapter 15) \[
\partial_t \mathbf{v}+ (\mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla) \mathbf{v}=\mathbf{g}-
\frac{\nabla p}{\rho} + \nu \nabla^2 \mathbf{v}, \qquad \nabla \cdot
\mathbf{v}= 0,
\tag{17.1}\] where \(\mathbf{g}\) is some external acceleration field, typically gravity in astrophysical applications.
A turbulent flow has structure on many scales (Figure 17.2). To separate the large-scale motion from the small-scale fluctuations, we decompose the velocity into an average and a fluctuating component: \[
\mathbf{v} = \bar{\mathbf{v}} + \delta\mathbf{v}, \qquad \bar{\mathbf{v}} (\mathbf{x}) = \int K (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}') \, \mathbf{v} (\mathbf{x}') \mathrm{d}^3 x',
\tag{17.2}\] where the filter \(K\) is a smooth, positive function of width \(\ell\), with integral equal to one. In other words, \(\bar{\mathbf{v}}\) is the average of \(\mathbf{v}\) over a region of size \(\ell\), and \(\delta\mathbf{v}\) contains the motions on scales smaller than \(\ell\).
We will assume that the average obeys the Reynolds rules: it is linear, it commutes with derivatives, and an averaged quantity can be treated as a constant under the average, \(\overline{\bar{a} b} = \bar{a} \bar{b}\). In particular, averaging twice does not change the result, so \[
\bar{\bar{\mathbf{v}}} = \bar{\mathbf{v}} \Longrightarrow \overline{\delta\mathbf{v}} = 0 .
\tag{17.3}\] These rules hold exactly for averages over time, in a statistically steady flow, or over many realizations of the flow. A spatial filter like the one in Figure 17.2 does not satisfy them in general. We will come back to this point in Section 17.5.






Figure 17.2: Filtering a turbulent velocity field. Left: the filter \(K\), of width \(\ell\). Right: the velocity \(\mathbf{v}\) (black), its average \(\bar{\mathbf{v}}\) (blue), and the fluctuations \(\delta\mathbf{v}\) (red).



Since \(\nabla \cdot \mathbf{v} = 0\), we can write \((\mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla) \mathbf{v} = \nabla \cdot (\mathbf{v} \otimes \mathbf{v})\). Because the average is linear and commutes with derivatives (for a spatial filter, this requires \(K\) to be the same everywhere), the average of Equation 17.1 is \[
\partial_t \bar{\mathbf{v}} + \nabla \cdot \overline{\mathbf{v} \otimes \mathbf{v}} = \bar{\mathbf{g}} - \frac{\nabla \bar{p}}{\rho} + \nu \nabla^2 \bar{\mathbf{v}},
\tag{17.4}\] with \(\nabla \cdot \bar{\mathbf{v}} = 0\). However, \(\overline{\mathbf{v} \otimes \mathbf{v}} \neq \bar{\mathbf{v}} \otimes \bar{\mathbf{v}}\). Instead, \[
\overline{\mathbf{v} \otimes \mathbf{v}} = \overline{(\bar{\mathbf{v}} + \delta\mathbf{v}) \otimes (\bar{\mathbf{v}} + \delta\mathbf{v})} = \bar{\mathbf{v}} \otimes \bar{\mathbf{v}} + \overline{\delta\mathbf{v} \otimes \delta\mathbf{v}},
\tag{17.5}\] where we have used \(\overline{\bar{\mathbf{v}} \otimes \bar{\mathbf{v}}} = \bar{\mathbf{v}} \otimes \bar{\mathbf{v}}\) and \(\overline{\bar{\mathbf{v}} \otimes \delta\mathbf{v}} = \bar{\mathbf{v}} \otimes \overline{\delta\mathbf{v}} = 0\) (and the same for \(\delta\mathbf{v} \otimes \bar{\mathbf{v}}\)). The last term is the Reynolds stress tensor \[
\mathbf{R} = \overline{\delta\mathbf{v} \otimes \delta\mathbf{v}} ,
\tag{17.6}\] so the filtered equations read \[
\partial_t \bar{\mathbf{v}} + \nabla \cdot (\bar{\mathbf{v}} \otimes \bar{\mathbf{v}}) = \bar{\mathbf{g}} - \frac{\nabla \bar{p}}{\rho} + \nu \nabla^2 \bar{\mathbf{v}} - \nabla \cdot \mathbf{R} .
\tag{17.7}\] These are the equations for a fluid with velocity \(\bar{\mathbf{v}}\) and pressure \(\bar{p}\), with an additional stress \(\mathbf{R}\) due to the fluctuations on scales smaller than \(\ell\). They are exact, but they are not closed, because we do not have a way to compute \(\mathbf{R}\) from \(\bar{\mathbf{v}}\). This is the so-called turbulence closure problem. We will come back to it in Section 17.5.
The simplest case is that of homogeneous and isotropic turbulence, which has no mean flow: \(\bar{\mathbf{v}} = 0\) and \(\delta\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{v}\). This also applies locally, in a small region in which the mean flow is nearly uniform, after we remove it by working in the frame moving with \(\bar{\mathbf{v}}\).

title: 17  Turbulence
text:
17.3 Kolmogorov’s Theory
Fluid motion is driven by external forces, such as gravity, which have a characteristic scale \(\ell_0\) comparable to the size of the system of interest. For example, for a star \(\ell_0 \sim R_*\), the radius of the star. The starting point of Kolmogorov’s theory is to assume that, if the size \(\ell\) of the region under consideration is sufficiently small, \(\ell \ll \ell_0\), the fluctuating component of the velocity \(\delta\mathbf{v}\), not necessarily assumed to be small, is universal, at least in a statistical sense, meaning that it does not depend on the particular system, but that is set by the equations of motion.
To keep our notation simple, we consider homogeneous and isotropic turbulence, so that \(\bar{\mathbf{v}} = 0\) and \(\delta\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{v}\). As discussed above, this is not a restriction on the theory we are developing, because on small scales the mean flow is nearly uniform, and we can remove it by working in the appropriate reference frame.
The equation for the evolution of the kinetic energy is obtained by multiplying Equation 17.1 by \(\mathbf{v}\): \[
\frac{1}{2}  [\partial_t v^2 + (\mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla) v^2] =\mathbf{g}
\cdot \mathbf{v}- \frac{1}{\rho} \nabla p \cdot \mathbf{v}+ \nu \nabla^2
\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{v}.
\tag{17.8}\] Consider the first term on the RHS, representing the work done by the external force on the flow. If \(\ell \ll \ell_0\), then we can take \(\mathbf{g} \sim \mathrm{const}\) over this region and \[
\overline{\mathbf{g} \cdot \mathbf{v}} \simeq \mathbf{g} \cdot \bar{\mathbf{v}} = 0.
\tag{17.9}\] This suggests that the evolution of \(v\) for \(\ell \ll \ell_0\) is independent of the details of the external force \(\mathbf{g}\), so \(v\) can be universal. Of course, if \(\ell \sim \ell_0\), then \(\overline{\mathbf{g} \cdot \mathbf{v}} > 0\) in general, meaning that kinetic energy is injected at the scale \(\ell_0\) by gravity and then evolves according to Equation 17.8.
Let’s now consider the role of pressure (note that \(\rho = \mathrm{const}\)): \[
\overline{\nabla p \cdot \mathbf{v}} = \frac{1}{V} \int_V \nabla p
\cdot \mathbf{v} \mathrm{d} V = \frac{1}{V} \int_V [\nabla \cdot (p
\mathbf{v}) - p \nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}] \mathrm{d} V = \frac{1}{V} \oint_S
p\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{n} \mathrm{d} S = 0.
\tag{17.10}\] In the last equation we have assumed that \(\mathbf{v}\) is isotropic (no preferred direction), so \(\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{n}\) is zero on average.
In a similar way, we can rewrite the average of the last term in the RHS of Equation 17.8 as \[
\begin{aligned}
\int_V \nabla^2 \mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{v} \mathrm{d} V
&= \oint_S \mathbf{n} \cdot \nabla \left( \tfrac{1}{2} v^2 \right) \mathrm{d} S \\
&\quad {} - \int_V | \nabla \mathbf{v} |^2 \mathrm{d} V \\
&= - \int_V | \nabla \mathbf{v} |^2 \mathrm{d} V .
\end{aligned}
\tag{17.11}\] This means that, on average, we can simplify the kinetic energy equation to read \[
\partial_t v^2 = 2\mathbf{g} \cdot \mathbf{v}- (\mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla) v^2
- 2 \nu | \nabla \mathbf{v} |^2 .
\tag{17.12}\] As already mentioned, the first term on the RHS is responsible for energy injection. The last term describes kinetic energy dissipation. We can estimate this term as \[
\nu | \nabla \mathbf{v} |^2 \sim \nu \left( \frac{v (\ell)}{\ell} \right)^2,
\tag{17.13}\] where \(v (\ell)\) is the characteristic velocity fluctuation on a length scale \(\ell\): \[
v (\ell) = \overline{| \mathbf{v} (\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{l}) -\mathbf{v}
(\mathbf{x}) |} = \frac{1}{V} \int_V | \mathbf{v}
(\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{l}) -\mathbf{v} (\mathbf{x}) | \mathrm{d} V.
\tag{17.14}\] Here \(| \mathbf{l} | = \ell\). We use the notation \(A \sim B\) to signify that two quantities, \(A\) and \(B\), are equal up to factors of order unity.
The quantity on the RHS of Equation 17.13 has units of power per unit mass, as expected, since it is the rate at which the kinetic energy per unit mass is dissipated. Equation 17.13 suggests that the energy is dissipated at a scale \(\ell_d\) (the dissipation or Kolmogorov scale) at which the dissipation rate is equal to the mean power of the global flow: \[
\nu \left( \frac{v (\ell_d)}{\ell_d} \right)^2 \sim \frac{v^3
(\ell_0)}{\ell_0} \Longrightarrow \ell_d \sim \ell_0  \left[
\frac{\nu}{\ell_0 v (\ell_0)} \right]^{1 / 2}  \left[ \frac{v (\ell_d)}{v
(\ell_0)} \right] = \frac{\ell_0}{\mathrm{Re}^{1 / 2}}  \left[ \frac{v
(\ell_d)}{v (\ell_0)} \right] .
\tag{17.15}\] In the previous equation, we have introduced the Reynolds number \[
\mathrm{Re} = \frac{\ell_0 v (\ell_0)}{\nu} .
\tag{17.16}\] Experimental observations of fluids in pipes suggest that turbulence sets in when \(\mathrm{Re} \gtrsim 10^3\). In astrophysical situations, \(\mathrm{Re}\) can be much larger. For example, in the interstellar medium \(\mathrm{Re} \sim 10^9\). In neutron star mergers we contend with flows having \(\mathrm{Re} \sim 10^{15}\). Consequently, Equation 17.15 implies that \(\ell_d \ll \ell_0\) for turbulent flows.
Summarizing, in our analysis of Equation 17.12 we have found that kinetic energy is injected at large scale \(\ell_0\) (first term on the RHS) and dissipated at the dissipation scale \(\ell_d \ll \ell_0\) (last term on the RHS). This means that there is a range of scales \(\ell_d \ll \ell \ll \ell_0\), the so-called inertial range, in which the dynamics is dominated by the nonlinear term \((\mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla) v^2\). We can estimate it as \[
(\mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla) v^2 \sim \frac{v^3 (\ell)}{\ell} .
\tag{17.17}\] Note that, for an incompressible flow, the nonlinear term can also be written as a divergence, \((\mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla) v^2 = \nabla \cdot (\mathbf{v} v^2)\). So, by the same argument we used for the pressure, its average over a region vanishes. In other words, the nonlinear term does not create or destroy kinetic energy. Instead, it moves kinetic energy between different scales. In a steady state, the energy per unit mass and per unit time injected at the scale \(\ell_0\), \[
\mathcal{P} = \frac{v^3 (\ell_0)}{\ell_0},
\tag{17.18}\] must flow through all the scales in the inertial range, without losses, until it reaches the dissipation scale, where it is dissipated. At the scale \(\ell\), the kinetic energy per unit mass \(v^2 (\ell)\) is passed on to smaller scales in a time \(\ell / v (\ell)\), so the flux of energy is \(v^3 (\ell) / \ell\). Since this must be the same at all scales, we have \[
\frac{v^3 (\ell)}{\ell} \sim \mathcal{P} \Longrightarrow \boxed{v
(\ell) \sim (\mathcal{P} \ell)^{1/3} = v (\ell_0)  \left( \frac{\ell}{\ell_0} \right)^{1 / 3}} .
\tag{17.19}\] This result is key to the theory of turbulence and is called Kolmogorov’s second similarity hypothesis1. It has been verified many times through direct numerical simulations and experiments. Note that \(v (\ell)\) decreases at smaller scales, so the flow is subsonic at sufficiently small scales, as we anticipated.
Often this hypothesis is formulated in terms of the energy spectrum \(E (k)\). This is defined so that \(E (k) \mathrm{d} k\) is the kinetic energy per unit mass in eddies with wave numbers between \(k\) and \(k + \mathrm{d} k\): \[
\frac{1}{2} \overline{| \mathbf{v} |^2} = \int_0^{\infty} E (k) \mathrm{d} k .
\tag{17.20}\] Eddies of size \(\ell\) have wave numbers \(k \sim 1 / \ell\). The kinetic energy per unit mass in eddies of size \(\sim \ell\) is the energy in a range of wave numbers of width \(\sim k\) around \(k\), so \[
v^2 (\ell) \sim k E (k) \Longrightarrow E (k) \sim \frac{v^2 (1 / k)}{k} \sim \mathcal{P}^{2/3} k^{- 5 / 3} .
\tag{17.21}\] This is the famous Kolmogorov \(k^{- 5 / 3}\) spectrum. A comparison between data and theory over about 16 orders of magnitude in scale is shown in Figure 17.3. The figure collects measurements of density fluctuations in the interstellar medium from several types of observations, with spacecraft data, including Voyager 1, at the smallest scales. It shows the three-dimensional spectrum of density fluctuations, which in Kolmogorov’s theory scales as \(k^{- 11 / 3}\). The extra factor \(k^{- 2}\) with respect to \(E (k)\) comes from the area of a shell of radius \(k\) in Fourier space. Deviations from the Kolmogorov scaling only appear at very small scales, when plasma kinetic effects become important.






Figure 17.3: Power spectrum of electron density fluctuations in the interstellar medium from several types of observations, including Voyager 1 (points), and Kolmogorov spectrum (dashed). From Lee and Lee (2019); © Springer Nature, reproduced for non-commercial educational use and not covered by the license of these notes.



A physical interpretation of the K41 model is given by the Richardson cascade (which actually predates K41). In this model, energy is injected at large scale by \(\mathbf{g}\) and dissipated at small scales by the viscosity. The nonlinear term \((\mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla) v^2\) couples different scales and is responsible for the transport of energy from large scale to small scale, as illustrated in Figure 17.4.






Figure 17.4: The Richardson cascade. Redrawn after Frisch (1995).



The main mechanisms for the transport of energy are vortex stretching and shear (Kelvin–Helmholtz) instabilities (Chapter 14).
We can interpret \(v^3 (\ell) / \ell\) as a term that controls the kinetic energy dissipation: \[
\frac{v^3 (\ell)}{\ell} = \frac{v^2 (\ell)}{\tau}, \qquad \tau =
\frac{\ell}{v (\ell)},
\tag{17.22}\] where \(\tau\) is the eddy turnover time, the time over which the specific kinetic energy \(v^2 (\ell)\) is transferred to smaller scales. To see this, notice that for \(\ell_d \ll \ell \ll \ell_0\), Equation 17.12 reduces to \[
\boxed{\frac{\mathrm{d} v^2 (\ell)}{\mathrm{d} t} \sim - \frac{v^2 (\ell)}{\tau}
.}
\tag{17.23}\] The constancy of \(v^3 (\ell) / \ell\) implies that the rate at which turbulence dissipates kinetic energy is independent of \(\nu\) or of the detailed form of the physical processes responsible for dissipation! Instead, it is set by the dynamics at large scale. In other words, when kinetic energy is injected by mechanical work at large scale in a turbulent flow, turbulence efficiently transports this energy to small scales (generating large velocity gradients) at which point it is dissipated. This is the reason why turbulence theory applies equally well to the flow of water around the propeller of a ship and to the motion of rarefied gas in the intergalactic medium. This finding also justifies turbulence modeling approaches used in simulations.
With Kolmogorov’s second similarity law, we can provide a better estimate for \(\ell_d\). Using Equation 17.19 into Equation 17.15, we can eliminate \(v (\ell_d)\) to find \[
\boxed{\ell_d \sim \left( \frac{\nu}{\ell_0 v (\ell_0)} \right)^{3 / 4}
\ell_0 = \mathrm{Re}^{- 3 / 4} \ell_0} .
\tag{17.24}\] Equivalently, using Equation 17.19, \(\ell_d\) is the scale at which the dissipation term, Equation 17.13, is comparable to the transport term, Equation 17.17: \[
\nu \left( \frac{v (\ell_d)}{\ell_d} \right)^2 \sim \frac{v^3 (\ell_d)}{\ell_d} \Longrightarrow \frac{v (\ell_d) \ell_d}{\nu} \sim 1,
\tag{17.25}\] that is, the Reynolds number of the eddies of size \(\ell_d\) is of order unity. On smaller scales the flow is smooth, so \(v (\ell) \sim | \nabla \mathbf{v} | \ell \propto \ell\), with \(| \nabla \mathbf{v} | \sim v (\ell_d) / \ell_d\). On scales larger than \(\ell_0\), \(v (\ell)\) stops growing, because the velocities at points farther apart than \(\ell_0\) are uncorrelated. These results are summarized in Figure 17.5.






Figure 17.5: Velocity fluctuations \(v (\ell)\) as a function of the scale \(\ell\) (sketch).



Equation 17.24 shows that the scale separation in developed turbulence can be enormous. A direct numerical simulation needs to resolve all scales between \(\ell_d\) and \(\ell_0\), so it needs \((\ell_0 / \ell_d)^3\) grid cells. It also needs a number of time steps \(\sim \ell_0 / \ell_d\), because the time step must be smaller than the time it takes for the flow to cross one cell. So the cost of a direct numerical simulation scales as \[
\mathrm{cost} \sim \left( \frac{\ell_0}{\ell_d} \right)^4 \sim \mathrm{Re}^3,
\tag{17.26}\] which makes it impossible to directly simulate very turbulent flows. The largest simulations today have about \(10^4\) grid cells in each direction, so they can reach \(\mathrm{Re} \sim 10^5\). To study flows with higher Reynolds numbers, it is necessary to give up the idea of simulating all scales in the flow and instead resort to modeling the dynamics below the numerical grid scale using turbulence theory.






TipExample



Consider the wind in the atmosphere of the Earth, with \(\ell_0 \sim 1\,\mathrm{km}\) and \(v (\ell_0) \sim 10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). The kinematic viscosity of air is \(\nu \approx 1.5 \times 10^{-5}\,\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}\), so \(\mathrm{Re} \sim 7 \times 10^8\). The dissipation scale is \(\ell_d \sim \mathrm{Re}^{-3/4} \ell_0 \sim 0.2\,\mathrm{mm}\), and a direct numerical simulation would cost \(\sim \mathrm{Re}^3 \sim 10^{26}\), many orders of magnitude beyond what is possible. Even a cup of coffee stirred with a spoon, with \(\ell_0 \sim 3\,\mathrm{cm}\), \(v (\ell_0) \sim 0.1\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), and \(\nu \approx 10^{-6}\,\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}\), has \(\mathrm{Re} \sim 3000\) and \(\ell_d \sim 70\,\mu\mathrm{m}\).


Before we discuss some applications of Kolmogorov’s theory, it is worth mentioning its limitations. Astrophysical flows are often supersonic and highly magnetized. Compressibility and magnetic fields can have a profound role on the turbulent cascade. Shocks can dissipate kinetic energy directly at large scales (Chapter 11). Magnetic fields can give rise to inverse cascade whereby small magnetic field structures self-organize into large scale ordered fields (turbulent dynamo process, Chapter 20). The study of compressible, magnetized turbulence is still an active area of research and beyond the scope of this course. However, even for compressible, magnetized flows, Kolmogorov’s theory provides a good starting point and can often be applied directly.

title: 17  Turbulence
section: 17.4 Shredding of Clouds in a Turbulent Flow
text:
17.4 Shredding of Clouds in a Turbulent Flow
Consider a cloud of gas of radius \(R\), for example a patch of material enriched by a supernova, that is carried by the turbulent flow of the interstellar medium. We want to compute the evolution of \(R\) with time. We will consider three cases, illustrated in Figure 17.6.






Figure 17.6: Distortion of a cloud in a turbulent medium. The three different cases are \(R \sim \ell_d\) (case A), \(\ell_d \ll R \ll \ell_0\) (case B), and \(R \sim \ell_0\) (case C).



If \(R \sim \ell_d\) the particles in the cloud will undergo Brownian random motion, so, as in the case of the random diffusion of photons (Chapter 6), we have \(R \sim t^{1 / 2}\). If \(R \sim \ell_0\), then the cloud is primarily advected by the mean flow. The edges of the cloud will still experience random diffusion, so \(R \sim t^{1 / 2}\), but with an effective diffusion coefficient \(\sim \ell_0 v (\ell_0)\), which is much larger than the molecular one. Indeed, eddies of size \(\ell_0\) act like particles with mean free path \(\ell_0\) (compare with Equation 1.1) moving with velocity \(v (\ell_0)\). We will see that this is the same estimate used for the turbulent viscosity.
The more interesting case is when \(\ell_d \ll R \ll \ell_0\). In this case, the cloud undergoes rapid distortion: \[
\frac{\mathrm{d} R}{\mathrm{d} t} \sim v \sim R^{1 / 3} \Longrightarrow \frac{\mathrm{d}
R^2}{\mathrm{d} t} \sim Rv \sim R^{4 / 3} .
\tag{17.27}\] This is Richardson’s 4/3-law. We can use the second Kolmogorov similarity hypothesis to find the time dependence for \(R\): \[
\frac{\mathrm{d} R}{\mathrm{d} t} \sim v (\ell_0)  \left( \frac{R}{\ell_0} \right)^{1 / 3}
\Longrightarrow R^{2 / 3} \sim \frac{v (\ell_0)}{\ell_0^{1 / 3}} t
\Longrightarrow R^2 \sim \mathcal{P} t^3 .
\tag{17.28}\] In other words, \(R \propto t^{3 / 2}\): the cloud grows faster and faster, because, as it grows, it is torn apart by larger and faster eddies. This is an example of superdiffusion: the cloud grows faster than by ordinary diffusion, for which \(R \propto t^{1 / 2}\).
Turbulence significantly accelerates the mixing of new elements produced in supernovae with the interstellar medium, where they can subsequently form new stars, planets, and people.






TipExample



Consider the metals ejected by a supernova into the warm interstellar medium, with \(T \sim 10^4\,\mathrm{K}\) and \(n \sim 1\,\mathrm{cm^{-3}}\). The turbulence in the interstellar medium is driven on scales \(\ell_0 \sim 100\,\mathrm{pc}\), with \(v (\ell_0) \sim 10\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}\). So turbulence mixes the metals over \(\sim 100\,\mathrm{pc}\) in a time \(\sim \ell_0 / v (\ell_0) \sim 10\,\mathrm{Myr}\). How long would it take without turbulence? The mean free path of the particles in this gas is \(\lambda \sim 10^{10}\,\mathrm{m}\), and their thermal velocity is \(v_{\mathrm{th}} \sim 10\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}\), so the diffusion coefficient is \(D \sim \lambda v_{\mathrm{th}} / 3 \sim 3 \times 10^{13}\,\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}\) (Chapter 6). Molecular diffusion would take \(\sim \ell_0^2 / D \sim 10^{16}\,\mathrm{yr}\), much longer than the age of the Universe. Note also that the ratio of the two timescales is \(\ell_0 v (\ell_0) / D \sim 10^9\), which is the Reynolds number of the interstellar medium.

title: 17  Turbulence
text:
17.5 Turbulence Modeling
Directly simulating turbulent flows is impossible, so one of the goals of turbulence theory is to develop effective strategies to deal with unresolved turbulence in simulations. The idea is to solve the filtered equations, Equation 17.7, instead of the Navier–Stokes equations. Because \(\bar{\mathbf{v}}\) is much smoother than \(\mathbf{v}\), Equation 17.7 can be solved on a coarse computational mesh. The problem of modeling turbulence is then reduced to that of finding a good model for \(\mathbf{R}\). There are many such models in the literature.
Commonly used frameworks are the Reynolds averaged Navier–Stokes (RANS) and Large-Eddy Simulations (LES). In RANS, the average is over time or over many realizations of the flow, so \(\mathbf{R}\) describes the fluctuations on all scales. In LES, \(\ell\) is comparable to the size of the grid cells, and \(\mathbf{R}\) describes only the unresolved eddies. In this case, the Reynolds rules do not hold: for example, \(\overline{\bar{\mathbf{v}} \otimes \delta\mathbf{v}} \neq \bar{\mathbf{v}} \otimes \overline{\delta\mathbf{v}}\). So the Reynolds stress is defined as \(\mathbf{R} = \overline{\mathbf{v} \otimes \mathbf{v}} - \bar{\mathbf{v}} \otimes \bar{\mathbf{v}}\), which reduces to Equation 17.6 for averages over time or over realizations. With this definition, Equation 17.7 follows from Equation 17.4 for any filter that commutes with derivatives.
The simplest model, which is also the most commonly used for astrophysical applications, is the turbulent (or eddy) viscosity model. Accordingly, one takes \[
\mathbf{R}= \frac{1}{3} (\mathrm{tr} \mathbf{R}) \mathbf{I} - \nu_T  (\nabla \bar{\mathbf{v}}+ \nabla^T \bar{\mathbf{v}}) .
\tag{17.29}\] The first term is needed because \(\mathrm{tr} \mathbf{R} = \overline{|\mathbf{v}|^2} - |\bar{\mathbf{v}}|^2\) is positive: it is equal to \(\overline{|\delta\mathbf{v}|^2}\) in RANS and to \(\int K (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}') \, |\mathbf{v} (\mathbf{x}') - \bar{\mathbf{v}} (\mathbf{x})|^2 \mathrm{d}^3 x'\) in LES, while the trace of the second term vanishes for an incompressible flow. The first term is isotropic, so it acts like an additional pressure, the turbulent pressure \(\rho \mathrm{tr} \mathbf{R} / 3\), which we include in \(\bar{p}\). We will meet the turbulent pressure again in the in-class worksheet. With this choice, using \(\nabla \cdot \bar{\mathbf{v}} = 0\) and taking \(\nu_T\) constant, Equation 17.7 becomes \[
\partial_t  \bar{\mathbf{v}} + \nabla \cdot \left(\bar{\mathbf{v}}
\otimes \bar{\mathbf{v}} + \frac{\bar{p}}{\rho} \mathbf{I} \right) = \bar{\mathbf{g}} + (\nu
+ \nu_T) \nabla^2 \bar{\mathbf{v}} .
\tag{17.30}\] That is, turbulence is described simply as a dissipative process and \(\nu_T\) is an effective turbulent viscosity. The turbulent viscosity, in turn, is often obtained using dimensional analysis arguments: \[
\nu_T = \ell_{\mathrm{mix}} V,
\tag{17.31}\] where \(\ell_{\mathrm{mix}}\) is a characteristic length, also called the mixing length, and \(V\) is a characteristic velocity. For example, in accretion disk theory (Chapter 16), \(V = c_s\) and \(\ell_{\mathrm{mix}}\) is taken to be proportional to the scale-height of the disk \(H\): \[
\ell_{\mathrm{mix}} = \alpha H = \alpha \frac{c_s}{\Omega} \Longrightarrow
\nu_T = \alpha \frac{c_s^2}{\Omega},
\tag{17.32}\] where \(\Omega\) is the angular velocity of the flow. This is the so-called \(\alpha\)-viscosity model.
For shear flows along \(x\) with shear in the \(y\)-direction, one can use the velocity gradient instead of \(V\): \[
\nu_T = \ell_{\mathrm{mix}}^2  \left| \frac{\partial \bar{v}_x}{\partial
y} \right| .
\tag{17.33}\] This is Prandtl’s mixing-length model. The Smagorinsky model, which is often used in large-eddy simulations, is a generalization of this model, in which \(\ell_{\mathrm{mix}}\) is proportional to the size of the grid cells and \(| \partial \bar{v}_x / \partial y |\) is replaced by the magnitude of the rate of strain of \(\bar{\mathbf{v}}\).
For industrial applications, a popular strategy is to solve additional equations for \(\partial_t \mathbf{R}\), with coefficients calibrated to experimental (wind tunnel) results. More sophisticated “subgrid” models have also been proposed for astrophysical applications, but their detailed description is beyond the scope of this course. See Brandenburg and Nordlund (2011) for more information.
Another popular approach is the Implicit Large-Eddy Simulations (ILES) method, in which \(\mathbf{R}\) is not included explicitly in the equations. Instead, a numerical scheme is chosen that has a numerical viscosity \(\nu_{\mathrm{num}} \approx \nu_T\). This approach is often effective, but ILES simulations need to be accompanied by careful resolution studies to assess their reliability, because accurate results can only be obtained if a sufficient portion of the inertial range is resolved by the simulations.






Figure 17.7: Density in a high-resolution simulation of compressible turbulence in the interstellar medium (Federrath et al. 2021), as shown on the cover of Nature Astronomy, April 2021. © Springer Nature, reproduced for non-commercial educational use and not covered by the license of these notes.

title: 17  Turbulence
text:
17.6 In-class worksheet
Turbulence in Core-Collapse Supernovae. We construct here a simplified model showing the role of turbulence in aiding shock revival in core-collapse supernovae.

Consider a steady accretion shock near the protoneutron star. Assume that the in-falling material is cold and that the velocity downstream of the shock is small. Show that the Rankine–Hugoniot conditions simplify to \[
p_2 \approx \rho_1 v_1^2, \qquad \frac{\rho_2}{\rho_1} = \frac{\Gamma +
1}{\Gamma - 1},
\tag{17.34}\] where all quantities have their usual meaning.
Find the equilibrium pressure \(p_2\) needed to support the accretion shock at a fixed radius \(r_s\), given the mass of the protoneutron star \(M\), and the accretion rate \(\dot{M}\). Assume that the gas upstream of the shock falls freely from rest at infinity.
Consider angular averages of the flow, e.g., \[
\langle \mathbf{v} \rangle = \frac{1}{4 \pi} \oint \mathbf{v} \mathrm{d}
\Omega .
\tag{17.35}\] Decompose the velocity downstream of the shock as the sum of an average (laminar) component \(\langle \mathbf{v} \rangle\) and a turbulent fluctuating component \(\delta \mathbf{v}\), \(\mathbf{v}= \langle \mathbf{v} \rangle + \delta \mathbf{v}\). Assume that \(\rho\) depends only on radius, so that \(\langle \rho \mathbf{v} \rangle = \rho \langle \mathbf{v} \rangle\). Define the Reynolds stress as \[
\mathbf{R}= \langle \delta \mathbf{v} \otimes \delta \mathbf{v} \rangle
.
\tag{17.36}\] Show that the conservation of momentum across the shock can be written as \[
\rho_2  \langle v_2 \rangle^2 + \rho_2 R_{r r} + p_2 = \rho_1 v_1^2 .
\tag{17.37}\]
Define the specific turbulent kinetic energy as \[
\varepsilon_{\mathrm{turb}} = \frac{1}{2}  | \delta \mathbf{v} |^2 =
\frac{1}{2}  (R_{rr} + R_{\theta \theta} + R_{\phi \phi}) .
\tag{17.38}\] Assume that \(R_{rr} = R_{\theta \theta} + R_{\phi \phi}\) and show that with this definition Equation 17.37 can be written as \[
\begin{aligned}
& \rho_2  \langle v_2 \rangle^2 \\
& \quad + \rho_2  [(\Gamma_{\mathrm{turb}} - 1)
\varepsilon_{\mathrm{turb}} + (\Gamma - 1) \varepsilon_2] \\
& \quad = \rho_1 v_1^2 .
\end{aligned}
\tag{17.39}\] What is the effective adiabatic index of turbulence \(\Gamma_{\mathrm{turb}}\)?
At early times, before the turbulence develops, the accretion shock is stalled at a radius \(r_s\). What happens to the shock, once turbulence develops?

title: 17  Turbulence
text:
17.7 Exercises

Exercise 17.1 (Brownian and Lévy random walks) Consider the random walk of a particle. At each step \(i\) a particle at position \(\mathbf{x}_i\) jumps to position \[
\mathbf{x}_{i + 1} =\mathbf{x}_i + R_i \mathbf{d}_i,
\tag{17.40}\] where \(\mathbf{d}_i\) is a random direction on the sphere (uniform in \(\phi\) and \(\cos \theta\)) and \(R_i\) is either

a fixed constant (Brownian random walk); or
it has a Pareto distribution \(p (R) \sim R^{- 1 - \beta}\), for a given \(\beta\) (Lévy random walk).

The Brownian random walk can be used to model ordinary diffusion process, while Lévy random walks can be used to model effective diffusion and mixing in a turbulent flow (superdiffusion).
Write a code to simulate Brownian and Lévy random walks with \(\beta = 2 / 3\), then compute the median of the traveled distance \(D_N = | \mathbf{x}_N -\mathbf{x}_0 |\) as a function of \(N\) for the two. For \(\beta < 1\) the mean length of a step is infinite, so the median is a better measure than the mean.
Show that \(D_N \sim N^{\gamma}\) and estimate \(\gamma\) in the two cases. Compare the results with the predictions from Kolmogorov theory for diffusion in a turbulent flow (\(R \sim t^{3 / 2}\)). Explain why the Lévy random walk gives \(D_N \sim N^{1 / \beta}\).
[You can use numpy.random.uniform and numpy.random.pareto to generate \(R_i\) and \(\mathbf{d}_i\).]

title: 18  Introduction to Plasma
text: 18.1 Electromagnetism Refresher

title: 18  Introduction to Plasma
text:
18.1.1 Lorentz Force and Maxwell Equations
Most of the baryonic matter in the Universe is in the form of plasma, a state of matter characterized by large electrical conductivity and charge mobility. Not surprisingly, plasma physics plays an important role in many astrophysical systems. Before we are ready to discuss plasmas, or even before we can precisely state what plasma is, it is a good idea to refresh some key concepts from electromagnetism. We will write the equations of electromagnetism in SI units, as in the rest of these notes.
The starting point for electromagnetism is the observation that some particles, electrons and protons, are endowed with electric charge, which is an intrinsic property, like mass. When two lumps of matter with net charge \(Q_1\) and \(Q_2\) are placed at a distance \(r\), the two experience a force \[
F = \frac{Q_1 Q_2}{4 \pi \epsilon_0 r^2} .
\tag{18.1}\] The force is repulsive if \(Q_1 Q_2 > 0\) and attractive if \(Q_1 Q_2 < 0\). In SI units, charge is measured in coulomb (\(1\,\mathrm{C} = 1\,\mathrm{A\,s}\)), and the constant \(\epsilon_0\), called the vacuum permittivity, is \[
\epsilon_0 = 8.854 \times 10^{- 12}\,\mathrm{C^2\,N^{-1}\,m^{-2}} .
\tag{18.2}\] The charge of the electron is \[
e = 1.602176634 \times 10^{- 19}\,\mathrm{C} .
\tag{18.3}\] The Coulomb force on particle 2 can also be thought of as the effect on particle 2 of an electrostatic field produced by particle 1. In a system of coordinates centered on particle 1, the electrostatic field produced by particle 1 is \[
\mathbf{E}= \frac{Q_1}{4 \pi \epsilon_0 r^2}  \hat{\mathbf{r}}
\tag{18.4}\] and the force on particle 2 is given by \[
\mathbf{F}= \frac{Q_1 Q_2}{4 \pi \epsilon_0 r^2}  \hat{\mathbf{r}} = Q_2 \mathbf{E}.
\tag{18.5}\] In general, a charged particle with charge \(Q\) moving in an electromagnetic field experiences the so-called Lorentz force: \[
\mathbf{F}= Q ( \mathbf{E}+ \mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B} ) .
\tag{18.6}\] The electric \(\mathbf{E}\) and magnetic \(\mathbf{B}\) fields are defined by Equation 18.6, as the force per unit charge on a particle at rest, and the additional force on a moving particle. Their units are \[
[\mathbf{E}] = \mathrm{N\,C^{-1}} = \mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}, \qquad [\mathbf{B}] = \mathrm{N\,s\,C^{-1}\,m^{-1}} = \mathrm{T}\ (\mathrm{tesla}) .
\tag{18.7}\] In astronomy, magnetic fields are customarily measured in gauss, with \(1\,\mathrm{G} = 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{T}\). We will give field strengths in tesla, followed by their value in gauss. Note that \(\mathbf{E}\) and \(c \mathbf{B}\), where \(c\) is the speed of light, have the same units. This makes sense, because electric and magnetic fields are different manifestations of a single field: the electromagnetic field, as is revealed by special relativity. The electromagnetic field can be found as solution of the Maxwell’s field equations \[
\begin{array}{ll}
\nabla \cdot \mathbf{E}= \dfrac{q}{\epsilon_0}, & \nabla \cdot \mathbf{B}= 0,\\
\nabla \times \mathbf{E}= - \dfrac{\partial
\mathbf{B}}{\partial t}, & \nabla \times \mathbf{B}= \mu_0
\mathbf{j}+ \mu_0 \epsilon_0 \dfrac{\partial \mathbf{E}}{\partial t} .
\end{array}
\tag{18.8}\] In the previous equation, \(q\) is the charge density, \(\mathbf{j}\) the current density, and \(\mu_0 \approx 4 \pi \times 10^{- 7}\,\mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}\) is the vacuum permeability. The two constants are related to the speed of light by \(\mu_0 \epsilon_0 = 1 / c^2\). The equations in the first row are called the Gauss law for electric and magnetic fields. The second two equations are the Faraday, or induction, equation (left column), and the Ampère–Maxwell law (right column).






NoteGaussian units



Most astrophysics texts and papers, including Kulsrud (2005), write the equations of electromagnetism in Gaussian (CGS) units. In these units there is no \(\epsilon_0\) or \(\mu_0\), charge is measured in statcoulomb, and \(\mathbf{E}\) and \(\mathbf{B}\) have the same units. To translate a formula from Gaussian to SI units, replace \(B / \sqrt{4 \pi}\) with \(B / \sqrt{\mu_0}\), \(e^2\) with \(e^2 / (4 \pi \epsilon_0)\), and \(\mathbf{E}\) with \(\sqrt{4 \pi \epsilon_0}\, \mathbf{E}\), and write every \(\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B} / c\) as \(\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B}\). For example, the Gaussian plasma frequency \(\sqrt{4 \pi n e^2 / m_e}\) becomes \(\sqrt{n e^2 / (\epsilon_0 m_e)}\) (Equation 18.50), and the Gaussian magnetic pressure \(B^2 / 8 \pi\) becomes \(B^2 / 2 \mu_0\).




18.1.2 Electrostatics
If the fields do not depend on time, the Maxwell equations for \(\mathbf{E}\) simplify to \[
\nabla \cdot \mathbf{E}= \frac{q}{\epsilon_0}, \qquad \nabla \times \mathbf{E}= 0.
\tag{18.9}\] The second equation tells us that \(\mathbf{E}= - \nabla \Phi\), where \(\Phi\) is the electrostatic potential. The latter satisfies the Poisson equation \[
\nabla^2 \Phi = - \frac{q}{\epsilon_0} .
\tag{18.10}\] Apart from a minus sign and the constant, \(1 / \epsilon_0\) instead of \(4 \pi G\), this is the same equation satisfied by the gravitational potential (Chapter 7).
The force experienced by a charge \(Q\) in an electrostatic field is \[
\mathbf{F}= Q\mathbf{E}= - Q \nabla \Phi .
\tag{18.11}\]






TipExample



Consider the electrostatic potential generated by a spherical distribution of charge density \(q\) and the force experienced by an electron outside the sphere, as illustrated in Figure 18.1.






Figure 18.1: Spherical distribution of charge.



The radial component of the force experienced by an electron, which has charge \(- e\), at a distance \(r\) from a charged sphere, with charge density \(q\), is given by: \[
F_r = e \partial_r \Phi .
\tag{18.12}\] From the Poisson equation \[
\nabla \cdot \nabla \Phi = - \frac{q}{\epsilon_0} .
\tag{18.13}\] Integrating both sides over a sphere of radius \(r\), we find \[
- \frac{1}{\epsilon_0} \int_V q \mathrm{d} V = - \frac{Q}{\epsilon_0} = \int_V \nabla \cdot \nabla \Phi
\mathrm{d} V.
\tag{18.14}\] The RHS gives (using the divergence theorem) \[
\int_V \nabla \cdot \nabla \Phi \mathrm{d} V = \int_S \nabla \Phi \cdot
\hat{\mathbf{r}} \mathrm{d} S = 4 \pi r^2 \partial_r \Phi \Longrightarrow
\partial_r \Phi = - \frac{Q}{4 \pi \epsilon_0 r^2} \Longrightarrow F_r = - \frac{Qe}{4 \pi \epsilon_0 r^2} .
\tag{18.15}\] So the electron is attracted by the sphere if \(Q > 0\), and repelled if \(Q < 0\).


Even though electrostatic and gravitational forces have a similar mathematical structure, these forces are very different for two reasons. First, gravity is always attractive, because no forms of matter are known to possess negative mass, while electric charge can be positive or negative and objects of similar charge repel each other. Second, gravity is a very weak force, as we explore with the next example.






TipExample



Consider a proton on the surface of the Sun. It is subject to an attractive gravitational force: \[
F_g = - \frac{GM_{\odot} m_p}{R_{\odot }^2} .
\tag{18.16}\] The proton is also subject to an electrostatic force: \[
F_e = \frac{Q_{\odot} e}{4 \pi \epsilon_0 R_{\odot}^2},
\tag{18.17}\] where \(Q_{\odot} \approx \frac{M_{\odot}}{m_p} \delta e\) is the net charge of the Sun, and \(\delta = (N_p - N_e) / N_p\) is the fractional charge imbalance. Gravity and electrostatic forces balance each other when \[
\delta = \frac{4 \pi \epsilon_0 G m_p^2}{e^2} \sim 10^{- 36} .
\tag{18.18}\] The Sun must be very close to neutral, because even a small charge imbalance would cause particles of the same charge as the Sun to be evaporated from the surface.


The argument we have just made for the Sun applies to most astrophysical systems. This implies that the charge imbalance in astronomical objects must be very small. In other words, they are quasi-neutral. As we will see shortly, quasi-neutrality is one of the key characteristics an ionized gas must have to be considered to be plasma. At this point, it is important to remark that, while we will be concerned only with systems that have zero net charge, these systems can still contain electric currents, which give rise to magnetic fields and internal stresses via the Lorentz force.






NoteGoing further: Conservation Laws in Electrodynamics



If we take the divergence of Ampère’s law we find \[
\epsilon_0 \frac{\partial \nabla \cdot \mathbf{E}}{\partial t} +
\nabla \cdot \mathbf{j}= 0.
\tag{18.19}\] Using Gauss’ law \[
\frac{\partial q}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \mathbf{j}= 0.
\tag{18.20}\] So the charge density satisfies a continuity equation, just like the mass density for a fluid (Equation 1.15). In other words, the Maxwell equations imply charge conservation.
It is also possible to show that the Maxwell equations imply conservation of the energy in the electromagnetic field. To see this, consider the work done by the electromagnetic field on a fluid with charge density \(q\) and velocity \(\mathbf{v}\). The Lorentz force per unit volume is \[
\mathbf{f}= q ( \mathbf{E}+ \mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B} ) .
\tag{18.21}\] So the work per unit volume is (using \(\mathbf{j}= q\mathbf{v}\) and Ampère’s law) \[
w =\mathbf{f} \cdot \mathbf{v}= q\mathbf{E} \cdot \mathbf{v}=\mathbf{E}
\cdot \mathbf{j}= \frac{1}{\mu_0} (\nabla \times \mathbf{B}) \cdot
\mathbf{E}- \epsilon_0 \mathbf{E} \cdot \frac{\partial \mathbf{E}}{\partial t} .
\tag{18.22}\] Using the vector identity \[
\mathbf{E} \cdot (\nabla \times \mathbf{B}) =\mathbf{B} \cdot (\nabla \times
\mathbf{E}) - \nabla \cdot (\mathbf{E} \times \mathbf{B})
\tag{18.23}\] and \[
\mathbf{E} \cdot \frac{\partial \mathbf{E}}{\partial t} = \frac{1}{2}
\dfrac{\partial E^2}{\partial t},
\tag{18.24}\] we can write \[
\mathbf{E} \cdot \mathbf{j}= \frac{1}{\mu_0} [\mathbf{B} \cdot
(\nabla \times \mathbf{E}) - \nabla \cdot (\mathbf{E} \times \mathbf{B})] -
\frac{\epsilon_0}{2}  \frac{\partial E^2}{\partial t} .
\tag{18.25}\] We can use Faraday’s law to get rid of \(\nabla \times \mathbf{E}\) to rewrite the last equation as \[
\frac{\partial}{\partial t} \left( \frac{\epsilon_0 E^2}{2} + \frac{B^2}{2 \mu_0} \right) + \nabla \cdot
\left( \frac{1}{\mu_0} \mathbf{E} \times \mathbf{B} \right) = -\mathbf{E}
\cdot \mathbf{j}.
\tag{18.26}\] We can recognize that this is a conservation law in the form \[
\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{EM}}}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \mathbf{S}=
-\mathbf{E} \cdot \mathbf{j}.
\tag{18.27}\] The last term is the work done by the electric field, so we can interpret \(u_{\mathrm{EM}} = \tfrac{1}{2} \epsilon_0 E^2 + \tfrac{B^2}{2 \mu_0}\) as the energy in the electromagnetic field and the vector \(\mathbf{S}= \frac{1}{\mu_0} \mathbf{E} \times \mathbf{B}\), called the Poynting flux, as the flux of electromagnetic energy. Equation 18.26 is also called the Poynting theorem. As we will see in Chapter 19, the equation for energy conservation for a plasma is just the sum of the energy conservation equations for the matter, which we already know as the energy equation (Chapter 6), and the energy conservation equation for the electromagnetic field.




18.1.3 Electromagnetic Waves
The propagation of electromagnetic waves in vacuum can be studied with a similar formalism as that used to study sound waves (Chapter 9). Actually, since Maxwell equations are linear, the derivation of the dispersion relation for electromagnetic waves is simpler than that for sound waves. The starting point are the Maxwell equations in vacuum: \[
\begin{array}{lll}
\nabla \cdot \mathbf{E}= 0, &  & \nabla \cdot \mathbf{B}= 0,\\
\nabla \times \mathbf{E}= - \dfrac{\partial
\mathbf{B}}{\partial t}, &  & \nabla \times \mathbf{B}= \dfrac{1}{c^2}
\dfrac{\partial \mathbf{E}}{\partial t} .
\end{array}
\tag{18.28}\] We look for solutions in the form \[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{E} (t, \mathbf{x}) &= \hat{\mathbf{E}}_0 \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i} (\mathbf{k}
\cdot \mathbf{x}- \omega t)}, \\
\mathbf{B} (t, \mathbf{x}) &=
\hat{\mathbf{B}}_0 \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i} (\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{x}- \omega t)} .
\end{aligned}
\tag{18.29}\] Inserting this ansatz into the first row of Equation 18.28, we obtain \[
\nabla \cdot \mathbf{E}= 0 \Longrightarrow \mathrm{i} \mathbf{k} \cdot
\hat{\mathbf{E}}_0 \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i} (\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{x}- \omega t)} = 0
\Longrightarrow \mathbf{k} \perp \hat{\mathbf{E}}_0
\tag{18.30}\] and, similarly, \(\mathbf{k} \perp \hat{\mathbf{B}}_0\). This means that, differently from sound waves, electromagnetic waves in vacuum are transverse, meaning that \(\mathbf{E}\) and \(\mathbf{B}\) are perpendicular to the direction of propagation of the wave.
From Faraday’s law, we obtain that \[
\mathrm{i} \omega  \hat{\mathbf{B}}_0 \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i} (\mathbf{k} \cdot
\mathbf{x}- \omega t)} = \mathrm{i} \mathbf{k} \times \hat{\mathbf{E}}_0
\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i} (\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{x}- \omega t)} \Longrightarrow
\omega  \hat{\mathbf{B}}_0 =\mathbf{k} \times \hat{\mathbf{E}}_0 .
\tag{18.31}\] This implies that \(\hat{\mathbf{E}}_0 \perp \hat{\mathbf{B}}_0\). From Ampère’s law, we obtain \[
\mathbf{k} \times \hat{\mathbf{B}}_0 = - \frac{\omega}{c^2}
\hat{\mathbf{E}}_0 .
\tag{18.32}\] Substituting Equation 18.32 into Equation 18.31, we obtain (using the properties of the double vector product) \[
\omega  \hat{\mathbf{B}}_0 = - \frac{c^2}{\omega} \mathbf{k} \times
(\mathbf{k} \times \hat{\mathbf{B}}_0) = \cancel{- \frac{c^2}{\omega} \mathbf{k}
(\mathbf{k} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{B}}_0)} + \frac{c^2}{\omega} k^2
\hat{\mathbf{B}}_0 = \frac{c^2}{\omega} k^2  \hat{\mathbf{B}}_0
\Longrightarrow \boxed{\omega^2 = c^2 k^2} .
\tag{18.33}\] So electromagnetic waves satisfy the same dispersion relation as sound waves (Equation 9.18), but with \(c\), the speed of light, instead of the sound speed \(c_s\).

title: 18  Introduction to Plasma
text:
18.2 Plasma

18.2.1 What is a Plasma?
Consider a quasi-neutral gas made of electrons and ions. Assume that, due to a thermal fluctuation, a small overdensity of electrons \(\delta n\) is created in a region with characteristic size \(L\). How large can this fluctuation be?






Figure 18.2: Schematic representation of an overdensity of electrons.



The electrostatic potential created by this overdensity is of order \[
\delta \Phi \sim \frac{L^2 e \delta n}{\epsilon_0} .
\tag{18.34}\] The potential energy of each electron is \[
e \delta \Phi \sim \frac{L^2 e^2 \delta n}{\epsilon_0} .
\tag{18.35}\] Their thermal energy is \(\sim k_B T\) (in thermodynamic equilibrium). Thermal fluctuations should have potential energy comparable to the thermal energy, so \[
\frac{L^2 e^2 \delta n}{\epsilon_0} \sim k_B T \Longrightarrow \frac{\delta n}{n} \sim
\frac{1}{L^2}  \left( \frac{\epsilon_0 k_B T}{ne^2} \right) =: \left(
\frac{\lambda_D}{L} \right)^2,
\tag{18.36}\] where \(n\) is the density of free electrons (we will also write it as \(n_e\)) and we have introduced the Debye length \[
\boxed{\lambda_D = \sqrt{\frac{\epsilon_0 k_B T}{ne^2}} .}
\tag{18.37}\] The Debye length is a characteristic length scale for charge fluctuations in the gas. Over scales \(L \gg \lambda_D\), one can assume that the medium is neutral, if the density of the gas is sufficiently high.
To see this, consider again a uniform gas of electrons and ions. The ion masses are of order \(A m_p \approx 1836 A m_e\), so if ions and electrons have on average the same kinetic energy, as would be expected in equilibrium, \(v_{\mathrm{ions}} \ll v_e\). To a first approximation, we can consider the ions to be static and immersed in a sea of electrons. If electrons are abundant, each ion will then be surrounded by a sea of electrons, which effectively shield its charge hiding it from the other ions, as shown in Figure 18.3.






Figure 18.3: Electron cloud around an ion of charge \(Q\).



It turns out that, in this situation, the electrostatic potential around the ion is \[
\Phi (r) = \frac{Q}{4 \pi \epsilon_0 r} \mathrm{e}^{- r / \lambda_D},
\tag{18.38}\] where \(\lambda_D\) is the Debye length (see the box below). In other words, the Debye length is also the characteristic screening length. However, screening can only take place if electrons are sufficiently mobile to screen each ion. To quantify this, we define the plasma parameter: \[
\Lambda = \frac{4}{3} \pi n \lambda_D^3 = \frac{4 \pi}{3 e^3}  (\epsilon_0 k_B
T)^{3 / 2} n^{- 1 / 2} .
\tag{18.39}\] The plasma parameter is just the number of electrons in each Debye sphere. We say that an ionized gas for which \(\lambda_D \ll L\) and \(\Lambda \gg 1\) is a plasma. Typical plasma parameters for astrophysical systems are given in Table 18.1. As we can see, astrophysical plasmas span a tremendous range in scales.



Table 18.1: Temperature, free electron density, Debye length, and plasma parameters for various systems. The electrons in protoneutron stars and white dwarfs are degenerate (and, in protoneutron stars, relativistic), so for these systems the values computed with the classical formulas are only indicative.

We can derive Equation 18.38 as follows. Consider an ion of charge \(Q\) at the origin, surrounded by electrons with temperature \(T\) and average density \(n_e\), and by other ions, which we assume to have uniform charge density \(e n_e\), so that the plasma is neutral on average. In thermal equilibrium, the electrons follow the Boltzmann distribution. An electron has potential energy \(- e \Phi\), so \[
n (r) = n_e \mathrm{e}^{e \Phi / k_B T} \approx n_e \left( 1 + \frac{e \Phi}{k_B T} \right),
\tag{18.40}\] where we have assumed \(| e \Phi | \ll k_B T\), which is true sufficiently far from the ion. The charge density is then \[
q = e n_e - e n (r) = - \frac{n_e e^2}{k_B T} \Phi ,
\tag{18.41}\] and the Poisson equation (Equation 18.10) becomes \[
\nabla^2 \Phi = \frac{n_e e^2}{\epsilon_0 k_B T} \Phi = \frac{\Phi}{\lambda_D^2} .
\tag{18.42}\] For a spherically symmetric potential, \(\nabla^2 \Phi = \frac{1}{r} \frac{\mathrm{d}^2 (r \Phi)}{\mathrm{d} r^2}\), so \(r \Phi\) satisfies \(\frac{\mathrm{d}^2 (r \Phi)}{\mathrm{d} r^2} = \frac{r \Phi}{\lambda_D^2}\). The solution that does not grow at large \(r\) is \(r \Phi = A \mathrm{e}^{- r / \lambda_D}\). Close to the ion, the potential must be that of the ion alone, \(\Phi \approx Q / (4 \pi \epsilon_0 r)\), so \(A = Q / (4 \pi \epsilon_0)\), and we recover Equation 18.38.




18.2.2 When is a Plasma a Fluid?
In Chapter 1 we have seen that a gas can be treated as a fluid if the mean free path \(\lambda\) of its particles is small compared to the scales of interest. In a plasma, the particles interact via the Coulomb force. Two particles are strongly deflected if they come so close that their electrostatic energy is comparable to their thermal energy, \(e^2 / (4 \pi \epsilon_0 r) \sim k_B T\). This gives a cross section \(\sigma \sim \pi [e^2 / (4 \pi \epsilon_0 k_B T)]^2\), and a mean free path \(\lambda \sim 1 / (n \sigma)\). Many weak collisions at larger distances make the particles lose their direction somewhat faster, and a more careful calculation gives \[
\lambda \approx 100\,\mathrm{m} \left( \frac{T}{1\,\mathrm{K}} \right)^2 \left( \frac{n}{1\,\mathrm{cm^{-3}}} \right)^{-1} .
\tag{18.43}\] Note that \(\lambda\) increases very quickly with temperature: hot plasmas are almost collisionless.
Magnetic fields change this picture. A particle with charge \(Q\) and mass \(m\) moving with velocity \(v\) perpendicular to a magnetic field \(B\) experiences a Lorentz force \(|Q| v B\) perpendicular to its velocity. So it moves on a circle around the field lines, with radius \(r_L\) given by \[
\frac{m v^2}{r_L} = | Q | v B \Longrightarrow r_L = \frac{m v}{| Q | B} .
\tag{18.44}\] \(r_L\) is called the Larmor radius, or gyroradius. In other words, particles cannot move freely across the magnetic field lines, even if they never collide. On scales much larger than \(r_L\), a magnetized plasma behaves like a fluid in the directions perpendicular to the magnetic field. Along the field lines, instead, particles can travel a distance \(\sim \lambda\). This is why magnetohydrodynamics (Chapter 19) works well even in plasmas in which collisions are rare. However, processes along the field lines, such as heat conduction, can be very different from those in an ordinary gas.






TipExample



Consider the warm interstellar medium, with \(T \sim 10^4\,\mathrm{K}\), \(n \sim 1\,\mathrm{cm^{-3}}\), and \(B \sim 0.3\,\mathrm{nT}\) (\(3\,\mu\mathrm{G}\)). From Equation 18.43, \(\lambda \sim 10^{10}\,\mathrm{m}\), which is much smaller than the scales of interest, \(\sim 1\,\mathrm{pc} \approx 3 \times 10^{16}\,\mathrm{m}\). A thermal proton has velocity \(v \sim \sqrt{k_B T / m_p} \approx 9\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}\), so its Larmor radius is \(r_L \approx 300\,\mathrm{km}\), even smaller.
The solar wind close to the Earth is different. It has \(T \sim 10^5\,\mathrm{K}\) and \(n \sim 5\,\mathrm{cm^{-3}}\), so \(\lambda \sim 2 \times 10^{11}\,\mathrm{m}\), about the distance between the Earth and the Sun. The solar wind is essentially collisionless! However, the magnetic field is \(B \sim 5\,\mathrm{nT}\) (\(5 \times 10^{-5}\,\mathrm{G}\)), so a thermal proton has \(r_L \approx 60\,\mathrm{km}\). On large scales, the solar wind can still be described as a magnetized fluid.




18.2.3 Cold Plasma Approximation
The cold plasma approximation is used to study the propagation of electromagnetic waves, particularly radio waves, in the interstellar medium. As the name suggests, in the cold plasma approximation we ignore the thermal motion of the electrons. We also take the ions to be stationary. Let’s consider the propagation of an electromagnetic wave through such a medium, as illustrated in Figure 18.4.






Figure 18.4: Lorentz force experienced by an electron due to a passing electromagnetic wave.



The Lorentz force experienced by an electron is (assuming \(v \ll c\)): \[
\mathbf{F}= - e ( \mathbf{E}+ \mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B} ) \approx - e\mathbf{E}.
\tag{18.45}\] So, if we take \(\mathbf{E}= \hat{\mathbf{E}}_0 \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i} (\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{x}- \omega t)}\) and \(\mathbf{v}= \hat{\mathbf{v}}_0 \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i} (\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{x}- \omega t)}\), we have \[
\hat{\mathbf{v}}_0 = \frac{e \hat{\mathbf{E}}_0}{\mathrm{i} \omega m_e} .
\tag{18.46}\] The induced current density in the plasma is \[
\hat{\mathbf{j}} = - ne \hat{\mathbf{v}}_0 = \left( \frac{\mathrm{i}
ne^2}{\omega m_e} \right)  \hat{\mathbf{E}}_0 = : \sigma \hat{\mathbf{E}}_0,
\tag{18.47}\] where we have introduced the conductivity \(\sigma\). Charge conservation is \[
\frac{\partial q}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \mathbf{j}= 0 \Longrightarrow -
\mathrm{i} \omega \hat{q}_0 + \mathrm{i} \mathbf{k} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{j}}_0 = 0
\Longrightarrow \hat{q}_0 = \frac{\mathbf{k} \cdot
\hat{\mathbf{j}}_0}{\omega} = \frac{\sigma}{\omega} \mathbf{k} \cdot
\hat{\mathbf{E}}_0 .
\tag{18.48}\] Gauss’ law reads \[
\mathrm{i} \mathbf{k} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{E}}_0 = \frac{\hat{q}_0}{\epsilon_0} \Longrightarrow
\mathrm{i} \mathbf{k} \cdot \left( 1 - \frac{\sigma}{\mathrm{i} \omega \epsilon_0}
\right) \hat{\mathbf{E}}_0 = 0.
\tag{18.49}\] Introducing the dielectric constant \[
\begin{aligned}
\epsilon &= 1 - \frac{\sigma}{\mathrm{i} \omega \epsilon_0} = 1 - \left(
\frac{\omega_p}{\omega} \right)^2, \\
\omega_p &= \sqrt{\frac{ne^2}{\epsilon_0 m_e}} \\
&\approx 5.6 \times 10^4\,\mathrm{s^{-1}} \left( \frac{n}{1\,\mathrm{cm}^{- 3}} \right)^{1 /
2} .
\end{aligned}
\tag{18.50}\] To evaluate \(\omega_p\), we have used \(1\,\mathrm{cm^{-3}} = 10^6\,\mathrm{m^{-3}}\). The corresponding frequency is \(f_p = \omega_p / 2 \pi \approx 9\,\mathrm{kHz}\,(n / 1\,\mathrm{cm^{-3}})^{1/2}\). \(\omega_p\) is called the plasma frequency, and \(\epsilon\) (not to be confused with the internal energy \(\varepsilon\), or with the vacuum permittivity \(\epsilon_0\)) is the dielectric constant. The plasma frequency has a simple physical meaning: if the electrons are displaced with respect to the ions, the electric field pulls them back, and they oscillate around their equilibrium positions with angular frequency \(\omega_p\) (Exercise 18.1). Note also that \(\lambda_D = v_{\mathrm{th}} / \omega_p\), where \(v_{\mathrm{th}} = \sqrt{k_B T / m_e}\) is the thermal velocity of the electrons. In other words, the Debye length is the distance traveled by a thermal electron during one plasma oscillation.
With these definitions, we find that the Maxwell equations reduce to \[
\begin{array}{lll}
\mathrm{i} \mathbf{k} \cdot \epsilon \hat{\mathbf{E}}_0 = 0, &  & \mathrm{i}
\mathbf{k} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{B}}_0 = 0,\\
\mathrm{i} \mathbf{k} \times \hat{\mathbf{E}}_0 = \mathrm{i} \omega
\hat{\mathbf{B}}_0, &  & \mathrm{i} \mathbf{k} \times \hat{\mathbf{B}}_0 = -
\mathrm{i} \frac{\omega}{c^2} \epsilon \hat{\mathbf{E}}_0 .
\end{array}
\tag{18.51}\] These can be solved in the same way as the vacuum Maxwell equations to find the dispersion relation for electromagnetic waves in a cold plasma \[
c^2 k^2 = \epsilon \omega^2 \Longrightarrow k = \frac{\omega}{c}  \sqrt{1 -
\left( \frac{\omega_p}{\omega } \right)^2} \Longrightarrow \boxed{k =
\frac{1}{c}  \sqrt{\omega^2 - \omega_p^2} .}
\tag{18.52}\] For example, if the wave is propagating in the \(z\)-direction, \(\mathbf{k}= k \hat{\mathbf{z}}\). Then

If \(\omega < \omega_p\), then \(k\) is imaginary and the wave cannot propagate. Its amplitude decays exponentially over a distance \(\sim c / \omega_p\): \[
\mathbf{E}= \hat{\mathbf{E}}_0 \mathrm{e}^{- \mathrm{i} \omega t} \mathrm{e}^{- \frac{z}{c}
\sqrt{\omega_p^2 - \omega^2}} .
\tag{18.53}\] Note that this is not due to dissipation. The electrons respond to the wave fast enough to cancel its electric field, so the wave is reflected by the plasma. This is the same mathematics we found for sound waves below the acoustic cutoff frequency (Equation 10.21).
If \(\omega > \omega_p\) the wave can propagate, but different frequencies propagate at different speeds: \[
v_g = \frac{\partial \omega}{\partial k} = c \sqrt{1 -
\frac{\omega_p^2}{\omega^2}} .
\tag{18.54}\] This leads to the phenomenon of dispersion, which can be used to measure the column density of free electrons between us and sources of radio pulses, such as pulsars and fast radio bursts, and hence to estimate their distance, as illustrated in Figure 18.5.






Figure 18.5: Different arrival time of a fast radio burst at different frequencies as a result of dispersion in the ISM: the first fast radio burst, FRB 010724. From Lorimer (2018) (figure by E. Keane); © Springer Nature, reproduced for non-commercial educational use and not covered by the license of these notes.










TipExample



Consider the ionosphere of the Earth, which has \(n_e \sim 10^6\,\mathrm{cm^{-3}}\). Its plasma frequency is \(f_p \approx 9\,\mathrm{MHz}\). AM radio, with \(f \sim 1\,\mathrm{MHz}\), is reflected by the ionosphere. This is why AM stations can be received beyond the horizon, especially at night. FM radio and TV, with \(f \sim 100\,\mathrm{MHz}\), pass through the ionosphere. For the same reason, radio astronomy at frequencies below \(\sim 10\,\mathrm{MHz}\) is only possible from space.

18.3 In-class worksheet
Fast radio bursts are thought to be millisecond-long broad-band radio flares, produced during particularly violent magnetar flares, and possibly other astrophysical events. As the radio waves propagate from the source to Earth through the interstellar medium, the signal is dispersed, as shown in Figure 18.6:

18.4 Exercises

Exercise 18.1 (Plasma oscillations and the Debye length) Consider a slab of plasma with uniform electron density \(n_e\). The ions are at rest and have uniform charge density \(e n_e\). At \(t = 0\), all electrons in the slab are displaced by a small distance \(x\) in the direction perpendicular to the slab.

Show that the displacement creates an electric field \(E = n_e e x / \epsilon_0\) inside the slab.
Show that the electrons oscillate around their equilibrium positions with angular frequency \(\omega_p = \sqrt{n_e e^2 / (\epsilon_0 m_e)}\).
Show that \(\lambda_D = v_{\mathrm{th}} / \omega_p\), where \(v_{\mathrm{th}} = \sqrt{k_B T / m_e}\). Interpret this result.
Compute \(\omega_p\), \(f_p = \omega_p / 2 \pi\), and \(\lambda_D\) for the ionosphere of the Earth (\(n_e \sim 10^6\,\mathrm{cm^{-3}}\), \(T \sim 10^3\,\mathrm{K}\)) and for the warm interstellar medium (\(n_e \sim 1\,\mathrm{cm^{-3}}\), \(T \sim 10^4\,\mathrm{K}\)).

title: 19  The MHD Equations
text:
19.1 Lorentz Force
These notes present a concise derivation of the equations of magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) and a discussion of the underlying assumptions. We consider a quasi-neutral gas of ions and electrons immersed in a magnetic field. Let \(\mathbf{w}_e\) and \(\mathbf{w}_i\) be the drift velocities of electrons and ions, respectively. The Lorentz force experienced by each electron is \[
\mathbf{F}_e = - e \mathbf{w}_e \times \mathbf{B}.
\tag{19.1}\] The force experienced by the ions is \[
\mathbf{F}_i = Ze \mathbf{w}_i \times \mathbf{B}.
\tag{19.2}\] So the total force per unit volume is \[
\mathbf{f}= n_e \mathbf{F}_e + n_i \mathbf{F}_i = e (n_i
Z\mathbf{w}_i - n_e \mathbf{w}_e) \times \mathbf{B} =: \mathbf{j}
\times \mathbf{B}.
\tag{19.3}\] Here \(\mathbf{j}\) is the electric current density, measured in \(\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}\). Note that we have not included the electric force. The electric force per unit volume is \(q \mathbf{E}\), where \(q\) is the charge density, and it is negligible because the plasma is quasi-neutral, \(q \approx 0\) (Chapter 18).
The equations of MHD are just the “usual” hydrodynamics equations with the addition of the Lorentz force on the RHS: \[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\mathrm{d} \rho}{\mathrm{d} t} &= - \rho \nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}, \\
\rho \frac{\mathrm{d} \mathbf{v}}{\mathrm{d} t} &= \boxed{\mathbf{j} \times \mathbf{B}} - \nabla p, \\
\rho \frac{\mathrm{d} \varepsilon}{\mathrm{d} t} &= - p \nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{19.4}\] These equations look deceptively simple. The real complication is that \(\mathbf{j}\) and \(\mathbf{B}\) are not prescribed, but are self-consistently produced by the fluid. We have also implicitly made the following assumption:
This assumption is satisfied in most situations encountered in terrestrial and astrophysical applications, because the currents are sufficiently weak and the charge densities sufficiently large that we can treat the plasma as being a single fluid. This can be violated in very tenuous plasmas, for example in the magnetosphere of dying pulsars, in which the field and spin have decayed to the point that pair production is no longer efficient. In this case, one needs to go beyond magnetohydrodynamics and use the multi-fluid magnetohydrodynamics equations, or employ a fully kinetic treatment. Another situation in which this assumption can fail is if the degree of ionization of the plasma is small, so there is drift between the charged component of the gas and the neutrals, ambipolar diffusion. As we will see in Chapter 20, ambipolar diffusion plays an important role, for example, in star formation.

title: 19  The MHD Equations
text: Assumption 19.1 (Negligible drift momentum) The drift motion of the charged particles in the plasma that gives rise to the current is sufficiently small that we can neglect its contribution to the macroscopic momentum \(\rho \mathbf{v}\). In other words, in a frame in which \(\mathbf{v}= 0\), we have \(m_i n_i \mathbf{w}_i + m_e n_e \mathbf{w}_e \approx 0\).

title: 19  The MHD Equations
text:
19.2 Ohm’s Law
We need two more equations, in addition to the equation of state, to close Equation 19.4. A first equation is the equation prescribing how currents \(\mathbf{j}\) arise in the plasma. The simplest model for the current is to assume that it is proportional to the electric field.

Assumption 19.2 (Ohm’s law) The electric current in the plasma \(\mathbf{j}\) is proportional to the electric field \(\mathbf{E}'\) in the frame of the plasma (in which \(\mathbf{v}= 0\)): \(\mathbf{j}= \sigma \mathbf{E}'\).

The quantity \(\sigma\) is called the electrical conductivity, it is the inverse of the electrical resistivity \(1 / \sigma\), which you might be familiar with from electromagnetism. In SI units1 \[
[\mathbf{E}] = \mathrm{V\,m^{-1}},
\qquad [\mathbf{j}] = \mathrm{A\,m^{-2}},
\tag{19.5}\] so the units of electrical conductivity are \[
[\sigma] = \mathrm{A\,V^{-1}\,m^{-1}} = \mathrm{S\,m^{-1}} .
\tag{19.6}\] Here \(\mathrm{S} = \mathrm{A\,V^{-1}}\) is the siemens, the inverse of the ohm. Again, note that in SI units the current is an independent quantity, measured in ampere, so the Maxwell and MHD equations contain the constants \(\epsilon_0\) and \(\mu_0\). Be very careful not to mix Gaussian and SI units, because the equations are different in the two cases (Chapter 18).
One subtlety with the new assumption is what we mean for the “electric field in the frame of the plasma”. The hydrodynamics equations are invariant with respect to Galilean transformations, that is, if \(\mathbf{u}\) is a velocity in the Eulerian frame, then in the fluid frame we have \[
\mathbf{u}' =\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{v}.
\tag{19.7}\] On the other hand, Maxwell equations are invariant with respect to Lorentz transformations. As such, Maxwell equations and the equations of non-relativistic hydrodynamics are fundamentally incompatible. To be able to put them together in a consistent way, we need to assume that \(\mathbf{E}\) and \(\mathbf{B}\) transform according to Lorentz transformations in the nonrelativistic limit.

Assumption 19.3 (Nonrelativistic limit) We assume \(v \ll c\), \(| \mathbf{E} | \ll c | \mathbf{B} |\), and \(\left| \epsilon_0 \frac{\partial \mathbf{E}}{\partial t} \right| \ll | \mathbf{j} |\). The second two assumptions are needed to ensure that charges are not relativistic and the plasma quasi-neutral.

Under these assumptions, it is possible to show that \[
\mathbf{B}' =\mathbf{B}, \qquad \mathbf{E}' =\mathbf{E}+ \mathbf{v}
\times \mathbf{B}, \qquad \mathbf{j}' =\mathbf{j}.
\tag{19.8}\] Accordingly, Ohm’s law becomes \[
\mathbf{j}' = \sigma \mathbf{E}' \Longrightarrow \mathbf{j}= \sigma \left(
\mathbf{E}+ \mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B} \right) .
\tag{19.9}\] In Ampère’s law, \[
\nabla \times \mathbf{B}= \mu_0 \mathbf{j}+ \frac{1}{c^2}  \frac{\partial
\mathbf{E}}{\partial t},
\tag{19.10}\] where we have used \(\mu_0 \epsilon_0 = 1 / c^2\), we can drop the displacement current (Assumption 19.3). This makes sense, because \(E \sim v B\), so if the fields change over a length \(L\) and a time \(T \sim L / v\), the displacement current is of order \(v B / (c^2 T) \sim (v / c)^2 B / L\), while \(\nabla \times \mathbf{B}\) is of order \(B / L\). So we obtain \[
\nabla \times \mathbf{B}= \mu_0 \mathbf{j}.
\tag{19.11}\] Then the Lorentz force becomes \[
\boxed{\mathbf{f}=\mathbf{j} \times \mathbf{B}= \frac{1}{\mu_0}  (\nabla
\times \mathbf{B}) \times \mathbf{B}.}
\tag{19.12}\] With this, we have completely eliminated the current from the MHD equations: \[
\boxed{\rho \frac{\mathrm{d} \mathbf{v}}{\mathrm{d} t} = \frac{1}{\mu_0}
(\nabla \times \mathbf{B}) \times \mathbf{B}- \nabla p.}
\tag{19.13}\] We still need another equation for \(\mathbf{B}\) to completely close the MHD equations.

title: 19  The MHD Equations
text:
19.3 Faraday’s Law
The missing equation is given by Faraday’s law, also known as the induction equation: \[
\frac{\partial \mathbf{B}}{\partial t} = - \nabla \times \mathbf{E}.
\tag{19.14}\] Here, we use again Ohm’s law to eliminate \(\mathbf{E}\): \[
\frac{1}{\sigma} \mathbf{j} =\mathbf{E}+
\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B} \Longrightarrow \mathbf{E}= \frac{1}{\sigma}
\mathbf{j}- \mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B} .
\tag{19.15}\] We use again Ampère’s law to remove \(\mathbf{j}= \frac{1}{\mu_0} \nabla \times \mathbf{B}\): \[
\mathbf{E}= \frac{1}{\mu_0 \sigma} \nabla \times \mathbf{B}- \mathbf{v}
\times \mathbf{B} =: \eta \nabla \times \mathbf{B}- \mathbf{v}
\times \mathbf{B} .
\tag{19.16}\] Inserting this back into the induction equation yields: \[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial \mathbf{B}}{\partial t} &= - \nabla \times \mathbf{E} \\
&= \nabla \times (\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B}) - \nabla \times
(\eta \nabla \times \mathbf{B}) .
\end{aligned}
\tag{19.17}\] If \(\eta\) is constant, then \[
\nabla \times (\nabla \times \mathbf{B}) = \nabla (\nabla \cdot \mathbf{B})
- \nabla^2 \mathbf{B},
\tag{19.18}\] so we find \[
\boxed{\frac{\partial \mathbf{B}}{\partial t} = \nabla \times
(\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B}) + \eta \nabla^2 \mathbf{B}.}
\tag{19.19}\] The coefficient \(\eta = 1 / (\mu_0 \sigma)\) has units of \(\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}\) and is called the magnetic diffusivity. Note that some texts use \(\eta\) for the resistivity \(1 / \sigma\) instead. The magnetic diffusivity is extremely small in most astrophysical systems.






TipExample



Consider the warm interstellar medium, with \(T \approx 10^4\,\mathrm{K}\). Its magnetic diffusivity is \(\eta \approx 500\,\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}\) (Equation 20.27). Consider a region of size \(L \sim 1\,\mathrm{pc}\) in which the gas moves with velocity \(v \sim 10\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}\). The ratio between the time it takes for the magnetic field to diffuse over the region, \(L^2 / \eta\), and the time it takes for the gas to cross it, \(L / v\), is \[
\mathrm{R}_M = \frac{L v}{\eta} \sim 6 \times 10^{17} .
\tag{19.20}\] This is the magnetic Reynolds number, which we will discuss in Chapter 20. For comparison, copper has a conductivity of about \(6 \times 10^{7}\,\mathrm{S\,m^{-1}}\), so its magnetic diffusivity is \(1 / (\mu_0 \sigma) \approx 1.3 \times 10^{-2}\,\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}\). A copper bar of length \(1\,\mathrm{m}\) moving with velocity \(1\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) has \(\mathrm{R}_M \sim 100\). In other words, resistivity is negligible in astrophysics, but not in the laboratory. Even liquid-metal experiments designed to study the generation of magnetic fields struggle to reach \(\mathrm{R}_M \sim 10^3\).


This is the last equation. The full set of MHD equations is \[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\mathrm{d} \rho}{\mathrm{d} t} &= - \rho \nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}, \\
\rho \frac{\mathrm{d} \mathbf{v}}{\mathrm{d} t} &= \frac{1}{\mu_0}  (\nabla
\times \mathbf{B}) \times \mathbf{B}- \nabla p - \rho \nabla \Psi, \\
\rho \frac{\mathrm{d} \varepsilon}{\mathrm{d} t} &= - p \nabla \cdot \mathbf{v} + \frac{j^2}{\sigma}, \\
\frac{\partial \mathbf{B}}{\partial t} &= \nabla \times (\mathbf{v} \times
\mathbf{B}) + \eta \nabla^2 \mathbf{B}, \\
\nabla \cdot \mathbf{B} &= 0,
\end{aligned}
\tag{19.21}\] where \(\mathbf{j} = \nabla \times \mathbf{B} / \mu_0\). The last term in the energy equation, \(j^2 / \sigma = \mu_0 \eta j^2\), describes the heating of the plasma by the electric currents, also known as Joule (or Ohmic) heating. It vanishes in ideal MHD. The last equation, \(\nabla \cdot \mathbf{B} = 0\), is a constraint on the initial data. If it is satisfied at \(t = 0\), the induction equation guarantees that it is satisfied at all times, because the divergence of a curl vanishes (see the in-class worksheet).
The first three equations can be converted to the Eulerian frame with the usual substitution \[
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} t} \longrightarrow \frac{\partial}{\partial t} +
(\mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla) .
\tag{19.22}\] If \(\eta = 0\), these are known as the ideal-MHD equations. If \(\eta > 0\), these are called the resistive-MHD equations.

title: 19  The MHD Equations
text:
19.4 Conservation Laws
It is possible to rearrange the terms of the momentum equation to obtain an equation that shows the conservation of the linear momentum: \[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
& \frac{\partial (\rho \mathbf{v})}{\partial t} \\
& \quad + \nabla \cdot \biggl[ \rho \mathbf{v} \otimes \mathbf{v}+ \Bigl( p + \frac{B^2}{2 \mu_0}
\Bigr) \mathbf{I} \\
& \qquad\qquad - \frac{\mathbf{B} \otimes \mathbf{B}}{\mu_0} \biggr]
=\mathbf{f},
\end{aligned}}
\tag{19.23}\] where \(\mathbf{f}\) is some external force, e.g., gravity. To derive this equation, we use the vector identity \[
(\nabla \times \mathbf{B}) \times \mathbf{B} = (\mathbf{B} \cdot \nabla) \mathbf{B} - \nabla \left( \frac{B^2}{2} \right)
\tag{19.24}\] and the fact that, since \(\nabla \cdot \mathbf{B} = 0\), \[
\nabla \cdot (\mathbf{B} \otimes \mathbf{B}) = (\mathbf{B} \cdot \nabla) \mathbf{B} + \mathbf{B} (\nabla \cdot \mathbf{B}) = (\mathbf{B} \cdot \nabla) \mathbf{B} .
\tag{19.25}\] So the Lorentz force can be written as the divergence of a tensor, \(\frac{1}{\mu_0} (\nabla \times \mathbf{B}) \times \mathbf{B} = - \nabla \cdot \left[ \frac{B^2}{2 \mu_0} \mathbf{I} - \frac{\mathbf{B} \otimes \mathbf{B}}{\mu_0} \right]\), and the rest of the derivation is the same as in Chapter 6. Here, we limit ourselves to discuss a couple of the consequences of this equation. The first is that the magnetic field does not contribute to the momentum \(\rho \mathbf{v}\), consistently with Assumption 19.1. This is not the case in relativistic MHD, in which the inertia of the electromagnetic field is also taken into account. Second, we see that the Lorentz force splits into two components: one that resembles an additional pressure term \(B^2 / 2 \mu_0\), plus a term proportional to \(\mathbf{B} \otimes \mathbf{B}\). We will discuss these terms in more detail in Chapter 21.
The energy conservation equation now takes into account both the gas energy and the energy in the electromagnetic field and can be obtained by combining the gas-dynamics energy equation with the Poynting theorem. For simplicity, we consider ideal MHD (\(\eta = 0\)). The equation describing the energy conservation for the gas (Equation 6.22) is \[
\begin{aligned}
& \frac{\partial}{\partial t} \left[ \rho \left( \varepsilon + \tfrac{1}{2} v^2 \right) \right] + \nabla \cdot \left[ \left( \rho \varepsilon + \tfrac{1}{2} \rho v^2 + p \right) \mathbf{v} \right] \\
& \qquad =\mathbf{f} \cdot \mathbf{v}+ (\mathbf{j} \times \mathbf{B}) \cdot
\mathbf{v} .
\end{aligned}
\tag{19.26}\] This is just the usual energy equation, with the inclusion of a new term representing the work done by the Lorentz force. The latter can be rewritten using Equation 19.16 as \[
(\mathbf{j} \times \mathbf{B}) \cdot \mathbf{v}= - (\mathbf{v} \times
\mathbf{B}) \cdot \mathbf{j}= \mathbf{E} \cdot \mathbf{j}.
\tag{19.27}\] You might recognize this as being the energy sink term in the Poynting theorem (Equation 18.26), which reads \[
\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{EM}}}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \mathbf{S}= -
\mathbf{j} \cdot \mathbf{E},
\tag{19.28}\] where \(u_{\mathrm{EM}}\) is the electromagnetic field energy, which in our case is: \[
u_{\mathrm{EM}} = \frac{\epsilon_0 E^2}{2} + \frac{B^2}{2 \mu_0} \approx \frac{B^2}{2 \mu_0} =
u_{\mathrm{B}},
\tag{19.29}\] consistently with our assumption that the dynamics is nonrelativistic. The Poynting vector is, using again Equation 19.16: \[
\mathbf{S}= \frac{1}{\mu_0}  (\mathbf{E} \times \mathbf{B}) =
\frac{\mathbf{B} \times (\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B})}{\mu_0} .
\tag{19.30}\] Combining Equation 19.26 and Equation 19.28, we obtain \[
\begin{aligned}
& \frac{\partial}{\partial t} \left[ \rho \left( \varepsilon + \tfrac{1}{2} v^2 \right) + u_{\mathrm{B}} \right] \\
& \quad + \nabla \cdot \left[ \left( \rho \varepsilon + \tfrac{1}{2} \rho v^2 + p \right) \mathbf{v}+\mathbf{S} \right] =\mathbf{f} \cdot \mathbf{v}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{19.31}\] In full form: \[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
& \partial_t  \left[ \rho \left( \varepsilon + \tfrac{1}{2} v^2
\right) + \frac{B^2}{2 \mu_0} \right] \\
& \quad + \nabla \cdot \biggl[ \left( \rho \varepsilon + \tfrac{1}{2} \rho v^2 + p \right)
\mathbf{v} \\
& \qquad\qquad + \frac{\mathbf{B} \times (\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B})}{\mu_0}
\biggr] =\mathbf{f} \cdot \mathbf{v}.
\end{aligned}}
\tag{19.32}\] This equation highlights the fact that magnetic and fluid energies are not separately conserved, but their sum is. In other words, it is possible to convert gas kinetic energy into magnetic energy (dynamo effect) or magnetic energy into kinetic and internal energy (magnetic reconnection, Chapter 20). In resistive MHD, Equation 19.32 still holds. In this case, Equation 19.27 has an additional term, \(- j^2 / \sigma\), and the Poynting flux has an additional term proportional to \(\eta\). However, these are exactly compensated by the Joule heating in the energy equation of the gas. In other words, the magnetic energy dissipated by the electric currents is transferred to the internal energy of the gas.

title: 19  The MHD Equations
text:
19.6 Exercises

Exercise 19.1 (Angular momentum of the solar wind)  

Starting from the equations of ideal MHD, show that the angular momentum of the plasma, \[
\mathbf{J} = \int_V \mathbf{r} \times \rho \mathbf{v} \mathrm{d} V,
\tag{19.34}\] subject to an external force per unit volume \(\mathbf{f}\), satisfies \[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\mathrm{d} \mathbf{J}}{\mathrm{d} t} &= \int_V \mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{f} \mathrm{d} V \\
&\quad {} - \oint_S \biggl[ (\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathrm{d} \mathbf{S}) (\mathbf{r} \times
\rho \mathbf{v}) \\
&\qquad\quad {} + (p + B^2 / 2 \mu_0) \mathbf{r}
\times \mathrm{d} \mathbf{S} \\
&\qquad\quad {} - (\mathbf{r} \times
\mathbf{B}) (\mathbf{B} \cdot \mathrm{d} \mathbf{S}) / \mu_0 \biggr] .
\end{aligned}
\tag{19.35}\] [Hint. Follow the steps of Exercise 6.1.]
Assume that the magnetic field is stationary in a frame rotating with the angular velocity of the Sun. Show that if the solar wind is infinitely conducting, then (in cylindrical coordinates \(R, \phi, z\)) \[
B_{\phi} v_R = (v_{\phi} - \Omega R) B_R,
\tag{19.36}\] where \(\Omega\) is the angular velocity of the Sun.
Let \(\dot{J}\) be the \(z\)-component of the torque across a cylinder of radius \(R\) and height \(2 R\). Assume that \(\dot{J}\) does not depend on \(R\), and neglect the flux of angular momentum through the top and bottom of the cylinder. Show that \(\dot{J}\) can be written as \[
- \dot{J} = 2 \pi \int_{- R}^R \left( R \rho v_R v_{\phi} - R
\frac{B_{\phi} B_R}{\mu_0} \right) R \mathrm{d} z.
\tag{19.37}\] Assume that the expression in parentheses is independent of \(z\), and that \(4 \pi \rho R^2 v_R\), the mass flux of the solar wind through the cylinder, is a constant. Show that \[
- \frac{\dot{J}}{4 \pi \rho R^2 v_R} = Rv_{\phi}  \left( 1 - \frac{B_R^2}{\mu_0 \rho v_R^2} \right) + \frac{B_R^2}{\mu_0 \rho v_R^2} \Omega R^2 .
\tag{19.38}\]
There is a radius, \(R_A\), called the Alfvén radius where the radial Alfvén speed \(v_A = B_R / \sqrt{\mu_0 \rho}\) is equal to \(v_R\). Evaluate the angular momentum loss per unit mass at this radius and show that it is equal to \(\Omega R_A^2\).
If \(R_A\) is 10 \(R_{\odot}\), approximately what fraction of its mass must the Sun lose to slow its rotation down by a factor of 2? Take the moment of inertia of the Sun to be \(0.06 M_{\odot} R_{\odot}^2\). What fraction of its mass has the Sun lost in 5 billion years if the solar wind was steady and the number density at the Earth is \(10\,\mathrm{cm^{-3}}\) and the velocity is \(300\,\mathrm{km/s}\)?
