title: 20  Flux Freezing
text:
20.1 The Ideal-MHD Limit
Flux freezing is an important phenomenon in highly conducting plasmas. In these notes, we derive flux freezing in ideal magnetohydrodynamics (MHD), however it is important to remark that flux freezing also applies beyond ideal MHD, at least in an approximate way. We also discuss the role of flux freezing in the context of some important astrophysical systems. The key equation we will consider is the induction equation (or Faraday’s Law), which reads (when \(\eta = \mathrm{const}\), see Equation 19.19): \[
\frac{\partial \mathbf{B}}{\partial t} = \nabla \times (\mathbf{v} \times
\mathbf{B}) + \eta \nabla^2 \mathbf{B}.
\tag{20.1}\]
Let \(L\) and \(V\) be characteristic length and velocity scales for the plasma. We can introduce the dimensionless time and space coordinates and velocity \[
\hat{t} = t \frac{V}{L}, \qquad \hat{x} = \frac{x}{L}, \qquad
\hat{\mathbf{v}} = \frac{\mathbf{v}}{V} .
\tag{20.2}\] Faraday’s law can be written as \[
\frac{V}{L}  \frac{\partial \mathbf{B}}{\partial \hat{t}} = \frac{V}{L}
\hat{\nabla} \times (\hat{\mathbf{v}} \times \mathbf{B}) + \frac{\eta}{L^2}  \hat{\nabla}^2 \mathbf{B}.
\tag{20.3}\] That is \[
\frac{\partial \mathbf{B}}{\partial \hat{t}} = \hat{\nabla} \times
(\hat{\mathbf{v}} \times \mathbf{B}) + \left( \frac{\eta}{LV}
\right)  \hat{\nabla}^2 \mathbf{B}= \hat{\nabla} \times (\hat{\mathbf{v}}
\times \mathbf{B}) + \frac{1}{\mathrm{R}_M}  \hat{\nabla}^2 \mathbf{B}.
\tag{20.4}\] We have introduced the magnetic Reynolds number, by analogy with the Reynolds number of Equation 17.16, \[
\mathrm{R}_M = \frac{LV}{\eta} .
\tag{20.5}\] The magnetic Reynolds number measures the relative importance of advection and resistivity in the evolution of the magnetic field. It is analogous to the “usual” Reynolds number, which measures the ratio of inertial to viscous forces in a fluid. When \(\mathrm{R}_M \gg 1\), we say that we are in the ideal-MHD limit. As we have seen in Chapter 19, \(\mathrm{R}_M\) is enormous in most astrophysical systems, for example \(\mathrm{R}_M \sim 6 \times 10^{17}\) in the warm interstellar medium.
In the ideal-MHD limit, the Faraday law simplifies to \[
\frac{\partial \mathbf{B}}{\partial t} = \nabla \times (\mathbf{v} \times
\mathbf{B}) \Longrightarrow \frac{\partial \mathbf{B}}{\partial t} + \nabla
\times (\mathbf{B} \times \mathbf{v}) = 0.
\tag{20.6}\] Remarkably, this is identical to the vorticity equation for a barotropic, inviscid fluid (Equation 13.6): \[
\frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\omega}}{\partial t} + \nabla \times (\boldsymbol{\omega}
\times \mathbf{v}) = 0.
\tag{20.7}\] The analogy between vorticity and magnetic field plays an important role in our understanding of MHD phenomena such as dynamos and is sometimes known as the Batchelor’s analogy.
Consider now a surface \(S (t)\) that moves with the fluid, and the magnetic flux across it \[
\Phi (t) = \int_{S (t)} \mathbf{B} \cdot \mathrm{d} \mathbf{A} .
\tag{20.8}\] The flux can change for two reasons: because \(\mathbf{B}\) changes with time, and because the surface moves. In a time \(\mathrm{d} t\), each element \(\mathrm{d} \mathbf{l}\) of the boundary \(C (t)\) of the surface sweeps an area \(\mathbf{v} \mathrm{d} t \times \mathrm{d} \mathbf{l}\), so the boundary adds a flux \(\mathbf{B} \cdot (\mathbf{v} \mathrm{d} t \times \mathrm{d} \mathbf{l}) = - (\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B}) \cdot \mathrm{d} \mathbf{l} \, \mathrm{d} t\). Using Stokes’ theorem, we find \[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\mathrm{d} \Phi}{\mathrm{d} t} &= \int_{S (t)} \frac{\partial \mathbf{B}}{\partial t} \cdot \mathrm{d} \mathbf{A} - \oint_{C (t)} (\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B}) \cdot \mathrm{d} \mathbf{l} \\
&= \int_{S (t)} \left[ \frac{\partial \mathbf{B}}{\partial t} - \nabla \times (\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B}) \right] \cdot \mathrm{d} \mathbf{A} = 0,
\end{aligned}
}
\tag{20.9}\] where we have used Equation 20.6 in the last step. In other words, the magnetic flux across any surface co-moving with the flow is constant in ideal MHD. The same argument applied to the vorticity gives Kelvin’s circulation theorem (Equation 13.7): the circulation \(\mathcal{C} = \oint_{C (t)} \mathbf{v} \cdot \mathrm{d} \mathbf{l} = \int_{S (t)} \boldsymbol{\omega} \cdot \mathrm{d} \mathbf{A}\) around a curve moving with a barotropic, inviscid fluid is conserved.
This fact is called flux freezing and is one of the most important properties of MHD. To understand this consider a magnetic flux tube. As the name suggests, a flux tube is an imaginary bundle of magnetic field lines dragged by the plasma. This is illustrated in Figure 20.1.
Consider the surface bounding the flux tube on the sides. This surface is such that the magnetic flux across it is zero, since there is no component of the field perpendicular to it. If we let this surface move with the plasma velocity, the flux freezing condition requires the magnetic field to deform to stay always parallel to it, as illustrated in Figure 20.1. In other words, the magnetic field is dragged by the plasma as if it was painted on the fluid elements. As we will see shortly, flux freezing has other important consequences.
At the microscopic level, the reason why flux freezing occurs in highly conducting plasmas is that the charged particles are “stuck” to the magnetic field lines1. Another way to think about flux freezing is in terms of induced currents. In order for the magnetic field lines to drift with respect to the plasma with velocity \(\mathbf{v}_d\), one would need to induce an electric field (in the plasma frame) \[
\mathbf{E}' = \mathbf{v}_d \times \mathbf{B}
\tag{20.10}\] which corresponds to a current \(\mathbf{j}' = \sigma \mathbf{E}'\). However, \(\sigma \rightarrow \infty\) (that is, \(\eta \rightarrow 0\)) in the ideal-MHD limit, meaning that an infinite current is required to cause the field lines to slip.

title: 20  Flux Freezing
text:
Figure 20.1: Effect of flux freezing.






20.1.1 Magnetic Field Amplification
Flux freezing also implies that, if a flux tube is compressed by the flow, then its magnetic field intensity is amplified. To see this, consider the situation illustrated in Figure 20.2.






Figure 20.2: Field amplification from the compression of a magnetic flux tube: a wide tube of cross-section \(A_1\) and field \(\mathbf{B}_1\) is squeezed from the sides by a velocity \(\mathbf{v}\) into a thinner tube of cross-section \(A_2\) and field \(\mathbf{B}_2\). Redrawn after Kulsrud (2005).



When a flux tube is compressed and its area changes from \(A_1\) to \(A_2\), the B-field strength needs to change in such a way so that the magnetic flux remains unchanged: \[
A_1 B_1 = A_2 B_2 .
\tag{20.11}\] So the magnetic field strength must be amplified: \[
B_2 = \frac{A_1}{A_2} B_1 .
\tag{20.12}\] It is instructive to compare this with the rate at which the plasma density is changed during the same process. In this case, the quantity that is conserved is the mass of the plasma in the flux tube, so \[
\rho A \ell = \mathrm{const} \Longrightarrow \rho_1 A_1 \ell = \rho_2 A_2 \ell
\Longrightarrow \rho_2 = \frac{A_1}{A_2} \rho_1 .
\tag{20.13}\] In this situation, we find that the ratio of magnetic field strength to density in the plasma stays constant: \[
\frac{B}{\rho} = \mathrm{const} .
\tag{20.14}\] Things are very different if the magnetic flux tube is compressed in the direction parallel to the magnetic field, as illustrated in Figure 20.3.






Figure 20.3: Compression along a flux tube.



In this case, the density of the plasma changes according to \[
\rho A \ell = \mathrm{const} \Longrightarrow \frac{\rho_2}{\rho_1} =
\frac{\ell_1}{\ell_2} .
\tag{20.15}\] However, \(B\) remains constant, because the cross-section of the flux tube, \(A\), is unchanged.






TipExample: Stellar collapse



A star with radius \(r_1 \sim 10^9\,\mathrm{m}\) collapses to form a neutron star with radius \(r_2 \sim 10\,\mathrm{km}\), and all its magnetic flux ends up in the neutron star.

By what factor does the magnetic field increase?
By what factor does the density increase?
If the initial field is \(B_1 \sim 10^{-2}\,\mathrm{T}\) (\(100\,\mathrm{G}\)), what will be the field of the neutron star?

Answer. The density evolves according to \(\rho r^3 = \mathrm{const}\), while the magnetic field evolves according to \(Br^2 = \mathrm{const}\) (assuming the field to be approximately radial), this means that \[
\begin{gathered}
B_2 = \left( \frac{r_1}{r_2} \right)^2 B_1, \qquad \rho_2 = \left(
\frac{r_1}{r_2} \right)^3 \rho_1, \\
B \sim \rho^{2 / 3} .
\end{gathered}
\tag{20.16}\] For example, an initial field of \(10^{-2}\,\mathrm{T}\) (\(100\,\mathrm{G}\)) is amplified to \(10^{8}\,\mathrm{T}\) (\(10^{12}\,\mathrm{G}\)) as result of the collapse of the star. The strong amplification of the magnetic field during the collapse of a star is the reason why neutron stars have extremely strong magnetic fields, up to \(10^{11}\,\mathrm{T}\) (\(10^{15}\,\mathrm{G}\)).




20.1.2 Resistive Evolution
If the resistivity \(1/\sigma\) is finite, \(\eta > 0\), then the magnetic field lines are not stuck to the plasma, but can drift. To understand how this process operates, we consider the evolution of a magnetic field under the sole influence of Ohmic diffusion: \[
\frac{\partial \mathbf{B}}{\partial t} = \eta \nabla^2
\mathbf{B}.
\tag{20.17}\] If the typical curvature radius of the field lines is \(L\), then we can approximate the previous equation as \[
\frac{\partial B}{\partial t} \sim \frac{\eta}{L^2} B =
\frac{1}{T_{\mathrm{decay}}} B, \qquad T_{\mathrm{decay}} = \frac{L^2}{\eta} .
\tag{20.18}\] For many astrophysical applications \(L\) is very large, so \(T_{\mathrm{decay}}\) is very long. We will put actual numbers for \(\eta\) and \(L\) when we discuss the problem of star formation below. If the magnetic field has more than one characteristic scale, then the smaller scales will be dissipated more rapidly by the resistivity. This has the effect of “smoothing” the field lines. To quantify this, we can use the Fourier transform. Accordingly, we represent the magnetic field as a superposition of plane waves \[
\mathbf{B} (t, \mathbf{x}) = \int \mathrm{d}^3 \mathbf{k}
\hat{\mathbf{B}}_{\mathbf{k}} (t) \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i} \mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{x}},
\qquad \hat{\mathbf{B}}_{\mathbf{k}} = \frac{1}{(2 \pi)^3} \int \mathbf{B} (t, \mathbf{x}) \mathrm{e}^{- \mathrm{i} \mathbf{k} \cdot
\mathbf{x}} \mathrm{d} V .
\tag{20.19}\] Note that the \(\mathbf{k}= 0\) mode of the B-field is proportional to the average value of the field in the volume \(V\): \[
\hat{\mathbf{B}}_0 = \frac{1}{(2 \pi)^3} \int \mathbf{B} (t,
\mathbf{x}) \mathrm{d} V = \frac{V}{(2 \pi)^3} \langle \mathbf{B} \rangle .
\tag{20.20}\] Inserting Equation 20.19 into Equation 20.17, we obtain: \[
\int \mathrm{d}^3 \mathbf{k}\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i} \mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{x}}  \left[
\frac{\mathrm{d} \hat{\mathbf{B}}_{\mathbf{k}}}{\mathrm{d} t} + \eta k^2  \hat{\mathbf{B}}_{\mathbf{k}} \right] = 0
\tag{20.21}\] The integral vanishes for all \(\mathbf{x}\) only if the quantity in square brackets vanishes for every \(\mathbf{k}\): \[
\frac{\mathrm{d} \hat{\mathbf{B}}_{\mathbf{k}}}{\mathrm{d} t} = - \eta k^2  \hat{\mathbf{B}}_{\mathbf{k}} .
\tag{20.22}\] So we have transformed Equation 20.17 into a simple system having an infinite number of decoupled equations, with solutions \[
\hat{\mathbf{B}}_{\mathbf{k}} (t) = \hat{\mathbf{B}}_{\mathbf{k}} (0) \exp
\left( - \eta k^2 t \right) .
\tag{20.23}\] We can see that different modes of the B-field decay exponentially and that large \(k\) modes are damped exponentially more quickly than smaller \(k\) modes. On the other hand, the \(k = 0\) mode is not affected at all and stays constant for all times. This means that the action of the resistivity is not really to make the field decay, but rather to straighten out all field lines, as illustrated in Figure 20.4.






Figure 20.4: Evolution of the magnetic field under the effect of resistivity.

title: 20  Flux Freezing
text:
20.2 Star Formation
One situation in which flux freezing must be violated is star formation. Consider the collapse of a region of a molecular cloud to form a star. If flux freezing were to hold, using the same approach as for the stellar collapse example, we would find \[
\begin{array}{clcc}
\rho : & 10^{- 24}\,\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}} & \to &
1\,\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}\\
B : & 10^{- 10}\,\mathrm{T}\ (1\,\mu\mathrm{G}) & \to & 10^{6}\,\mathrm{T}\ (10^{10}\,\mathrm{G})
\end{array}
\tag{20.24}\] That is, the protostar would be embedded with a pulsar-like magnetic field. This is actually impossible. Indeed, the gravitational binding energy of the protostar would be \[
W \sim - \frac{3 GM^2}{5 R} \sim 2 \times 10^{48} M_1^2\,\mathrm{erg},
\tag{20.25}\] where \(M_1\) is the protostar mass in solar masses. The magnetic energy would be \[
U_B \sim \frac{4}{3} \pi R^3 \cdot \frac{B^2}{2 \mu_0} \sim 8 \times 10^{51}\,
\mathrm{erg} \gg | W | !
\tag{20.26}\] The protostar would be unbound, meaning that the magnetic stresses would tear it apart. In reality, the magnetic field halts the collapse of an ideal-MHD cloud well before these levels of magnetic field strength can be achieved. To see why, note that both the gravitational binding energy and the magnetic energy scale as \(1 / R\) during the collapse (see the in-class worksheet). So, if flux freezing holds, the ratio \(U_B / | W |\) does not change during the collapse. With the numbers above, the cloud already has \(U_B \gg | W |\) before it starts to collapse. In other words, if flux freezing holds, a cloud for which the magnetic energy exceeds the binding energy can never collapse. To form a star, the cloud must get rid of most of its magnetic flux. Obviously, Nature has a way to form stars from magnetized clouds, so how does it defeat flux freezing?
It turns out that resistivity is not sufficient to do the trick. The magnetic diffusivity \(\eta = 1/(\mu_0 \sigma)\) of ionized hydrogen plasma depends weakly on density and can be approximated as (Kulsrud 2005) \[
\eta \approx \frac{420}{T_{\mathrm{eV}}^{3 / 2}}\,
\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}.
\tag{20.27}\] For a star \(T_{\mathrm{eV}} \approx 10^2\) and \(L \sim R_{\odot} \approx 7 \times 10^8\,\mathrm{m}\), so the decay time is \[
T_{\mathrm{decay}} = \frac{L^2}{\eta} \approx 1.2 \times 10^{18}\,\mathrm{s} \approx
40\,\mathrm{Gyr} .
\tag{20.28}\] This is longer than the age of the Universe, so the magnetic fields of stars are also frozen in the plasma. For a molecular cloud core, with \(T \approx 10\,\mathrm{K}\) and \(L \approx 0.1\,\mathrm{pc}\), the decay time is even longer, \(\sim 10^{16}\,\mathrm{yr}\). So resistivity is clearly not sufficient to release the magnetic flux and allow stars to form.
The mechanism currently thought to be responsible for the drift between magnetic fields and the plasma is ambipolar diffusion. The details go beyond the scope of this course, but the key observation is that molecular clouds are only weakly ionized. The neutral component of the gas is not affected by the Lorentz force, so it can flow perpendicular to field lines. The Lorentz force on the ions, on the other hand, is orders of magnitude larger than gravity, so the ions are stuck on the field lines. The mutual friction between ions and neutrals has the effect of regulating the rate of collapse and determines the time for the formation of protostars. This physics is illustrated in Figure 20.5.






Figure 20.5: Ambipolar diffusion.



Magnetic fields do not just regulate the collapse of clouds into protostars. They also play a key role enabling it. Indeed, magnetic fields allow the protostar to lose angular momentum and prevent the gas from getting stuck at the centrifugal barrier (see Exercise 22.1). This happens because the collapsing cloud forces a large column of gas, parallel to the mean magnetic field, to corotate with it. This allows the forming protostar to dissipate angular momentum. We explore this in a more quantitative way in Exercise 19.1, for the case of the solar wind.

title: 20  Flux Freezing
text:
20.3 Io and Jupiter
The unipolar-inductor model for the interaction between Jupiter and its moon Io is one of the early successes of plasma astrophysics. This model has also been adopted to explain a variety of other astrophysical systems, including the launching of electromagnetic waves by black holes moving through plasma. The main idea of this model is that the motion of a conductor, in this case Io, in an external magnetic field, in this case Jupiter’s field, generates an electric current.
The original motivation for this model was the discovery in the 1960s of radio flares from Jupiter in phase with the rise and setting of Io. More precisely, Jupiter has a rotation period of about 10 hours, while Io has an orbital period of about 42 hours. Radio flares are preferentially detected when Io has a longitude of \(90^{\circ}\) or \(240^{\circ}\) with respect to Jupiter, as shown in Figure 20.6, taken from Duncan (1965).






Figure 20.6: Number of radio bursts detected from Jupiter as a function of the phase of Io. From Duncan (1965); © Elsevier, reproduced for non-commercial educational use and not covered by the license of these notes.



In 1969, Goldreich and Lynden-Bell (Goldreich and Lynden-Bell 1969) proposed a model to explain:

the mechanism generating the radiation;
the reason for the phase difference between the rising and setting of Io and the radiation bursts.

We explain this model in a qualitative way and then build a semi-quantitative simplified model below.
Io is primarily composed of silicates and iron, so it has a good electrical conductivity. This means that there is no electric field inside Io, in Io’s frame of reference, and the magnetic field lines of Jupiter are stuck to it (flux freezing). However, because in Jupiter’s frame of reference Io completes a revolution every 13 hours, the field lines cannot be frozen everywhere, otherwise the magnetic energy in the magnetosphere would grow without bound2. This means that the field lines must slip somewhere. It turns out that this happens in Jupiter’s atmosphere, where the gas resistivity is the highest, due to the presence of a neutral gas. The geometry of the magnetic flux tube connecting Jupiter and Io is illustrated in Figure 20.7.






Figure 20.7: Magnetic flux tube connecting Io and Jupiter. Redrawn after Goldreich and Lynden-Bell (1969).



The slippage of the field lines on Jupiter’s surface drives a current along the flux tube connecting the planet to the moon. Electrons gyrate in the field lines producing cyclotron radiation, which is beamed primarily in the direction perpendicular to the field lines, explaining the offset between Io’s rises and settings and the radio bursts. This is illustrated in more detail in Figure 20.8.






Figure 20.8: Left panel: footprint of the magnetic-flux tube connecting Io and Jupiter on Jupiter’s atmosphere. Right panel: cross-section of the magnetic-flux tube connecting Jupiter and Io and direction in which the current \(I\) flows between the planet and the moon. Redrawn after Goldreich and Lynden-Bell (1969).



A strong electric field is created in the direction perpendicular to the \(B\)-field, in the \(Y\)-direction shown in the figure. The potential difference across the flux tube is \(\Delta \Phi \sim v B D\), where \(v \approx 57\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}\) is the velocity of Io with respect to Jupiter’s corotating magnetic field, \(B \approx 2\,\mu\mathrm{T}\) (\(0.02\,\mathrm{G}\)) is the magnetic field at Io, and \(D \approx 3600\,\mathrm{km}\) is the diameter of Io. This gives \(\Delta \Phi \sim 4 \times 10^5\,\mathrm{V}\)3. However, the motion of electrons perpendicular to the field lines is suppressed by the Lorentz force, so a current is driven along the field lines, through the moon, and back to the planet, as shown in the right panel of Figure 20.8. The current intensity is \(I \sim 10^6\,\mathrm{A}\), which is sufficient to produce cyclotron and synchrotron radiation.
Here, we consider a toy model in which we see how the electric field is created by the slippage of the field lines. We consider a conductor moving in an external B-field anchored in a wall with infinite conductivity, as shown in Figure 20.9.






Figure 20.9: Toy model for the Io and Jupiter problem.



In our analogy, the conductor is Jupiter’s atmosphere, while the wall represents Io. We imagine that initially the field is vertical and the conductor is at rest. At \(t = 0\), we start moving the conductor with velocity \(\mathbf{v}\) in the \(x\)-direction. The field is dragged up to a distance \(L\) and then starts to slip, realizing the configuration shown in Figure 20.9.
There is no external electric field, so the electric field in the frame of the conductor is \[
\mathbf{E}' =\mathbf{E}+ \mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B} =
\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B} = v_x B_y
\hat{\mathbf{z}},
\tag{20.29}\] and the associated current is \(\mathbf{j}= \sigma (\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B}) = \sigma v_x B_y \hat{\mathbf{z}}\). The current is responsible for the creation of the \(x\)-component of the \(B\)-field (with \(\eta = 1 / \mu_0 \sigma\)): \[
\nabla \times \mathbf{B}= \mu_0 \mathbf{j} \Longrightarrow - \partial_y B_x
= \mu_0 j_z \Longrightarrow B_x = - \mu_0 j_z y = - \frac{1}{\eta} v_x
B_y y.
\tag{20.30}\] On the other hand, from the geometry of the system, we have: \[
B_x = \left. \frac{B_y L}{D} \right|_{y = d} \Longrightarrow L = \frac{v_x
Dd}{\eta} = v_x T_{\mathrm{decay}} ,
\tag{20.31}\] where now \(T_{\mathrm{decay}}\) is computed as in Equation 20.18, with \(L^2\) replaced by \(D d\).
This shows the two key features of the system. The relative motion of the conductor and the walls generates an electric field (a consequence of Faraday’s law). The electric field drives a current in the system. The current, in turn, causes the field lines to bend and slip (from Ampère’s law).






NoteGoing further: Pulsars



Pulsars were discovered by Jocelyn Bell Burnell and Antony Hewish in 1967. It was later realized that pulsars are rotating neutron stars endowed with strong magnetic fields. In 1969, Goldreich and Julian (Goldreich and Julian 1969) developed the first model of a pulsar. Like the unipolar induction model, Goldreich and Julian’s model applies to a variety of astrophysical systems and shows another key physical effect associated with flux freezing. Namely, the fact that rotating neutron stars fill their surroundings with a dense plasma, creating the so-called magnetosphere.






Figure 20.10: Schematic illustration of a pulsar magnetosphere. Redrawn after Goldreich and Julian (1969).



In this model, shown in Figure 20.10, we neglect the misalignment between magnetic North pole and rotational axis, which would be needed to produce the pulsed emission. However, this model contains all required physical ingredients. We assume at first that the pulsar is a neutron star with a dipole magnetic field in vacuum. The magnetic field is then given by \[
\mathbf{B}= B_0  \left( \tfrac{R}{r} \right)^3  (2 \cos \theta
\hat{\mathbf{r}} + \sin \theta \hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}) .
\tag{20.32}\] The angular velocity of the star is given by \[
\boldsymbol{\Omega}= \Omega \hat{\mathbf{z}}, \qquad \hat{\mathbf{z}} = \cos
\theta \hat{\mathbf{r}} - \sin \theta \hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}} .
\tag{20.33}\] In the previous equation \(\hat{\mathbf{z}}\) is the unit vector in the \(z\)-direction. Since neutron stars are essentially perfect conductors, there should be no electric field in their frame \(\mathbf{E}' = 0\). This means that in the inertial frame there is an electric field inside the star given by \[
\mathbf{E}= - \mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B} = -
(\boldsymbol{\Omega} \times \mathbf{r}) \times \mathbf{B}= B_0 \Omega
r  \left( \frac{R}{r} \right)^3 (\sin^2 \theta \hat{\mathbf{r}} - 2 \cos
\theta \sin \theta \hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}) .
\tag{20.34}\] In the previous equation we have used the fact that \[
\boldsymbol{\Omega} \times \mathbf{r}= \Omega r \sin \theta
\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}
\tag{20.35}\] and \[
\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}} \times (2 \cos \theta \hat{\mathbf{r}} + \sin \theta
\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}) = 2 \cos \theta \hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}} - \sin \theta
\hat{\mathbf{r}} .
\tag{20.36}\] If there is vacuum in the exterior (and assuming axisymmetry), then the external electric potential is \[
\Phi (r, \theta) = \sum_{\ell = 0}^{\infty} \frac{\phi_{\ell}}{r^{\ell + 1}}
P_{\ell} (\cos \theta), \qquad r > R
\tag{20.37}\] where \(\phi_{\ell}\) are fixed by the fact that the tangential component of the electric field should be continuous on the surface of the star4 \[
\left[\!\left[ \mathbf{E}_{\parallel} \right]\!\right] = 0 \Longrightarrow E_{\theta} (r =
R) = - \frac{1}{R} \partial_{\theta} \Phi (r = R) .
\tag{20.38}\] Inside the star, \(E_{\theta} \propto \sin \theta \cos \theta \propto \partial_{\theta} P_2 (\cos \theta)\), so only the \(\ell = 2\) term can match it (the \(\ell = 0\) term is fixed by the total charge of the star, which we assume to be zero). So the external field is quadrupolar, meaning that \[
\Phi (r, \theta) = \frac{\phi_2}{r^3} P_2 (\cos \theta),
\tag{20.39}\] then Equation 20.38 implies \[
\boxed{\Phi = - \frac{2 B_0 \Omega R^5}{3 r^3} P_2 (\cos \theta) .}
\tag{20.40}\] So we find that there is an enormous electrostatic potential at the surface of the star: \[
| \Phi | \approx 4
\times 10^{16}  (B_8 R^2_4 / P)\,\mathrm{V},
\tag{20.41}\] where \(B_8 = B_0 / 10^8\,\mathrm{T}\) (\(10^{12}\,\mathrm{G}\)), \(R_4 = R / 10^4\,\mathrm{m}\), and \(P = 2 \pi / \Omega\) is the period in seconds. For example, the ratio of electrostatic to gravitational force for a neutron star with \(M = 1.4\,M_{\odot}\) is \[
\frac{| \mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{EM}} |}{| \mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{G}} |} \sim
\frac{\Phi e}{\frac{GM}{R} m} = \left\{\begin{array}{ll}
2 \times 10^8, & \text{protons},\\
4 \times 10^{11}, & \text{electrons} .
\end{array}\right. \gg 1.
\tag{20.42}\] The electromagnetic forces are strong enough to pull charges out of the surface of the neutron star and fill all the region around it with plasma. The field is so strong that electron-positron cascade production is triggered once the first particles are extracted. This is the so-called magnetosphere. The magnetosphere creates currents that to leading order short out the electric potential to infinity.
In the extreme conditions found in pulsar or black-hole magnetospheres, the electromagnetic energy density is so large compared to the plasma inertia that the plasma is forced to move in such a way as to cancel the Lorentz force, \(q \mathbf{E} + \mathbf{j} \times \mathbf{B} = 0\). This is the so-called force-free electrodynamics approximation. Electrons, positrons, and ions can flow freely along the \(B\)-field lines, so they short out any electric field along \(\mathbf{B}\). If, in addition, the plasma moves with velocity \(\mathbf{v}\), the electric field is given by the ideal-MHD condition: \[
\mathbf{E} \cdot \mathbf{B}= 0, \qquad \mathbf{E}+ \mathbf{v}
\times \mathbf{B}= 0.
\tag{20.43}\] From the first condition, if the system is axisymmetric, we have that \[
\mathbf{E}= E_0  \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}} \times \mathbf{B} \Longrightarrow
\mathbf{E}= - \Omega r \sin \theta  \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}} \times
\mathbf{B}.
\tag{20.44}\] From the last two equations, we find \[
0 = (\mathbf{v}- \Omega r \sin \theta \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}) \times \mathbf{B}
\Longrightarrow \mathbf{v}= \Omega r \sin \theta \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}
+ v_d  \hat{\mathbf{B}} .
\tag{20.45}\] So the plasma velocity has two components. The plasma is forced to co-rotate with the pulsar (first term in the first equation). However, when \(\Omega r \sin \theta \geq c\), the drift velocity \(v_d\) of plasma along the field lines must be non-zero so that \(| \mathbf{v} | < c\). The region at which \(\Omega r \sin \theta = c\) is called the light cylinder. It is the boundary of the region in which magnetic field lines can be closed. Outside the light cylinder, the \(B\)-field lines bend and reach infinity so that plasma can flow away from/to the pulsar (depending on its charge) creating a current.
The plasma charge density is given by Gauss’ law of electrodynamics: \[
q = \epsilon_0 \nabla \cdot \mathbf{E} .
\tag{20.46}\] Note that \[
\frac{q}{\epsilon_0} = \nabla \cdot \mathbf{E}= \nabla \cdot \left[ -
\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B} \right] = - \mathbf{B} \cdot
(\nabla \times \mathbf{v}) + \mathbf{v} \cdot (\nabla \times
\mathbf{B}) .
\tag{20.47}\] This can be computed using \[
\nabla \times \mathbf{v}= \nabla \times (\boldsymbol{\Omega} \times
\mathbf{r}) =\boldsymbol{\Omega} (\nabla \cdot \mathbf{r}) -
(\boldsymbol{\Omega} \cdot \nabla) \mathbf{r}= 2\boldsymbol{\Omega}
\tag{20.48}\] and \[
\nabla \times \mathbf{B}= \mu_0 \mathbf{j}= \mu_0 q \mathbf{v}
\tag{20.49}\] So the charge density is \[
\frac{q}{\epsilon_0} = - 2 \mathbf{B} \cdot \boldsymbol{\Omega}+ \frac{q}{\epsilon_0}
\frac{v^2}{c^2} \Longrightarrow q_{\mathrm{GJ}} = - 2 \epsilon_0 \boldsymbol{\Omega}
\cdot \mathbf{B}  \frac{1}{1 - v^2 / c^2} .
\tag{20.50}\] Note that \(\boldsymbol{\Omega} \cdot \mathbf{B}\) changes sign across a critical line in the magnetosphere. This means that there is charge separation in the magnetosphere.
The minimum electron number density is the so-called Goldreich–Julian density \[
n_{\mathrm{GJ}} = \frac{| q_{\mathrm{GJ}} |}{e} \approx 7 \times 10^{10}  (B_8 / P)\,\mathrm{cm}^{-
3} .
\tag{20.51}\] This is \(\sim 10\) orders of magnitude larger than the typical density of electrons in the ISM. More recent theoretical models show that the plasma number density can be several orders of magnitude larger than the Goldreich-Julian density. This is because the plasma is rich in electron-positron pairs and \(n_{\mathrm{GJ}}\) only measures the net density of charges. For example, see Figure 20.11.






Figure 20.11: \(\log_{10} (n / n_{\mathrm{GJ}})\) in a particle-in-cell simulation with approximate treatment of pair creation. Coherent plasma waves are thought to be responsible for the production of the radio pulses. From Philippov et al. (2015); © The American Astronomical Society, reproduced for non-commercial educational use and not covered by the license of these notes.

20.4 In-class worksheet
Spherical Collapse. A spherical distribution of plasma (a star or a molecular cloud) is endowed with a dipolar magnetic field, as shown in Figure 20.12.






Figure 20.12: Dipolar magnetic field of a sphere.



The sphere contracts from an initial radius \(R_0\) to a new radius \(R_1 < R_0\).

How do the gravitational binding energy \(W\) and the magnetic energy \(U_B\) change? What does this imply for the collapse of a magnetized cloud?
In the process of forming a neutron star, an object with mass \(M \sim 10^{31}\,\mathrm{kg}\) contracts from an initial radius \(R_0 \sim 10^9\,\mathrm{m}\) to \(R_1 \sim 10\,\mathrm{km}\). By what factor is the magnetic field amplified? If the typical magnetic field strength for a star is \(B \sim 10^{-2}\,\mathrm{T}\) (\(100\,\mathrm{G}\)), what is the field strength expected for a neutron star?
Gas in a molecular cloud with density \(\rho \sim 10^{- 24}\,\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}\) and typical magnetic field \(B \sim 0.1\,\mathrm{nT}\) (\(1\,\mu\mathrm{G}\)) contracts to form a star with \(\rho \sim 1\,\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}\). What is the strength of the resulting field if flux freezing holds?

title: 20  Flux Freezing
text:
20.5 Exercises

Exercise 20.1 (Flux freezing in an Alfvén wave) In this exercise we check, for a simple wave, that the magnetic field lines move together with the plasma. Consider a plasma with uniform density \(\rho\) and pressure \(p\), in the uniform magnetic field \(B_0 \hat{\mathbf{z}}\). We perturb it with a transverse wave travelling along the field, with velocity and magnetic field \[
\mathbf{v}= \epsilon v_A \sin (kz - \omega t)  \hat{\mathbf{x}}, \qquad
\mathbf{B}= B_0  \hat{\mathbf{z}} - \epsilon B_0 \sin (kz - \omega t)
\hat{\mathbf{x}} ,
\tag{20.52}\] where \(\epsilon \ll 1\) and \(v_A = B_0 / \sqrt{\mu_0 \rho}\).

Show that Equation 20.52 solves the ideal-MHD equations to first order in \(\epsilon\), provided that \(\omega = k v_A\). In other words, we neglect all terms of order \(\epsilon^2\) and higher.
The ideal-MHD equations neglect the displacement current. Use the ideal-MHD electric field to compute the displacement current of this wave, and compare it with the term \(\mu_0 \mathbf{j}\) in Ampère’s law. Show that the displacement current is negligible when \(v_A \ll c\).
Now consider a plasma with finite resistivity, that is, with magnetic diffusivity \(\eta > 0\). Compare the resistive term in the induction equation with the term \(\nabla \times (\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B})\), and show that the resistive term is negligible when \(\omega T_{\mathrm{decay}} \gg 1\), where \(T_{\mathrm{decay}} = 1 / (k^2 \eta)\) is the decay time of Equation 20.18 for \(L = 1/k\).
To first order in \(\epsilon\), the field lines are the curves \(x (z)\) that solve \[
\frac{\mathrm{d} x}{\mathrm{d} z} = \frac{B_x}{B_0} .
\tag{20.53}\] Find these curves. Then compute the displacement of the fluid elements, \[
x (z, t) = \int v_x \mathrm{d} t ,
\tag{20.54}\] and show that it gives the same curves. This is what we expect if the field lines are frozen into the plasma.

Adapted from Kulsrud (2005), Problem 3.1.

Imagine a single flux tube wound around Jupiter multiple times. The magnetic flux in the tube must be conserved, so the intensity of the field is constant. However, as the flux tube is wound around, more and more of the magnetosphere is filled by the coils of the flux tube, so the integrated magnetic energy (\(B^2 / 2 \mu_0\)) grows linearly with time over the winding timescale.↩︎
Goldreich and Lynden-Bell estimated \(\Delta \Phi \approx 7 \times 10^5\,\mathrm{V}\), with the values of Jupiter’s magnetic field known at the time.↩︎
In other words, we are matching the interior solution with the exterior solution.↩︎

title: 21  Magnetic Tension and Hydromagnetic Equilibria
text:
21.1 Magnetic Tension Force
Up to now we have been primarily concerned with the consequences of the induction equation (Faraday’s law). We have seen that, in the ideal-MHD limit, the magnetic field lines are frozen in the flow and explored some of the consequences of this fact. Now, we consider the feedback of the magnetic field on the plasma, that is the impact of the \(\mathbf{j} \times \mathbf{B}\) term in the momentum equation.
A first somewhat obvious, but important remark is that the magnetic force \(\mathbf{j} \times \mathbf{B}\) is always perpendicular to the magnetic field, as is obvious from the cross product. In other words, there is no impediment to the plasma flow along field lines. On the other hand, the field might resist or drive plasma motion perpendicular to the field lines. The latter, in turn, causes the field lines to move, in accordance with the induction equation. It is important to keep this in mind, because we are now going to rewrite the Lorentz force in a form in which this constraint is not manifest. Using the vector identity \[
\begin{aligned}
\nabla (\mathbf{A} \cdot \mathbf{B}) &= \mathbf{A} \times (\nabla \times
\mathbf{B}) +\mathbf{B} \times (\nabla \times \mathbf{A}) \\
&\quad {} + (\mathbf{A}
\cdot \nabla) \mathbf{B}+ (\mathbf{B} \cdot \nabla) \mathbf{A}
\end{aligned}
\tag{21.1}\] (see also Equation 19.24) and Ampère’s law (\(\mu_0 \mathbf{j}= \nabla \times \mathbf{B}\)), we can rewrite the Lorentz force as \[
\mathbf{j} \times \mathbf{B}= \frac{(\nabla \times \mathbf{B}) \times
\mathbf{B}}{\mu_0} = \frac{(\mathbf{B} \cdot \nabla) \mathbf{B}}{\mu_0} -
\nabla \frac{B^2}{2 \mu_0} .
\tag{21.2}\] The second term is often improperly referred to as the magnetic pressure, because it is reminiscent of the \(- \nabla p\) term in the momentum equation, while the first term is improperly referred to as magnetic tension. However, remember that magnetic pressure is only effective perpendicular to the field lines, as we have already remarked. To better understand the nature of the Lorentz force in MHD, we factor \[
\mathbf{B}= B \hat{\mathbf{b}},
\tag{21.3}\] where \(\hat{\mathbf{b}}\) is a unit vector. Accordingly, we can write \[
\begin{aligned}
(\mathbf{B} \cdot \nabla) \mathbf{B} &= B (\hat{\mathbf{b}} \cdot \nabla)
(B \hat{\mathbf{b}}) \\
&= B^2  (\hat{\mathbf{b}} \cdot \nabla) \hat{\mathbf{b}}
+ B \hat{\mathbf{b}}  (\hat{\mathbf{b}} \cdot \nabla) B \\
&= B^2  (\hat{\mathbf{b}} \cdot \nabla)  \hat{\mathbf{b}} + \frac{1}{2}
\hat{\mathbf{b}}  (\hat{\mathbf{b}} \cdot \nabla) B^2 .
\end{aligned}
\tag{21.4}\] The last term on the RHS is, apart from a factor 1/2, the projection of \(\nabla B^2\) parallel to \(\mathbf{B}\): \[
[\hat{\mathbf{b}}  (\hat{\mathbf{b}} \cdot \nabla) B^2]_i = \sum_{j = 1}^3
\hat{b}_i  \hat{b}_j \partial_j  (B^2) = [(\hat{\mathbf{b}} \otimes
\hat{\mathbf{b}}) \nabla (B^2)]_i =: \nabla_{\parallel} B^2 .
\tag{21.5}\] Plugging this back into Equation 21.2 yields \[
\mathbf{j} \times \mathbf{B}= \frac{B^2}{\mu_0}  (\hat{\mathbf{b}} \cdot
\nabla)  \hat{\mathbf{b}} - [\mathbf{I}- \hat{\mathbf{b}} \otimes
\hat{\mathbf{b}}]  \frac{\nabla B^2}{2 \mu_0} = \frac{B^2}{\mu_0}
(\hat{\mathbf{b}} \cdot \nabla)  \hat{\mathbf{b}} - \nabla_{\perp}
\frac{B^2}{2 \mu_0} .
\tag{21.6}\] The last term is the component of \(\nabla (B^2 / 2 \mu_0)\) perpendicular to the field lines. This is the correct form of the magnetic pressure, while the first term on the RHS is the proper form of the magnetic tension.
We remark that \(u_B = B^2 / 2 \mu_0\) is the energy density of the magnetic field, so the magnetic pressure is \[
p_B = (\Gamma_B - 1) u_B,
\tag{21.7}\] which has the same form as the equation of state of an ideal gas (Equation 2.16), with an effective adiabatic index \(\Gamma_B = 2\). This makes sense, because, if we compress a flux tube perpendicular to the field, flux freezing (Chapter 20) gives \(B \propto \rho\), so \(p_B \propto \rho^2\). For ionized hydrogen \(\Gamma = 5 / 3\), so magnetic energy is more effective at resisting compression than gas internal energy. Of course, magnetic pressure can only resist compression perpendicular to the field lines.
To understand the meaning of the first term on the RHS of Equation 21.6, note that \[
(\hat{\mathbf{b}} \cdot \nabla)  \hat{\mathbf{b}} =\boldsymbol{\kappa},
\tag{21.8}\] where \(1 / | \boldsymbol{\kappa} |\) is the curvature radius of the field lines and \(\boldsymbol{\kappa}\) points towards the centre of curvature. In other words, \(\boldsymbol{\kappa}= 0\) for straight field lines. For a circular field line, \(1 / | \boldsymbol{\kappa} |\) is the radius of the circle spanned by the line. This means that the magnetic field lines back-react on the plasma as if they were elastic strings under a tension \(B^2 / \mu_0\) per unit area.
Summarizing, we find that there are two components of the Lorentz force. The first is the magnetic pressure, according to which the magnetic field lines resist being bundled together. The second is the magnetic tension, according to which the magnetic field lines resist bending. This situation is illustrated in Figure 21.1. We will see that magnetic tension is the restoring force for Alfvén waves (Chapter 22) and the driver of the magnetorotational instability (Chapter 23).
As we have already anticipated (see Equation 19.23), the Lorentz force can be rewritten as the divergence of the magnetic stresses: \[
\frac{(\mathbf{B} \cdot \nabla) \mathbf{B}}{\mu_0} - \nabla \frac{B^2}{2
\mu_0} = \nabla \cdot \left[ \frac{\mathbf{B} \otimes \mathbf{B}}{\mu_0} -
\frac{B^2}{2 \mu_0} \mathbf{I} \right] =: \nabla \cdot
\mathbf{T}_{\mathrm{EM}} .
\tag{21.9}\] This follows from Equation 19.25. Including both the fluid stresses \(\mathbf{T}\) and the magnetic stresses, the momentum equation reads: \[
\rho \frac{\mathrm{d} \mathbf{v}}{\mathrm{d} t} = \nabla \cdot
[\mathbf{T}+\mathbf{T}_{\mathrm{EM}}] .
\tag{21.10}\] For an ideal fluid \(\mathbf{T}= - p\mathbf{I}\), however shear and bulk viscosity can also be included in \(\mathbf{T}\) to obtain the viscous MHD equations. In conservation form, the momentum equation reads \[
\frac{\partial (\rho \mathbf{v})}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot [\rho
\mathbf{v} \otimes \mathbf{v}-\mathbf{T}-\mathbf{T}_{\mathrm{EM}}] = 0,
\tag{21.11}\] where \(\rho \mathbf{v} \otimes \mathbf{v}\) is the flux of momentum carried by the flow1.

title: 21  Magnetic Tension and Hydromagnetic Equilibria
text:
Figure 21.1: Left panel: effect of the magnetic pressure force. Right panel: effect of the magnetic tension force.










TipExample: Solar prominence



Solar prominences are plasma arches which rise above the solar photosphere and are supported by the magnetic tension, as illustrated by Figure 21.2 and Figure 21.3. Prominences are made of cool gas, \(T \sim 10^4\,\mathrm{K}\), with densities \(n \sim 10^{10}\)–\(10^{11}\,\mathrm{cm^{-3}}\), about 100 times denser than the surrounding corona, which has \(T \sim 10^6\,\mathrm{K}\) and \(n \sim 10^9\,\mathrm{cm^{-3}}\). The scale height of a gas at \(10^4\,\mathrm{K}\) in the gravity of the Sun is only a few hundred km, while prominences extend for tens of thousands of km above the photosphere. So the gas pressure alone cannot support them against gravity.






Figure 21.2: Solar prominence in UV. Credit: NASA (What is a solar prominence?); not covered by the license of these notes.









Figure 21.3: Force diagram for a Solar prominence.



To understand how prominences are supported against gravity, let us consider the balance of forces on the region in the volume \(V\) with boundary surface \(S\): \[
\begin{aligned}
0 &= \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} t} \int_V \rho \mathbf{v} \mathrm{d} V \\
&= - \int_V \nabla \cdot [\rho \mathbf{v} \otimes
\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{T}-\mathbf{T}_{\mathrm{EM}}] \mathrm{d} V \\
& \quad + \int_V \rho \mathbf{g} \mathrm{d} V \\
&= - \int_S \rho \mathbf{v}\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathrm{d} \mathbf{S} \\
& \quad - \int_S \left( p + \frac{B^2}{2 \mu_0} \right) \mathrm{d} \mathbf{S} \\
& \quad + \int_S \frac{\mathbf{B}}{\mu_0} \mathbf{B} \cdot \mathrm{d} \mathbf{S}+ \int_V \rho
\mathbf{g} \mathrm{d} V.
\end{aligned}
\tag{21.12}\] For a prominence at rest, \(\mathbf{v} = 0\) and the first term vanishes. Note that the field lines enter \(V\) going down on the left and leave it going up on the right. In other words, the prominence sits in a dip of the field lines, like a weight on a hammock. The main force balancing gravity is the magnetic tension, arising from the \(\mathbf{B}\mathbf{B} \cdot \mathrm{d} \mathbf{S}\) term. On the left, \(\mathbf{B}\) points into \(V\), so \(\mathbf{B} \cdot \mathrm{d} \mathbf{S} < 0\) and the force is opposite to \(\mathbf{B}\). Since \(\mathbf{B}\) points down, the force points up. On the right, \(\mathbf{B}\) points out of \(V\), so \(\mathbf{B} \cdot \mathrm{d} \mathbf{S} > 0\) and the force is along \(\mathbf{B}\), which also points up. The horizontal components cancel. The magnetic pressure, arising from the squeezing of the field lines below the prominence, also contributes, but is subdominant. We work out a simple model of this configuration in Exercise 21.1.
The attentive reader might have noticed that the term \(\mathbf{B}\mathbf{B} \cdot \mathrm{d} \mathbf{S}\) gives a force along \(\mathbf{B}\), with magnitude \(B^2 | \hat{\mathbf{b}} \cdot \mathrm{d} \mathbf{S} | / \mu_0\). How can this be possible? We have seen that the magnetic force is always perpendicular to \(\mathbf{B}\). The point is that this term represents the net force from the magnetic tension on the whole volume \(V\), not the force at a specific point. In other words, we should not confuse the force on individual fluid elements, which is always perpendicular to \(\mathbf{B}\), with the net force on a control volume, which can be in any direction.

title: 21  Magnetic Tension and Hydromagnetic Equilibria
text:
21.2 Hydromagnetic Equilibria
Consider the hydrostatic equilibrium of a plane-parallel, magnetized atmosphere in a gravitational potential \(\Psi (z)\), as illustrated in Figure 21.4. This equilibrium configuration could be representative of the disk in a spiral galaxy, or of the photosphere of the Sun.






Figure 21.4: Force diagram for a plane-parallel magnetized atmosphere.



The force-balance equation for hydromagnetic equilibrium is \[
- \nabla p - \rho \nabla \Psi + \frac{1}{\mu_0} (\nabla \times \mathbf{B})
\times \mathbf{B}= 0.
\tag{21.13}\] We will make two simplifying assumptions.

The gas is isothermal, so \(p = c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2 \rho\). This means that, in absence of magnetic fields, \[
\rho (z) = \rho_0 \exp (- \Psi / c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2) .
\tag{21.14}\]
We assume that the magnetic field is planar and does not depend on \(x\), meaning that \[
\mathbf{B}= B_y (y, z)  \hat{\mathbf{y}} + B_z (y, z)  \hat{\mathbf{z}} .
\tag{21.15}\] This means that there exists a vector potential \(\mathbf{A}= A (y, z) \hat{\mathbf{x}}\) such that \(\nabla \times \mathbf{A}=\mathbf{B}\). In particular, \[
\begin{aligned}
& B_y = \partial_z A, \quad B_z = - \partial_y A \\
& \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \mathbf{B}= \nabla A \times \hat{\mathbf{x}} .
\end{aligned}
\tag{21.16}\] Note that \(\mathbf{A} \perp \mathbf{B}\) and that the function \(A (y, z)\) is constant along the field lines, because \(\mathbf{B} \cdot \nabla A = 0\). So the isocontours of \(A (y, z)\) are the field lines.

To compute the Lorentz force we use \[
\nabla \times \mathbf{B}= \nabla \times (\nabla \times \mathbf{A}) = -
\nabla^2 \mathbf{A}+ \nabla (\nabla \cdot \mathbf{A}) = - \hat{\mathbf{x}}
\nabla^2 A
\tag{21.17}\] and \[
(\nabla \times \mathbf{B}) \times \mathbf{B}= - (\nabla^2 A)
\hat{\mathbf{x}} \times (- \hat{\mathbf{x}} \times \nabla A) = - (\nabla^2
A) \nabla A.
\tag{21.18}\] For reasons that will be more clear later, we rewrite \[
\nabla p + \rho \nabla \Psi = \mathrm{e}^{- \Psi / c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2} \nabla q, \qquad q = p\,\mathrm{e}^{\Psi
/ c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2} .
\tag{21.19}\] The force equation finally reduces to \[
\boxed{- \frac{1}{\mu_0} (\nabla^2 A) \nabla A = \mathrm{e}^{- \Psi / c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2} \nabla
q.}
\tag{21.20}\] The last equation shows that \(\nabla q \parallel \nabla A\), which means that \(q = q (A)\). Since \(\nabla q = (\mathrm{d} q / \mathrm{d} A) \nabla A\), the force equation becomes \[
\nabla^2 A = - \mu_0 \mathrm{e}^{- \Psi / c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2} \frac{\mathrm{d} q}{\mathrm{d} A} .
\tag{21.21}\] This is a nonlinear Poisson equation for \(A\), analogous to the Grad–Shafranov equation used to model the magnetic equilibria of tokamaks and of pulsar magnetospheres. One can then find equilibrium configurations by specifying \(q = q (A)\), which encodes the amount of matter enclosed by the field lines \(A\) and \(A + \mathrm{d} A\), and solving Equation 21.21 for \(A\). We shall not follow this line of reasoning here, instead we will make two more simplifying assumptions, following Parker (1966).

We assume that the magnetic field lines are horizontal, \(\mathbf{B}= B (z) \hat{\mathbf{y}}\).
We assume that the ratio of magnetic to gas pressure is constant \[
\frac{B^2}{2 \mu_0 p} = \alpha_0 .
\tag{21.22}\]

With these simplifications, the equation for equilibrium becomes \[
(1 + \alpha_0)  \frac{\mathrm{d} p}{\mathrm{d} z} = - \frac{p}{c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2}  \frac{\mathrm{d}
\Psi}{\mathrm{d} z} .
\tag{21.23}\] Apart from the additional factor \(1 + \alpha_0\), this is the usual equation for hydrostatic equilibrium of a plane-parallel isothermal atmosphere (Equation 10.2). The solution is \[
\begin{gathered}
p (z) = p_0 \exp \left( - \frac{\Psi (z)}{(1 + \alpha_0) c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2} \right),
\\ B (z) = B_0 \exp \left( - \frac{\Psi (z)}{2 (1 + \alpha_0) c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2}
\right) .
\end{gathered}
\tag{21.24}\] For a uniform gravitational field, \(\Psi = g z\), the scale height of the gas is \(H = (1 + \alpha_0) c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2 / g\). In other words, the magnetic field makes the atmosphere thicker, because part of the weight of the gas is supported by the magnetic pressure. The inverse of \(\alpha_0\), \[
\beta = \frac{2 \mu_0 p}{B^2},
\tag{21.25}\] is called the plasma beta. Plasmas with \(\beta \gg 1\) are dominated by the gas pressure, while plasmas with \(\beta \ll 1\) are dominated by the magnetic field.






TipExample: Magnetic support of the Galactic disk



Consider the gas in the disk of the Milky Way near the Sun. The magnetic field is \(B \approx 0.5\,\mathrm{nT}\) (\(5\,\mu\mathrm{G}\)), so the magnetic pressure is \(B^2 / 2 \mu_0 \approx 1 \times 10^{-13}\,\mathrm{Pa}\). The thermal pressure of the gas is \(p / k_B \approx 3000\,\mathrm{K\,cm^{-3}}\), that is \(p \approx 4 \times 10^{-14}\,\mathrm{Pa}\). So \(\alpha_0 \approx 2\), or \(\beta \approx 0.4\). In other words, the magnetic field is as important as the gas pressure in supporting the disk against the gravity of the stars2. In the model of Equation 21.24, the field increases the scale height of the gas by a factor \(1 + \alpha_0 \approx 3\).


Remarkably, the solution in Equation 21.24 turns out to be unstable for any \(\alpha_0 > 0\) to long-wavelength perturbations, if the perturbations are also isothermal. This is the so-called Parker instability (Parker 1966). Note that, if the perturbations have adiabatic index \(\Gamma\) and are allowed to vary across the field lines, the atmosphere is unstable for \(\Gamma < 1 + \alpha_0\) (Newcomb 1961). Without magnetic field, \(\alpha_0 = 0\), this is the condition \(N^2 < 0\) for the onset of convection in an isothermal atmosphere (Section 10.2). In other words, an isothermal atmosphere is marginally stable to isothermal perturbations, \(N = 0\), and the magnetic field makes it unstable. The Parker instability is demonstrated in the MHD simulations shown in Figure 21.5.






Figure 21.5: Development of the Parker instability in 3D MHD simulations, at three times, shown in a vertical slice. From Matsumoto and Shibata (1992); © Astronomical Society of Japan, reproduced for non-commercial educational use and not covered by the license of these notes.



Imagine starting from horizontal field lines, like in the left panel of the figure, and adding a small bend to them. The gas in the regions where the field lines are inclined can now slide down along them, because the magnetic force has no component along the field. In doing so, the gas loses gravitational potential energy and collects in the valleys, as shown by the arrows in the middle panel. The crests of the field lines are now lighter, so they are pushed further up by the magnetic pressure below them, the gas drains more efficiently, and the perturbation grows. This instability is responsible, for example, for the emergence of magnetic flux tubes from the solar interior, which gives rise to the type of prominence we have discussed previously.
In the case of the solar corona, the field lines at the foot of the prominences are anchored in the outer convection layers of the Sun. The motion of plasma in this region moves the field lines in random ways and builds enormous tension in the field. When field lines of opposite polarities find themselves sufficiently close they can annihilate in a so-called reconnection event. This might seem in contradiction with flux freezing, since the magnetic Reynolds number in the corona is enormous (Chapter 20). However, reconnection takes place in thin current sheets, in which the field changes direction over a very short distance. The magnetic Reynolds number computed with this length is small, so the field lines can diffuse through the plasma. Reconnection suddenly releases the magnetic tension and generates solar flares and coronal mass ejections. Solar eruptions can significantly impact satellites and space communication and can be hazardous for astronauts. The prediction of solar eruptions using ground- and space-based observations, in conjunction with MHD simulations, is a field of its own: space weather modeling.

text:
21.3 In-class worksheet
Explosive Reconnection. Plasma is contained in a region bounded by two perfectly conducting plates. Two magnetic flux tubes are anchored on the plates and stretched by the application of an external force \(\mathbf{f}\) as shown in panel (a) of Figure 21.6.






Figure 21.6: Explosive reconnection of two magnetic flux tubes anchored on conducting plates: (a) before and (b) after reconnection.



When \(\ell \approx D\), the field lines reconnect and snap to a new configuration shown in panel (b). This process releases energy stored in the magnetic tension of the field to accelerate the plasma to a velocity \(\mathbf{v}\), which reaches a maximum when the field lines are perfectly straight. Assume that the ideal-MHD approximation holds at all times, except when reconnection takes place.

Show that, apart from geometric factors of order unity, the force per unit volume necessary to hold the field lines bent to a height \(\ell\) is \[
| \mathbf{f} | \approx \frac{B^2}{\mu_0}  \frac{\ell}{D^2} .
\tag{21.26}\]
Show that, apart from factors of order unity, the maximum velocity of the plasma after the reconnection event is \[
v \approx v_A,
\tag{21.27}\] where \(v_A\) is the Alfvén velocity \[
v_A = \frac{B}{\sqrt{\mu_0 \rho}} .
\tag{21.28}\]
Magnetic fields in solar active regions have strengths \(B \sim 0.03\,\mathrm{T}\) (\(300\,\mathrm{G}\)) and extend over regions of size \(L \sim 3 \times 10^4\,\mathrm{km}\). Estimate the magnetic energy available. Compare it with the energy released by a large solar flare, \(\sim 10^{32}\,\mathrm{erg} = 10^{25}\,\mathrm{J}\).

title: 21  Magnetic Tension and Hydromagnetic Equilibria
text:
21.4 Exercises

Exercise 21.1 (A model for solar prominences) Consider the model of a solar prominence of Kippenhahn and Schlüter (1957). The prominence is a vertical sheet of isothermal gas, with isothermal sound speed \(c_{\mathrm{iso}}\) (Equation 9.16), in a uniform gravitational field \(\mathbf{g} = - g \hat{\mathbf{z}}\). The magnetic field is \[
\mathbf{B} = B_x \hat{\mathbf{x}} + B_z (x) \hat{\mathbf{z}},
\tag{21.29}\] where \(B_x\) is a constant, and all quantities depend only on \(x\).

Show that \(\nabla \cdot \mathbf{B} = 0\) and that the horizontal component of the force balance gives \[
p + \frac{B_z^2}{2 \mu_0} = \mathrm{const} .
\tag{21.30}\]
Show that the vertical component of the force balance is \[
\rho g = \frac{B_x}{\mu_0} \frac{\mathrm{d} B_z}{\mathrm{d} x} .
\tag{21.31}\] Which component of the Lorentz force holds the gas up?
Assume that \(p \to 0\) and \(B_z \to \pm B_{\infty}\) for \(x \to \pm \infty\). Show that \[
B_z = B_{\infty} \tanh (x / w), \qquad w = \frac{2 B_x}{B_{\infty}} \frac{c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2}{g},
\tag{21.32}\] and find \(\rho (x)\). Sketch the field lines.
Show that the mass per unit area of the sheet is \[
\Sigma = \int_{- \infty}^{\infty} \rho \, \mathrm{d} x = \frac{2 B_x B_{\infty}}{\mu_0 g} .
\tag{21.33}\] Evaluate \(w\), the central number density \(n (0)\) and \(\Sigma\) for \(B_x = 1\,\mathrm{mT}\) (\(10\,\mathrm{G}\)), \(B_{\infty} = 0.2\,\mathrm{mT}\) (\(2\,\mathrm{G}\)), \(T = 7000\,\mathrm{K}\), mean molecular weight \(\mu = 0.6\), and \(g = 270\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Compare with observed prominences, which have widths of a few thousand km and densities \(n \sim 10^{10}\)–\(10^{11}\,\mathrm{cm^{-3}}\).

title: 22  MHD Waves
text:
22.1 Waves in a Homogeneous Plasma
Waves play a very important role in the dynamics of magnetized plasmas. Particle-wave interaction with the interstellar medium regulates the propagation of cosmic rays in the Galaxy. In strong MHD turbulence (Chapter 17), the non-linear interaction between Alfvén waves acts as the main driver of the turbulence cascade. Torsional Alfvén waves extract angular momentum from proto-stellar cores allowing them to collapse and form stars (Exercise 22.1). These are just a few examples. In this chapter, we discuss the phenomenology of waves in compressible MHD.
We consider a homogeneous plasma described by the ideal-MHD equations with \[
\rho_0 = \mathrm{const}, \qquad \mathbf{v}_0 = 0, \qquad \mathbf{B}_0 = B_0
\hat{\mathbf{z}} .
\tag{22.1}\] We proceed in the same way as when we derived the dispersion relation for sound waves in unmagnetized media (Chapter 9). However, as we will see shortly, the phenomenology of MHD waves is significantly more complex than that of sound waves. As before, we introduce a perturbation with a Lagrangian displacement \(\boldsymbol{\xi}\), shown in Figure 22.1.
The pressure and density perturbations in the Lagrangian frame are \[
\delta \rho = - \rho_0 \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}, \qquad \delta p =
\frac{\Gamma p_0}{\rho_0} \delta \rho = - \Gamma p_0 \nabla \cdot
\boldsymbol{\xi}.
\tag{22.2}\] Since the background is uniform, the Lagrangian and Eulerian perturbations coincide. The magnetic field perturbations can be computed from the linearized induction equation: \[
\frac{\partial \delta \mathbf{B}}{\partial t} = \nabla \times \left(
\frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial t} \times \mathbf{B}_0 \right)
\Longrightarrow \delta \mathbf{B}= \nabla \times (\boldsymbol{\xi} \times
\mathbf{B}_0) .
\tag{22.3}\] The linearized momentum equation becomes (note that the unperturbed current vanishes \(\mathbf{j}_0 = 0\)): \[
\rho \frac{\mathrm{d} \mathbf{v}}{\mathrm{d} t} = - \nabla p +\mathbf{j} \times
\mathbf{B} \Longrightarrow \rho_0  \frac{\partial^2 \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial
t^2} = - \nabla \delta p + \delta \mathbf{j} \times \mathbf{B}_0 .
\tag{22.4}\] The perturbed current is \[
\delta \mathbf{j}= \frac{1}{\mu_0} \nabla \times \delta \mathbf{B}=
\frac{1}{\mu_0} \nabla \times [\nabla \times (\boldsymbol{\xi} \times
\mathbf{B}_0)],
\tag{22.5}\] so putting everything together we get the oscillation equation \[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\rho_0  \frac{\partial^2 \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial t^2} = {} & \Gamma p_0
\nabla (\nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}) \\
& + \frac{1}{\mu_0} \{ \nabla \times
[\nabla \times (\boldsymbol{\xi} \times \mathbf{B}_0)] \} \times \mathbf{B}_0 .
\end{aligned}}
\tag{22.6}\] Of course, if \(\mathbf{B}_0 = 0\), this equation reduces to the equation for sound waves. All the new physics is in the last term on the RHS. To derive a dispersion relation, we take the usual ansatz \[
\boldsymbol{\xi} (t, \mathbf{x}) =\boldsymbol{\xi}_1 \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i} (\mathbf{k} \cdot
\mathbf{x}- \omega t)},
\tag{22.7}\] which we plug into the oscillation equation. This yields \[
\begin{aligned}
- \rho_0 \omega^2 \boldsymbol{\xi}_1 = {} & - \Gamma p_0 \mathbf{k} (\mathbf{k} \cdot
\boldsymbol{\xi}_1) \\
& - \frac{1}{\mu_0}  \{ \mathbf{k} \times [\mathbf{k} \times
(\boldsymbol{\xi}_1 \times \mathbf{B}_0)] \} \times \mathbf{B}_0 .
\end{aligned}
\tag{22.8}\] As we have seen for sound waves (Chapter 9), the oscillation equation gives rise to an eigenvalue problem in the form \[
- \rho_0 \omega^2 \boldsymbol{\xi}_1 =\mathbf{F} (\mathbf{k}) \boldsymbol{\xi}_1,
\tag{22.9}\] where \(\mathbf{F} (\mathbf{k})\) is a matrix. This equation has solutions with \(\boldsymbol{\xi}_1 \neq 0\) if and only if \[
\det [\mathbf{F} (\mathbf{k}) + \rho_0 \omega^2 \mathbf{I}] = 0.
\tag{22.10}\] The last equation defines the dispersion relation \(\omega = \omega (\mathbf{k})\). The eigenvectors of \(\mathbf{F} (\mathbf{k})\) define the polarization vector \(\boldsymbol{\xi}_1\) of the wave.

title: 22  MHD Waves
text: Figure 22.1: Lagrangian displacement of a fluid element from position \(\mathbf{x}\) to position \(\mathbf{x}+\boldsymbol{\xi}\).

title: 22  MHD Waves
text:
22.2 Families of MHD Waves
In general, there are three solutions to the eigenvalue problem Equation 22.9, corresponding to three different modes. In the unmagnetized case, one of the modes is the sound wave, while the other two are the transverse modes with \(\omega = 0\) we found in Chapter 9. In the magnetized case, the magnetic field provides a restoring force also for transverse displacements, and there are three types of waves: Alfvén waves, slow-, and fast-magnetosonic waves.
Without loss of generality, we can choose the axes so that \(\mathbf{B}_0\) is along \(z\) and \(\mathbf{k}\) is in the \(x z\)-plane, at an angle \(\theta\) from \(\mathbf{B}_0\). We will see that the \(y\) component of the displacement decouples from the other two. So the eigenvalue problem splits into a \(1 \times 1\) problem (the Alfvén wave) and a \(2 \times 2\) problem (the slow and fast waves). We consider these separately below.

22.2.1 Alfvén Waves
We first consider displacements along \(y\), as depicted in Figure 22.2:

\(\mathbf{B}_0\) is along \(z\)
\(\mathbf{k}\) is in the \(x z\)-plane
\(\boldsymbol{\xi}\) is along \(y\)

Note that \(\mathbf{k} \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}= 0\), meaning that \(\delta \rho = \delta p = 0\).






Figure 22.2: Geometry of the Alfvén wave: \(\mathbf{B}_0\) along \(z\), \(\mathbf{k}\) in the \(xz\)-plane at an angle \(\theta\) from \(\mathbf{B}_0\), and displacement \(\boldsymbol{\xi}\) along \(y\).



To compute the Lorentz force we proceed as follows. In Fourier space, \(\nabla \rightarrow \mathrm{i} \mathbf{k}\), so each derivative in Equation 22.3 and Equation 22.5 is replaced by a factor \(\mathrm{i} \mathbf{k}\). First we note that \[
\boldsymbol{\xi} \times \mathbf{B}_0 = \xi_y B_0  \hat{\mathbf{x}} .
\tag{22.11}\] Next, we compute the magnetic field perturbation as \[
\delta \mathbf{B} = \mathrm{i} \mathbf{k} \times (\boldsymbol{\xi} \times \mathbf{B}_0) = \mathrm{i} k \xi_y B_0 \cos
\theta \hat{\mathbf{y}} .
\tag{22.12}\] The current is given by \[
\begin{aligned}
\mu_0 \delta \mathbf{j} &= \mathrm{i} \mathbf{k} \times \delta \mathbf{B} = - \mathbf{k} \times [\mathbf{k} \times (\boldsymbol{\xi} \times \mathbf{B}_0)] \\
&= k^2 \xi_y B_0 \cos \theta \hat{\mathbf{k}}_{\perp} .
\end{aligned}
\tag{22.13}\] Finally, the Lorentz force is \[
\mu_0 \delta \mathbf{j} \times \mathbf{B}_0 = - k^2 B_0^2 \cos^2 \theta \xi_y
\hat{\mathbf{y}} = - (\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{B}_0)^2 \boldsymbol{\xi}.
\tag{22.14}\] So \(\boldsymbol{\xi}\) evolves as a mass attached to an elastic spring with spring constant \((\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{B}_0)^2 / \mu_0\). In formulas, \[
\begin{aligned}
- \rho_0 \omega^2 \xi_y &= - \tfrac{1}{\mu_0} k^2 B_0^2 \cos^2 \theta \xi_y \\
\Longrightarrow \quad & \boxed{\omega = \pm \frac{B_0}{\sqrt{\mu_0 \rho_0}} k
\cos \theta = \pm \mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{v}_A ,}
\end{aligned}
\tag{22.15}\] where \(\mathbf{v}_A = \mathbf{B}_0 / \sqrt{\mu_0 \rho_0}\). We call \(\omega_A = \mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{v}_A\) the Alfvén frequency. These waves are called Alfvén waves, after Alfvén (1942) (Physics Nobel Prize in 1970). Some comments are in order.

If \(\theta = 0\), these waves propagate along the field lines with velocity (Alfvén velocity): \[
v_A = \frac{B_0}{\sqrt{\mu_0 \rho_0}} .
\tag{22.16}\] If \(\theta > 0\), the phase velocity is reduced to \(v_A \cos \theta\). However, the group velocity is \(\partial \omega / \partial \mathbf{k} = \pm v_A \hat{\mathbf{z}}\), for any \(\theta\). In other words, Alfvén waves always transport energy along the magnetic field lines, with velocity \(v_A\).
The displacement \(\boldsymbol{\xi}\) is perpendicular to the background field \(\mathbf{B}_0\), so these waves are transverse. More precisely, Alfvén waves behave as transverse waves in an elastic string (the magnetic field). Indeed, the restoring force for these waves is magnetic tension (Chapter 21).
As already mentioned \(\delta \rho = \delta p = 0\) for these waves. As such, Alfvén waves are incompressible and exist also in incompressible flows.

Although we have derived Alfvén waves as small perturbations, it turns out that Alfvén waves with \(\delta \mathbf{B} = \mp \sqrt{\mu_0 \rho} \, \delta \mathbf{v}\), propagating in the \(\pm z\) direction, are an exact solution to the full non-linear equations, as long as the magnetic pressure \(B^2 / 2 \mu_0\) stays uniform. This means that MHD flows can support arbitrarily strong waves. We check the small-amplitude case in Exercise 20.1.


22.2.2 Magnetosonic Waves
We now consider displacements in the \(x z\)-plane, as depicted in Figure 22.3:

\(\mathbf{B}_0\) is along \(z\)
\(\mathbf{k}\) is in the \(x z\)-plane
\(\boldsymbol{\xi}\) is also in the \(x z\)-plane

Note that \(\delta p, \delta \rho\) are no longer necessarily zero.






Figure 22.3: Geometry of the magnetosonic wave: \(\mathbf{B}_0\) along \(z\), \(\mathbf{k}\) in the \(xz\)-plane at an angle \(\theta\) from \(\mathbf{B}_0\), and displacement \(\boldsymbol{\xi}\) also in the \(xz\)-plane.



We can compute the current using the following vector identity \[
\mathbf{a} \times (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}) =\mathbf{b} (\mathbf{a}
\cdot \mathbf{c}) -\mathbf{c} (\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b})
\tag{22.17}\] and the fact that \(\mathbf{k} \perp \boldsymbol{\xi} \times \mathbf{B}_0\), since the latter is in the \(y\)-direction, we can write \[
\mathbf{k} \times [\mathbf{k} \times (\boldsymbol{\xi} \times \mathbf{B}_0)]
=\mathbf{k} [\mathbf{k} \cdot (\boldsymbol{\xi} \times \mathbf{B}_0)] - k^2
(\boldsymbol{\xi} \times \mathbf{B}_0) = - k^2 (\boldsymbol{\xi} \times
\mathbf{B}_0) .
\tag{22.18}\] Plugging this into the expression for the Lorentz force gives \[
\begin{aligned}
\delta \mathbf{j} \times \mathbf{B}_0 &= - \frac{1}{\mu_0}  \{ \mathbf{k}
\times [\mathbf{k} \times (\boldsymbol{\xi} \times \mathbf{B}_0)] \} \times
\mathbf{B}_0 \\
&= \frac{k^2}{\mu_0}  (\boldsymbol{\xi} \times \mathbf{B}_0)
\times \mathbf{B}_0 = - \frac{k^2 B_0^2 \xi_x}{\mu_0}  \hat{\mathbf{x}} .
\end{aligned}
\tag{22.19}\] The pressure force is \[
- \Gamma p_0 \mathbf{k} (\mathbf{k} \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}) = - k^2 \Gamma p_0
(\xi_x \sin \theta + \xi_z \cos \theta)  (\sin \theta \hat{\mathbf{x}} +
\cos \theta \hat{\mathbf{z}}) .
\tag{22.20}\] Using \(c_s^2 = \Gamma p_0 / \rho_0\) and \(v_A = B_0 / \sqrt{\mu_0 \rho_0}\), we find \[
\omega^2  \left(\begin{array}{c}
\xi_x\\
\xi_z
\end{array}\right) = k^2 \left(\begin{array}{cc}
c_s^2 \sin^2 \theta + v_A^2 & c_s^2 \sin \theta \cos \theta\\
c_s^2 \sin \theta \cos \theta & c_s^2 \cos^2 \theta
\end{array}\right) \left(\begin{array}{c}
\xi_x\\
\xi_z
\end{array}\right) .
\tag{22.21}\] The eigenvalues of this matrix are \(\omega^2 = T / 2 \pm \sqrt{T^2 / 4 - D}\), where \(T = k^2 (c_s^2 + v_A^2)\) and \(D = k^4 c_s^2 v_A^2 \cos^2 \theta\) are its trace and determinant. After some algebra, we find the dispersion relation \[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\left( \frac{\omega}{k} \right)^2 = {} & \frac{v_A^2 + c_s^2}{2} \\
& \pm \frac{1}{2} \sqrt{(v_A^2 - c_s^2)^2 + 4 c_s^2 v_A^2 \sin^2 \theta} .
\end{aligned}}
\tag{22.22}\] So there are two solutions and two corresponding polarization vectors \(\boldsymbol{\xi}_s\) and \(\boldsymbol{\xi}_f\). Note that \(\boldsymbol{\xi}_s \perp \boldsymbol{\xi}_f\), since the matrix \(\mathbf{F} (\mathbf{k})\) in Equation 22.21 is self-adjoint (see Equation 9.29). Conventionally, \(\boldsymbol{\xi}_s\) is taken to be the polarization corresponding to the minus sign in Equation 22.22, i.e., to the smaller phase velocity. This is the so-called slow magnetosonic wave. Conversely, \(\boldsymbol{\xi}_f\) is called the fast magnetosonic wave. As we will see shortly, these have a mixed character of sound and magnetic waves.

title: 22  MHD Waves
text:
22.3 Effect of Propagation Direction
We can get additional insight into the nature of the three modes by considering the properties of waves propagating along the magnetic field lines, or perpendicular to them. The general case will turn out to be intermediate between these two limits.

22.3.1 Parallel Propagating Waves (\(\theta = 0\))
Let us consider the case of waves propagating along the background magnetic field lines, that is \(\theta = 0\). In this case, the dispersion relation for Alfvén, slow, and fast modes are \[
\left( \frac{\omega}{k} \right)^2 = v_A^2, \qquad \left( \frac{\omega}{k}
\right)^2 = \frac{1}{2}  [v_A^2 + c_s^2 \pm |v_A^2 - c_s^2 |] .
\tag{22.23}\] There are two different cases, depending on whether \(v_A > c_s\) or \(v_A < c_s\), shown in Figure 22.4.






Figure 22.4: Polarization diagram for MHD waves propagating along the background magnetic field.




If \(v_A > c_s\), then

The slow mode polarization is along the magnetic field, the mode propagates at speed \(c_s\) and its restoring force is pressure.
Fast and Alfvén modes are orthogonal to the magnetic field and to each other and both have the character of Alfvén waves propagating with speed \(v_A\). Magnetic tension is their restoring force.

If \(v_A < c_s\), then the situation is similar as before, but the slow and fast modes exchange character: the fast mode is now a sound wave, while the slow mode is an Alfvén wave.



22.3.2 Perpendicularly Propagating Waves (\(\theta = 90^{\circ}\))
Let us consider the case of waves propagating perpendicular to the field lines. In this case, Alfvén and slow modes cannot propagate (they have \(\omega_{A, s} = 0\)). The fast-magnetosonic wave satisfies the dispersion relation \[
\left( \frac{\omega}{k} \right)^2 = v_A^2 + c_s^2 .
\tag{22.24}\] In this case \(\boldsymbol{\xi}_f\) is parallel to \(\mathbf{k}\). The restoring force for the mode is the sum of the magnetic and gas pressures, which explains why this mode is called the “magnetosonic” mode. In other words, the field lines are compressed, as in a sound wave, but they are not bent.


22.3.3 Friedrichs Diagrams
Friedrichs diagrams show the propagation velocity of the different MHD modes as a function of a generic propagation angle \(\theta\). The special cases of \(\theta = 0, 90^{\circ}\) discussed above correspond to the \(x\)- and \(y\)-axis in Figure 22.5. In general, slow and fast modes have a mixed character between sound waves and Alfvén waves.






Figure 22.5: Friedrichs diagrams for ideal MHD, for \(v_A = 2 c_s\) (left) and \(v_A = c_s / 2\) (right). The phase speeds are in units of the smaller of \(v_A\) and \(c_s\).

title: 22  MHD Waves
text:
22.4 Weak and Strong Field Limits
Finally, it is also instructive to compare slow- and fast-magnetosonic waves in the limits of weak magnetic field (\(c_s \gg v_A\)) and strong magnetic field \((v_A \gg c_s)\), as illustrated in Figure 22.6. Note that when \(v_A\) becomes a sizable fraction of the speed of light, we can no longer use Newtonian MHD, because the displacement current becomes important. In this limit, one needs to use the (significantly more complex) equations of relativistic magnetohydrodynamics.






Figure 22.6: Slow and fast magnetosonic waves in the limits of weak (left panel) and strong (right panel) magnetic fields.




Left panel: the fast mode is \(\sim\) a sound wave, with \(\omega \approx k c_s\), and the slow mode is nearly perpendicular to \(\mathbf{k}\), with \(\omega \approx k v_A \cos \theta\).
Right panel: the fast mode is \(\sim\) an Alfvén wave, with \(\omega \approx k v_A\), and the slow mode is nearly parallel to \(\mathbf{B}_0\), with \(\omega \approx k c_s \cos \theta\). In other words, the slow mode is a sound wave guided along the magnetic field lines. This is the situation in the solar corona.

title: 22  MHD Waves
text:
22.5 Shock Waves
As for unmagnetized gases, MHD waves can steepen into shock waves. Alfvén waves can steepen into rotational discontinuities, in which the magnetic field direction suddenly changes across an interface. Slow- and fast-magnetosonic waves can give rise to (slow and fast) shocks and rarefaction waves. The theory of MHD shocks is very complex and beyond the scope of this course. A good overview is given in Bazer and Ericson (1959). It is important to be aware that, even in the case of shocks propagating along magnetic field lines, MHD effects can be important. For example, a shock propagating along the magnetic field can create a component of the field parallel to the shock front (a switch-on shock), and the opposite process is also possible (a switch-off shock).
We treat in detail only one case that is relevant for the interstellar medium: a shock propagating in an isothermal flow with perpendicular magnetic field, as illustrated in Figure 22.7.






Figure 22.7: Isothermal shock propagating in a medium with perpendicular magnetic field.



The shock conditions for the shock shown in Figure 22.7 are: \[
\left[\!\left[ \rho u \right]\!\right] = 0, \quad \left[\!\left[ Bu \right]\!\right] = 0,
\quad \left[\!\left[ p + \rho u^2 + \frac{B^2}{2 \mu_0} \right]\!\right]
= 0,
\tag{22.25}\] where \(\left[\!\left[ \cdot \right]\!\right]\) denotes the jump across the shock.
In the absence of a magnetic field, the shock conditions for an isothermal gas, \(p = c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2 \rho\), are \(\rho_1 u_1 = \rho_2 u_2\) and \(c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2 \rho_1 + \rho_1 u_1^2 = c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2 \rho_2 + \rho_2 u_2^2\). Using the first condition to eliminate \(u_2\) from the second, we find \(c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2 (\rho_2 - \rho_1) = \rho_1 u_1^2 (1 - \rho_1 / \rho_2) = \rho_1 u_1^2 (\rho_2 - \rho_1) / \rho_2\). So the compression factor of an isothermal shock is \[
\frac{\rho_2}{\rho_1} = \left( \frac{u_1}{c_{\mathrm{iso}}} \right)^2,
\tag{22.26}\] which can become arbitrarily large for large upstream Mach numbers. We discuss isothermal shocks in more detail in Section 11.5.3. This is dramatically different when a magnetic field is present, as long as it is sufficiently strong: \[
u_1 \gg v_A = \frac{B_1}{\sqrt{\mu_0 \rho_1}} \gg c_{\mathrm{iso}}.
\tag{22.27}\] In this case, from \(\left[\!\left[ \rho u \right]\!\right] = \left[\!\left[ Bu \right]\!\right] = 0\), we conclude that \[
\frac{B_1}{\rho_1} = \frac{B_2}{\rho_2} .
\tag{22.28}\] From the conservation of momentum, we have (using \(u_1 \gg v_A \gg c_{\mathrm{iso}}\)) \[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\rho_2}{\rho_1} &= \frac{c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2 + u_1^2 + \frac{1}{2} v_A^2}{c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2 + u_2^2 +
\frac{B_2^2}{2 \mu_0 \rho_2}} \\
&\approx \frac{u_1^2}{c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2 + u_2^2 +
\frac{B_2^2}{2 \mu_0 \rho_2^2} \rho_2} \\
&= \frac{u_1^2}{c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2 + u_2^2 +
\frac{B_1^2}{2 \mu_0 \rho_1}  \frac{\rho_2}{\rho_1}} \\
&\approx \frac{u_1^2}{\frac{v_A^2}{2}  \frac{\rho_2}{\rho_1}} .
\end{aligned}
\tag{22.29}\] Solving for \(\rho_2 / \rho_1\), we obtain \[
\boxed{\frac{\rho_2}{\rho_1} = \sqrt{2}  \frac{u_1}{v_A} .}
\tag{22.30}\] This shows that the compression ratio now scales with the Alfvénic Mach number of the upstream gas, \(\mathrm{Ma}_A = u_1 / v_A\), instead of the square of its Mach number. This is another example showing that magnetic fields play an important role in the dynamics of the interstellar medium and in star formation.






TipExample: Shocks in molecular clouds



Consider a molecular cloud with temperature \(T \approx 10\,\mathrm{K}\), number density \(n \approx 100\,\mathrm{cm^{-3}}\) and magnetic field \(B \approx 1\,\mathrm{nT}\) (\(10\,\mu\mathrm{G}\)). The gas has \(\rho = \mu m_u n \approx 4 \times 10^{- 22}\,\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}} = 4 \times 10^{- 19}\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}\) (with \(\mu \approx 2.3\)) and \(c_{\mathrm{iso}} \approx 0.2\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}\). The Alfvén velocity is \[
v_A = \frac{B}{\sqrt{\mu_0 \rho}} \approx 1.4\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}} .
\tag{22.31}\] Note that \(v_A \gg c_{\mathrm{iso}}\), so the magnetic pressure is much larger than the gas pressure. Suppose that the cloud is hit by a shock with \(u_1 = 10\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}\), for example driven by a nearby supernova remnant. Then \(u_1 \gg v_A \gg c_{\mathrm{iso}}\), and Equation 22.30 applies. Without the magnetic field, the compression factor would be \((u_1 / c_{\mathrm{iso}})^2 \approx 2500\). With the magnetic field, it is only \(\sqrt{2} u_1 / v_A \approx 10\). In other words, the magnetic field makes the shocked gas about 250 times less dense. So it is much harder to form dense cores in molecular clouds with shocks alone.

title: 22  MHD Waves
text:
22.6 In-class worksheet
Fast Magnetosonic Waves. Consider a homogeneous plasma described by the ideal-MHD equations with \[
\rho_0 = \mathrm{const}, \qquad \mathbf{v}_0 = 0, \qquad \mathbf{B}_0 =
B_0  \hat{\mathbf{z}} .
\tag{22.32}\]

Introduce a small perturbation in the form of a displacement \(\boldsymbol{\xi} (t, \mathbf{x})\) of the fluid elements and show that the oscillation equation is \[
\begin{aligned}
& \rho_0  \frac{\partial^2 \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial t^2} = \Gamma p_0 \nabla
(\nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}) \\
& \quad + \frac{1}{\mu_0} \{ \nabla \times [\nabla
\times (\boldsymbol{\xi} \times \mathbf{B}_0)] \} \times \mathbf{B}_0 .
\end{aligned}
\tag{22.33}\]
Introduce the ansatz \(\boldsymbol{\xi} (t, \mathbf{x}) = \boldsymbol{\xi}_1 \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i} (\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{x}- \omega t)}\) and show that Equation 22.33 reduces to \[
\begin{aligned}
& - \rho_0 \omega^2 \boldsymbol{\xi}_1 = - \Gamma p_0 \mathbf{k} (\mathbf{k}
\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}_1) \\
& \quad - \frac{1}{\mu_0}  \{ \mathbf{k} \times
[\mathbf{k} \times (\boldsymbol{\xi}_1 \times \mathbf{B}_0)] \} \times
\mathbf{B}_0 .
\end{aligned}
\tag{22.34}\] [Hint. Use \(\partial_t \rightarrow - \mathrm{i} \omega\) and \(\nabla \rightarrow \mathrm{i} \mathbf{k}\).]
Consider waves with \(\mathbf{k} \parallel \hat{\mathbf{x}}\) and \(\boldsymbol{\xi} \parallel \mathbf{k}\). Find the dispersion relation \(\omega = \omega (\mathbf{k})\) and compute group and phase velocities for these waves.

title: 22  MHD Waves
text:
22.7 Exercises

Exercise 22.1 (Torsional Alfvén waves)  

Consider the torsional Alfvén wave, in cylindrical coordinates \((R, \phi, z)\), \[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{v} &= \epsilon v_A g (R) f (z - v_A t)  \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}, \\
\mathbf{B} &= B_0  \hat{\mathbf{z}} - \epsilon B_0 g (R) f (z - v_A t)
\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}},
\end{aligned}
\tag{22.35}\] where \(f\) and \(g\) are arbitrary functions and \(\epsilon\) is a small parameter. Show that it is a solution of the ideal-MHD equations to first order in \(\epsilon\).
Consider a uniform plasma at rest, threaded by the magnetic field \(B_0 \hat{\mathbf{z}}\). A thin disk of radius \(a\), made of a perfectly conducting material, lies in the \(x y\)-plane with its centre at the origin. At \(t = 0\), the disk is set into rotation with a constant angular velocity \(\Omega\), with \(\Omega a \ll v_A\). The plasma just above and below the disk must move with the same tangential velocity as the disk. Use the solution of part 1 to show that, at time \(t\), the plasma with \(R < a\) and \(| z | < v_A t\) rotates with angular velocity \(\Omega\), while the rest of the plasma is still at rest.
Let \(\Sigma\) be the mass per unit area of the disk. Estimate how long it takes before the disk starts to slow down. [Hint. Compare the angular momentum of the disk with that of the plasma set in motion by the wave.]

Adapted from Kulsrud (2005), Problem 3.4.
