title: 23  The Magnetorotational Instability
text:
23.1 Qualitative Picture
The magnetorotational instability (MRI) was first discovered by Velikhov (1959) and Chandrasekhar (1961), who studied the stability of a conducting fluid between two rotating cylinders, and then rediscovered in the context of accretion disks by Balbus and Hawley (1991). This is the instability thought to be responsible for the \(\alpha\)-viscosity (Chapter 16) in many astrophysical systems: from X-ray binaries to AGN disks. It is one of the most important, among the many instabilities operating in plasmas, so we will cover it in detail in these notes.
It was long known that a way to transport angular momentum in the disk is through magnetic stresses, that is the \(B_R B_{\phi} / \mu_0\) term in the momentum equation (Chapter 21). However, to explain the observed luminosities from accretion disks, the magnetic stresses must be similar in magnitude to the pressure in the disk \(p\) (the proportionality constant being the \(\alpha\)-viscosity coefficient). Given a small component of the field in the radial direction, flux freezing (Chapter 20) can grow \(B_{\phi}\) linearly in time. However, since \(B_R\) is small, this mechanism can transport angular momentum efficiently only if \(B_{\phi}^2 / 2 \mu_0 \gg p\). Such a strong toroidal field cannot be contained in the disk, because it is buoyant and rises out of it. The requirement for the magnetic stresses to do the job of transporting angular momentum is that \(B_R B_{\phi} / \mu_0 \approx \alpha \rho c_s^2\), with \(B_R \sim B_{\phi}\). Detailed simulations have shown that MRI is a mechanism that naturally produces the required field strengths over a short timescale. Note that a vertical field can also carry angular momentum away from the disk, through torsional Alfvén waves (Exercise 22.1).
Consider an accretion disk with Keplerian angular velocity profile \[
\Omega (R) = \Omega_0  \left( \frac{R_0}{R} \right)^{3 / 2},
\tag{23.1}\] initially threaded by a vertical magnetic field \(B_0 \hat{\mathbf{z}}\). Let \(A\) and \(B\) be two fluid elements connected by a magnetic field line (initially vertical) and displace their positions according to \(\xi_r = \epsilon \cos k z\), as shown in Figure 23.1. Because inner orbits are faster, \(A\) moves ahead of \(B\), as shown in the right panel of Figure 23.1. As a result, the field line that connects them is stretched in the azimuthal direction, and a toroidal component of the field, \(B_{\phi}\), is generated.
The magnetic tension (Chapter 21) then creates an attractive force between \(A\) and \(B\), which has the effect of transporting angular momentum from \(A\) to \(B\). This causes \(A\) to lose angular momentum and sink further inwards, while \(B\) gains angular momentum and starts moving outwards. In turn, because the angular velocity decreases with radius, \(A\) increases its angular velocity, while \(B\) slows down, further separating the two points. This in turn enhances the magnetic tension force. The cycle we have just described is unstable, so the initial perturbation grows exponentially in time, until the system becomes nonlinear.
The mechanism we have just described involves the magnetic tension force, so it is natural to expect a characteristic growth rate of \[
\lambda \approx kv_A, \qquad v_A = \frac{B_z}{\sqrt{\mu_0 \rho}} .
\tag{23.2}\] In our derivation, we have assumed the field to be sufficiently weak, so that the displaced fluid elements can acquire the angular velocity of their surroundings. This should be valid as long as \[
\omega_A = kv_A \lesssim \Omega ,
\tag{23.3}\] where \(\omega_A\) is the Alfvén frequency (Equation 22.15). We will find that the exact condition for instability is \(kv_A < \sqrt{3} \Omega\), so the maximum growth rate is achieved by taking \(k\) sufficiently large, so that \(\lambda \approx kv_A \approx \Omega\). This is a very short timescale: the amplitude of the fastest mode grows by a factor of about 100 every orbit! Moreover, the maximum growth rate is independent of the field strength, as long as \(v_A\) is not so large that the required \(k\) to satisfy \(kv_A < \sqrt{3} \Omega\) corresponds to perturbations with characteristic size larger than the vertical size of the disk. We will see that this requires \(v_A \lesssim c_s\).

title: 23  The Magnetorotational Instability
text: Figure 23.1: Qualitative description of the magnetorotational instability transporting angular momentum between fluid elements \(A\) and \(B\). Left panel: meridional view. Right panel: orbital plane.

title: 23  The Magnetorotational Instability
text:
23.2 Detailed Calculation
The starting point is the momentum equation of ideal MHD (Equation 19.4), with the Lorentz force written as the sum of magnetic pressure and tension (Equation 21.6). We write it in vector form. We use cylindrical coordinates \((R, \phi, z)\). \[
\rho \left[ \frac{\partial \mathbf{v}}{\partial t} + (\mathbf{v} \cdot
\nabla) \mathbf{v} \right] = - \nabla \left( p + \frac{B^2}{2 \mu_0} \right) +
\frac{(\mathbf{B} \cdot \nabla) \mathbf{B}}{\mu_0} +\mathbf{g} \rho .
\tag{23.4}\] We consider a disk that is Keplerian and threaded by a vertical magnetic field: \[
\mathbf{v}= R \Omega \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}} +\mathbf{u}, \qquad \mathbf{B}=
B_0  \hat{\mathbf{z}} +\mathbf{b}, \qquad p + \frac{B^2}{2 \mu_0} = P_0 + P.
\tag{23.5}\] We will treat \(\mathbf{u}\) and \(\mathbf{b}\) as (small) Eulerian perturbations. We will only consider modes that are axisymmetric (no \(\phi\) dependence) and incompressible \[
\nabla \cdot \mathbf{u}= \frac{1}{R}  \frac{\partial (Ru_R)}{\partial R} +
\frac{\partial u_z}{\partial z} = 0.
\tag{23.6}\] In equilibrium, the centrifugal force balances gravity, \(R \Omega^2 = G M / R^2\), and \(P_0\) is constant. We neglect the self-gravity of the disk, so that \(\mathbf{g}\) is not perturbed. To first order in \(\mathbf{u}\), and using Kepler’s law, we have \[
\begin{alignedat}{2}
(\mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla) \mathbf{v} &{}\rightarrow{} && (R \Omega)
(\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}} \cdot \nabla) \mathbf{u}+(\mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla) (R
\Omega \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}) \\
&{}={} && - 2 \Omega u_{\phi}  \hat{\mathbf{R}} + \left( R \frac{\mathrm{d}
\Omega}{\mathrm{d} R} + 2 \Omega \right) u_R \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}} \\
&{}={} && \frac{1}{2} \Omega u_R  \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}} - 2 \Omega u_{\phi}
\hat{\mathbf{R}} .
\end{alignedat}
\tag{23.7}\] Similarly, \[
\begin{alignedat}{2}
(\mathbf{B} \cdot \nabla) \mathbf{B} &{}\rightarrow{} && B_0  (\hat{\mathbf{z}}
\cdot \nabla) \mathbf{b}+(\mathbf{b} \cdot \nabla) (B_0  \hat{\mathbf{z}}) =
\\
& && B_0  \dfrac{\partial b_R}{\partial z}  \hat{\mathbf{R}} + B_0
\frac{\partial b_{\phi}}{\partial z}  \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}} + B_0
\frac{\partial b_z}{\partial z}  \hat{\mathbf{z}} .
\end{alignedat}
\tag{23.8}\] Since the unit vectors do not depend on \(z\), this is \(B_0 \, \partial \mathbf{b} / \partial z\). So the linearized momentum equation reads \[
\frac{\partial \mathbf{u}}{\partial t} + \frac{1}{2} \Omega u_R
\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}} - 2 \Omega u_{\phi}  \hat{\mathbf{R}} = -
\frac{1}{\rho} \nabla P + \frac{B_0}{\mu_0 \rho} \frac{\partial \mathbf{b}}{\partial z} .
\tag{23.9}\] The induction equation, Equation 19.19 with \(\eta = 0\), can be linearized in a similar way: \[
\begin{aligned}
& \nabla \times (\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B}) \\
& \quad \rightarrow \nabla \times \bigl[(R \Omega \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}) \times (b_R \hat{\mathbf{R}} + b_{\phi} \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}} + b_z \hat{\mathbf{z}}) \\
& \qquad\qquad + (u_R \hat{\mathbf{R}} + u_{\phi} \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}} + u_z \hat{\mathbf{z}}) \times (B_0 \hat{\mathbf{z}})\bigr] \\
& \quad = \nabla \times [- R \Omega b_R \hat{\mathbf{z}} + R \Omega b_z \hat{\mathbf{R}} \\
& \qquad\qquad - u_R B_0 \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}} + u_{\phi} B_0 \hat{\mathbf{R}}] \\
& \quad = \nabla \times [ (R \Omega b_z + u_{\phi} B_0) \hat{\mathbf{R}} \\
& \qquad\qquad - u_R B_0 \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}} - R \Omega b_R \hat{\mathbf{z}}] \\
& \quad = \left( \frac{\partial u_R}{\partial z} B_0 \right) \hat{\mathbf{R}} + \biggl( R \Omega \frac{\partial b_z}{\partial z} + \frac{\partial u_{\phi}}{\partial z} B_0 \\
& \qquad\qquad - \frac{3}{2} \Omega b_R + \Omega \frac{\partial (Rb_R)}{\partial R} \biggr) \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}} \\
& \qquad\qquad - \frac{1}{R} \left[ \frac{\partial (Ru_R B_0)}{\partial R} \right] \hat{\mathbf{z}} \\
& \quad = \left( \frac{\partial u_R}{\partial z} B_0 \right) \hat{\mathbf{R}} + \left( \frac{\partial u_{\phi}}{\partial z} B_0 - \frac{3}{2} \Omega b_R \right) \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}} \\
& \qquad\qquad - \frac{1}{R} \left[ \frac{\partial (Ru_R B_0)}{\partial R} \right] \hat{\mathbf{z}} .
\end{aligned}
\tag{23.10}\] In the last equation we have also used the condition that \(\nabla \cdot \mathbf{b}= 0\).
We will consider a small patch of the disk, so that we can use the Fourier (WKB) ansatz: \[
\mathbf{u}=\mathbf{u}_0 \mathrm{e}^{\lambda t + \mathrm{i} (k_R R + k_z z)}, \qquad
\mathbf{b}=\mathbf{b}_0 \mathrm{e}^{\lambda t + \mathrm{i} (k_R R + k_z z)}
\tag{23.11}\] where \(k_R R, k_z R \gg 1\), so that we can neglect terms of order \(1 / R\). We also assume \(k_z \gg k_R\), which simplifies the algebra and turns out to give the fastest-growing modes. Here \(\lambda = - \mathrm{i} \omega\), so that modes with \(\lambda^2 > 0\) grow exponentially, while modes with \(\lambda^2 < 0\) oscillate. Substituting this into the linearized equations of motion yields \[
\begin{alignedat}{2}
\lambda u_R - 2 \Omega u_{\phi} &{}={} && - \mathrm{i} k_R  \frac{P}{\rho} +
\frac{\mathrm{i} k_z B_0 b_R}{\mu_0 \rho},  \\
\lambda u_{\phi} + \frac{\Omega}{2} u_R &{}={} && \frac{\mathrm{i} k_z B_0
b_{\phi}}{\mu_0 \rho}, \\
\lambda u_z &{}={} && - \mathrm{i} k_z  \frac{P}{\rho} + \frac{\mathrm{i} k_z B_0 b_z}{\mu_0
\rho} .
\end{alignedat}
\tag{23.12}\] We can eliminate \(P / \rho\) from the last equation and insert it into the first to obtain (in the limit \(k_z \gg k_R\)): \[
\lambda u_R - 2 \Omega u_{\phi} = \mathrm{i} k_z  \frac{B_0 b_R}{\mu_0 \rho} .
\tag{23.13}\] The linearized induction equation yields \[
\begin{alignedat}{2}
\lambda b_R &{}={} && \mathrm{i} k_z B_0 u_R  \\
\lambda b_{\phi} &{}={} && - \frac{3}{2} \Omega b_R + \mathrm{i} k_z B_0
u_{\phi} .
\end{alignedat}
\tag{23.14}\] Eliminating \(b_R\) in the second equation yields \[
\lambda b_{\phi} = - \frac{3}{2}  \frac{\mathrm{i} k_z B_0 \Omega}{\lambda}
u_R + \mathrm{i} k_z B_0 u_{\phi} .
\tag{23.15}\] Eliminating \(b_{\phi}\) and \(b_R\) in the momentum equations above and introducing the Alfvén frequency \(\omega_A = k_z v_A\), with \(\omega_A^2 = k_z^2 B_0^2 / \mu_0 \rho\), yields \[
\begin{alignedat}{2}
(\lambda^2 + \omega_A^2) u_R &{}={} && 2 \lambda \Omega u_{\phi},  \\
(\lambda^2 + \omega_A^2) u_{\phi} &{}={} && \left( - \frac{\lambda}{2} \Omega
+ \frac{3}{2}  \frac{\omega_A^2 \Omega}{\lambda} \right) u_R .
\end{alignedat}
\tag{23.16}\] Introducing \[
\mu^2 = \lambda^2 + \omega_A^2,
\tag{23.17}\] the dispersion relation becomes \[
f (\mu^2) = \mu^4 + \Omega^2 \mu^2 - 4 \Omega^2 \omega_A^2 = 0.
\tag{23.18}\] The product of the two roots of \(f (\mu^2)\) is negative, so there is one positive and one negative root. Since \(\lambda^2 = \mu^2 - \omega_A^2\), the instability is present when the positive root is larger than \(\omega_A^2\). Since \(f (0) < 0\), this occurs if \[
f (\omega_A^2) = \omega_A^4 - 3 \Omega^2 \omega_A^2 < 0 \Longrightarrow
\boxed{\frac{k_z B_0}{\sqrt{\mu_0 \rho}} = \omega_A < \sqrt{3} \Omega .}
\tag{23.19}\] We find that if \(k_z\) is sufficiently small (long wavelengths), then the mode is unstable. However, if the background field is too large, then the condition in Equation 23.19 might only be satisfied for \(k_z\) that corresponds to modes larger than the disk thickness \(H \approx c_s / \Omega\) (Exercise 16.1), so the disk is stable to the MRI. The unstable modes have wavelengths longer than \(2 \pi v_A / (\sqrt{3} \Omega)\), so they fit in the disk only if \(v_A \lesssim c_s\). In other words, the MRI operates when the plasma \(\beta\) (Equation 21.25) is larger than about one, that is, when the magnetic pressure is smaller than the gas pressure.
The growth rate of the instability is found by solving the dispersion relation to find \[
\lambda^2 = \frac{\Omega}{2}  \left( - \Omega + \sqrt{\Omega^2 + 16
\omega_A^2} \right) - \omega_A^2,
\tag{23.20}\] which is maximized when \[
\omega_A = \frac{\sqrt{15}}{4} \Omega \approx \Omega,
\tag{23.21}\] which corresponds to \[
k_{\max} = \frac{\sqrt{15}}{4} \frac{\Omega}{v_A} \approx \frac{\Omega}{v_A} .
\tag{23.22}\] The growth rate of the most unstable mode is \[
\boxed{\lambda_{\max} = \frac{3}{4} \Omega .}
\tag{23.23}\]






TipExample: The MRI in a protoplanetary disk



Consider the disk of gas and dust around a young star like the Sun, at a distance \(R = 1\,\mathrm{AU}\) from the star. In the minimum-mass solar nebula, a standard model for the early solar system, the gas at this distance has \(T \approx 280\,\mathrm{K}\) and \(\rho \approx 1.4 \times 10^{- 9}\,\mathrm{g\,cm^{- 3}} = 1.4 \times 10^{- 6}\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{- 3}}\). The gas is mostly molecular hydrogen, with \(\mu \approx 2.3\), so \(c_s \approx 1\,\mathrm{km\,s^{- 1}}\). The angular velocity is \(\Omega = (G M_{\odot} / R^3)^{1 / 2} \approx 2 \times 10^{- 7}\,\mathrm{s^{- 1}}\), corresponding to an orbital period of one year, and the thickness of the disk is \(H \approx c_s / \Omega \approx 5 \times 10^{9}\,\mathrm{m} \approx 0.03\,\mathrm{AU}\).
Suppose that the disk is threaded by a vertical field \(B_0 \approx 10^{- 4}\,\mathrm{T}\) (\(1\,\mathrm{G}\)). The Alfvén speed is \[
v_A = \frac{B_0}{\sqrt{\mu_0 \rho}} \approx 75\,\mathrm{m\,s^{- 1}},
\tag{23.24}\] and the plasma \(\beta \approx 360\). The fastest-growing mode has wavelength \(2 \pi / k_{\max} \approx 2.5 \times 10^{9}\,\mathrm{m} \approx H / 2\), so it fits in the disk. Its growth time is \(1 / \lambda_{\max} = 4 / (3 \Omega) \approx 80\) days. In other words, even a field with magnetic pressure 360 times smaller than the gas pressure makes the disk unstable, and the perturbations grow by a factor of about 100 every year.


It is instructive to check the limit of our analysis when \(B_0 \rightarrow 0\), which corresponds to \(\omega_A \rightarrow 0\). If \(\omega_A \equiv 0\), then Equation 23.16 reduces to \[
\lambda^2 u_R = - \Omega^2 u_R, \qquad \lambda^2 u_{\phi} = - \Omega^2
u_{\phi} .
\tag{23.25}\] In other words, the perturbations oscillate with the epicyclic frequency \(\kappa\), which for a Keplerian disk equals \(\Omega\). More in general, an unmagnetized rotating fluid is stable to axisymmetric perturbations as long as its specific angular momentum \(R^2 \Omega\) increases outward. This is called the Rayleigh criterion, and it is satisfied by Keplerian disks.
In the limit of \(0 < \omega_A \ll \Omega\) (long wavelength perturbations, or weak magnetic field), we can drop all the \(\omega_A\) terms in Equation 23.16, with the exception of the term multiplied by \(\Omega\) to obtain \[
\begin{alignedat}{2}
\lambda^2 u_R &{}={} && 2 \lambda \Omega u_{\phi},  \\
\lambda^2 u_{\phi} &{}={} && \left( - \frac{\lambda}{2} \Omega + \frac{3}{2}
\frac{\omega_A^2 \Omega}{\lambda} \right) u_R .
\end{alignedat}
\tag{23.26}\] Eliminating \(u_{\phi}\), we obtain: \[
\lambda^2 u_R = \left( \frac{3 \omega_A^2 \Omega^2}{\lambda^2} - \Omega^2
\right) u_R,
\tag{23.27}\] which has unstable solutions with \(\lambda^2 > 0\) as long as \(\omega_A > 0\). For \(\omega_A \ll \Omega\), the growing solution is \(\lambda \approx \sqrt{3} \omega_A\). This growth rate goes to zero for \(B_0 \to 0\), at fixed \(k_z\). However, the fastest-growing mode always grows at the rate \(\frac{3}{4} \Omega\), for any \(B_0 > 0\). In other words, an arbitrarily weak magnetic field makes the disk unstable, even though the disk is stable without the field. Note that the MRI only requires the angular velocity to decrease outward (see Section 23.3), while the Rayleigh criterion is about the angular momentum. This is why the MRI is so important for accretion disks.

title: 23  The Magnetorotational Instability
text:
23.3 In-class worksheet
There is a simple mechanical equivalent of the magnetorotational instability (MRI) in a disk with vertical magnetic field. This model is concerned with two particles of mass \(m\) orbiting a central object with angular velocity \(\Omega = \Omega (R)\) (not necessarily Keplerian). The particles are connected by a spring, as shown in Figure 23.2. The spring pulls each mass towards the common center of mass with a force equal to \(-mK\) times its displacement.






Figure 23.2: Mechanical analogue of the magnetorotational instability: two masses connected by a spring, orbiting a central object.



The coordinates \(x\) and \(y\) denote the displacement of one of the two masses from the common center of mass.

Assuming \(|x|, |y| \ll R\), show that the displacement satisfies the differential equations \[
\begin{alignedat}{2}
\ddot{x} - 2 \Omega \dot{y} &{}={} && - \left( K + \frac{\mathrm{d}
\Omega^2}{\mathrm{d} \ln R} \right) x, \\
\ddot{y} + 2 \Omega \dot{x} &{}={} && - Ky.
\end{alignedat}
\tag{23.28}\] Note that these are the same equations as those obtained for the MRI in a disk threaded by a vertical magnetic field, \(k_R = 0\), and \(K = (v_A k_z)^2 = \omega_A^2\).
Look for solutions in the form \(x (t) = x_0 \mathrm{e}^{\lambda t}\), \(y (t) = y_0 \mathrm{e}^{\lambda t}\). Find \(\lambda\).
Under what conditions is the system unstable?

title: 23  The Magnetorotational Instability
text:
23.4 Exercises

Exercise 23.1 (Dead zones in protoplanetary disks) In this exercise we estimate how much ionization is needed for the MRI to operate in a protoplanetary disk.

Consider the MRI in a disk with finite resistivity, that is, with magnetic diffusivity \(\eta > 0\). Argue that a mode with wavenumber \(k\) is damped by Ohmic diffusion on the time scale \(T_{\mathrm{decay}} = 1 / (k^2 \eta)\) (see Equation 20.18). Show that the fastest-growing mode, with \(k \approx \Omega / v_A\), grows faster than it is damped only if \[
v_A^2 \gtrsim \eta \Omega .
\tag{23.29}\]
In a weakly ionized gas, the magnetic diffusivity is approximately \[
\eta \approx 2.34 \times 10^{- 2} \left( \frac{T}{\mathrm{K}} \right)^{1 / 2} x_e^{- 1}\,\mathrm{m^2\,s^{- 1}},
\tag{23.30}\] where \(x_e = n_e / n\) is the ionization fraction. Find the minimum ionization fraction for the MRI to operate in the disk of the protoplanetary-disk Example (\(T \approx 280\,\mathrm{K}\), \(\Omega \approx 2 \times 10^{- 7}\,\mathrm{s^{- 1}}\), \(v_A \approx 75\,\mathrm{m\,s^{- 1}}\)).
Close to the star, where \(T \gtrsim 1000\,\mathrm{K}\), alkali metals such as sodium and potassium are thermally ionized, and \(x_e\) is large. Further out, the gas is ionized only by X-rays from the star and by cosmic rays. These ionize the surface layers of the disk, but they do not reach its dense midplane, unless the column density of the disk is small. Where in the disk do you expect the MRI to operate? Sketch your answer in the \(R z\)-plane.

title: Appendix A — Vector Calculus
text:
A.1 Vector fields
Fluid mechanics is most concisely and generally written in the language of vector calculus. This appendix gives key definitions and theorems used throughout the rest of these notes. A more extended, but still concise treatment can be found in Griffiths (2023, chap. 1 and Appendix A). The point of view we follow in these notes is geometrical: we will introduce the elements of vector calculus in terms of geometrical/physical quantities without reference to any coordinate system.
In a given coordinate system, the position of a point is given by three numbers \(x_1, x_2, x_3\) and we will write, with slight abuse of notation, \(A = (x_1, x_2, x_3)\). For example, in Cartesian coordinates each point will be associated to one triple \(A = (x,y,z)\), while in spherical coordinates the same point will be written as \(A = (r,\theta,\phi)\).
We can picture \(\overrightarrow{AB}\) as an arrow connecting \(A\) to \(B\), and pointing from \(A\) to \(B\). Since a translation moves all points in the same way, the arrow can be moved parallel to itself without changing the vector: \(\overrightarrow{AB} = \overrightarrow{CD}\) whenever \(A\), \(B\), \(D\), and \(C\) are the vertices of a parallelogram. We will choose a special point in Euclidean space called the origin \(O\) and define as the position vector of a point \(P\) the vector \(\mathbf{r}_P :=
\overrightarrow{OP}\).
Most frequently, we deal with vector fields in these notes. An example is the fluid velocity \(\mathbf{v}\). Vector fields associate to each point in Euclidean space a vector in another Euclidean space, e.g., the space of velocities in the case of \(\mathbf{v}\).
Vector fields can be decomposed over a vector basis as \[
    \mathbf{v} = v_1(x_1,x_2,x_3) \mathbf{e}_1 + v_2(x_1,x_2,x_3) \mathbf{e}_2 + v_3(x_1,x_2,x_3) \mathbf{e}_3,
\tag{A.1}\] where \(\mathbf{e}_1, \mathbf{e}_2, \mathbf{e}_3\) are, at each point, linearly independent vectors. For example, the Cartesian basis is \(\mathbf{e}_1 =
\hat{\mathbf{x}}\), \(\mathbf{e}_2 = \hat{\mathbf{y}}\), and \(\mathbf{e}_3 = \hat{\mathbf{z}}\). Alternatively, we might take a spherical basis \(\mathbf{e}_1 = \hat{\mathbf{r}}\), \(\mathbf{e}_2 = \hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\), and \(\mathbf{e}_3 = \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}\). Note that, in the latter case, the basis vectors are themselves position dependent, since, e.g., the radial direction is different for different \((\theta,\phi)\). This must be taken into account when computing derivatives of vector fields in the spherical basis. Note that, because vector fields live in a different space from the coordinates, we can, in principle, combine vector basis and coordinate choices in an arbitrary way. For example, we could work in spherical coordinates, but still consider the \(\hat{\mathbf{x}}\), \(\hat{\mathbf{y}}\), and \(\hat{\mathbf{z}}\) components of vector fields. In practice, throughout these notes we will use the vector basis naturally associated with the chosen coordinate system. For a coordinate system \((x_1, x_2, x_3)\), the natural vector basis is chosen so that the unit vector \(\mathbf{e}_i\) points along the direction in which \(x_i\) increases, while all other coordinates are kept constant. In other words, the natural basis is formed by unit vectors that are tangent to the coordinate lines.

title: Appendix A — Vector Calculus
text:
Definition A.1 (Point) We define a point to be an element of three-dimensional Euclidean space \(\mathbb{E}^3\). We will denote points with capital letters, \(A, B, C \in \mathbb{E}^3\).



Definition A.2 (Vector) A vector is a translation of Euclidean space, that is, a shift that moves every point by the same distance in the same direction. For any two points \(A\) and \(B\) there is exactly one translation that moves \(A\) to \(B\). We denote it by \(\overrightarrow{AB} = B - A\).

title: Appendix A — Vector Calculus
text:
A.2 Gradient

Definition A.3 (Gradient) If \(f\) is a scalar function, we define its gradient \(\nabla f\) as being the only vector field such that, for every pair of points \(A\) and \(B\) and any (smooth) curve connecting them \[
    f(B) - f(A) = \int_A^B \nabla f \cdot \mathrm{d} \mathbf{l}.
\tag{A.2}\]

In Cartesian coordinates, we can find the expression of the gradient by considering two points \(A = (x,y,z)\) and \(B = (x+\mathrm{d} x, y+\mathrm{d} y, z + \mathrm{d}
z)\). Taylor expanding to first order, the LHS of Equation A.2 is \[
    f(B) - f(A) = f(x+\mathrm{d} x, y+\mathrm{d} y, z + \mathrm{d} z) - f(x,y,z) =
    \partial_x f \mathrm{d} x + \partial_y f \mathrm{d} y + \partial_z f \mathrm{d} z .
\tag{A.3}\] The RHS is \[
    \int_A^B \nabla f \cdot \mathrm{d} \mathbf{l} = (\nabla f)_x {} \mathrm{d} x + (\nabla f)_y {} \mathrm{d} y + (\nabla f)_z {} \mathrm{d} z ,
\tag{A.4}\] so we conclude that \[
    \nabla f = \left(\begin{array}{c}
        \partial_x f \\
        \partial_y f \\
        \partial_z f
    \end{array}
    \right).
\tag{A.5}\] For the generalization to curvilinear coordinates, see Griffiths (2023, Appendix A).
Note that the definition of gradient can be extended to vectors. In this case the gradient is a matrix \(\nabla \mathbf{v}\) such that \[
    \mathbf{v}(B) - \mathbf{v}(A) = \int_A^B (\nabla\mathbf{v}) \cdot \mathrm{d} \mathbf{l}.
\tag{A.6}\] The dot in the integral denotes a matrix–vector multiplication, \([(\nabla\mathbf{v}) \cdot \mathrm{d}\mathbf{l}]_i = \sum_j (\nabla\mathbf{v})_{ij}\, \mathrm{d} l_j\). Repeating the calculation done for Equation A.5 for each component of \(\mathbf{v}\), we find that, in Cartesian coordinates, \[
    (\nabla\mathbf{v})_{ij} = \partial_j v_i ,
\tag{A.7}\] that is, the \(i\)-th row of \(\nabla\mathbf{v}\) is the gradient of \(v_i\). Be aware that some textbooks use the transposed convention, \((\nabla\mathbf{v})_{ij} = \partial_i v_j\). The derivative of \(\mathbf{v}\) along a vector \(\mathbf{a}\) is written as \[
    (\mathbf{a}\cdot\nabla)\mathbf{v} = (\nabla\mathbf{v}) \cdot \mathbf{a} , \qquad
    \left[ (\mathbf{a}\cdot\nabla)\mathbf{v} \right]_i = \sum_j a_j \partial_j v_i .
\tag{A.8}\]

title: Appendix A — Vector Calculus
text:
A.3 Curl

Definition A.4 (Curl) Given a vector field \(\mathbf{v}\), we define its curl \(\nabla\times\mathbf{v}\) as being the only vector field such that, for every smooth two-dimensional surface \(S\) bounded by a closed curve \(C\), we have \[
    \oint_C \mathbf{v} \cdot \mathrm{d}\mathbf{l} = \int_S (\nabla\times\mathbf{v}) \cdot \mathrm{d} \mathbf{A},
\tag{A.9}\] where \(\mathrm{d}\mathbf{A} = \hat{\mathbf{n}}\, \mathrm{d} A\), \(\hat{\mathbf{n}}\) is the unit normal to \(S\), and the direction in which \(C\) is traversed is related to \(\hat{\mathbf{n}}\) by the right-hand rule (Figure A.1).







Figure A.1: Stokes’ theorem. With the thumb of the right hand along \(\mathrm{d}\mathbf{A}\), the fingers curl in the direction of \(\mathrm{d}\mathbf{l}\) along \(C\).



The expression in Equation A.9 is known as Stokes’ theorem. We take it as the operational definition of the curl. In Cartesian coordinates, the curl can be written as the following formal determinant \[
    \nabla\times\mathbf{v} = \left|
        \begin{array}{ccc}
            \hat{\mathbf{x}} & \hat{\mathbf{y}} & \hat{\mathbf{z}} \\
            \partial_x & \partial_y & \partial_z \\
            v_x & v_y & v_z
        \end{array}
        \right| =
        \left( \partial_y v_z - \partial_z v_y \right) \hat{\mathbf{x}} +
        \left( \partial_z v_x - \partial_x v_z \right) \hat{\mathbf{y}} +
        \left( \partial_x v_y - \partial_y v_x \right) \hat{\mathbf{z}}.
\tag{A.10}\] This is formally the same expression as the vector product between the “vector” \(\nabla = \partial_x \hat{\mathbf{x}} + \partial_y \hat{\mathbf{y}} +
\partial_z \hat{\mathbf{z}}\) and \(\mathbf{v}\). However, note that this equivalence breaks down in curvilinear coordinates.

title: Appendix A — Vector Calculus
text:
A.4 Divergence

Definition A.5 (Divergence) Given a vector field \(\mathbf{v}\), we define its divergence \(\nabla\cdot\mathbf{v}\) as being the only scalar field such that, for every closed surface \(S\) enclosing a volume \(V\), we have \[
    \oint_S \mathbf{v} \cdot \mathrm{d} \mathbf{A} = \int_V \nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}\, \mathrm{d} V,
\tag{A.11}\] where \(\mathrm{d}\mathbf{A} = \hat{\mathbf{n}}\, \mathrm{d} A\) and \(\hat{\mathbf{n}}\) is the outward-pointing unit normal to \(S\) (Figure A.2).







Figure A.2: The divergence theorem. The area elements \(\mathrm{d}\mathbf{A}\) are normal to the closed surface \(S\) and point out of the volume \(V\).



The expression in Equation A.11 is known as Gauss’ theorem, or the divergence theorem. In Cartesian coordinates, we can find the expression for the divergence by considering Equation A.11 applied to a rectangular region centered at \((x,y,z)\) with sides of length \(\mathrm{d} x\), \(\mathrm{d} y\), and \(\mathrm{d} z\). The derivation is analogous to the calculation leading to Equation 1.12 in Chapter 1 and will not be repeated here. The result is that \[
    \nabla\cdot\mathbf{v} = \partial_x v_x + \partial_y v_y + \partial_z v_z.
\tag{A.12}\] This is formally the same expression as if we were to take the dot product between \(\nabla\) and \(\mathbf{v}\). However, once again, this equivalence breaks down in curvilinear coordinates.
The divergence can be extended to tensor fields, such as the stress tensors that appear in the equations of fluid dynamics.

Definition A.6 (Divergence of a tensor) Given a tensor field \(\mathbf{T}\), we define its divergence \(\nabla\cdot\mathbf{T}\) as being the only vector field such that, for every closed surface \(S\) enclosing a volume \(V\), we have \[
    \oint_S \mathbf{T} \cdot \mathrm{d} \mathbf{A} = \int_V \nabla \cdot \mathbf{T}\, \mathrm{d} V,
\tag{A.13}\] where \((\mathbf{T}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{A})_i = \sum_j T_{ij}\, \mathrm{d} A_j\).

In Cartesian coordinates, the \(i\)-th component of the LHS of Equation A.13 is the flux of the vector field formed by the \(i\)-th row of \(\mathbf{T}\), \((T_{ix}, T_{iy}, T_{iz})\). Applying Equation A.11 to each row, we find \[
    (\nabla\cdot\mathbf{T})_i = \partial_x T_{ix} + \partial_y T_{iy} + \partial_z T_{iz} .
\tag{A.14}\] For a symmetric tensor, \(T_{ij} = T_{ji}\), it does not matter which index is summed over. All the stress tensors in these notes are symmetric.

title: Appendix A — Vector Calculus
text:
A.5 Laplacian

Definition A.7 (Laplacian) If \(f\) is a scalar function, we define its Laplacian as \(
abla^2 f = 
abla\cdot(
abla f)\). If \(\mathbf{v}\) is a vector field, we define its Laplacian as \(
abla^2 \mathbf{v} = 
abla\cdot(
abla \mathbf{v})\).

In Cartesian coordinates \[
    
abla^2 f = \partial_x^2 f + \partial_y^2 f + \partial_z^2 f.
	ag{A.15}\]
From Equation A.7 and Equation A.14, the Cartesian components of \(
abla^2\mathbf{v}\) are the Laplacians of the components of \(\mathbf{v}\), \((
abla^2\mathbf{v})_i = 
abla^2 v_i\). This is not true for the components in a curvilinear basis.

title: Appendix A — Vector Calculus
text:
A.6 Vector identities
The identities involving derivatives of vector fields that we use in these notes, such as the product rules (Equation B.2) and the expression for the advective term (Equation B.5), are collected in Appendix B. They can all be verified by writing them out in Cartesian components. However, because gradient, curl, and divergence are geometrical objects, these identities hold in any coordinate system. Here, we prove two particularly important identities.

Theorem A.1 (Curl of a gradient and divergence of a curl) For any smooth scalar field \(f\) and vector field \(\mathbf{a}\), \[
\nabla \times (\nabla f) = 0 , \qquad \nabla \cdot (\nabla \times \mathbf{a}) = 0 .
\tag{A.16}\]







Figure A.3: Proof that \(\nabla \cdot (\nabla \times \mathbf{a}) = 0\). A closed surface is cut along the curve \(C\) into \(S_1\) and \(S_2\), here pulled apart. On both pieces \(\mathrm{d}\mathbf{A}\) points out of the enclosed volume, so, by the right-hand rule, \(C\) is traversed in opposite directions for the two pieces.




Proof. For the first identity, consider any surface \(S\) bounded by a closed curve \(C\). By Equation A.9 and Equation A.2, \[
\int_S [\nabla \times (\nabla f)] \cdot \mathrm{d}\mathbf{A}
= \oint_C \nabla f \cdot \mathrm{d}\mathbf{l} = f(P) - f(P) = 0 ,
\tag{A.17}\] because a closed curve starts and ends at the same point \(P\). Since this holds for every surface, \(\nabla \times (\nabla f) = 0\).
For the second identity, consider a closed surface \(S\) enclosing a volume \(V\), and cut it along a closed curve \(C\) into two pieces \(S_1\) and \(S_2\) (Figure A.3). Applying Equation A.9 to each piece, with \(\mathrm{d}\mathbf{A}\) pointing out of \(V\), we find \[
\begin{aligned}
\oint_S (\nabla \times \mathbf{a}) \cdot \mathrm{d}\mathbf{A}
&= \int_{S_1} (\nabla \times \mathbf{a}) \cdot \mathrm{d}\mathbf{A} \\
&\quad {} + \int_{S_2} (\nabla \times \mathbf{a}) \cdot \mathrm{d}\mathbf{A} \\
&= \oint_C \mathbf{a} \cdot \mathrm{d}\mathbf{l} - \oint_C \mathbf{a} \cdot \mathrm{d}\mathbf{l} = 0 .
\end{aligned}
\tag{A.18}\] The two line integrals have opposite signs because the outward normals of \(S_1\) and \(S_2\) lie on opposite sides of \(C\), so the right-hand rule traverses \(C\) in opposite directions. By Equation A.11, the integral of \(\nabla \cdot (\nabla \times \mathbf{a})\) then vanishes over every volume, so \(\nabla \cdot (\nabla \times \mathbf{a}) = 0\).

title: Appendix A — Vector Calculus
text:
A.7 In-class worksheet

Compute the gradient of the function \[
f (x, y, z) = \frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2}} .
\tag{A.19}\]
Consider the vector field \[
\mathbf{E}= \hat{\mathbf{r}} = \left(\begin{array}{c}
\frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2}}\\
\frac{y}{\sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2}}\\
\frac{z}{\sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2}}
\end{array}\right) .
\tag{A.20}\] Its gradient \(\nabla \mathbf{E}\) is the matrix \[
\begin{pmatrix}
\partial_x E_x & \partial_y E_x & \partial_z E_x\\
\partial_x E_y & \partial_y E_y & \partial_z E_y\\
\partial_x E_z & \partial_y E_z & \partial_z E_z
\end{pmatrix} .
\tag{A.21}\] Compute

the gradient \(\nabla \mathbf{E}\);
\(\nabla \cdot \mathbf{E}\);
\(\nabla \times \mathbf{E}\).

Prove that \[
\nabla \cdot \nabla f = \nabla^2 f = \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2} +
\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y^2} + \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial z^2} .
\tag{A.22}\]
The divergence of a tensor field \[
\mathbf{T}= \left(\begin{array}{ccc}
T_{x x} & T_{x y} & T_{x z}\\
T_{y x} & T_{y y} & T_{y z}\\
T_{z x} & T_{z y} & T_{z z}
\end{array}\right)
\tag{A.23}\] is the vector with components \[
\begin{aligned}
(\nabla \cdot \mathbf{T})_x &= \partial_x T_{x x} + \partial_y T_{x y} + \partial_z T_{x z} , \\
(\nabla \cdot \mathbf{T})_y &= \partial_x T_{y x} + \partial_y T_{y y} + \partial_z T_{y z} , \\
(\nabla \cdot \mathbf{T})_z &= \partial_x T_{z x} + \partial_y T_{z y} + \partial_z T_{z z} .
\end{aligned}
\tag{A.24}\] Prove that \[
\nabla \cdot (p\mathbf{I}) = \nabla \cdot \left(\begin{array}{ccc}
p &  & \\
& p & \\
&  & p
\end{array}\right) = \nabla p.
\tag{A.25}\]





Griffiths, David J. 2023. Introduction to Electrodynamics. 5th ed. Cambridge University Press.

title: Appendix B — Useful Formulae
text:
B.2 Curvilinear Coordinates

B.2.1 Cylindrical coordinates \((R, \phi, z)\)
\(x = R \cos \phi\), \(y = R \sin \phi\), \(\mathrm{d} V = R \mathrm{d} R \mathrm{d} \phi \mathrm{d} z\), \(\partial_{\phi} \hat{\mathbf{R}} = \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}\), \(\partial_{\phi} \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}} = - \hat{\mathbf{R}}\). \[
\begin{aligned}
\nabla f &= \partial_R f \, \hat{\mathbf{R}} + \frac{1}{R} \partial_{\phi} f \, \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}} + \partial_z f \, \hat{\mathbf{z}}, \\
\nabla \cdot \mathbf{A} &= \frac{1}{R} \partial_R (R A_R) + \frac{1}{R} \partial_{\phi} A_{\phi} + \partial_z A_z, \\
\nabla^2 f &= \frac{1}{R} \partial_R (R \, \partial_R f) + \frac{1}{R^2} \partial_{\phi}^2 f + \partial_z^2 f,
\end{aligned}
\tag{B.10}\] \[
\begin{aligned}
\nabla \times \mathbf{A} &= \left[ \frac{1}{R} \partial_{\phi} A_z - \partial_z A_{\phi} \right] \hat{\mathbf{R}} \\
& \qquad {} + [\partial_z A_R - \partial_R A_z] \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}} \\
& \qquad {} + \frac{1}{R} [\partial_R (R A_{\phi}) - \partial_{\phi} A_R] \hat{\mathbf{z}}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{B.11}\] With \(\mathbf{A} \cdot \nabla = A_R \partial_R + \frac{A_{\phi}}{R} \partial_{\phi} + A_z \partial_z\) acting on the components: \[
\begin{aligned}
[(\mathbf{A} \cdot \nabla) \mathbf{B}]_R &= \mathbf{A} \cdot \nabla B_R - \frac{A_{\phi} B_{\phi}}{R}, \\
[(\mathbf{A} \cdot \nabla) \mathbf{B}]_{\phi} &= \mathbf{A} \cdot \nabla B_{\phi} + \frac{A_{\phi} B_R}{R}, \\
[(\mathbf{A} \cdot \nabla) \mathbf{B}]_z &= \mathbf{A} \cdot \nabla B_z,
\end{aligned}
\tag{B.12}\] \[
\begin{aligned}
(\nabla^2 \mathbf{A})_R &= \nabla^2 A_R - \frac{A_R}{R^2} - \frac{2}{R^2} \partial_{\phi} A_{\phi}, \\
(\nabla^2 \mathbf{A})_{\phi} &= \nabla^2 A_{\phi} - \frac{A_{\phi}}{R^2} + \frac{2}{R^2} \partial_{\phi} A_R, \\
(\nabla^2 \mathbf{A})_z &= \nabla^2 A_z.
\end{aligned}
\tag{B.13}\]


B.2.2 Spherical coordinates \((r, \theta, \phi)\)
\(x = r \sin \theta \cos \phi\), \(y = r \sin \theta \sin \phi\), \(z = r \cos \theta\), \(\mathrm{d} V = r^2 \sin \theta \mathrm{d} r \mathrm{d} \theta \mathrm{d} \phi\), \(\hat{\mathbf{z}} = \cos \theta \, \hat{\mathbf{r}} - \sin \theta \, \hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\). \[
\begin{aligned}
\nabla f &= \partial_r f \, \hat{\mathbf{r}} + \frac{1}{r} \partial_{\theta} f \, \hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}} + \frac{1}{r \sin \theta} \partial_{\phi} f \, \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}, \\
\nabla \cdot \mathbf{A} &= \frac{1}{r^2} \partial_r (r^2 A_r) + \frac{1}{r \sin \theta} \partial_{\theta} (\sin \theta A_{\theta}) \\
& \qquad {} + \frac{1}{r \sin \theta} \partial_{\phi} A_{\phi}, \\
\nabla^2 f &= \frac{1}{r^2} \partial_r (r^2 \partial_r f) + \frac{1}{r^2 \sin \theta} \partial_{\theta} (\sin \theta \, \partial_{\theta} f) \\
& \qquad {} + \frac{1}{r^2 \sin^2 \theta} \partial_{\phi}^2 f,
\end{aligned}
\tag{B.14}\] \[
\begin{aligned}
\nabla \times \mathbf{A} &= \frac{1}{r \sin \theta} [\partial_{\theta} (\sin \theta A_{\phi}) - \partial_{\phi} A_{\theta}] \hat{\mathbf{r}} \\
& \qquad {} + \frac{1}{r} \left[ \frac{1}{\sin \theta} \partial_{\phi} A_r - \partial_r (r A_{\phi}) \right] \hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}} \\
& \qquad {} + \frac{1}{r} [\partial_r (r A_{\theta}) - \partial_{\theta} A_r] \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{B.15}\] With \(\mathbf{A} \cdot \nabla = A_r \partial_r + \frac{A_{\theta}}{r} \partial_{\theta} + \frac{A_{\phi}}{r \sin \theta} \partial_{\phi}\) acting on the components: \[
\begin{aligned}
[(\mathbf{A} \cdot \nabla) \mathbf{B}]_r &= \mathbf{A} \cdot \nabla B_r - \frac{A_{\theta} B_{\theta} + A_{\phi} B_{\phi}}{r}, \\
[(\mathbf{A} \cdot \nabla) \mathbf{B}]_{\theta} &= \mathbf{A} \cdot \nabla B_{\theta} + \frac{A_{\theta} B_r}{r} \\
& \qquad {} - \frac{A_{\phi} B_{\phi} \cot \theta}{r}, \\
[(\mathbf{A} \cdot \nabla) \mathbf{B}]_{\phi} &= \mathbf{A} \cdot \nabla B_{\phi} + \frac{A_{\phi} B_r}{r} \\
& \qquad {} + \frac{A_{\phi} B_{\theta} \cot \theta}{r}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{B.16}\]

title: Appendix B — Useful Formulae
text:
B.3 Thermodynamics
Composition: mass density, mean molecular weight, and mass fractions, with \(Y_i = n_i / n\) the particle number fractions, \[
\rho = \mu m_u n, \qquad \mu = \sum_i Y_i \frac{m_i}{m_u}, \qquad X_i = \frac{\rho_i}{\rho}.
\tag{B.17}\] First law, also per unit mass with \(v = 1/\rho\), and the specific enthalpy \(h\): \[
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{d} E &= T \mathrm{d} S - p \mathrm{d} V, \\
\mathrm{d} \varepsilon &= T \mathrm{d} s - p \mathrm{d} v = T \mathrm{d} s + \frac{p}{\rho^2} \mathrm{d} \rho, \\
h &= \varepsilon + \frac{p}{\rho}, \qquad \mathrm{d} h = T \mathrm{d} s + \frac{\mathrm{d} p}{\rho}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{B.18}\] Ideal gas and \(\Gamma\)-law equation of state, with \(u = \rho \varepsilon\) the internal energy density (\(\Gamma = 5/3\) for a monatomic gas, \(7/5\) for a diatomic gas, \(4/3\) for radiation): \[
p = n k_B T = \frac{\rho k_B T}{\mu m_u}, \qquad p = (\Gamma - 1) \rho \varepsilon = (\Gamma - 1) u.
\tag{B.19}\] Adiabatic changes, with \(K\) a function of the entropy only, and the polytropic equation of state: \[
p = K \rho^{\Gamma}, \qquad p = K \rho^{1 + 1 / n}.
\tag{B.20}\] Adiabatic and isothermal sound speeds: \[
c_s^2 = \left( \frac{\partial p}{\partial \rho} \right)_s, \qquad c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2 = \left( \frac{\partial p}{\partial \rho} \right)_T.
\tag{B.21}\] Radiation: energy density, pressure, the flux from a blackbody, and the Planck function: \[
\begin{aligned}
u &= a T^4, \qquad p = \frac{1}{3} u, \\
a &= \frac{4 \sigma}{c}, \qquad F = \sigma T^4, \\
B_{\nu} &= \frac{2 h \nu^3}{c^2} \frac{1}{\mathrm{e}^{h \nu / k_B T} - 1}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{B.22}\] Mean free path, with \(\sigma\) the cross section and \(\kappa\) the opacity: \[
\lambda = \frac{1}{n \sigma} = \frac{1}{\kappa \rho}.
\tag{B.23}\]

title: Appendix B — Useful Formulae
text:
B.4 Hydrodynamics and Gravity
Rate of change following a fluid element: \[
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} t} = \frac{\partial}{\partial t} + \mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla.
\tag{B.24}\] Equations of hydrodynamics in Lagrangian form, with \(\mathbf{f}\) the external force per unit volume and \(\dot{q}\) the heating rate per unit mass: \[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{1}{\rho} \frac{\mathrm{d} \rho}{\mathrm{d} t} &= - \nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}, \\
\rho \frac{\mathrm{d} \mathbf{v}}{\mathrm{d} t} &= - \nabla p + \mathbf{f}, \\
\rho \frac{\mathrm{d} \varepsilon}{\mathrm{d} t} &= \rho \dot{q} - p \nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{B.25}\] In conservation form, \(\partial_t U + \nabla \cdot \mathbf{F} = S\): \[
\begin{aligned}
& \frac{\partial \rho}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot (\rho \mathbf{v}) = 0, \\
& \frac{\partial (\rho \mathbf{v})}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot [\rho \mathbf{v} \otimes \mathbf{v} + p \mathbf{I}] = \mathbf{f}, \\
& \frac{\partial}{\partial t} \left[ \rho \left( \varepsilon + \frac{1}{2} v^2 \right) \right] \\
& \quad {} + \nabla \cdot \left[ \left( \rho \varepsilon + \frac{1}{2} \rho v^2 + p \right) \mathbf{v} \right] = \rho \dot{q} + \mathbf{f} \cdot \mathbf{v}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{B.26}\] Gravity: potential, Poisson equation, and gravitational energy: \[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{g} &= - \nabla \Psi, \qquad \nabla^2 \Psi = 4 \pi G \rho, \\
\Psi (\mathbf{r}) &= - G \int \frac{\rho (\mathbf{r}')}{|\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}'|} \mathrm{d}^3 r', \\
W &= \frac{1}{2} \int \rho \Psi \mathrm{d} V.
\end{aligned}
\tag{B.27}\] Hydrostatic equilibrium, and the virial theorem for a system in equilibrium, with \(K\) the kinetic energy: \[
\nabla p = - \rho \nabla \Psi, \qquad 2 K + W + 3 \int p \mathrm{d} V = 0.
\tag{B.28}\] Vorticity equation and Bernoulli’s constant, with \(\mathcal{H} = \int \mathrm{d} p / \rho\) for a barotropic gas: \[
\begin{aligned}
\boldsymbol{\omega} &= \nabla \times \mathbf{v}, \qquad \mathcal{B} = \frac{1}{2} v^2 + \mathcal{H} + \Psi, \\
\frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\omega}}{\partial t} &= \nabla \times (\mathbf{v} \times \boldsymbol{\omega}) + \frac{1}{\rho^2} \nabla \rho \times \nabla p.
\end{aligned}
\tag{B.29}\]
Linear perturbations. The Eulerian perturbation \(q'\) and the Lagrangian perturbation \(\delta q\) of a quantity \(q\) are related by \(q' = \delta q - \boldsymbol{\xi} \cdot \nabla q_0\), where \(\boldsymbol{\xi}\) is the displacement. Plane waves go as \(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i} (\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{x} - \omega t)}\), so that \[
\begin{aligned}
& \nabla \to \mathrm{i} \mathbf{k}, \qquad \frac{\partial}{\partial t} \to - \mathrm{i} \omega, \\
& v_{\mathrm{ph}} = \frac{\omega}{k}, \qquad \mathbf{v}_g = \frac{\partial \omega}{\partial \mathbf{k}}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{B.30}\]
Jump conditions for a conservation law \(\partial_t U + \partial_x F = 0\) across a discontinuity moving with speed \(s\), with \(\mathrm{L}\) and \(\mathrm{R}\) the states on its left and right: \[
s (U_{\mathrm{L}} - U_{\mathrm{R}}) = F (U_{\mathrm{L}}) - F (U_{\mathrm{R}}).
\tag{B.31}\] Across a steady shock, in the shock frame, with 1 and 2 the upstream and downstream states: \[
\begin{aligned}
\rho_1 u_1 &= \rho_2 u_2, \\
p_1 + \rho_1 u_1^2 &= p_2 + \rho_2 u_2^2, \\
h_1 + \frac{1}{2} u_1^2 &= h_2 + \frac{1}{2} u_2^2.
\end{aligned}
\tag{B.32}\]

title: Appendix B — Useful Formulae
text:
B.5 Diffusion and Viscosity
Diffusion equation: \[
\frac{\partial P}{\partial t} = \nabla \cdot (D \nabla P).
\tag{B.33}\] Rate-of-strain tensor, viscous stress tensor, and Navier–Stokes equation: \[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{S} &= \frac{1}{2} (\nabla \mathbf{v} + \nabla \mathbf{v}^T), \\
\boldsymbol{\tau} &= \zeta (\nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}) \mathbf{I} \\
& \qquad {} + \rho \nu \left[ \nabla \mathbf{v} + \nabla \mathbf{v}^T - \frac{2}{3} (\nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}) \mathbf{I} \right], \\
\rho \frac{\mathrm{d} \mathbf{v}}{\mathrm{d} t} &= - \nabla p + \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\tau} + \mathbf{f}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{B.34}\] Reynolds number, for a flow with velocity \(V\) on a scale \(L\): \[
\mathrm{Re} = \frac{L V}{\nu}.
\tag{B.35}\] Thin disks: surface density, Keplerian angular velocity, scale height, and \(\alpha\) viscosity: \[
\begin{aligned}
& \Sigma = \int \rho \mathrm{d} z, \qquad \Omega = \left( \frac{G M}{R^3} \right)^{1 / 2}, \\
& H = \frac{c_s}{\Omega}, \qquad \nu = \alpha c_s H.
\end{aligned}
\tag{B.36}\]

title: Appendix B — Useful Formulae
text:
B.6 Electromagnetism and Magnetohydrodynamics
Maxwell’s equations, with \(q\) the charge density and \(\mathbf{j}\) the current density, and the Lorentz force on a particle of charge \(Q\): \[
\begin{aligned}
\nabla \cdot \mathbf{E} &= \frac{q}{\epsilon_0}, \qquad \nabla \cdot \mathbf{B} = 0, \\
\nabla \times \mathbf{E} &= - \frac{\partial \mathbf{B}}{\partial t}, \\
\nabla \times \mathbf{B} &= \mu_0 \mathbf{j} + \mu_0 \epsilon_0 \frac{\partial \mathbf{E}}{\partial t}, \\
\mathbf{F} &= Q (\mathbf{E} + \mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B}), \qquad \mu_0 \epsilon_0 = \frac{1}{c^2}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{B.37}\] Debye length, plasma frequency, and Larmor radius: \[
\lambda_D = \sqrt{\frac{\epsilon_0 k_B T}{n e^2}}, \qquad \omega_p = \sqrt{\frac{n e^2}{\epsilon_0 m_e}}, \qquad r_L = \frac{m v_{\perp}}{|Q| B}.
\tag{B.38}\] Ohm’s law, Ampère’s law without displacement current, magnetic diffusivity, and the induction equation: \[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{j} &= \sigma (\mathbf{E} + \mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B}), \qquad \nabla \times \mathbf{B} = \mu_0 \mathbf{j}, \\
\eta &= \frac{1}{\mu_0 \sigma}, \\
\frac{\partial \mathbf{B}}{\partial t} &= \nabla \times (\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B}) - \nabla \times (\eta \nabla \times \mathbf{B}).
\end{aligned}
\tag{B.39}\] Magnetic Reynolds number: \[
\mathrm{R}_M = \frac{L V}{\eta}.
\tag{B.40}\] Equations of ideal MHD (\(\eta = 0\), so that \(\mathbf{E} = - \mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B}\)) in conservation form: \[
\begin{aligned}
& \frac{\partial \rho}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot (\rho \mathbf{v}) = 0, \\
& \frac{\partial (\rho \mathbf{v})}{\partial t} \\
& \qquad {} + \nabla \cdot \biggl[ \rho \mathbf{v} \otimes \mathbf{v} + \left( p + \frac{B^2}{2 \mu_0} \right) \mathbf{I} \\
& \qquad\qquad {} - \frac{\mathbf{B} \otimes \mathbf{B}}{\mu_0} \biggr] = \mathbf{f}, \\
& \frac{\partial}{\partial t} \left[ \rho \left( \varepsilon + \frac{1}{2} v^2 \right) + \frac{B^2}{2 \mu_0} \right] \\
& \qquad {} + \nabla \cdot \biggl[ \left( \rho \varepsilon + \frac{1}{2} \rho v^2 + p \right) \mathbf{v} \\
& \qquad\qquad {} + \frac{\mathbf{B} \times (\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B})}{\mu_0} \biggr] \\
& \qquad = \rho \dot{q} + \mathbf{f} \cdot \mathbf{v}, \\
& \frac{\partial \mathbf{B}}{\partial t} = \nabla \times (\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B}).
\end{aligned}
\tag{B.41}\] The momentum equation in Lagrangian form, and the magnetic force split into tension and pressure: \[
\begin{aligned}
\rho \frac{\mathrm{d} \mathbf{v}}{\mathrm{d} t} &= \mathbf{j} \times \mathbf{B} - \nabla p + \mathbf{f}, \\
\mathbf{j} \times \mathbf{B} &= \frac{(\mathbf{B} \cdot \nabla) \mathbf{B}}{\mu_0} - \nabla \frac{B^2}{2 \mu_0}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{B.42}\] Plasma beta and Alfvén speed: \[
\beta = \frac{2 \mu_0 p}{B^2}, \qquad v_A = \frac{B}{\sqrt{\mu_0 \rho}}.
\tag{B.43}\]
